News.title: Microsoft Outlook outage hits police and schools as 'underlying issue' explained
News.content:
Microsoft Outlook outage hits police and schools as 'underlying issue' explained

Microsoft online services are gradually returning but only after a global outage that impacted millions of users around the world

Microsoft doesn't believe they are 'dealing with a cyber attack'

Microsoft’s email meltdown sparked global chaos, with everything from police to schools across Britain hit

‌



‌



Patients needing to book GP appointments were told to try calling surgeries, people were unable to email police with crime reports, and the government used contingency plans to “minimise the disruption”. Courts, councils, pharmacies and countless businesses were among others impacted.

‌



In some cases, staff were told to dust off old-fashioned paper based ways of working as organisations tried to find a way around the IT shutdown.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Issues with Microsoft’s widely used Office 365 suite of software - which includes email, as well as Teams video conferencing and its CoPilot AI tool - were first reported on Thursday evening and spread across the world.

View 2 Images An outage impacted millions of Microsoft email users (Image: Yui Mok/Press Association)

‌



Microsoft outage could leave people in hospital for longer and others low on medication, warns top pharmacist READ MORE :

It was only by mid-afternoon, more than 20 hours after the disruption began, that Microsoft said its email services are “approaching normal levels”. “Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues,” the firm added.

The US tech giant insisted: “At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident.” It said it had "addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service" earlier, repeating that the issue was "not related to cyber or AI/agents".

‌



"The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change," it added.

James Ferryman, a computer science professor at the University of Reading, warned it was one of the “longest and most disruptive” IT failures ever.

‌



Schools used social media to encourage parents to call, rather than email, to report pupil absences.

Rachel Harrison, national officer at the GMB union, warned of a “serious impact across ambulance and NHS trusts” due to the outage. "Those who work in 111 and 999 service are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos,” she said. "Luckily, emergency and life threatening call outs appear to be unaffected.”

‌



View 2 Images Microsoft's Office 365 programs include email, Teams and CoPilot

The Met Police said "some online form submissions may be affected", while supermarket Asda revealed customers were unable to reset online passwords, or new shoppers complete the registration process.

‌



National Rail said passengers who bought train tickets online after the outage began may struggle to access them. Various local authorities reported that they were unable to access emails.

Cheltenham Racecourse had urged racegoers to arrive early on Friday for the opening day of the November meeting as the outage threatened to cause disruption for those carrying digital tickets.

‌



The outage fuelled Friday the 13th jokes on social media. Sainsbury’s posted on Facebook: “Microsoft being down is the most Friday 13th thing ever.” Aldi wrote it was “the equivalent of an adult snowy day right?!”

However, there was a serious side, with around two thirds of hospital trusts and GP practices using Microsoft for emails and meetings. Dr Tim Frank, a GP from Penzanze, Cornwall, said: “This is going to be very disruptive. Fridays are a heavily laden day due to the upcoming weekend.”

‌



A spokesperson for the UK National Pharmacy Association said the outage affected access to the NHS email system, limiting chemists’ ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients.

The outage also impacted some courts across the country . The BBC quoted a member of staff at Westminster Magistrates’ Court reporting “a lot of delays”, adding: “Judges have been unable to access systems, the prosecution hasn’t been able to send papers through, and we’ve been unable to get pre-sentence reports.”

‌



More than 430 million people use Microsoft’s Office 365 suite of software, although it is unclear how many were unable to use it.

Downing Street urged the public to follow advice on “alternative ways to get in touch” where services are disrupted.

‌



A Government spokesperson said earlier in the day: “We are aware of the ongoing global technical issues affecting Microsoft services. We are working closely with Microsoft to assess any impact on government services, with robust contingency plans in place to minimise disruption.” Defence minister Luke Pollard: “We’re assessing the impact.”

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said: “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.

‌



“My committee’s report on delivering a digital government concluded that the UK is hugely dependent on a small number of US-based technology providers for our public services, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.”

UK Minister for Cyber, Liz Lloyd, said: "The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has been working with Microsoft and departments across Government to establish the full picture around the global outage at Microsoft and activate public sector contingency plans where needed. I have spoken to the CEO of Microsoft UK about their plans for a full return to normal services as soon as possible, which is well underway and seeing positive results.

‌



"The outage has mainly affected back-office functions, such as messaging and email. 999 calls are unaffected, as are NHS 111 services. HMRC and DWP phone lines remain fully operational, though people may experience longer than usual waiting times, and we have no reports of disruption to our transport network as a result of the outage.

"The Government recognises this incident has been inconvenient and disruptive. Affected departments and public sector organisations have plans in place for these events to mitigate potential impacts and continue their business operations. Throughout the day, we have seen limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery, and I encourage people to follow advice from the services they need on alternative ways to get in touch where email or web forms may be unavailable.

Article continues below

"We will review this incident and the lessons learned to inform our ongoing work to raise digital resilience across the UK, just as we are doing under the Government Cyber Action Plan and the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill."

News.title: 'Brits should not struggle to contact doctors or report crimes when one tech company suffers a breakdown'
News.content:
'Brits should not struggle to contact doctors or report crimes when one tech company suffers a breakdown'

GP surgeries, police forces, courts, schools and councils were caught out by today's Microsoft outage...

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

When a single technology company suffers a breakdown, Britain should not be left struggling to contact doctors, report crimes or keep vital public services running. Yet Microsoft's latest outage did exactly that.

‌



‌



GP surgeries, police forces, courts, schools and councils were caught in the chaos as systems failed around the world. Even emergency services were affected, while some workers were reduced to pen and paper. There is something extremely worrying about how we now place so much of our essential infrastructure in the hands of a handful of multinational giants.

‌



Technology makes our lives easier, but convenience is a poor excuse for allowing one company's failure to bring so much to a standstill. Ministers must demand tougher safeguards, reliable backup systems and far greater accountability from firms whose software underpins our daily lives. Public services must be able to function when technology giants falter because the next outage could have consequences far more serious than a missed email.

‌



Farage's £5m question

Nigel Farage has a £5 million question to answer. Again. The Reform leader insisted a billionaire’s gift would keep him safe for life. Yet reports now suggest his party has spent more than £150,000 on his security in the past year. So what happened to the money, and what was it for? Nobody disagrees that politicians facing threats deserve protection. But Farage reportedly turned down a taxpayer-funded security detail, leaving his party to foot the bill while an overseas crypto tycoon bolstered his personal fortune.

Reform says it distinguishes between political security and longer-term personal protection. Fine. Then explain precisely how the arrangement works, and whether a penny of that gift has been spent. A man forever insisting on transparency from others should welcome some himself.

Article continues below

Surprise call from Kate

Owain Wyn Evans has raised a remarkable £4 million for Children in Need, earning a surprise call from the Princess of Wales. Kate even spoke to him in his native Welsh. After his gruelling challenge, Owain probably had enough trouble finding the words in any language.

News.title: Nigel Farage’s personal security paid for with Reform funds despite claim over £5million gift
News.content:
Nigel Farage’s personal security paid for with Reform funds despite claim over £5million gift

Nigel Farage’s personal security has been paid for using Reform UK’s central funds despite him saying it would be covered by a £5million gift from a crypto billionaire

View 2 Images Nigel Farage is under investigation by Parliament’s standards watchdog over his alleged failure to declare the £5million gift (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Nigel Farage’s personal security has been paid for using Reform UK’s central funds despite his claim it was being covered by a £5million gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire.

‌



Mr Farage has insisted the cash from Thailand-based tycoon Christopher Harborne is to pay for his security bill for the “rest of my life”. But the Reform party has reportedly paid for a security team and two cars for the Reform leader.

And the Mirror has been told by an insider that the £5m has not been spent as it is for Mr Farage’s security after his official political career is over. It is unclear what has been done with the money, including whether it is accruing interest in a bank account

According to the Guardian, Mr Farage charged Reform costs for security including changes to his properties, with costs amounting to £150,000. The Mirror understands Reform disputes this point, but not that the central party pays for his security as leader of the party more generally.

Close Nigel Farage ally appears to admit £5million Brexit comment slip up in undercover footage READ MORE :

View 2 Images Thai-based billionaire Christoper Harborne gave Farage a £5m gift before the 2024 general election (Image: Linedin)

A Reform spokesman said: “As a standard practice, we do not comment on security matters.” Mr Farage has previously said: “This money was given to me so that I would be safe and secure for the rest of my life.”

Mr Farage is being investigated by Parliament’s standards watchdog over his failure to declare the cash, which he insists was not necessary as it was a personal gift. Newly elected MPs must declare any financial benefits they received in the 12 months before they were elected.

Mr Farage has offered varying explanations for the purpose of the money. In May, he suggested the £5m gift was a reward for his Brexit campaigning. In interviews in June, the Reform leader claimed it was not the public's business how he spends it - and he could splash it on Ferraris or betting on horseracing if he wanted.

Undercover footage last month showed one of Mr Farage's closest allies, Dan Jukes, admitting the Reform leader was not following the party line when he said the £5m gift was a reward for his Brexit campaigning. The former aide appeared to suggest Mr Farage slipped up, saying the comment was not the "line to take from the press office".

According to The Guardian, Reform makes a distinction between security needed for Mr Farage’s political activities as leader of the party, which it pays for, and his potential longer-term personal security needs, which the gift was intended to provide for.

In April, Mr Farage told the Telegraph the state had failed to fund his security. The i Paper later reported he received taxpayer-funded security when he became an MP in 2024 but that he later declined it when it was reviewed the following year.

Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses over his secret £5m ‘gift’ have fallen apart. You can’t trust a word he says... It’s time for him to get his story straight and be honest with the public.”

A Conservative party spokesman said: “Nigel Farage should come clean about where the £5m has gone and what it was really for.”

News.title: BBC Weather issues ‘unprecedented’ polar vortex verdict as snow forecast for UK
News.content:
BBC Weather issues ‘unprecedented’ polar vortex verdict as snow forecast for UK

While snow and freezing temperatures are on the cards this weekend, weather forecasters say we have now seen the 'earliest major sudden stratospheric warming on record'

What is the bizarre weather phenomenon Sudden Stratospheric Warming?

Following a summer of record-breaking temperatures and heatwaves, experts say another weather record has now tumbled.

‌



‌



BBC Weather says winds in the polar vortex have switched from their typical westerly direction to easterly, marking the “earliest major sudden stratospheric warming on record”.

‌



Temperatures rising in the stratosphere can cause shifts in the polar vortex, a ring of powerful winds that keeps freezing air near the North Pole. When these winds weaken, Arctic air rushes downwards and often impacts the jet stream.

‌



The previous earliest SSW on record came on November 28 in both 1969 and 2025. The same process led to the infamous 'Beast from the East' in 2018, a historic weather system which brought 22 inches of snow to some parts of the country.

View 2 Images The polar vortex is a ring of powerful winds that keeps freezing air near the North Pole (Image: weathershot)

Met Office weather maps show 20 counties face snow on Monday and Tuesday – list READ MORE :

However, as there are “very few historical examples of early season major SSWs to compare with”, BBC Weather says it remains unclear just how the current SSW will impact our weather. “This event happening so early in autumn is unprecedented in modern observations,” forecasters explain.

‌



Temperatures have dropped below freezing this week, reaching -7C in some rural areas overnight, while snow is expected in some regions this weekend. However, this isn’t a result of SSW.

“We do know that it is definitely not connected to the cold spell right now,” BBC Weather said. The Met Office previously linked the current conditions to developments in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

‌



View 2 Images SSW can lead to snow falling in the UK (stock) (Image: PA)

The world is also in the grips of a strengthening El Nino, set to be the most powerful in decades. El Ninos have previously been linked with SSW events in the latter half of winter, but BBC Weather says “further research” is needed to draw any links between the current El Nino and the SSW event this week.

‌



Met Office forecasts snow for UK

Met Office Deputy Chief Forecaster Steven Keates has said “spells of rain, sleet and some hill snow” are on the cards this weekend.

In Scotland, “there is an increasing chance of snow developing later in the day”. While most of the snow will be confined to higher ground, he added some “could fall to lower levels too”.

Article continues below

“Into next week, unsettled and cold conditions remain with rain, sleet and (mainly hill) snow key features,” the Met Office said.

News.title: Heavily pregnant woman killed in 'particularly tragic' two-car crash in Amesbury
News.content:
Heavily pregnant woman killed in 'particularly tragic' two-car crash in Amesbury

A heavily pregnant woman has died in a two vehicle crash on a busy road in Amesbury, Wiltshire, while a second person suffered minor injuries, police said

View Image The scene of the collision in Amesbury

A heavily pregnant woman has been killed in what police described as a "particularly tragic" crash on a busy road in Wiltshire.

‌



‌



Emergency services were called to the scene on Countess Road in Amesbury at around 8pm on Thursday following a two vehicle collision involving a Toyota Aygo and a Volkswagen Polo.

‌



The woman, aged in her 30s, was travelling in the Toyota and tragically died at the scene, Wiltshire Police said.

‌



The driver of the vehicle, a man in his 30s, sustained minor injuries, while the occupants of the second vehicle were uninjured.

The road was closed overnight while police carried out enquiries but it has since re-opened.

‌



Roads Policing Unit Insp Neil Duffin said the collision was "particularly tragic," adding that emergency services "did everything they could" at the crash site.

He said those who attended the scene will be given the necessary welfare support.

‌



"Firstly, I would like to express my sincere condolences to the family involved," Duffin said. "Every collision which results in the loss of a life is devastating, but this incident was particularly tragic.

"The family are being supported by specialist trained officers at this time.

Article continues below

"Emergency services did everything they could at the scene, and I know those who attended will be deeply affected – they will be provided with the necessary welfare support."

News.title: Former NSW MP Rory Amon found guilty of sexually assaulting 13-year-old boy
News.content:
Former NSW MP Rory Amon found guilty of sexually assaulting 13-year-old boy

Former NSW Liberal MP Rory Amon, 37, has been found guilty by a jury of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old boy after claiming he believed the boy was over the age of 16

View 2 Images Former NSW Liberal MP Rory Amon (Image: 7NEWS)

A former NSW Liberal MP could face a lengthy jail term after a jury found him guilty of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old boy.

Rory Amon was found guilty on Friday of one count of sexual intercourse with a person aged between 10 and 14, and of indecently assaulting a child. The jury reached a verdict after around four hours of deliberations.

The 37-year-old was standing trial for a second time at the New South Wales Supreme Court after a previous jury cleared him of eight separate child sex offences in March, but failed to reach a verdict on the other two.

The case centred on Amon's contact with a 13-year-old boy, who he met through an adults-only website, the court heard.

Amon had consistently denied the allegations, claiming he genuinely believed the boy was over 16. His original trial heard the boy had given a false age when signing up to the gay dating app and repeated it during conversations with Amon.

The pair exchanged explicit images before arranging to meet in 2017 in the car park of the boy's apartment block, the court heard.

View 2 Images Amon has maintained that he believed the boy was over 16 (Image: 7NEWS)

At the time, Amon was working full-time for Jason Falinski, a federal MP representing the Australian constituency of Mackellar. He later served two terms on the Northern Beaches council before being elected as the Liberal MP for Pittwater in 2023.

But the charges brought his fledging political career to an abrupt end, with Amon expelled from the Liberal Party and forced to resign just months after his election in March 2023.

His departure triggered a by-election, in which the Liberals lost the previously safe seat to an independent candidate.

Amon remains on bail and is due back in court for a sentencing hearing on November 27. He is the third former NSW MP to be convicted of sexual offences in recent years.

Former Kiama MP and Coalition minister Gareth Ward was jailed in 2025 for sexually abusing two young men, including a political staffer who was drunk following an event at NSW Parliament House.

His minimum prison term of three years and nine months is due to expire in April 2029.

Former NSW minister Milton Orkopoulos was convicted in 2023 of sexually abusing teenage boys while serving as a state Labor MP.

The 65-year-old was found guilty of 26 offences involving four underage boys, as well as supplying them with drugs over a decade-long period ending in 2003.

He had previously served more than a decade in prison for separate offences, including the sexual assault of a minor, indecent assault and supplying heroin and cannabis.

News.title: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11
News.content:
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.

The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.

Here's what we know.

News.title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
News.content:
The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.

No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.

It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved.

"We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.

West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved".

"Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.

Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.

They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.

News.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

News.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
News.content:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.

News.title: Watch: Children in Need 2026... in 90 seconds
News.content:
Almost Â£40m was raised by the end of Friday night's Children In Need 2026 live programme.

The money will help disadvantaged young people across the United Kingdom.

It includes more than Â£3.8m raised by BBC Radio 2 host Owain Wyn Evans, who completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations - riding almost 400 miles between Glasgow and Cardiff.

Elsewhere in the show, actors TimothÃ©e Chalamet, Zendaya, and the stars of Dune: Part 3 pranked presenter Rylan Clark with the help of some hysterical youngsters.

The total is set to rise as more money comes in.

News.title: Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban
News.content:
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during the closing stages of the second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.

De Miguel died the following day, aged 30.

The disciplinary committee said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'.

"The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge."

The committee added the "nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances" means that "the maximum sanction, a 12-match suspension, is justified".

Separately, the federation has decided the game between the two sides, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred, will not be replayed.

"This avoids having to resume play from the precise moment at which the tragic incident occurred," it said.

The teams were drawing 2-2 at the time and that result will now stand, with a federation committee saying that was the "most respectful course of action, given the extraordinary and tragic circumstances of this case".

Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on 4 November, in which he said he was experiencing "the most difficult days" of his life and felt "enormous pain" about De Miguel's death.

On Thursday, FC Andorra manager Carles Manso said Equatorial Guinea international Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the incident.

Manso said Owono is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return, adding: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to âhim.

"We will âgive him space so that he feels completely free to make âany â decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.

"When he feels it is appropriate and when âhe feels genuinely ready to take a âdecision â like that [he will do so]."

News.title: Widespread frost and freezing fog forecast as cold health alerts continue
News.content:
Arctic air will maintain its grip on the UK to start the weekend, as cold health alerts remain in place for a large swathe of England.

Saturday will dawn with another sharp and widespread frost with the coldest conditions expected in England and Wales.

Patches of freezing fog could also be a hazard, reducing visibility and bringing a risk of very slippery surfaces in southern and eastern England.

Then it is all change by Sunday with most areas having a frost-free start, but heavy bursts of rain and brisk winds will sweep across the country later.

News.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
News.content:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

News.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
News.content:
Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.

She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.

Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.

When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.

Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.

What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.

He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.

This article contains details some readers may find upsetting

Dolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.

A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.

The car did not stop.

As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.

News.title: Probation officers to take industrial action over pay and early release scheme
News.content:
Probation officers have voted to reject a 5% pay rise and take industrial action, citing growing pressure created by the government's prisoner early release scheme.

Members of Napo, the probation service union, voted to refuse overtime from 23 November - and could take strike action should the union "deem that option to be necessary".

Its general secretary Ian Lawrence said the service was "already in crisis" before the early release scheme came into force, which relies on probation staff monitoring freed prisoners in the community.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government had put forward a "strong offer" and was recruiting an extra "1,300 officers to significantly cut workloads".

They added that the government has "robust contingency plans in place" to ensure offenders "are still subject to the same rigorous supervision" in the event of industrial action.

Probation service unions have warned that officers have too many cases and the rate at which staff are leaving the profession has increased.

The service has come under renewed pressure in recent months as a result of the early release scheme, the union said, which the government introduced as prisons were dangerously close to capacity.

Seven-hundred eligible offenders originally sentenced to up to 19 months were released on 1 October, with another two groups of 650 prisoners released on 13 October and 10 November.

Another nine groups are expected to leave prison in the next seven months, with inmates who received longer sentences included in the later cohorts.

Some 250 prisoners serving more than 12 years are expected to be released on 9 June.

Napo's leader said staff had tried "desperately" to implement early release schemes introduced by the Labour government and previous Conservative government, but had been asked to do so with "inadequate staff and a lack of resources".

The government has said electronic tags and probation intervention will help to manage prisoners freed early.

The Probation Service uses electronic monitoring to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order, with most of those eligible for early release now requiring tagging.

But a September report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements were not fitted on time.

News.title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of UK knife attack
News.content:
A former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.

Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2021.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.

Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year.

The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.

During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.

He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than Â£2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines.

Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.

News.title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
News.content:
A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.

The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.

In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.

Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.

Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.

Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.

He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.

"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.

He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".

Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.

Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."

Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.

As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."

Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".

McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."

While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.

News.title: 'Hardest challenge of my life' - Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need ride
News.content:
Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised Â£3,853,530 in the process.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.

"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."

The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.

During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.

It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.

News.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
News.content:
Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.

Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.

NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.

Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.

The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.

The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.

Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.

The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.

NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

News.title: Man jailed for grooming at least 70 girls online
News.content:
A man who groomed at least 70 girls and manipulated them into sending sexually explicit videos and images of themselves has been sentenced to 30 years in prison.

Bilal Kazi, 27, targeted his victims - aged between 10 and 17 - using apps including Snapchat, Wink and Roblox between August 2021 and August 2025.

Kazi, a student from India who was studying at the University of Chester, posed as a 14-year-old white British teenage boy and made his victims believe they were in a relationship with him.

He was jailed after pleading guilty to 37 charges including making indecent images, blackmail and inciting a child to engage in sexual activity.

Warning: This article contains distressing information

Kazi must serve a minimum of 20 years in prison before being eligible for parole and will be on the sex offenders register for life.

Once eligible for parole he will be on licence for eight years.

In a personal impact statement read out at Chester Crown Court earlier, one victim said she had struggled with anxiety as Kazi, who later moved to Birmingham, had "taken away a sense of privacy and security".

"I am doing my best to move forward but the effects are still with me," she said.

"The harm caused is not limited to the time events took place - they continue to affect my daily life."

The court heard that some of the victims had attempted suicide, struggled with anxiety and developed eating disorders.

One victim, who was 13 years old when Kazi first contacted her, said he took her "innocence away".

"I hope one day I can get on with my life," she said.

News.title: Eleanor Donaldson given supervision order and placed on sex offenders' register
News.content:
The wife of former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson has been placed under a supervision order for three years.

Appearing before Newry Crown Court, via video link, for the first time since 2025, a tearful Eleanor Donaldson was also told she would be placed on the sex offenders' register for five years.

When Judge Paul Ramsey asked if she understood that she would be subjected to a supervision treatment order (STO), she nodded her head and said "yes".

Eleanor Donaldson could not be given a prison sentence as she faced a 'trial of the facts' as it was determined she was medically unfit for a criminal trial.

She was found to have done the acts in relation to five charges, including four of aiding and abetting her husband's offending.

Last month Jeffrey Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.

His wife has also applied to appeal the verdict from her trial of the facts.

News.title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction set for Los Angeles, with many big names skipping the stage
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It may feel like '80s night at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, with the new members including Billy Idol, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, New Order, Luther Vandross and Iron Maiden.

But it's hard to say exactly what the vibe will be on Saturday at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, with many of the inductees opting out of performing or appearing, and the Hall of Fame revealing next-to-nothing about the show during the run-up.

After streaming the ceremony live the past few years, the Rock Hall is returning to its previous model, where the public won’t see it until an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ on Dec. 9.

Here's what we do know about the show:

Oasis, youngest of the inductees, won’t be coming. Guitarist Noel Gallagher is playing a gig back home in Britain, and his little brother, Liam Gallagher, just doesn't want to come.

“It’s too far to be going for the night,” he said in a post on the social platform X. He added in another, “I dont like award ceremonies they freak me out I dont know why I just get weird vibes."

Iron Maiden will be on tour in Australia. Sade is opting to sit it out, too. Collins is likely to appear, but he said he has to decline from playing his songs for health reasons. Key members of New Order, getting a joint induction with their previous incarnation Joy Division, will also be out for health reasons. Vandross died in 2005.

But the show will go on, and hip-hop could be the highlight. Wu-Tang Clan will be inducted along with Queen Latifah and MC Lyte, and all are expected to appear and probably perform.

And Idol, being inducted with his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens, will take the stage ready to rock.

Latifah and Lyte enter the hall as recipients of the Early Influence Award along with posthumous nominees Gram Parsons, Fela Kuti and Celia Cruz.

Parsons, an essential figure at the crossroads of country and rock in the 1960s and '70s, got his own separate tribute Wednesday night at the legendary Troubadour club in West Hollywood, where his duet partner Emmylou Harris along with Rock Hall-of-Famers Elvis Costello and Sheryl Crow sang his songs and saluted his legacy.

Kuti will become the first African-born artist in the hall, and Cruz will become the first member who sang primarily in Spanish.

A group of producers will be inducted via the Musical Excellence Award: Rick Rubin, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller. And TV host Ed Sullivan will get in as the winner of the Ahmet Ertugun award, which goes to nonmusicians who've made rock history.

Many other major stars are likely to appear to induct the new members or to play the absentees' songs in tribute. The past few years, the hall has announced several special guests, though not their roles, the week of the show, but with no live airing this year it has returned to a model of keeping nearly everything secret until it happens.

The show is in Los Angeles for the second straight year, and organizers have said it will be here more often while still rotating to New York and Cleveland, where the actual hall resides.

News.title: 'The Sun Also Rises' at 100: Women are now leaders in Hemingway scholarship
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hilary K. Justice, an Ernest Hemingway scholar at Boston's John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, remembers having to defend her chosen field of expertise as a graduate student some 30 years ago.

“I was told that studying Hemingway amounted to committing professional suicide — ‘Haven’t we killed him yet?’ was the comment of one professor in my PhD program,” she said in a recent interview. Justice oversees the Hemingway collection at the JFK library, where the author's papers are stored.

“I used to be able to count on being asked ‘How do you, as a woman, justify studying Hemingway?’ at every Q&A session at every public speaking event.”

This year marks the centennial of Hemingway's classic breakout novel, “The Sun Also Rises,” an occasion for scholars and fans to celebrate his work — and express relief that his outsized legend has receded enough that his books can stand or fall on their own. Hemingway died more than 60 years ago, and at least a generation of students has come of age knowing little about the man who for countless predecessors embodied the very ideal — or anti-ideal — of the writing life: the macho adventurer, drinker and womanizer who once famously defined courage as “grace under pressure.”

A grandson's coming of age

At a centennial event last month at the 92nd Street Y Unterberg Poetry Center in Manhattan, Maya Hawke, Will Harrison, Sarah Pidgeon and other actors read from “The Sun Also Rises,” and a panel discussion featured “Bright Lights, Big City” novelist Jay McInerney and a handful of Hemingway descendants. Grandson Brendan Hemingway, a teenager during the rise of second-wave feminism in the 1970s, spoke of female classmates approaching him in high school hallways just to tell him how much they despised the author.

“People decided that they'd project on to me whatever they liked or didn't like about Ernest Hemingway and were surprised that wasn't a great experience for me,” said Brendan Hemingway, now 65. “And the big thing for me at 100 (years of “The Sun Also Rises”) is for my daughter's generation that's all gone. We've outlasted the baggage. We've outrun the backlash. For my daughter's generation, you read him or you don't."

Justice and other Hemingway scholars say they generally encounter little resistance these days. Verna Kale, an associate research professor at Penn State, says she recently asked a group of students if they had ever read Hemingway and was told that none of them had. Ross K. Tangedal, an associate professor of English at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point and a member of the Hemingway Letters Project editorial team, said his students usually were “exposed to his work in small doses in high school.”

“So when they come to my college classroom they encounter the work before the myth,” he added.

Hemingway's 1926 novel follows British and American expatriates adrift in Europe, sustaining themselves on sex, alcohol, boxing and bullfights. It was a foundational text for the so-called “Lost Generation” of the post World War I era, and for many aspiring writers after. McInerney, 71, told the audience gathered at the Poetry Center that he first read “The Sun Also Rises” while in college and remembered how the novel “blew me away.”

“I couldn't believe how fresh it was and how it seemed really cool, to me” he said. "When the book was published, it essentially revolutionized English prose. It was a really radical new voice that somehow still spoke directly to me."

No longer ‘required’ reading, but the book still sells

“The Sun Also Rises” is still popular, although its numbers fall well short of the book's famous contemporary, F. Scott Fitzgerald's “The Great Gatsby.” According to Circana, which tracks around 85% of the print market, “The Sun Also Rises” has sold just under 40,000 copies this year so far, down from a peak of more than 60,000 for each of several years in the 2010s. Over the past 20 years, sales in the U.S. have topped 1 million copies ("Gatsby" sales over the same time period approached 8 million).

Debra Moddelmog, who serves on the editorial board of The Hemingway Review, acknowledges that many readers familiar with Hemingway's image regard the women in his books as stereotyped and marginalized. But she thinks of Hemingway as a “deceptive” writer whose famously terse prose holds unexpected dimensions. She cites the libertine Lady Brett Ashley of “The Sun Also Rises" as someone whom close reading reveals to be a “complex character rather than the typical femme fatale.”

Justice notes that women hold many of the leading roles in Hemingway scholarship, including Moddelmog; Sandra Spanier, general editor of the Hemingway Letters Project; and Suzanne del Gizzo, editor of The Hemingway Review.

Kale, an associate editor for the Hemingway letters project and the editor of a Norton Library edition of “The Sun Also Rises,” is a self-identified Gen-Xer who started out as a student of medieval literature. She changed her focus after experiencing a Hemingway-esque epiphany as she read “The Sun Also Rises” — on a night train to Spain during a trip to Europe.

“I was just the right age to read it, and I became very interested in the expatriate modernists,” she said. “I’ve never had any misgivings about studying Hemingway whatsoever. I find his writing captivating, and documenting his life through his letters has become my life’s work.”

News.title: French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Emmanuel Macron is set to attend a biennial meeting of French-speaking territories beginning Saturday in Cambodia, where the French president contending with public unrest at home will face international political challenges as an African conflict hangs over the proceedings.

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie is holding the three-day meeting through Monday in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh. Macron is expected to engage in bilateral discussions and join the summit meeting of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers where French is spoken.

Cambodia will take over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, who served as chair in 2024 when France was the host nation.

Before departing for Malaysia on Monday, Macron is scheduled to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site near the city of Siem Reap, where he and King Norodom Sihamoni will mark the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.

The French leader's trip comes at a time of widespread domestic protests. France’s Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people took to the streets earlier this month in a demonstration to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement, which has resulted in thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.

Conflict in eastern Congo may roil the proceedings

The summit's sticky diplomacy for Macron and other leaders will take place when participants decide on Monday who will serve for the next four years as the group’s leader and chief executive in the role of secretary-general.

The choices include candidates from two bitterly feuding African members, Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who is seeking reelection to a third four-year term, and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country’s martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.

Congo, the United States and experts from the United Nations accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups that have been vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.

Congo has threatened to leave the OIF if Mushikiwabo is reelected. With a population exceeding 110 million people, over 40 million more than France, Congo is the most populous nation where French is the official language and its withdrawal would mark a significant blow to the Francophonie organization.

Two other candidates, from Romania and Mauritania, are poised to serve as compromise picks.

France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of €71.7 million ($79 million).

The outcome also could be delicate because the challenge comes on the heels of the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.

Mali said the suspensions infringed on sovereignty, but the withdrawals also came in the context of Francophone African countries in recent decades shedding French political, military and cultural influence that they regarded as overbearing.

Cambodia welcomes world leaders

The summit's slogan, “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability,” is seen as a reflection of Cambodia’s recovery from years of war and unrest in the last quarter of the 20th century.

About 20 government leaders, including Canada’s Mark Carney, Vietnam’s To Lam, Rwanda’s Paul Kagame and the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Félix Tshisekedi, are expected to attend the summit and likely will meet with Cambodia's king as well as Prime Minister Hun Manet.

Most of the summit’s agenda is uncontroversial. Documents set to be approved concern political commitment to peaceful coexistence, social, cultural and economic cooperation, resolution of crisis situations and peace-building, and the protection of cultural heritage and the promotion of cultural diversity.

Host Cambodia, which has an opportunity to showcase tourism potential and business opportunities, is holding side events highlighting commercial partnerships, cultural exchanges, science and technology.

Local political activists see the meeting as an occasion to press for more democratic freedoms in a de facto one-party state. U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews issued a statement pleading with summit delegates to uphold OIF values and pressure the Cambodian government for the release of detained rights activists.

“No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.

Cambodia can lay claim to helping birth the OIF, as its late king and mercurial independence leader, Norodom Sihanouk, was one of four founders in 1970 of the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation. Sihanouk was overthrown and his immediate successors did not join, as Cambodia subsequently endured civil war and the brutal rule of the communist Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979. Cambodia joined the Francophonie as an observer in 1991 and became a full member in 1993.

___

Peck reported from Bangkok.

News.title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer’s, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn’t have Alzheimer’s but advanced CTE instead.

The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn’t involved with the research.

Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed.

The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan.

—-

News.title: Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In September, comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident, something that could happen to anyone. But one thing stood out: the men in the other car were unusually polite, and even offered to cover his medical bills and the damage to his car.

Huang later received a call from Taiwanese police telling him it wasn't an ordinary accident.

Taipei prosecutors in October charged five men for deliberately attempting to injure Huang in a case that has drawn attention across Taiwan. Authorities say it is part of a growing trend where operatives paid by China harass or attack people on the self-ruled island who are seen as critical of the government in Beijing.

“In the beginning, it was verbal harassment, then it morphed to pouring paint and property damage ... to the level of causing a fake car accident," Chiu Shao-Chou, the commissioner of Taiwan's Criminal investigation Bureau, said. "There's a trend of increasing severity, and that's something we have to take seriously.”

China's transnational repression an increasing worry

Taiwan is a democratic island claimed by Beijing, which hasn't ruled out using force to annex it. Taiwanese authorities have long worried about Chinese infiltration attempts, including spy plots targeting senior military officials and the president's bodyguards, disinformation schemes during elections or the use of cultural exchanges as a way to spread Communist Party ideology.

China's tactics to harass, spy on or even harm dissidents abroad have come to light in recent years. In 2023, authorities in New York made arrests in connection with secret police stations set up on behalf of the Chinese government to surveil Chinese dissidents.

Huang said the car attack might have been linked to his performance at the end of last year, in which he criticized Chinese President Xi Jinping and compared him to Winnie the Pooh. Huang is a comedian trained in the xiangsheng tradition, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue that relies heavily on wordplay and rhymes.

Prosecutors say the five men accepted about 450,000 New Taiwan dollars ($13,900) from someone from China who went by the alias “K” and wanted them to injure Huang seriously enough that he could no longer perform.

Huang said he had stopped collaborating with other comedians and believes his criticism of Xi is the reason. He said he knows of other comedians who had performances canceled in China and Taiwan because they had collaborated with him. He has no plans of taking his shows to China.

His solo shows, however, have sold out since the attack.

“The Communist Party is very childish. Your country’s leader was criticized by a comedian and as a result, you give such an aggressive response?” Huang said.

Hong Kong gangsters were involved in another attack

Hong Kong gangsters have been accused of plotting to assault Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in what Taiwanese prosecutors called another instance of “transnational repression."

According to an October statement from prosecutors, five Hong Kong triad members, paid by a fellow gangster, entered Taiwan in early July and inspected the area around the hotel where Yaita was expected to give a speech. But before the attack, two withdrew, and the pair, alongside another member, left Taiwan, the statement said.

One of the men was offered 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,750) to assault Yaita, the prosecutors said. He punched the commentator in the face and was later arrested, while another, who acted as a lookout, fled Taiwan.

Yaita, a former reporter in Beijing who now leads a think tank in Taiwan, believes the assault was linked to his remarks, including his criticism of the Chinese government’s policies.

“By violently attacking me, they hope to silence others who criticize China, including myself,” he said, adding that he wouldn't change his views.

The man who was arrested pleaded guilty on Tuesday and will be sentenced later, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.

Analyst says the escalation is alarming

Matt Brazil, a fellow at The Jamestown Foundation in Washington, D.C., said the recent attacks represented a “big step beyond" sending navy ships and warplanes around the island. He said anyone in Taiwan who speaks out against Xi and the Chinese Communist Party could be a target.

“(It) shows that Beijing may be turning toward a more militant stance in acting against its critics (in Taiwan). If successful, the party may expand such tactics elsewhere,” he said.

Taiwan's police say the threat of transnational repression isn't limited to Taiwan. They said they are in close coordination with U.S. authorities about similar cases that involve Taiwanese nationals overseas.

In October, U.S. authorities arrested a woman in Los Angeles for allegedly conducting surveillance on the son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te on behalf of the Chinese government.

“Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society, but with these types of actions which harm our national security, the investigation of this is of the highest importance,” Chiu, the police commissioner, said. He added that police treat the cases as national-level threats and coordinate with immigration authorities, the coast guard and other government agencies.

Catching the criminals before they leave Taiwan is a top priority, he said, adding that police would also investigate Taiwanese collaborators.

The island's Mainland Affairs Council, which handles relations with China, said it would seek to strengthen the Anti-Infiltration Act — a law designed to punish such acts.

China rejects claims of transnational repression

In response to the attack on Yaita, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said in July that the Hong Kong man who punched Yaita had acted out of “righteous indignation” and that it was an ordinary public security incident.

China denied any involvement in the attack on Huang. The Taiwan Affairs Office said Wednesday that “transnational repression” was a lie by Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party. It said that the party had created the Anti-Infiltration Act to suppress political dissidents and restrict cross-strait exchanges.

But for Huang, who now travels with a police escort to every performance, the intended message was clear.

“They want to tell everyone that there's a cost to criticizing the Chinese government and its leader. They want to tell people, clearly, ‘If you do something abroad, we will come deal with you, so shut your mouth and accept reunification.'”

___

Wu reported from Bangkok. Leung reported from Hong Kong.
