Sports.title: Choi pushing for first LPGA win at The Annika as Korda drops back
Sports.content:
Hye-Jin Choi opened with two bogeys, made up ground with a 15-foot eagle putt late and finished with a three-under 67 on Friday that gave her part of a three-way share of the lead at The Annika.

It was far more effective than the bogey-free round of Nelly Korda, the No. 1 player who could only laugh at her clean card because it was cleaner than she would have preferred - 15 straight pars, one birdie, two closing pars for a 69.

That left Korda four shots behind going into the weekend at Pelican Golf Club, where a victory would make the 28-year-old American eligible for the LPGA Hall of Fame.

"I had a lot of chances," said Korda, competing for the first time in two months. "But you can just tell that from yesterday morning to today afternoon with the wind, that's what the defence of this golf course is. It's as fast as Bermuda as I've putted on throughout my career."

It wasn't a problem for Solheim Cup star Carlota Ciganda, who birdied her last four holes for a 63 to join Choi and Lindy Duncan (66) atop the leaderboard at 12-under 128.

Image: Nelly Korda has dropped further behind the leaders. (AP Photo/Chris O'Meara)

The Japanese duo of Mao Saigo (65) and Minami Katsu (69) were two shots behind.

Choi has been an LPGA member for five years and it has been a curious chase for that first LPGA victory, particularly since she was 17 when she had a late lead in the 2017 US Women's Open and wound up as a runner-up.

She also had two good chances at winning during the recent Asia swing, where she was runner-up in Shanghai and South Korea.

Choi was playing in the group with Korda for the opening two rounds, which she believes has tested her enough to calm her nerves on the weekend. She wasn't rattled by the bogey-bogey start, or the bogey on the par-five 14th, her fifth hole of the round.

She pieced together enough birdies to regain some momentum, then hit an approach that got a nice kick around the green and rolled out to just under 15 feet for eagle on the par-five seventh.

"I have two rounds left, but I have recently played in a champion group on the tournament before, so I have that experience and I'm going just try my best and concentrate on my game," Choi said.

Scoring was low enough in the opening round that one-under 139 made the cut. This is the final regular-season event of the year, and the top 60 in the Race to CME Globe advance to the finale next week in Naples, where the winner gets $2 million.

Julia Lopez Ramirez of Spain, who defeated Yealimi Noh in a crucial singles match in her Solheim Cup debut, was among those at nine-under 131. That was important for the Spaniard, who came into the week at No. 66 in the Race to the CME Globe.

Image: Charley Hull was five shots off the leaders on seven-under. (AP Photo/Chris O'Meara)

Duncan, the 35-year-old Floridian, has yet to win on the LPGA Tour and this was the first time she had at least a share of the lead through 36 holes. She went 2-1 in her Solheim Cup debut.

"The week has gone by really fast, which is sometimes a good thing," Duncan said. "Because if you're playing a lot and you get some momentum going, that's kind of a nice way to play. So it's just been kind of rolling with it."

Charley Hull was five shots off the leaders on seven-under after shooting 67 on Friday. England's Lottie Woad finished the second round level with Hull on seven-under.

Sports.title: England respond to Jones' mind games ahead of Japan match
Sports.content:
England have hit back at Eddie Jones' claim they could be vulnerable to an upset by Japan on Saturday because they have one eye on their upcoming game with New Zealand.

Jones is aiming to disrupt Steve Borthwick's side by hitting them with the unexpected in the belief they will be "a little bit distracted" by the All Blacks' visit to Allianz Stadium on November 21.

New Zealand are the box-office fixture of the campaign ahead of finals weekend but England deny they are looking beyond Japan.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Japan head coach Eddie Jones fired England a warning to 'expect the unorthodox' ahead of the reunion with their former coach

"That's nowhere near the case because we understand how important this game is," scrum coach Tom Harrison said.

"We understand the challenge Japan can throw at us and we have to be alive in every single moment to the type of rugby they play.

"We understand that there might be unorthodox things coming our way but our need is to be alive.

"I've never worked with Eddie but I've met him a few times and he's a rugby genius, the way he thinks about the game and the way the players talk about him."

Murley: My best rugby will get me in the mix

Image: Cadan Murley is aiming to make an impression on Steve Borthwick

Cadan Murley wins his eighth cap but first at Twickenham after coming in for the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the left wing as one of 10 changes made for Japan.

Murley, Max Ojomoh and Will Joseph are aiming to make an impression on Borthwick after the head coach signalled that places in next year's World Cup squad are up for grabs.

"I just want go out there and play my best rugby," Murley said. "I'll focus on what I can do, control the controllables, and hopefully that will get me in the mix further down the line.

"But my sole focus is on this game and putting my best foot forward. It's my first game at Twickenham and that's what's on my mind at the moment."

Sports.title: Tearful Pochettino admits he 'couldn't say no to Man Utd'
Sports.content:
An emotional Mauricio Pochettino said that leaving his role with the United States was the "toughest decision of his career" but admitted he couldn't turn down the chance to become head coach of Manchester United.

Pochettino has been appointed as Michael Carrick's replacement at Old Trafford having signed a deal until the summer of 2029. It comes mere months after extending his stay with the USMNT until the 2030 World Cup.

The Argentine will begin his new role on November 18, after taking charge of the USA's two fixtures against Haiti.

Speaking in his pre-match press conference before his penultimate game, Pochettino broke down in tears as he explained his decision.

"In some part, this is a very sad decision. In another part, we are professionals. This is the next step to try and make your dreams come true," the former Spurs and Chelsea boss said.

"It all happened so quickly. By Sunday afternoon there was contact. You always were transparent and always tried to build something together. We learned a lot from you all, this amazing country and you amazing people. This is one of the most difficult decisions of my career. Thank you so much."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Rob Dorsett explains why Pochettino could be set for a busy January transfer window

Pochettino last held a club role in Europe during his one-season stint at Chelsea, which came to an end in 2024. When asked why he had opted to leave his post to return to the Premier League, Pochettino didn't hide the fact that taking the Old Trafford hot seat was a once in a lifetime opportunity.

"It's obvious," Pochettino added. "They [US Soccer Federation] know that not many opportunities can happen in your career like a side the size of Manchester United.

"When that arrives, it's difficult to turn down."

Liverpool

Manchester United Sunday 22nd November 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

Pochettino explains why he is staying for two more games

Pochettino will start life at Carrington following the international break, and will have three training sessions with the players before the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

The new head coach admitted that he would have started sooner if asked to, but explained why he wanted to see out the remainder of this camp.

"I am a professional person and the emotional link between us we have built in this two years is to show the commitment and respect and care and love," Pochettino said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports's Rob Dorsett explains why Pochettino has a VERY busy few days ahead of him

"Even if we take a decision which is not the best for one part, we've always been open. We have the respect of the players and staff, they understand the situation.

"Of course, if Manchester United and the federation agreed different terms, I would have respected between both. But this happened and of course, all the games are important.

"The last four games were important. We gave debuts to 13 players, before the cup I thought everyone had different ideas about it but we believe in the programme and are brave enough to go ahead. We're always optimistic and positive.

"After this camp, with four victories, we've been consistent in the same way, win or lose. We believe in the programme. It's an honour for us to be here, defend our patch and our players.

"We need to play tomorrow and the next game. We're not thinking in the future, it's about performing. We're very optimistic and it's a natural way to finish our partnership."

Emotional Poch rediscovered motivation in USA

Sky Sports News' chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:

"We've always known Mauricio Pochettino is an emotional person. He wears his heart on his sleeve. But I don't think you would normally expect a manager to break down and be so emotional in a press conference when he was leaving the USA to manage Manchester United.

"But that just tells you about the kind of guy he is because he's all about personal relationships. And obviously, he's made some very good friends in the US.

"He also said: 'We recovered our motivation here'. He was quite hurt and bruised by what happened to him at PSG and at Chelsea. It's almost like he's rediscovered his motivation by working in the US. And now he's ready to come back to the Premier League."

Carrick’s unintentional advice to Pochettino

In the wake of the announcement of Pochettino as the new head coach at Old Trafford, his predecessor Michael Carrick penned an emotional farewell off the back of his sacking on Wednesday.

Carrick took to social media to thank supporters saying, “you've shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing, and what most end up doing, would be to turn the other way".

In his post, the former Red Devils midfielder also lent an inadvertent word of advice for his replacement, giving an insight into what life is like at the club.

Sports.title: Riley determined to prove himself a world champion in waiting
Sports.content:
Viddal Riley will put himself on a path to a cruiserweight world title shot, if he can defend the European championship against Seydi Coupe on Saturday.

Only 14 fights into his pro career, Riley is already rated as the IBF's No. 2 contender for their world championship.

The Londoner wants to showcase himself as a world champion in waiting against Coupe.

"I think I'm the most well-rounded cruiserweight in the world," Riley told Sky Sports.

"I think we've trained for that because we want to cover every aspect of the game. We don't want to be lacking any area when it comes to movement, speed, IQ. All these things, I have them."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look back at Viddal Riley's best knockouts.

The IBF belt is currently vacant with Riley and New Zealand's David Nyika ranked one and two. Sooner or later a world title fight would surely lie ahead of Riley, if he's victorious.

"He's in the way. We can't worry about the other side of the door until we get past the doorman," Riley said of Coupe.

"I'm trying to get in the club, Seydi's asking for my ID at the door, I have to show him my ID or pull him out the way and get into the club."

It's a fight Riley is determined to dominate.

"I believe this will be a stoppage victory," the Londoner said. "You can't stop everybody, I'm aware of that as well. I won't be disappointed per se if I don't stop him. I'll be disappointed if I don't batter him.

"I just want to show for 12 rounds at least, it's not the level. We're completely different levels and I do, contrary to belief, possess good punch power."

Sports.title: Tearful Pochettino says United job was ‘difficult to turn down’ in USMNT farewell
Sports.content:
There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.

“These moments are not easy decisions,” a reflective Pochettino told the media. “Normally it’s the opposite. Normally you get sacked and you cry because you want to stay and you’re sacked by [the club]. It’s a tough decision but at the same time we are excited for the next step forward.”

Pochettino characterized United’s interest and negotiations as having come together at the last minute, essentially, with contact between the two sides first made Sunday.

“We cannot underestimate the staff and the players. When things became big and big and big, the players are very sensitive and the staff are too – they start to feel things as well. [Everything] was so quick, because we arrived here last Friday and Sunday afternoon this situation started to appear and some contact. We were very transparent, we were talking with [US Soccer CEO] JT [Batson] and the federation.”

Details were quickly ironed out between the sides, with the club and federation agreeing Pochettino would remain with the US through the upcoming matches.

“[Thursday], when things were positive in the way the agreement was, we had a meeting and I communicated to the players and the whole staff. I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation and they know us – how committed we are for the next two games. The decision between the federation and Manchester United, to agree that we’ll continue with our job in the camp; [nothing] can change our commitment and how important the next two games are.”

Pochettino bids tearful farewell to USA after Manchester United appointment – video

Pochettino and the US federation touted his contract renewal in August as the start of something new and significant, with the coach given a larger role in the overall direction of the US men at every level. That went by the wayside when United came knocking.

“They know that there are not too many opportunities that can happen in your career like [this one with Manchester United],” Pochettino said. “When they arrive, it’s difficult to turn down. But I want to make it clear, when we decided together to [stay another four years], it was always the commitment for the federation, too. Maybe the four games [in the September/October window] if we lose them, maybe you start to put pressure [on me]. And maybe something can be in a different way.

“Or even in the future,” he continued, “Things can happen. The federation and maybe new people arrive or don’t, or maybe have different ideas and you say, ‘We are thinking in different directions’ and maybe they say ‘Mauricio, maybe you need to go home.’ We cannot think in these extremes – I think we were very committed and never thought this would happen so quickly.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Pochettino was joined by Batson and US Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone on Friday. Batson was pressed on what will happen with the approximately $10m (£7.5m) Manchester United paid out for Pochettino’s services. A significant portion of Pochettino’s $6m salary was subsidized by billionaire hedge fund manager and US Soccer donor Ken Griffin. It’s unclear whether that generosity will extend towards Pochettino’s successor.

“The agreement with Manchester United, those funds – as you all know, US Soccer is a nonprofit and those funds are used to help us hire great coaches,” Batson said. “They help us do youth national team programs, coaching education … those funds are available for us to invest in order for us to make the biggest impact on our goals. Our supporters, our sponsors, our donors, are fans are very supportive around making sure that we have the resources that we need to achieve our goals, including having a world-class coach. We are appreciative of that support and look forward to our way of winning going forwards.”

Pochettino’s legacy, of course, is still to be defined. He was by no means a generational influence on the state of soccer in the US but he will be remembered fondly, by many, for a handful of standout performances and for guiding the US to a respectable, albeit disappointing, last-16 finish at this summer’s World Cup.

Pochettino was reluctant at first to define his own legacy, telling reporters he was “not arrogant” before jokingly conceding that he is “well, a little bit arrogant, but not too much.”

“We don’t take a project to be remembered forever,” Pochettino said, “and to have a picture here at the training center. It’s the impact on the human being. It’s for us to be a good partner and, through the vision of the federation, to add our quality and knowledge of the game and to be part of this family. I hope, in Manchester United, to do the same. That is what we can do – add our expertise about soccer … The key factor, though, that can have a key influence is the human being.”

Sports.title: ‘United is broken’: Guardian readers react to Michael Carrick’s sacking
Sports.content:
“As a United fan who was around for the early 90s seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation. He was the only likable thing about the club … I took my eight-year-old lad to Old Trafford for the Brighton game in the FA Cup in January and I’ve never experienced a more toxic atmosphere at a football ground. The fans deserve better … Better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment” – Chris

“Wilcox, [Berada] and [Jim] Ratcliffe should have fired themselves. They are the common denominator of all this failure. [Mauricio] Pochettino will last 12 months if he’s lucky” – Deb

“I have been a United supporter for over 60 years and this sacking just depresses me. Everyone knows the problem lies elsewhere … We were in desperate need of a left-back and centre-half. What did they do? Recruit several midfielders. So it starts again. Does anyone really believe changing manager will make any difference?” – Barry

“This feels sadder than every other time it’s happened since Alex Ferguson retired. Each of the previous managers had to go, as in large part the underperformance felt like it was their fault. This doesn’t feel like that … But, because the owners and executives aren’t going to sack themselves, and because you can’t fire the players, you change the only thing you can: the manager. And then repeat the cycle” – John

“I think it was Jonathan Liew who made the eminently sensible suggestion of a positional switch for Michael Carrick – by having him replace Jason Wilcox as director of football. That would have made sense” – Geoff

View image in fullscreen Manchester United minority shareholder Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), CEO Omar Berrada (centre) and technical director Jason Wilcox. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

“Just waiting for Mr Mediocrity Wilcox to do the honourable thing and admit he is out of his depth and responsible in part for the situation and resign” – Andrew

“Since Fergie left there have been 12 managers at United, including interims, with little reward. Can all of these have been wrong? Surely they could not have been? It highlights the systemic failures of the club at all levels” – Simon

“Carrick remains a Manchester United legend, he will always be. Without corresponding changes in the club’s recruitment process and the people driving it, we will be back here after 12-18 months” – Wale

“There are many problems at United but the biggest is short-termism. Carrick, like Ole Gunnar Solskjær, was given the permanent job because he did a good job as caretaker, but those roles are very different. Building for the long term, even at a well-run club with solid foundations, is different from getting the best from the hand you’ve been dealt over a few months. Since Fergie retired managers have been sacked because results have taken a downturn, and those who’ve suggested things might need to get worse before they get better (Ralf Rangnick and Ruben Amorim) have been shown the door. There are no reasons to think it will be any different for Pochettino” – Jason

“Is Pochettino a good manager? He did well at Spurs – albeit without winning anything – and in a short spell at Southampton but that was a long time ago. Since then his record has been pretty underwhelming, up to and including an uninspiring time in charge of the US men’s team. He just seems to have a reputation as a good manager but I’m not really sure what it’s based on any more” – Jon

“The similarities between ENIC’s ownership of Tottenham and the Glazers stewardship of United are striking. It doesn’t bode well for United given Tottenham’s unprecedented two-and-a-half decades of underachievement since then. The main difference, further bad news for United, is that Tottenham’s perilous debt load primarily funded a new stadium rather than facilitating the owners’ stake in the company and subsequent dividends to themselves. Football clubs can’t withstand money being extracted – it all has to be re-invested to keep the wheels turning” – Paul

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“In 53 years of supporting United this is the most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years. The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they see winning as nice to have [but] not the core objective of an elite football club … I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. It was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail and fail quickly. Our first team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us? It doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue” – Robert

“I have supported United for over 70 years through thick and thin but no more, to support United means supporting the Glazers. And I just wonder would a fans’ boycott get rid of them. An empty Old Trafford might do it” – Paul

“I am 62. I have followed Manchester United since the age of four (I found a picture of George Best, and told my mum I liked him). I stood on the Stretford End in my teens and took my son during the 90s. The fanbase needs to wrest control. The only way this will change is for the fanbase to boycott games. Stop going, stop providing matchday revenue. If the Glazers are only interested in the money, stop providing them with an income” – Bob

“Carrick delivered United back to the Champions League and have the team and the fans hope. He did more than I dared hope. But a one-front war is not a four-front war. He should never have been given a new mandate. A manager experienced at dealing with a totally new and different challenge, with Premier League experience, was always the need. Carrick is just another in a long list of managers who has a hands tied by the club. I’ve nothing but admiration for his effort and conduct” – Ben

Sports.title: John McGinn double saves Scotland’s blushes against North Macedonia
Sports.content:
A special occasion for Andy Robertson saw Scotland flirt with embarrassment. Collection of his 102nd cap moves him level with Kenny Dalglish in the all-time Scottish list. Robertson will soon be a record holder. This was, however, John McGinn’s night. A double from McGinn, the second a penalty, spared Scottish blushes against a North Macedonia team who threatened to administer red faces to those in navy blue.

This proved an almighty struggle for Scotland. Questions – and plenty of them – surround whether or not Sébastien Pocognoli can build on the excellent work of his predecessor Steve Clarke. For now, Scotland are a tough watch. Pocognoli looks tactically inflexible and this is not the new dawn many predicted.

“At times it wasn’t pretty,” admitted McGinn. The 32-year-old compared this Scotland process to a club team starting a new season. The rationale is fair enough, were this a remotely forgiving environment.

It was Robertson who led the dressing room inquest in the immediate aftermath of last month’s defeat to Slovenia. It is not in the Tottenham full-back’s make-up to personalise scenarios but shortcomings in the last international window, Pocognoli’s first as the Scotland manager, added to the sense that the bigger picture was important here. North Macedonia looked favourable visitors, having not scored a goal in eight outings.

Pocognoli could call upon Kieran Tierney, Scott McTominay and Ché Adams for the first time and deployed all three from the outset. It already appears the Belgian coach will not deviate from a back three. Ben Gannon-Doak took his place at right wingback, as is feasible against such weak opposition. Scotland’s approach will inevitably change for Monday’s meeting with Switzerland.

View image in fullscreen Andy Robertson, the Scotland captain, equalled Kenny Dalglish’s record of 102 caps. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Scotland had been ponderous until McTominay came within an excellent Stole Dimitrievski save of properly announcing his international return. The midfielder swivelled and struck, with Dimitrievski equal to the Napoli man’s effort.

Robertson was denied the opportunity to mark his special night with a goal by an errant whistle. The referee hauled play back for a Scotland free kick – McTominay had been upended – when the playing of advantage would have seen Robertson collect a Billy Gilmour pass in a scoring position. The Hampden crowd mumped and moaned, which rather summed up recent attitudes around this Scotland team. It feels as if the public are not yet fully engaged with Pocognoli’s project. Adams sought to lift the mood, the striker stooping for a header that took a deflection before Dimitrievski batted away.

In backing up their statistical position, North Macedonia were providing nothing by way of attacking threat. Their enjoyment came from frustrating the Scots. McTominay, who has previous for acrobatic excellence in this arena, tried a 34th minute bicycle kick that flew over the crossbar and Scotland’s most lively player tried again with a low shot which Dimitrievski blocked with his midriff. This lack of cutting edge was a Scottish concern long before Pocognoli entered the dugout. The boos that met the half-time whistle, seconds after North Macedonia had created their first chance of the evening, depicted a supporter base who remained unconvinced.

Less than a minute of the second half had been played when Gilmour produced one of the worst misses ever witnessed at this famous old venue. Calamity in the North Macedonia defence allowed Adams to steal in. The Torino striker laid the ball back to Gilmour six yards out and, with an open goal, he blazed his shot wildly over the bar. It was a genuine, utter howler.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Billy Gilmour reacts after shooting over from six yards against North Macedonia. Photograph: Russell Cheyne/Reuters

Route one broke the deadlock for Scotland. Ryan Porteous’s looping header from the halfway line caused panic in the North Macedonia defence. Adams capitalised, his pass to the advancing McGinn setting up the Aston Villa midfielder’s 23rd goal for his country. Relief was as obvious as celebration.

Although a North Macedonia response was not in the script, the equaliser epitomised Scottish slackness. A near post run from Elmin Rastoder saw him meet a menacing Enis Bardhi corner from the left. Angus Gunn in the home goal was helpless as Rastoder flicked home.

North Macedonia clearly now sensed Scottish vulnerability. While Pocognoli’s men continued to dominate the ball, North Macedonia’s counterattacking threat had increased. Officialdom, and sharp footwork from Gannon-Doak, were soon to come to Scotland’s rescue.

Gannon-Doak was instantly convinced of the foul by Dimitrievski after the Bournemouth man tried to skip past the goalkeeper. It took the VAR to inform the referee that the incident was worthy of further inspection. Intriguingly, it was not Oli McBurnie – still awaiting his maiden Scotland goal and on in place of Adams – who took the spot-kick. Up stepped McGinn, who made no mistake. While Gannon-Doak is due credit for winning the penalty, this appearance once more raised serious questions about his decision making.

That of the Scottish FA in hiring Pocognoli would be open to question had North Macedonia delivered a shock. That they did not do so spared Scotland ignominy. “It was not always perfect,” said Pocognoli. You aren’t kidding, Sébastien.

Sports.title: Jesús Owono given 12-match ban for tackle that resulted in Jesús de Miguel’s death
Sports.content:
The FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono was suspended for 12 matches by the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee on Friday after his challenge on Jesús de Miguel resulted in the death of the Tenerife striker last week.

Owono, an Equatorial Guinea international, was sent off in the second division match on 2 November after racing into midfield and colliding with De Miguel while trying to clear an aerial ball. After the collision, De Miguel, 30, was placed in intensive care in hospital and the Spanish forward died on 3 November.

“The assessment of the conduct under consideration in these proceedings must be based on the facts expressly recorded in the referee’s report, which states that the player was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play,’” said the committee in a statement.

“The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesús de Miguel, is public knowledge. In view of the nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances … the maximum sanction, 12 matches of suspension, is justified.”

Spanish police sources said last week that an investigation into what happened had been opened under judicial supervision.

Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after De Miguel’s death. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words, and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club last week.

“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesús. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesús and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

The FC Andorra head coach, Carles Manso, said on Thursday it would be Owono who decides if and when he returns to football after the tragic incident.

Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including the Spain head coach, Luis de la Fuente, and the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez.

Sports.title: Tuchel to remind England players of anti-racism protocols before game in Spain
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will remind his ­England players of the anti-racism protocols as they prepare to play Spain in Madrid for the first time since the notorious meeting between the countries in 2004. Spain won 1-0 at the Bernabéu but the occasion was ruined by racist abuse directed at England’s black players from the stands.

England have since played three games in Spain, although they refused to return to Madrid for the first of them in 2009. The match was moved to Seville. There were no ­problems in any of the three; the second was in Alicante in 2015, the third back in Seville in 2018.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Spanish federation was fined £44,750 in the wake of the 2004 fixture when Ashley Cole, Rio ­Ferdinand, Shaun Wright-Phillips, Jermaine Jenas and Jermain Defoe were targeted. England face Spain in the Nations League at Madrid’s other major stadium – the Metropolitano.

Spain were last month fined £15,000 and ordered to play their next friendly with a partial stadium closure after supporters sang a discriminatory chant about Muslims during a match against Egypt in Barcelona in March.

Tuchel said: “We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September of last year]. There is a protocol in place. Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]. It’s important that the players know about the protocol. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch.”

England’s head coach made it clear he did not anticipate any problems at the Metropolitano. “It’s unacceptable,” he said. “In any stadium, not even in stadiums … we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone. That’s just not who we are. I expect, of course, full support from the Spanish crowd for the Spanish team. But we will not expect anything [untoward].”

Sports.title: Branding it like Beckham: how Jude Bellingham is future-proofing his fame
Sports.content:
This Sunday, Jude Bellingham will line up with his England teammates for a match against Spain. But the footballer has been hitting the headlines way beyond the pitch recently – thanks to fronting a Calvin Klein underwear ad released this month, and becoming the first footballer to appear solo on the cover of British Vogue.

It’s a savvy move for the 23-year-old, future-proofing himself as a power player both on and off the pitch. This is a roadmap carved out by David Beckham, who since retiring in 2013 has become a brand and personality that transcends sport. Beckham – together with his wife, Victoria – became a billionaire this year.

The Calvin Klein ads, which feature Bellingham in underwear, sometimes in his signature Christ the Redeemer pose, have caused a stir since appearing in London and New York, with passersby stopping to take selfies. The popularity of a billboard in Soho, New York also cements his celebrity status in the US after this summer’s World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham on the cover of British Vogue. Photograph: Alasdair McLellan/British Vogue

Of course Bellingham is a bona fide star on the pitch. Mark Borkowski, a public relations consultant, says this factor is pivotal to the footballer’s crossover appeal. “Bellingham is an exceptional sporting talent, and his brand value is understandably enormous,” he says. “But fashion doesn’t create that value, football does. Fashion merely provides another means of exploiting it.”

This buzz is working out well for Calvin Klein. The fashion data firm Launchmetrics said in 48 hours the Calvin Klein campaign generated $35.8m (£27m) in media impact value, the metric that works out the monetary value of social media posts. The fashion platform Lyst reports that searches for Calvin Klein underwear have risen by 25% since the campaign was released.

Bellingham has a savvy team around him, with his mother, Denise, a former HR executive, working as his personal manager. Some are wondering if his 21-year-old brother, Jobe – in the England squad for the first time this month – might do similar campaigns, increasing the rise of the Bellingham brand.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham poses for Calvin Klein’s cotton stretch underwear campaign. Photograph: Oliver Hadlee Pearch

So far Bellingham – and his management team – have been strategic with his brand choices. As well as Calvin Klein, Bellingham works with Adidas, Kim Kardashian’s underwear brand Skims and Louis Vuitton.

Daniel-Yaw Miller, in his influential SportsVerse newsletter, compared him to Beckham. “It’s very intentional,” he says. “What [Bellingham is] doing is aimed at the higher tier of the market but at the same time, a big part of his personality is very relatable.”

Bellingham is also a heart-throb, with looks that, in another life, could belong to a boyband. Vogue have amped up this factor: the magazine comes with a pull-out poster. “It helps that he’s incredibly good-looking,” says Miller.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Fashion Statement Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Bellingham is not the only male footballer to work with the fashion industry. Bukayo Saka and Son Heung-min were in Burberry’s autumn campaign, Kylian Mbappé worked with Christian Dior, and Declan Rice is on the cover of GQ this month. “The earnings that they can get during their football career are obviously huge,” says Miller. “But what sets them up for life beyond that is being brands and businesses in their own right. It’s not only just a money thing. It’s about cementing a legacy and securing their profile in the game long term, commercially and culturally.”

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham posing for British Vogue in its December 2026 issue. Photograph: Alasdair McLellan/British Vogue

Not everyone is impressed by Bellingham’s foray into fashion. Felicia Pennant, the editor of the football and fashion magazine Season, says if he is following Beckham’s business model, the older footballer pushed the boundaries more, appearing in edgy photoshoots covered in (fake) blood for The Face magazine in 2001, and in artwork by Sam Taylor-Johnson. “Beckham was the subject of art and he was the art rather than selling the art,” she says. “I think what Jude’s doing feels quite transactional … there’s nothing that directional about anything he’s done so far.”

Borkowski sounds a note of caution going forward. “Fame surrounds exceptional young athletes with people whose livelihoods depend on telling them how wonderful they are. That can become a very dangerous echo chamber,” he says. “The football makes the myth. The business can preserve it. But hubris can destroy both.”

Sports.title: Why Chelsea and Manchester City’s WSL clash is not as season-defining as you think
Sports.content:
There was a time when the games between the top three – traditionally Chelsea, Manchester City and Arsenal – were title-deciders. Where every point taken off a title rival was key. Such was the gap in investment and quality between those teams and the rest of the Women’s Super League, it was extremely rare that points would be dropped to teams outside that elite clique.

As the WSL has grown in investment, profile and size, that narrative has started to shift a little. The investment gap is still large from the top to the bottom of the league. But increased investment among the best of the rest and even among those teams further down the table, as well as an increase in high-quality coaches with the tactical and technical vision to get more from players, is having an impact.

That’s a roundabout way of saying that when Chelsea welcome the title holders and current league leaders to Stamford Bridge on Saturday lunchtime, counterintuitively, the three points isn’t the most important takeaway. Instead, based on the state of play, it’s the momentum, confidence, belief and bragging rights that are critical.

Naturally, should Chelsea win and thus leapfrog Manchester City, then the title race will be considered wide open. If Andrée Jeglertz’s City extend their lead over Chelsea from two points to five, even at this early stage, they will be considered favourites for the title in May, but it will be said with a little less confidence than it might have been in previous years.

The WSL is more and more competitive year on year. There have been only two occasions, in the 15 years since the first WSL season was played (after it was launched to replace the FA Women’s Premier League National Division), when the title winners have lost more than two games in a season. Both of those have come in the last three years, with Chelsea the first to do so in 2023-24 and then Manchester City last season.

You could say that because wins are less consequential in the games between title rivals, those games are less thrilling, but the reality is that the growing unpredictability of almost every match across the WSL means that every game becomes a must-watch.

At Stamford Bridge on Saturday, the remaining two unbeaten teams have the opportunity to inflict a first defeat. Neither side has looked infallible this season. City have kept just two clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions, while Chelsea stuttered last weekend, with their second draw of the season allowing City to move above them.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City leapfrogged Chelsea at the top of the WSL after beating West Ham last weekend. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

Arguably, there has been a momentum shift between Sonia Bompastor’s and Jeglertz’s teams, with the former having dropped points against Everton before a 0-0 draw with the Swedish side Häcken in the Champions League while City earned a 5-0 win over West Ham and picked up a first win in Europe, after three draws, with a 4-1 defeat of Inter.

Jeglertz said that moving top had changed nothing before this clash. “We’re still early in the season. We want to win all games. That’s our focus this weekend,” he said. “Nothing has changed from that point of view and I don’t think it will have for them either.”

Chelsea have been defensively strong, and are the only WSL team to still be in single figures for goals conceded, on five to City’s 10, and they have kept nine clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions (not including Champions League qualifying).

However, the key to the west London side’s ambition of drawing first blood between the two teams this season will probably centre around how well they cope without Lauren James.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They may lead the way in goals scored too, 28 to City’s 27, but against Everton the absence of the England forward’s creativity was keenly felt and Chelsea’s attack looked a little predictable. Everton nullified the impact of the wide players Ellie Carpenter and Sandy Baltimore and Chelsea struggled to find another way through.

“My job is to make sure I find solutions when some players are not available and not playing for the team,” Bompastor said last week.

While Chelsea have to cope with the absence of James, who has a hamstring injury that Bompastor says means they “won’t see her until the end of this block” – up until at least the international break at the end of the month – City have players returning.

Rebecca Knaak is fine after a knock to the head against Inter and Vivianne Miedema, Beth Mead and Niamh Charles are on their way back. “All three of them, actually, were in the session today and I hope that they will be available for Saturday,” said Jeglertz. Advantage City then, just.

In a way, that it is unlikely that this result decides either team’s season makes it a more interesting and exciting contest, because players are free to play uninhibited by the pressure of how catastrophic a loss could be and, with the two dominant teams going head to head, we’re in for a show.

Sports.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
Sports.content:
It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

Reader, it did not. But it did set a precedent that is being enthusiastically revived. It’s even possible that, after several decades of hurt, the world’s favourite sport may finally be getting its artistic due. There have been three iterations of the Football Art Prize in the past 20 years, and the latest arrives at the National Football Museum this month (from the Sheffield Millennium Gallery) with a breadth of entries that demonstrate how resonant the subject can be.

View image in fullscreen Felix Higham’s Newcastle 2 Barcelona 7, one of many exhibits that focus on football culture rather than the game itself. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Meticulous still lives – of battered balls, or boots mid-clean – ache with memory. There’s haunting photo-documentary: Bangladeshi youths playing a pickup game in the middle of a rubbish dump, pitches affected by climate change. “You see the whole gamut of footballing experience on display,” says the museum’s exhibitions director, Pip Diment. Her assumptions – she initially imagined herself hanging portraits of famous moments and iconic players – were overturned. “Pretty much every one of the artists is expressing how football matters to them, but they’re responding and reacting in such different ways.”

There are a few famous faces nevertheless. One artist worked in charcoals to create a hyper-realist bust of N’Golo Kanté. Roy Keane appears twice, once proffering a plate of prawn sandwiches to his viewer, another time in a diptych with Micah Richards. The latter is the work of Conor Rogers, whose satirical series of paintings on abandoned betting slips took second prize. They include a poignant image of Sheffield United’s manager, Chris Wilder, head in hands, next to a repurposed bookmaker’s logo asking: “Lad r u ok?”

Diment says football and art are still perceived as almost entirely separate spheres, so it’s interesting that this year’s winning work – a video by Alina Akbar – explores the connection between “high” and “popular” culture. In Footwork, the multimedia artist segues between keepy-uppy skills and the choreographed movements of Kathak, an Indian classical dance style. The combined rhythms and sounds create a mesmerising meditation on identity, related to the northern South Asian community in which she grew up.

View image in fullscreen Kyle King-Jagger ‘s Roy’s Rolls riffs on Roy Keane’s famous ‘prawn sandwich brigade’ comment. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Football, she says, is a post-migration culture whose value is sometimes overlooked by the very people who adopted it. “Whenever I went to my great-grandparents’ house, football was on TV all the time and I’d be on their street, trying out tricks,” says Akbar. “My grandad and his brothers were really excited when I started playing, because they’d gone through the more racist era of the 70s, and they never went to games.”

For all its social themes, Akbar’s work still expresses the balletic movement and poise that Picasso once pursued in the flowing form of his ceramic sculpture Footballeur. It’s interesting how so much of the art in the show reflects football culture rather than the game itself – watching from the sofa, in the pub, on the touchline of a recreational game. Perhaps it’s hard for artists to compete with the volume of visual content that the games already provide. And we have moved a long way from a classically inspired fascination with athletes’ physiques (for comparison, check out the leaping goalkeeper in Cecil Beaton’s mid-20th-century painting Footballers, with his unashamedly pert buttocks).

Tim Marlow, the director of the Design Museum and chair of the judging panel, points out that “artists today have unashamedly adopted the position of the spectator or the fan” and that it’s rare to find works that try to get inside the experience of the footballer themselves. One of his favourite exceptions is the 2006 film, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait, which he calls “a great piece of conceptual art”. “It’s a really intimate study of the game, which in the current era, when you’ve got referees with head cams, might feel old hat, but nothing like it had been done before.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Keith Bird’s Full-time at Maine Road depicts Manchester City’s former home. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

And then there’s Tottenham’s stadium gallery, OOF, where exhibitions of football-related work have ranged from Roger Mayne’s 1950s street photography to AC Larsen’s polemic on the FA’s trans ban. This month brought the opening of Trackie McLeod’s celebration of Wag culture. Historic football art, meanwhile, is rocketing in value. Four years ago Lowry’s Going To The Match went for £7.8m at auction, a record price for the Salford artist’s work, and in 2022 one of Nicholas de Staël’s Parc des Princes 1952 abstract series – based on a friendly he watched between France and Sweden – became the most expensive football artwork when it sold for £16.7m.

Money has always been a key element in the art world, and there are notable collectors within the footballing world today, from billionaire club owners to cultured former players. Fabio Capello has a well documented passion for Kandinsky; David Beckham’s collection is said to include Andy Warhol, Banksy and Yayoi Kusama; Michael Ballack is spotted at major art fairs around the world. The whimsically named J St John, who organised Football and Fine Arts, told the Liverpool Daily Post 70 years ago that art needed a new form of patronage, to help people appreciate the painted canvas in the same they understood the artistry of Joe Mercer, Ferenc Puskas and Stanley Matthews. Could his dream finally be coming to pass?

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: I'm told control over transfers was key to Mauricio Pochettino taking Man United job. It seems they finally have a manager bullish enough to hold Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Jason Wilcox to account
Sports.content:
It only happened once. But if you search for it, there is footage. The date was February 23, 2000 and the place was the old Wembley Stadium. England 0-0 Argentina, the kind of friendly best forgotten, except for a single line of trivia.

Of all the games played by Jason Wilcox and Mauricio Pochettino, this was the sole example of them sharing a pitch. Wilcox was given the full 90 at a point when Kevin Keegan was low on options for the left wing and Pochettino came on with 35 minutes on the clock and kicked a few people.

He was good at kicking people, Pochettino. He flattened Paul Scholes once, then he nudged over David Beckham and twice he got stuck into Emile Heskey. But Wilcox was in a safe zone on the other side of the field that night. While Pochettino indulged his hobby, Wilcox kept out of harm’s way.

We might ask at this juncture if either of them ever changed their spots. But it’s more interesting to ponder what comes next, now they have been pitched together again at Manchester United.

United needed a big bull to replace Michael Carrick and they have got one. Wilcox’s preference? Well, United’s director of hopeless football quite fancied Eddie Howe, according to the whispers, and Howe is far from a shrinking violet, but he’s not Pochettino. And Pochettino certainly isn’t Carrick.

Pochettino won’t drive to work for three days straight while knowing his race is run. And he won’t have the same patience for incompetence from those below or above.

Manchester United needed a big bull to replace Michael Carrick and they have got one in Mauricio Pochettino

Pochettino is not the sort of manager to drive to work for three days straight while knowing his race is run, like Carrick did this week

With any luck, United knew this when they reached an agreement that was a decade in the making. If they did, it would demonstrate some self-awareness at last, because United have badly needed the right blend of bruiser and diplomat in that seat.

They have cried out for someone who isn’t too nice, too loyal, too whiny or too undermined by their own shortcomings to have the kind of rucks that are needed for change. By that logic, United may have invited their own worst enemy to dinner, or their best chance of a solution.

There have been few managerial appointments in recent years as inherently fascinating at this one. That instinct is partly driven by the thought it has all arrived a touch late – when United favoured Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to replace Jose Mourinho, it was a sliding-door moment for all parties.

But there’s another way of viewing this and that comes from the opposite angle. Maybe this is the perfect time, based on the qualifications needed to operate within the modern version of United.

There is no doubt that Pochettino has lost some of his sheen since his masterful handling of Daniel Levy at Tottenham, but what did he gain? He managed the vastest collection of footballing egos at PSG, worked under a convoluted tier of meddlers in the madhouse of Chelsea and was confronted by presidential interference in his time with the US national team at the World Cup.

Two schools of thought can exist here. One is that he failed to tear up any trees in each of those assignments. But the other talks to the point we are making: United require a manager who can navigate their unique brand of chaos and the new guy knows the dance.

Pochettino won’t ever thank Donald Trump for the Folarin Balogun fiasco in the summer, but Sir Jim Ratcliffe would have to work awfully hard to cause him a more uncomfortable press conference.

The scale of Pochettino’s challenge is obvious. In the micro, that means applying a playing style built on hard running to a squad that jogged its way to embarrassing statistics under Carrick. In the macro, it will be his challenge with Wilcox and a recruitment team that effectively cost Carrick his job.

Pochettino has had plenty to deal with as USA coach, not least the meddling of Donald Trump

Pochettino has the authority to challenge (above, from left) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox over United's failing transfer policy

Talking to one of Pochettino’s former colleagues on Friday, the expectation is that greater control over transfers will have been a key tenet of those negotiations with United.

As predictable as that might sound, it was a huge bone of contention for him at Chelsea and United’s failures in this area are clear. Time will tell if any promises are honoured.

But Pochettino has got what he wanted and pursued. His desire for the post has never been disguised, which can be mapped as a trail of breadcrumbs from that bottle of red he once shared with Sir Alex Ferguson all the way up to carefully planted mentions of the club in gatherings with media.

There were some acts of reassurance necessary for the final step, of course, and doubtless it will sting to leave the US - his farewell tears on Friday showed as much. But not enough to inspire a second thought.

To look back over Pochettino’s other stints in England, one main memory stands out from his time at Tottenham and I’ve cited in this space previously.

It traces to September 2016, when Pochettino was on the rise and had a game approaching against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City. In attempting to coax a decent line in the press conference, a few of us killed time before his arrival by digging up old footage of Pochettino’s Espanyol beating Barcelona, when he and Guardiola were on opposing sides.

Within the clip was an unexpected gem, because Pochettino murdered the Brazilian Ronaldo in a challenge. He took the ball, sure, but demolished the man, too, and his boot ended up shoulder-high. We were watching this when Pochettino wandered over and requested a replay – when it was shown, he laughed maniacally.

As a player, he always saw the value in a good reducer. And it’s a trait that might well be needed at United. If Wilcox and the other cronies upstairs don’t up their game, they might find that Carrington offers fewer hiding places than the old Wembley.

Pochettino's fondness for the USA job was apparent by his farewell tears on Friday

Was Tom Brady ever in the Blues' building?

Tom Brady has left Birmingham, but was he ever really there? Across three years, he attended only four games.

The club is on a steep upward trajectory and there is no doubt that the Brady association helped on their commercial side.

But I recall speaking to one Blues shareholder a couple of seasons back, and after attempting to establish some tangible detail about their star investor’s contribution, there was a period of silence. When I asked how often Brady might dial into meetings, there was laughter.

In this era of celebrity ownership of our football clubs, it’s easy to get blinded by a famous name. And easier still to get drawn in by suggestions of expertise that they have carried over from a different space.

But in the vast majority of cases, they are little more than mascots without the costume.

Tom Brady makes a rare appearance at a Birmingham match in 2025

Great delivery from Cummins - but it's not over yet

Pat Cummins stood for 70 minutes on Thursday and answered questions about Sandpapergate.

The Australia captain refused to budge, both from the microphone and his position that Usman Khawaja was incorrect in his claim that the entire team was in on the plot to cheat against South Africa in 2018.

It’s hard to know what was more impressive – Cummins’ commitment to answering every question, or his delusion in believing that it would be the last time he discusses it.

Sports.title: The four problems Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix at Man United: From big names causing unrest in the dressing room to an issue which plagued Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick before him, these are the items top of his Old Trafford in-tray
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino will see out his final two games as US national team boss with a double-header against Haiti before starting work at Manchester United on Wednesday. The 54-year-old won’t have any time to waste with a daunting first game against United’s bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday followed by a European clash with Sporting Lisbon in Portugal three days later. With United languishing in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League standings, it’s clear why Pochettino has been brought in to replace Michael Carrick on a two-and-a-half-year contract. Daily Mail Sport looks at the most pressing matters in Pochettino’s in-tray at Carrington as the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss and his backroom staff head for Manchester... Mauricio Pochettino is the new manager of Manchester United - but the problems he has to fix are already piling up Winning mentality It sounds obvious, but winning games to get United out of the Premier League drop zone has to be the first priority. Everything at a football club flows from the results on the pitch, and United’s humiliating decline this season has had ramifications throughout Old Trafford and Carrington. The players are clearly low on confidence which has only exacerbated the team’s dismal performances and brought just one win in 10 Premier League games, against newly-promoted Ipswich – United’s worst start in 40 years. Diogo Dalot is a prime example, after fans cheered his substitution in the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa last weekend, and the defender cut a crestfallen figure as he left Old Trafford to go on international duty with Portugal. The Stretford End also turned on the players as the atmosphere turned toxic after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth at the end of last month, having vented their anger towards the club’s ownership – the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – as well as chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox at every opportunity. That won’t go away anytime soon, but a winning team will at least take some of the sting out of the situation if appointing Pochettino can give United a ‘bounce’ and divert attention back onto the pitch. United players are low on confidence, not least Diogo Dalot (left) whose substitution was cheered by his own fans against Aston Villa The United team were also lambasted by the Stretford End after the 3-0 loss to Bournemouth last month Survival of the fittest Carrick enjoyed a good start, losing just two of his 17 games in charge in the second half of last season to earn a two-year contract, but United struggled under him this term due to a combination of poor recruitment, injuries and lack of fitness. These are all issues that Pochettino must try to put right. There is little he can do about recruitment until the January transfer window opens and United have a chance to atone for their mistake in not signing cover at left back and centre forward last summer, which backfired spectacularly when both Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko picked up injuries. He can, however, try to get more out of United’s £155million midfield signings Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again – Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, and a United squad that was good enough to finish third in the Premier League last season. Injuries have been a major problem with the hamstring strain that will keep Baleba out of action for Pochettino’s first few weeks in charge just the latest setback. As well as Shaw, Sesko, Baleba and long-term casualty Manuel Ugarte, United have also lost Amad Diallo, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Lisandro Martinez, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui for parts of this season. Pochettino must get more out of United’s £155million midfield signing Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again United have struggled to keep up with their opponents since the opening day - a lack of fitness has plagued every manager since Ole Gunnar Solskjaer The good news for Pochettino is that Shaw and Rashford are hoping to be fit for Anfield, while Matthijs de Ligt is available again after a year out with back problems. However, Sesko’s absence until the new year leaves the new boss without his most natural source of goals. Fitness is another matter and United have looked short of it since the opening-day defeat at Hull City amid concerns that the coaching levels dropped off under Carrick and were too relaxed. They covered 120.8 kilometres against Villa – the most in a league game under Carrick – and Pochettino will demand that and a whole lot more as he increases the work-rate among his new squad. It’s a problem that has hindered a succession of United bosses going back to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and the Argentine must find a way to drill a better work ethic into United. Get Bruno back to his best The problems at United this season have inevitably led to unrest in the dressing room, with the biggest issue centred around captain Bruno Fernandes. News that Fernandes has rejected United’s latest contract offer has come as no surprise given his dramatic change in fortunes from last season, and Pochettino must find a way to get arguably United’s best player back in form and onside. Having set a new Premier League record for assists and picked up a string of player of the year awards last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off a cliff as he struggled with an injury sustained at the World Cup, and he suffered the rare indignity of being benched for the loss to Bournemouth. Never one to hide his mood very well, the 32-year-old criticised Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat by Como in what was a major blow to his head coach. Never one to hide his mood very well, Bruno Fernandes has been disgruntled of late and rejected United's offer of a new contract Lisandro Martinez looks to be headed for the exit door - although the arrival of his fellow Argentine Pochettino may help things While the United hierarchy will try to persuade Fernandes to sign a new deal in keeping with their reduced wage structure and the fact he will turn 33 next year, Pochettino has to find a way of relighting the fire in his skipper. Whether the club will make as much effort to keep Lisandro Martinez as he comes towards the end of his contract remains to be seen after another member of United’s leadership team took aim at Wilcox’s recruitment after the defeat by Atletico Madrid. It is said to have caused an angry clash between Martinez and summer signing Tielemans on the way back from Spain. Martinez looks to be heading for the Old Trafford exit, but it will be interesting to see if the arrival of his compatriot Pochettino – a combative Argentine centre back in much the same mould as a player – has an impact on that. Plug the leaky defence As a former defender, Pochettino won’t need telling that leaking 15 goals in the last five games simply isn’t good enough. United have now let in 30 in all competitions this season, the most of any club in Europe’s top five leagues apart from Lens. They have been appalling at the back, conceding in the opening seconds to Atletico, Como and Villa. Had they been able to hold out and prevent late equalisers against Everton and Tottenham, the additional four points would have them 12th in the table rather than in the relegation zone.

Your browser does not support iframes.

A revolving door of makeshift left backs in the absence of Shaw and Dorgu, De Ligt’s belated comeback and Martinez’s needless red card at Chelsea haven’t helped. Goalkeeper Senne Lammens, so composed last season, looks considerably more shaky behind a leaky and ever-changing back-four, and had arguably his worst game against Villa last weekend. Pochettino couldn’t ask for a tougher first test than going to Anfield, and knows that United will have to start by being solid at the back.

Sports.title: 'He's an absolute joke': Experts break down 'unique' Henry Pollock's ability to play in the pack AND on the wing - from his exceptional work rate and physicality to his endless 'bravado'
Sports.content:
'He's an absolute joke': Experts break down 'unique' Henry Pollock's ability to play in the pack AND on the wing - from his exceptional work rate and physicality to his endless 'bravado'

England’s impressive win over Australia last week was bad news for Steve Borthwick’s detractors but also for those who argue Henry Pollock should focus on his rugby.

It was bad news for those who bizarrely seem to hate the fact that Pollock works with Eddie Hearn, for those who argue he does too much off the field. That he’s on the front covers of Tatler and Men’s Health.

Those outdated old fools who seemingly can’t grasp the bigger picture that by doing so, Pollock is not only broadening his own appeal, but that of the sport he plays, too – as long as he also does the business on the pitch.

Well, after appearing off the bench against the Wallabies for a second-half cameo in the unusual position of wing, Pollock – normally a back-row – certainly did that, scoring twice, playing beautifully and giving a metaphorical two fingers to the naysayers.

It was a performance which showcased his undoubted rugby ability and world-class athleticism. Now seemingly at the head of Test rugby’s ‘hybrid player’ phenomenon, Pollock’s versatility adds to his appeal, marketing ability and makes him a key figure in England rugby.

‘Henry is doing amazing things,’ England’s 2003 World Cup-winning livewire winger, Jason Robinson, tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘There are not many forwards, if any, who would be comfortable playing on the wing. Fair play to him.

'If the shoe was on the other foot and I’d been asked to play in the back-row back in my day, I’m not sure I’d have been keen!’

England's Henry Pollock celebrates his first try against Australia last weekend when the forward played as a winger - to great effect

Pollock touches down after a neat sidestep that befuddled Australia

In 2019, then England head coach Eddie Jones – who returns to Twickenham as the man in charge of Japan today – floated the idea his wing Jack Nowell could be deployed as a loose forward. Jones was broadly laughed at.

But seven years later, his idea has proved prophetic. In the international game, there are a number of players now comfortable playing as both forwards and backs.

South Africa’s Andre Esterhuizen (a centre who increasingly plays flanker) and Kwagga Smith and France’s Sekou Macalou (flankers who can cover wing) have done it, too, but it is Pollock – as he always seems to do – who is standing out in that way for England.

‘He’s got great ability, footwork, strength and speed,’ Robinson says of Pollock. ‘His second try against Australia showed the pace he’s got. He’s mobile. Henry knows how to play.

'What I like about Henry is that I look at him and I see all the razzle-dazzle. The off-field stuff he’s been up to. I’ve got no problem with that. But if you do that, you have to roll up your sleeves and get your hands dirty (on the pitch).

'That’s what you’re judged on in Test rugby. Those who know the game know you’re judged on getting your hands on the ball. Being prepared to be smashed. Putting your head where it hurts. Henry has got all the skills, but he does all that gritty stuff too.’

Pollock will win his 15th England cap against Japan, starting in a more customary position of No 8. In his 14 appearances to date, all but one of which have come as a replacement, he has scored eight tries.

In this year’s Nations Championship, he has scored five tries in just 111 minutes of action at an average of one every 22 minutes. He has the best try-scoring rate of any player. Only New Zealand superstar wing/full-back Will Jordan has more tries, with six.

Pollock will win his 15th England cap against Japan, starting in a more customary position of No 8

Pollock touches down for a second time against Australia. He has scored five Nations Championship tries in just 111 minutes of action

Against Australia, Pollock clocked a top speed of 20.4mph. In an era where the physical power and weight needed to play in the pack is significant, such speed is beyond rare. It’s what makes Pollock a unique property.

As Borthwick plans for next year’s World Cup – for which he can only name a squad of 33 – Pollock will already be inked in. His ability to cover multiple positions makes his selection a certainty, even if it might be the case that in England’s first-choice 23, he is better deployed as a replacement.

‘Henry has had an incredible impact off the bench,’ said England coach Borthwick ahead of the Japan match. ‘I want to ensure he's bringing that to the start of the game.

'He is talented, keeps it simple. And when he gets himself around the ball, moments happen. He has exceptional work-rate and that will put him in position for those carries and getting on the ball.’

Despite his shining contribution against Australia, Pollock will only act as emergency wing cover. He won’t start Tests there. But the fact he can even fill in, frankly, is more than impressive.

‘He’s an absolute joke,’ says Alex Coles, Pollock’s team-mate at both Northampton and England. ‘I was not surprised he did well on the wing. There’s been a bit of work done behind the scenes to get him ready for that scenario both at club and country.

'He just relishes those challenges. He wants that moment. He wants to be trying something new. He’s athletically built to be able to do that. He’s so fast. It’s mega-impressive he can go do that.

'It’s certainly going to add to his game, being able to play multiple positions. Good on him. I’m only jealous!’

The meeting with Japan is another chance for Pollock to prove his worth. He wasn’t tested defensively at all against Australia, who were poor. Jones, who is a big cricket fan, likened Pollock's two tries against the Wallabies to ‘cheap runs’ – ones scored when the result has already been decided.

‘He’s an absolute joke,’ says Alex Coles, Pollock’s team-mate at both Northampton and England. ‘I was not surprised he did well on the wing'

'He’s got some fantastic attributes and he’s a good player. But can he be a great in the game?' asks Eddie Jones

‘He’s got a good manager (Hearn) who seems to have his head screwed on and is giving some good advice,’ Jones says of Pollock. ‘His big test will come when he has to start against South Africa or New Zealand. Then we’ll find out how good a player he can be.

'He’s got some fantastic attributes and he’s a good player. But can he be a great in the game?'

So can Pollock deliver in big matches from the off, rather than in short bursts as a replacement? He is still a work in progress. But, then again, what 21-year-old isn’t?

‘I certainly didn’t play with anyone like him,’ says England assistant coach Kevin Sinfield. ‘In terms of media attention I have played with guy like that before. Sam Tomkins got a lot in rugby league.

'They are very different characters and personalities, but Sam had to deal with some intensity and a lot of noise around him. He handled it really well. Henry is a breath of fresh air around the group. He is different. If we were all the same, it would be boring. I really like him. He is keen to learn.

'For all the bravado that comes with him, he is a lovely guy who wants to win, who wants to improve and he wants to be an England player. It is a different way of doing it and I have not seen it done before.

‘He was great at the weekend. To come off the bench and play on the wing for a large period of time, I thought he did very well.’

Pollock’s only previous England start was a disappointing defeat by Ireland when he and his team-mates struggled at the contact area. But he should have plenty of chances to wreak havoc against Japan, even if one of rugby’s greatest characters Jones is likely to have some tricks up his sleeve.

Pollock’s energy will be key to Borthwick’s men backing up the win over Australia. Changing two thirds of the team risks upsetting attacking cohesion. But Borthwick hopes the presence of back-line experience in George Ford, Henry Slade and Freddie Steward will allow Max Ojomoh and Will Joseph to excel at 12 and wing respectively.

'For all the bravado that comes with him, he is a lovely guy who wants to win, who wants to improve and he wants to be an England player,' says coach Kevin Sinfield of Pollock

‘Henry just needs to keep doing what he does well,’ Jason Robinson says. ‘I knew what I was strong at – and I did that. It was enough for me to go on and win a World Cup'

In the pack, even with a new front row, England should wield too much power for Japan. Their maul, buoyed by notable law changes, is set to be dominant. And that could help Pollock end with at least another try – perhaps this time as part of a pile of bodies from close range instead of galloping in from 20 metres-plus in the wide channels.

As a league convert, who was a union superstar in England’s most successful team, Robinson knows what it takes to be successful at the highest level and to be adaptable.

‘Henry just needs to keep doing what he does well,’ Robinson says. ‘Sometimes our sport tries to fit players into a mould of what they should be or do. When I switched from league to union, I was completely out of the mould. But I knew what I was strong at – and I did that. It was enough for me to go on and win a World Cup.

‘As an international rugby player, you’ve got to back yourself, play to your strengths, and enjoy yourself. Henry is smiling and he’s doing what’s being asked of him.

‘Where can the complaints be?'

Sports.title: Inside football's Christian revolution: The Premier League stars who say God has saved them from their darkest moments, stopped them diving to win penalties - and why some still face mockery and abuse for their faith
Sports.content:
When Borussia Dortmund star Felix Nmecha transferred an imaginary crown from his head onto the pitch last weekend, he probably wasn't expecting to spark a firestorm.

Arriving at the German national team camp two days later, he was summoned for a grilling by sporting director Rudi Voller and manager Jurgen Klopp. His symbol of surrender before God, a goal celebration called ‘The King’s Return’, had blown up into an international news story.

Voller, alongside many of Dortmund’s fans, was concerned by Nmecha's ties to Ballers in God, a network of Christian players founded in 2015 by former Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

While its core mission is to promote faith in Jesus, the evangelical group is believed to hold a conservative stance on issues such as sexuality and gender – a perspective Nmecha has been in hot water for promoting before.

Nmecha insisted that his message was one of love, but as his celebration was dissected worldwide, the furore posed more questions than it answered.
