Ghana News.title: After 26 years, the US has lost its measles elimination status
Ghana News.content:
Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore.

An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday.

The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy.

The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country.

To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients.

Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission.

In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026.

There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states.

It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said.

The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it.

“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated.

Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived.

In 2025 and 2026, however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection.

More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year.

Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC, and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports.

‘Measles is back’

The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore.

“This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.”

But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago.

Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said.

Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea.

If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk.

In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal.

All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination.

The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.”

“Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added.

Could the US regain its elimination status?

Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it.

Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978.

Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO.

In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission.

That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces.

Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status.

Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it.

“That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said.

“So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.”

Ghana News.title: Police begin rolling out TraffiTech-GH speed camera warning signs after Mahama directive
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Police Service and road safety agencies have commenced processes for the installation of large advance warning signboards across key road corridors to alert motorists to the presence of automated TraffiTech-GH speed cameras.

The move follows a direct call by President John Dramani Mahama for administrative transparency in the deployment of the automated traffic enforcement system, insisting that drivers must be given clear prior notice of camera locations.

Photographs from the exercise show police personnel and technical crews preparing and mounting large blue-and-yellow reflective gantries equipped with heavy lifting machinery.

In one of the photos, ACP Alexander Kwaku Obeng, Director of Education, Research and Training at the MTTD, was captured by some of the signs bearing a 50 m speed limit sign.

Some of the newly introduced billboards prominently feature a camera icon alongside a red-ringed "80" km/h speed limit sign. Bold inscriptions on the panels read: "24-hrs speed camera monitoring" and "Speed kills, kill it now".

Fulfilling the transparency mandate

The signage rollout directly addresses public concerns raised following the launch of the TraffiTech-GH initiative on November 1, 2026. Several commercial transport operators and private motorists had criticized the initial phase of the system, arguing that enforcing automated fines without visible warning signs amounted to entrapment.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, President Mahama backed the technology as vital to reducing pedestrian fatalities while directing the police and implementing partners to erect visible advance notices.

"All I will urge is that the police and those implementing TraffiTech should put signs showing where the cameras are, because that is one of the things you need to do if you are introducing this kind of innovation," President Mahama stated. "You need to put signposts warning motorists that there is a speed camera ahead. I think that transparency is important."

How the TraffiTech-GH system operates

Operated under the Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) of the Ghana Police Service, TraffiTech-GH uses fixed, mobile, and radar camera sensors to capture speeding violations in real time.

Once a vehicle exceeds the posted speed limit, the system automatically generates an Electronic Notice of Violation (ENV) and dispatches an SMS alert containing details of the infraction and statutory fine to the registered owner’s mobile phone.

Road safety officials have indicated that the ongoing installation of warning signs will be extended across major highways and urban arteries nationwide as authorities prepare to activate additional enforcement modules covering red-light jumping and illegal parking.

Ghana News.title: AU Commission chairperson pays courtesy call on President Mahama
Ghana News.content:
A high-level African Union (AU) Commission delegation led by Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf paid a courtesy call on President John Dramani Mahama, the incoming AU Chairperson, in Accra today.

Mr Youssouf welcomed the opportunity to discuss key continental issues with the President. The delegation pledged full support to President Mahama as he assumes the AU Chairmanship in January.

They recognised his leadership and significant contributions, especially his advocacy for reparative justice and commitment to reforming Africa's financial institutions.

The delegation expressed strong confidence that President Mahama's leadership would make a substantial positive impact on the AU and shape its future direction constructively.

A key topic was achieving financial self-reliance for the African Union. Citing ECOWAS as a successful model with a 0.5% levy to cover costs, President Mahama urged AU member states to fully implement the Union’s 0.2% levy on eligible imports.

"It’s not government money to the AU; it’s the people’s money. Government is only a collecting agency," President Mahama stated.

They thanked President Mahama for supporting the AU's efforts to achieve financial independence, especially through the proposed 0.2% levy on eligible imports to fund the Union's work.

President Mahama pledged to engage other African leaders to secure their full support for the levy’s implementation.

He briefed the delegation on the Accra Reset Initiative, which seeks to advance Africa's sovereignty and resilience by enhancing vaccine production, increasing access, and strengthening health systems across the continent.

He reiterated the need to address Africa's debt portfolio by exploring effective debt treatment approaches and creating sustainable mechanisms to manage the continent's debt burden.

The two leaders also discussed regional security and intra-African relations. Chairperson Youssouf commended President Mahama for his ongoing efforts to bridge divides between ECOWAS and the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).

He also praised President Mahama's leadership in advancing the AU's reparations agenda worldwide.

Ghana News.title: Image on new GH¢50 note is Theodosia Okoh, not her sister – BoG
Ghana News.content:
GH¢50 note

The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has dismissed concerns that the portrait of the late Mrs Theodosia Salome Okoh on the new GH¢50 Heritage Series banknote was taken from a photograph of her sister, Dr Letitia Obeng.

The central bank says the image was developed from different photographs of Mrs Okoh, the designer of Ghana’s national flag, but underwent artistic adjustments to meet the technical and security requirements of currency production.

In a statement issued on Friday, November 13, 2026, the bank said the changes made during the engraving process, including replacing Mrs Okoh’s familiar head tie with a hairstyle common during the period, had contributed to the differences in her appearance.

It acknowledged that the alterations had resulted in the portrait bearing a close resemblance to Dr Obeng, giving rise to public concerns over the identity of the woman depicted.

“The Bank confirms that the portrait was developed from different photographs of Mrs Okoh and not from a photograph of her sister, Dr Letitia Obeng,” the statement said.

The Bank said it appreciated the constructive engagement of the Okoh family and the public interest in preserving Ghana’s national heritage.

It maintained that the portrait was intended to recognise Mrs Okoh’s contribution to Ghana’s national identity and pledged to ensure that distinguished personalities featured on the country’s currency were represented with dignity and respect.

The clarification comes ahead of the introduction of the Heritage Series banknotes, which the Bank says will enter circulation on December 1, 2026.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: ICC stops probe into alleged crimes by US troops in Afghanistan
World.content:
Although unrelated, the decision follows Trump’s refusal to have the court prosecute American citizens.

Share ICC stops probe into alleged crimes by US troops in Afghanistan on social media

Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have issued a decision to halt the prosecutor’s investigations into alleged crimes by American troops in Afghanistan and instead to focus on the Taliban’s actions since 2021, according to court documents released on Friday.

The ICC’s ruling, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence”.

The decision follows feuds between the United States and the Hague-based ICC, notably after Washington sanctioned 13 current and former ICC staff members over the investigation into alleged crimes by US personnel and arrest warrants issued against Israeli officials.

It closes not only the line of inquiry into alleged crimes by US troops, which had lain dormant since 2021, but also the probe into the ISIL affiliate in Khorasan Province (ISKP).

The prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press and Reuters news agencies that it has already appealed the decision.

US threatens to dismantle ICC

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously said, “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans.”

In the October statement, Rubio also warned that “the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”

It is not clear if the court’s decision to stop the investigation will affect Washington’s stance on the ICC.

Regardless, the US is not a member of the court and does not recognise its jurisdiction.



The court’s founding statute says that it can prosecute anyone accused of atrocity crimes committed on the territory of ICC member states.

The ICC issued four arrest warrants for Taliban leaders last year.

The investigation in Afghanistan began in 2020, covering offences allegedly committed by Afghan government forces, the Taliban, American troops and US foreign intelligence operatives dating back to 2002.

In 2021, Karim Khan, the probe’s prosecutor, announced he would “deprioritise” the investigation into American forces, citing challenges in obtaining evidence.

Khan was ousted from the court over sexual misconduct allegations earlier this year.

World.title: FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next?
World.content:
The FAA says nationwide ground stop disrupting thousands of US flights was caused by a telecommunications outage.

Share FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next? on social media

FAA grounds all fights across the US over ‘telecommunication outage’

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop imposed on Friday that halted departing flights, an order it issued citing “extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety”.

The halt, which grounded thousands of flights across the country, was lifted on Friday evening.

This was the third nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

“Everybody’s safe,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, adding that this was not “another 9/11”.

Here is what we know:

What happened?

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54pm Eastern Time (20:54 GMT) on Friday due to a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres, which handle flights travelling across the country.

The FAA confirmed that the nationwide ground stop had been lifted.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said airspace reopened at 8:15pm ET (01:15 GMT on Saturday), after more than four hours of disruption.

“We’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said, warning that flights would not resume immediately.

“It’s going to be slow,” he added, urging passengers to check with their airlines.

Duffy said flights would resume depending on the availability of pilots and flight attendants, with authorities trying to get as many flights moving as possible on Friday night.

Aviation analytics firm Cirium said that after 4pm ET (21:00 GMT) on Friday, about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were still scheduled to depart from US airports.



By 7:05pm ET (00:05 GMT on Saturday), at least 827 flights had been diverted, according to Cirium. Of those, 670 returned to their departure airports, while 157 were diverted elsewhere.

Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop.

During the ground stop, international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis, with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.

How many flights were affected?

More than 4,700 flights were cancelled and 10,000 delayed on Friday, while another 700 had already been cancelled for Saturday, according to FlightRadar24.

Aviation analysts said it could take days for airlines to restore their schedules.

Reporting from Los Angeles international airport, Al Jazeera’s John Hendren spoke to passenger Nicholas Erdodi, who travelled from New Zealand and was trying to reach Chicago for a conference.

Erdodi said he had been travelling for 16 to 18 hours before spending another six hours at the airport, where passengers had been forced to leave their plane.

“The challenge is you cannot ask anyone here what to do,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Lack of information is what bothers me, I mean, and not to mention find the hotel for the night, not to mention all the cost.”

Erdodi said he had been rebooked but remained uncertain whether his next flight would depart.

“I work in tech, I understand what could be going on, but someone needs to tell us,” he said.

“It doesn’t matter if someone tells us that we don’t know what’s happening, but please just let us know what’s going on,” he added.

What does a nationwide ground stop mean?

A nationwide ground stop temporarily requires departing aircraft to remain on the ground until cleared to take off.

Flights in the air are generally allowed to continue to their destination, but new departures are on strict orders to stay grounded.

The measure is intended to stop any further aircraft from entering the airspace as the authorities deal with the safety issues.

What caused the FAA nationwide ground stop?

The FAA said the ground stop was caused by a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control systems.

Duffy said the outage was caused by switches and routers that became overloaded with data and went down, adding that the incident did not involve a total loss of communications or radar capabilities.

Todd Curtis, an aviation safety expert and chief executive of AirSafe.com, told Al Jazeera that the failures appeared to be concentrated in the country’s air route traffic control centres.



“There are 21 across the United States, one in Alaska and the other 20 in the lower 48,” he said.

“These are the folks who handle the aircraft that are transiting from one part of the country to the other, and they rely on multiple handoffs between controllers.”

Speaking before Duffy provided further details, Ron Bartsch, a professor of international aviation law at the University of the South Pacific, raised questions about the apparent failure of backup systems.

“The whole aviation community is based on redundancy,” he told Al Jazeera.

“So the fact that a redundant system hasn’t kicked in immediately just raises more questions than what we’ve seen answers to at this stage.”

Mullin said that there was no cyberattack linked to the nationwide ground stop and that the public was never in danger.

Duffy acknowledged that tens of thousands of travellers had been stranded and called for $50bn in upgrades to the nation’s air traffic control system.

When will US flights return to normal?

Duffy said it will “take us some time to get back to capacity”, but he expected operations to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving”.

The Thanksgiving travel period, which begins in less than two weeks, is usually one of the busiest times of the year for air travel in the US.

Aviation safety expert Curtis also warned that the disruption could continue affecting passengers even after the technical problems were resolved.

“If it’s fully resolved, it would take more than a day to get back to normal, to reschedule aircraft,” he told Al Jazeera.

He explained that many airlines operate interconnected networks, meaning passengers often have to change planes at major hubs.

“So there could be a bit of a hassle on the part of the airlines trying to figure out how to get everyone to where they have to go,” he said.

Passengers have been advised to check their flight status directly with their airlines, as delays and cancellations might continue.

World.title: Measles-associated deaths reach 10 in US after two more deaths reported
World.content:
Share Measles-associated deaths reach 10 in US after two more deaths reported on social media

Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have announced one additional measles-associated death in each state, marking 10 total deaths in the United States linked to the disease this year.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services reported an infant’s death on Friday, while the Pennsylvania Department of Health said that its latest death was an unvaccinated patient who had tested positive for measles.

Pennsylvania has logged seven measles-associated deaths, while Wisconsin has reported two. On November 2, New York state said a child had died in the state’s first recorded measles death in more than 30 years.

More than 5,400 confirmed measles cases have been recorded in the US to date, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Johns Hopkins University International Vaccine Access Center tracker.

The number of confirmed cases as of November 2026 is more than double the 2,289 confirmed cases reported in 2025.

The CDC recorded six measles-related deaths, according to figures on its website. The newly reported data is twice the deaths the agency recorded in 2025.

Dispute over death toll

The CDC’s national death toll is lower than the number of measles-related deaths reported by state officials.

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr asked CDC director Erica Schwartz not to count the deaths in the official tally, claiming there was no evidence they were measles-associated.

The federal count of measles reports has been at the centre of a dispute between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Kennedy over how measles deaths are classified.



Pennsylvania, the state hardest hit by the outbreak, reports “measles-associated” deaths after a person with confirmed measles dies within 30 days of developing symptoms, unless the death resulted from an unrelated event.

The CDC has said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to establish a standardised definition for measles deaths.

Infectious disease experts warn that the dispute over how to classify the deaths puts the CDC at odds with a longstanding approach to tracking the consequences of measles.

Epidemiologists have told Al Jazeera that tracking “measles-associated” deaths has long been a standard used by the World Health Organization and the CDC.

Measles elimination on the brink

Measles, a highly contagious virus, was officially declared eliminated in the US in 2000.

The outbreak comes as vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners has decreased from 95.2 percent during the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4 percent in the 2025-2026 school year.

Local and state health departments have ramped up vaccination efforts.

Measles is preventable through the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which offers approximately 97 percent protection after two doses.

As of Friday, Pennsylvania’s Department of Health has logged 1,542 confirmed cases this year, while Wisconsin recorded 651 cases.

As a result of the ongoing outbreak, the US could lose its measles elimination status this week. Elimination status requires that the country in question is able to squash instances of measles transmission for 12 months or more.

World.title: Tanker collision leaves riverboat passengers clinging to railings
World.content:
NewsFeed Tanker collision leaves riverboat passengers clinging to railings

Passengers and crew have been rescued after a tanker ship collided with a riverboat docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans. The collision partially submerged the riverboat, forcing passengers to cling to railings.

World.title: Former FAA official says ‘nobody really knows what is going on’
World.content:
Former FAA official says ‘nobody really knows what is going on’

NewsFeed Former FAA official says ‘nobody really knows what is going on’

Former FAA safety team representative Kyle Bailey says grounding flights is the safest course of action amid the nationwide communications failure, adding ‘nobody really knows what is going on’.

World.title: UK police open sex offence probe into comedian and author David Walliams
World.content:
The children’s author and comedian denies the sexual assault allegations, says he has not broken the law.

London’s police have opened an investigation into allegations of serious sexual offences after media reports accused British comedian and children’s author David Walliams of grooming and sexually abusing girls and young women.

Walliams, 55, denies the allegations.

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement on Friday that it “has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s”.

In the statement, Met Police Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney urged anyone affected to come forward.

The Met said the new allegations are separate from those reported this week by ITV News and The Guardian.

The two news organisations published reports on Tuesday that several women had accused Walliams of sexual misconduct, with the allegations dating back as far as 2003.

The reports came out a day after comedian Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for rape and sexual assault.

Multiple allegations

The Guardian and ITV said they spoke to more than 100 people during a three-year investigation.

One woman said Walliams sexually assaulted her at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them as teenagers. The reports also included allegations that he harassed young female colleagues.

In a letter to ITV and The Guardian, he said: “Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator … I have not broken the law.”



The investigative reports were published after he lost a High Court bid to block the media outlets from naming him.

The judge, Matthew Nicklin, said an injunction would be “an exceptionally serious interference” with the media’s rights.

Dropped by BBC, literary agency

A spokesperson for the BBC told the AFP news agency that it had taken down some shows involving Walliams, including all episodes of Little Britain, the comedy sketch show that made him famous.

His literary agency, Independent Talent Group, said it was “no longer representing him in any capacity”.

Walliams’s publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him last year, following accusations that he harassed female staff, which he had also denied.

Walliams rose to fame as a comedian with sketch shows Little Britain and Come Fly With Me. He was also a judge on ITV’s Britain’s Got Talent.

He penned children’s books that have reportedly sold more than 50 million copies, including Mr Stink, Gangsta Granny and The Boy in the Dress.

World.title: Here’s the latest.
World.content:
Pinned

The nationwide ground stop that brought all air travel to a halt across the country and stranded thousands of passengers has been canceled, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Within minutes of flight traffic being restored, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, took to a podium Friday night at the White House to decry Congress, accusing lawmakers of dragging their feet when it came to fully funding upgrades he warned were vital to prevent similar failures from happening again.

“It’s going to continue to fail,” Mr. Duffy told reporters, adding: “How many times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?”

Mr. Duffy added that the antiquated radar and telecoms systems that controllers rely on to transmit data and other information between facilities began to falter at 3:36 p.m. The aging system, which has undergone a number of upgrades, became overloaded, officials said.

Appearing alongside him, Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, stressed that there was never any indication that the communications failures had been triggered by a cyberattack, but he added, “we are still looking, and we’re not going to rule it out.” He emphasized that lives were never in danger.

But the incident appeared to inject new fuel into Mr. Duffy’s now monthslong campaign to secure at least $30 billion in extra funding for air traffic control modernization.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, funds Mr. Duffy has repeatedly referred to as a “down payment” when asking for tens of billions more. On Friday night, Mr. Duffy appeared to up the ante, telling reporters that he didn’t just want another $30 billion for the project, but another $50 billion. He argued that it should be delivered in emergency funding before the end of the year, after which control of Congress — and the budget — switches from Republicans to Democrats.

Some Democratic lawmakers have already raised questions about how efficiently and effectively the F.A.A. has spent the money they have been given thus far. But Mr. Duffy has long argued that his department cannot be expected to complete a meaningful overhaul of the nation’s air traffic control system without a massive influx of funding.

Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the third that the F.A.A. has issued this century. It ranks as the second-longest, after the ground stop issued on Sept. 11, 2001, in the wake of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center in New York. There was a shorter one on Jan. 11, 2023, because of an outage in the F.A.A.’s system to alert pilots to safety issues.

The order on Friday halted nearly all departures and stranded thousands of passengers at airports across the country. Hundreds of flights were diverted to other airports and more were canceled, even as some internationally bound flights managed to secure permission to take off. Amid the delays and cancellations, many passengers were taken off flights or told to go home.

More than 2 million people pass through airport security checkpoints on a typical day, according to Transportation Security Administration data. On Thursday, the agency screened nearly 2.5 million people. According to FlightRadar24, an aviation tracking site, there were more than 1,000 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports during the nationwide ground stop. According to the flight tracking app Flighty, there were more than 30,000 departures and arrivals scheduled for the remainder of the day.

Passengers waiting to take off Friday afternoon were stuck in limbo.

In the Denver airport, passengers were taken off their flights with their suitcases. A handful began rebooking travel for the next day. But most waited patiently for any kind of update. A Southwest flight attendant announced that the airline expected an update in 30 minutes.

Before the advisory was published, the F.A.A. halted flights to Chicago’s O’Hare and Midway airports, citing equipment problems, and reported equipment-related departure delays at Newark, Las Vegas, Teterboro, Orlando, Houston and Phoenix.

Here’s what else to know:

If your flight is canceled: You are entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled in the United States, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it. Here are other travel tips that might be helpful. Read more ›

A busy travel month: The ground stop happened about two weeks before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest times of the year for air travel. On average, U.S. airlines are expected to fly about 2.7 million passengers each day over the holiday period, according to industry trade group Airlines for America.

Handling the chaos: Radio transmissions between air traffic controllers and pilots at major airports offered a peek at how they navigated the ground stoppage. Read more ›

The last ground stop: The last nationwide ground stop came in the early morning of Jan. 11, 2023, and lasted around 90 minutes. The disruption came after a system to alert pilots of real-time dangers went down. Read more ›

Christine Chung , Niraj Chokshi , Luke Broadwater , Dustin Volz , Lisa Lerer and Robert Chiarito contributed reporting.

World.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
World.content:
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.

The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.

World.title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery
World.content:
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.

Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

World.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
World.content:
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.

Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.

"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.

"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.

"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.

"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."

The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".

He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.

Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.

"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."

World.title: Watch: How a server outage took down Microsoft Teams and Outlook
World.content:
A Microsoft outage is affecting services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot.

Microsoft has said the problem was caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers but that systems were now showing "early signs of stabilisation" as work continued on a fix.

The BBC's technology reporter Shiona McCallum explains what we know.

World.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
World.content:
The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.

It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean.

During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely."

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space.

The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead, it has splashed down in the ocean.

Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it is in space.

If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

World.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
World.content:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

World.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
World.content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.

Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

World.title: The Peruvian city that has embraced Pope Leo as one of its own
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.

The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.

The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.

"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago.

Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began.

"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.

World.title: Lagos thugs, London protesters and the chaos before the ballot, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
On Thursday, 12 November, two incidents with red flags for the 2027 elections emerged. In London, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan was detained in his car by a group of protesters. In Lagos, thugs invaded a meeting venue, where supporters of the National Democratic Party (NDC) gathered for a town hall.

The Lagos and London incidents are not the same, but together they portend an increasingly fraught electoral season. They are early indicators of where we are headed if nothing is done to arrest them. The grievance in London concerned duplicate entries, AI-generated photographs and fake polling units in INEC’s preliminary voters’ register. For this, the protesters circled Amupitan’s car and prevented him from leaving Chatham House, where he had gone to give a presentation. They got what they wanted: an election umpire embarrassed on a foreign stage.

The irony is that Amupitan had already conceded much of their case. On 9 November, he disclosed that the commission had removed 1,608,660 invalid registrations and identified 54 people across ten states for possible disciplinary action or prosecution. At Chatham House, he also acknowledged that transmission glitches in the 2023 elections had eroded trust in the commission.

I’d say that Amupitan’s candour deserves applause. But a commission that discovers more than 1.6 million invalid entries in its own register has handed its critics a case, and the distrust that follows does not stay confined to demonstrations outside think tanks. The danger is that when citizens doubt the count will be fair, some will conclude that the contest must be settled by other means. That is where London ends and Lagos begins.

The kind of political violence Lagos witnessed on Thursday has happened so often that it has become a motif of our existence in this country: an enduring injury, a simmering sadness, an ambient terror. As supporters of the NDC gathered for their town hall, thugs descended on them, destroying property and hunting down those in attendance. As long as this continues, the Nigeria of our dreams will remain a mirage.

We have been here before. The 2011 general elections produced one of the deadliest outbreaks of post-election violence in the country’s history. After Goodluck Jonathan defeated Muhammadu Buhari, who would later become president, rioting erupted across major northern cities. Machetes and guns were freely used, and reports put the toll at more than 200 killed and 40,000 displaced. In February 2023, Oyibo Chukwu, the Labour Party’s senatorial candidate in Enugu East, was killed when his convoy was attacked days before the national election.

The catalogue is lengthening. The African Centre for Security, Governance and Development counts 70 election-related attacks and 27 deaths so far in 2026. The Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room, drawing on the CLEEN Foundation’s threat assessment, also reports 27 deaths in the first ten months of the year and names campaign rallies and party offices as principal targets. The counts differ in method, but they agree on direction.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigerians, to their credit, still want to vote. A September survey by Yiaga Africa found that while 84 per cent of Nigerians of voting age are keen to vote in 2027, about 61 per cent worry about their safety because of the risk of election violence. That gap between wanting to vote and fearing to is the first real cost of normalised violence, and it is paid before a single ballot is cast.

The course can still be reversed, but only if we stop treating the thug as a freelance nuisance. Researchers who have studied Nigeria’s thug networks link them to elected officials, political financiers and armed groups. Thugs, in other words, have backers, and backers have names.

First, the state’s response must be firm and even-handed. It must go beyond the tired quarrel over whether a party obtained a permit for its rally, meeting or town hall. When campaign events become dangerous, turnout on election day falls, because voters who fear the rally will also fear the polling unit.

Second, the police must act before the violence, not after it. Those who profit from violence learn that it works, and what works escalates. Political actors are already testing their strategies for 2027, thugs included, and the police must sharpen their intelligence to anticipate them rather than merely count the casualties.

Third, accountability must reach the sponsor, not stop at the implementers. Every election season, a handful of young men are paraded before cameras while the men who paid them return to their campaign councils untouched. The National Assembly has toyed for years with an electoral offences commission and has never found the urgency to establish one. Until those behind the violence answers in court for the mayhem the bankrolled, violence will remain what it has long been in our politics: a cheap and dependable campaign expense.

Fourth, INEC must win back the argument the London protesters won. Removing 1.6 million invalid entries is a beginning; publishing the cleaned register in a form that citizens and parties can audit, polling unit by polling unit, is the end. Trust does not return through press conferences. It returns when voters can check for themselves that the ghosts are gone and the phantom polling units have been struck off.

The two incidents of November 12 must be read together because they feed each other. A register that cannot be trusted makes violence look rational to the desperate; violence that goes unpunished makes a clean register irrelevant to the frightened. Break either link and the cycle weakens. Leave both intact, and 2027 may be settled by those other means, long before INEC announces a single result.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving global businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: A democratic landslide is not a blank cheque, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
The 2018 United States Senate election in Texas, held on 6 November, was quite remarkable. For the first time in several years, the race did not look like a straightforward Republican victory. Incumbent Senator Ted Cruz faced a formidable challenge from a Democratic congressman representing Texas’s 16th Congressional District. His name was Robert Francis O’Rourke, popularly known as Beto O’Rourke. In the end, Cruz prevailed, but by just 215,000 votes, or 2.6 percentage points. Beto’s performance was extraordinary for a Democrat challenging an incumbent in a deeply Republican state like Texas.

Yet, despite Beto’s spectacular performance, the outcome was deeply disappointing to many Democrats who believed that nobody else stood a better chance of turning such a reliably red state blue. Beto was the ideal candidate, and if anyone stood a chance, it had to be him. Young, charismatic and bilingual, he ran a campaign built around a statewide strategy and a message of inclusion. Though of Irish-American ancestry, he was born and raised in El Paso, Texas, a predominantly Hispanic border city. In other words, he was a white man with considerable appeal to Hispanic voters, one of the most important voting demographics in Texas. Yet he still lost.

Fast-forward to 2026, and we have another Senate race. This time, the contest was between Republican candidate Ken Paxton, the former Texas attorney general, and Democrat James Talarico, a relatively lesser-known politician serving in the Texas House of Representatives. Paxton was a deeply controversial candidate, dogged by considerable personal and political baggage, including his highly publicised marital infidelity and legal troubles. Even some Republicans considered Talarico the stronger candidate. But then, this is Texas, and Democrats were understandably reluctant to get their hopes up. That was until the midterm election results began trickling in.

American politics has just witnessed an extraordinary electoral earthquake. The 2026 midterm elections will be remembered as one of the most consequential political reversals in recent American history. Democrats have not only reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress but have also made remarkable inroads into territories that, until recently, appeared safely beyond their reach.

James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, and Annie Andrews in South Carolina are three Democratic candidates who prevailed in states long associated with Republican political dominance. Their victories, alongside four other Republican-held Senate seats that Democrats flipped, represent a stunning repudiation of the Republican establishment. In the House, according to CBS News, Democrats have flipped 43 congressional districts, with several victories coming in territory that Donald Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, hardly an admirer of the Democratic Party, described the Republican losses as close to an extinction-level event for his party.

The scale of this victory deserves acknowledgment. It is historic and, in several respects, extraordinary. Democrats made these gains against the backdrop of contentious battles over voting rights and access to the ballot, including Republican-led efforts to tighten election rules that critics argue disproportionately burden minority voters.

In the years that followed, thousands of polling places closed in jurisdictions previously subject to federal oversight, raising concerns about access to the ballot, particularly in some Black and Latino communities. Yet, as remarkable as this Democratic victory is, the party must not mistake an electoral repudiation of its opponents for an unconditional endorsement of its own agenda. The challenge now is to govern wisely, remain focused on the concerns of ordinary Americans and resist the temptation to overplay its hand.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

An electoral victory is not necessarily an endorsement of every policy position, ideological conviction or political ambition of the winning party. Sometimes, voters are not voting enthusiastically for one party so much as they are voting decisively against another. There is an important distinction here, and Democrats would be wise not to lose sight of it.

The immediate temptation, particularly among the more enthusiastic elements of the party, will be to turn this victory into an opportunity for political retribution. Already, there are renewed calls for the impeachment of Donald Trump. I understand the sentiment. There is certainly no shortage of reasons his political opponents might want to hold him accountable. However, at some point, political emotions must give way to realpolitik.

The question is not simply whether Trump deserves impeachment. It is whether pursuing impeachment is the most consequential use of the political capital Democrats have just acquired.

The House can impeach a president with a simple majority. Removal, however, requires conviction by a two-thirds majority of senators present. With all 100 senators voting, that means 67 votes. Even with control of the Senate, Democrats are nowhere near that threshold. I would wager that very few, if any, Republican senators would be willing to cross party lines to vote for Trump’s conviction.

There is another complication Democrats should not underestimate. Their congressional majority will not necessarily translate into a unified voting bloc. Some of the Democrats who have just won in deeply conservative states and Republican-leaning districts will have little appetite for participating in what their constituents might perceive as a partisan crusade against Trump. They know that Trump retains considerable loyalty among his political base, and they will be reluctant to jeopardise their own political futures by taking positions that could alienate the very voters who sent them to Washington.

This is the uncomfortable reality of American politics. A Democratic representative from a deeply conservative district does not suddenly become a progressive crusader simply because the Democratic Party has won control of Congress. These lawmakers have their own political survival to consider. They may agree with their party on oversight, healthcare, infrastructure and economic policy while disagreeing on impeachment or other highly polarizing questions.

Democrats should therefore resist the temptation to spend their newly acquired political capital on symbolic battles that have little prospect of producing meaningful outcomes. We have seen this movie before, not once but twice. Impeachment proceedings that culminate in acquittal may satisfy the party’s most ardent supporters, but they risk becoming another expensive political spectacle that distracts from more consequential fights. There are far more pressing matters demanding attention.
