Americans are struggling with the cost of living. Inflation has significantly eroded household purchasing power. Grocery bills remain painfully high, and fuel prices have become another source of economic anxiety, further aggravated by the war involving Iran. For millions of ordinary Americans, the question of whether they can afford groceries, pay their mortgages, maintain their health insurance and put something aside for retirement is considerably more immediate than the political fate of Donald Trump.

Democrats must understand that their victory is an opportunity to reconnect with these ordinary economic anxieties, not an invitation to lose themselves in Washington’s familiar political theatrics.

Indeed, the party needs an honest postmortem of its own. How did Democrats lose the confidence of enough Americans to allow a politician with Trump’s baggage to return to the White House? That question deserves more than convenient explanations about misinformation, racism or the gullibility of voters. Democrats must be willing to examine their own failures.

Immigration is a particularly important example. The party handled the issue poorly, and pretending otherwise would be a mistake. While many Americans are deeply uncomfortable with the manner in which some immigration enforcement operations are conducted by ICE, that discomfort should not be mistaken for opposition to immigration enforcement itself.

Americans want an orderly and secure border. They want immigration laws enforced. They do not want a return to the perception, during the Biden administration, that the southern border was overwhelmed and that the federal government had lost control of the situation. At the same time, they expect immigration enforcement to be conducted humanely, lawfully and with respect for due process.

These positions are not mutually exclusive. A country can enforce its immigration laws without abandoning its humanitarian obligations. Democrats must learn to articulate that distinction convincingly rather than allow Republicans to monopolise the language of border security.

There is also a broader question about the party’s political priorities. Democrats have sometimes given the impression that their most visible political preoccupations revolve around cultural and identity issues, including LGBTQ rights, while the economic struggles of ordinary working families receive comparatively less attention.

To be clear, protecting minority rights, defending individual liberties and ensuring equal treatment under the law are legitimate responsibilities of government. They should never be abandoned for political convenience. But there is a difference between defending fundamental rights and allowing cultural controversies to dominate the party’s political identity.

The economic circumstances of ordinary Americans must be at the centre of a Democratic legislative agenda. People want affordable healthcare, decent-paying jobs, lower housing costs, affordable education and an economy in which hard work offers a reasonable prospect of upward mobility. These are the issues that should define the party’s priorities.

Then there is the judiciary, perhaps the most formidable obstacle to the Democrats’ ability to exercise meaningful oversight of the Trump administration.

The United States Supreme Court currently has a 6–3 conservative majority. This is not an inconsequential detail. The Court has become an increasingly consequential player in the country’s political and constitutional disputes, and its ideological composition will matter enormously as the legislative and executive branches collide over the next two years. Ideally, the Court should have a more balanced ideological composition, one that encourages deliberation and makes it necessary to persuade members across ideological lines.

Unfortunately, that is not the case, and it will undoubtedly work against Democrats in certain disputes. The principle of checks and balances is weakened when one institution becomes so ideologically predictable that litigants can reasonably anticipate how a substantial category of politically consequential cases will be decided.

I fully expect significant litigation between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled Congress. Questions surrounding executive authority, immigration, presidential powers, federal spending and congressional oversight will almost certainly find their way into the courts. Ultimately, many of these disputes could end up before a Supreme Court whose conservative majority may be more receptive to the administration’s legal arguments.

That does not mean every conservative justice will automatically side with Trump. The Court has its own institutional interests and constitutional responsibilities. But Democrats should be under no illusion that winning Congress automatically gives them control over the broader machinery of government. This is precisely why strategic thinking matters.

Democrats have a historic opportunity to demonstrate that they can govern differently. They can use congressional oversight to expose wrongdoing, insist on accountability, scrutinise executive actions and challenge policies they consider unlawful. They can legislate on matters that directly improve the lives of Americans. They can also demonstrate that responsible government is not synonymous with political vengeance.

Most importantly, they must recognise that the voters who made this victory possible are not necessarily signing up for an ideological revolution. Many are simply exhausted by the chaos, economic uncertainty and political dysfunction that have characterised recent years.

The 2026 midterms were a powerful rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party. But they were not a blank cheque for Democrats to pursue every item on their ideological wish list. Nor should the party mistake the temporary collapse of Republican electoral fortunes for a permanent realignment of American political loyalties.

Republicans have been given a serious warning. Democrats have been handed an extraordinary opportunity. What they do with it will determine whether this election becomes the beginning of a durable political realignment or merely another temporary swing of the American political pendulum.

The Democrats have won the battle. Now comes the harder task of governing wisely enough to deserve the victory.

Osmund Agbo is a medical doctor, author, and the 2026 recipient of the Thabo Mbeki Prize for Scholarship and Public Service.

World.title: Towards a resilient Pan-Africanism: Tackling the scourge of Afrophobia, By Yusuf Tuggar
World.content:
These are but a very few of the reasons why Nigerians cannot fathom why they and other Black Africans are being targeted in South Africa. Call it Afrophobia, which may be better description than Xenophobia (as non-black Africans appear to be exempted) or the more euphemistic framing – anti-migration protests, it is wrong and must be condemned. It is also ill-timed, coming at a period when Nigeria’s foreign policy agenda of Strategic Autonomy precisely relies on Diaspora and robustness in assuring the dignity of Nigerian’s abroad as one of its 4D pillars. Yet at the same time, it is important to understand what exactly is going on in South Africa and put it into context.

The President of the Bridge Club, my dear friend and brother, Abdulhakeem Mustapha (SAN), members of the Executive Committee of The Bridge Club, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, I wish to begin by expressing how honoured I am to be invited to serve as chairman of this occasion by such an esteemed body of professionals and business leaders. Quite often in Africa, we make the mistake of failing to tap the experience of former office holders; the moment you depart, it’s out of sight, out of mind. Or worse, you become anathema for the simple crime of no longer having an official designation.

However, many of the polities that we look up to have devised ways of embracing and transiting public office

holders into think tanks (whether affiliated to political parties or standalone), to share and benefit from their experiences in policy conception and implementation. Therein lies one of the ways we can improve on putting theory into praxis. I therefore commend the Bridge Club for showing the path in this regard.

I would like to equally thank the Bridge Club for choosing the all-important topic of Xenophobia and Pan-Africanism as the theme of this year’s grand event. Who better to interrogate this subject than the erudite and peripatetic Professor PLO Lumumba? Africa is proud of you Prof. And my sister and former colleague in the Nigerian legislature, the Right Honourable Abike Dabiri-Erewa, who through sheer grit and determination, has built the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NIDCOM) into a globally recognised agency championing the dignity of Nigerians abroad. We are equally proud of you, chair and thank you for your service to the nation.

I belong to a generation of Nigerians whose worldview was shaped by the struggle against apartheid and the liberation of Africa from racist regimes. In secondary school, we had Mine Boy, Tell Freedom and Cry the Beloved Country as literature textbooks. Following the Soweto massacre in June 1976, many of us lived with its victims in our boarding schools and shared first-hand experiences, after Nigeria adopted them as its own, with full scholarships. This gesture extended to Namibians, Angolans and others under the yoke of oppression. A singular act of kindness by Mrs Maude Obanye (wife of a Nigerian diplomat) in donating money to the Soweto victims, set off a deluge that became the South African Relief Fund, which Nigerians competed to contribute to.

Our Ambassador Leslie Harriman of blessed memory chaired the United Nations Committee Against Apartheid and we hosted the World Conference Against Apartheid that framed it as a threat against international peace and security, and made it a global imperative. We did this at a time when we were financially constrained,

due to a slump in oil prices in 1976. And leading by example, Nigeria as the host, nationalised Barclays Bank and British Petroleum, at great risk of offending some of our Western partners. Again, this was a time when policy conception and implementation benefited from the intellectual heft of our think tanks and past and present public office holders; the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA), the Nigerian Institute of Social and Economic Research (NISER), among others, were tasked with scenario-building to weigh the pros and cons of such a course of action.

Theory was successfully put into praxis. These are but a very few of the reasons why Nigerians cannot fathom why they and other Black Africans are being targeted in South Africa. Call it Afrophobia, which may be better description than Xenophobia (as non-black Africans appear to be exempted) or the more euphemistic framing – anti-migration protests, it is wrong and must be condemned. It is also ill-timed, coming at a period when Nigeria’s foreign policy agenda of Strategic Autonomy precisely relies on Diaspora and robustness in assuring the dignity of Nigerian’s abroad as one of its 4D pillars. Yet at the same time, it is important to understand what exactly is going on in South Africa and put it into context.

First, there are endogenous factors at play. Those who laid the foundations of Apartheid were very intelligent individuals, strategic thinkers, whose influence continues to be felt globally. It began with the systemic creativity of Lord Frederick Lugard, a name well known to Nigerians and Ugandans. Lugard birthed cultural segregation to answer the native question – how a few thousand colonial officers and settlers can rule over millions. The black populace was kept separate along tribal lines. The concept of the Sabo and Sabon Gari was so effective, such that Mallam Ibrahim Gusau (later to become Nigeria’s First Republic minister of agriculture) was arrested and sanctioned by the colonial authorities for mingling with his Igbo and Yoruba compatriots in Sabon Gari. Worst of all, he was found to be in possession of Nnamdi Azikiwe’s ‘seditious’ West African Pilot newspaper.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Jan Smuts improved on this system to become the father of institutional segregation. By all accounts a very clever man, Smuts was one of the authors of the League of Nations Charter and chancellor of the University of Cambridge to boot. By the time it got to PW Botha’s Constellation of States, Apartheid was dividing South

Africans not just by race, but also by class and economics. The Homelands made everyone a foreigner from within and without. So, you can see, it was a segregation spectrum with varying degrees from Lugard to Botha, from Nigeria to South Africa, that has left a long-lasting psychological scar. It therefore brings South African exceptionalism into question, in this regard. And context is not justification.

Nigerian thinkers and scholars helped chart a course for dealing with the colonial trauma. Professor Kenneth Dike revolutionised historiography by proving the empiricism of the oral tradition and other methods of studying African history. He disproved Hegel’s declaration that Africa had no history or was ‘unhistorical’ prior to contact with enlightened outsiders. Such theoretical constructions provided the scaffolding for colonisation and ultimately for apartheid and its deep-seated scarring. Dike’s Africanist history developed

offshoots and spread across the continent from its Ibadan roots. We require such rigour and intellectual heft to tackle the Camp of The Saint’s level anti-migrant fear that exists well beyond South Africa.

Which brings me to the second part of today’s discussion – Pan-Africanism as a thesis, if Afrophobia is antithetical. Ironically, South Africa was expected to be to Africa what Japan was to Asia. In the 1970s and 80s, Japan was considered the challenger to the US’ global economic supremacy and ended up attracting punitive tariffs. Japan responded by diversifying its manufacturing base into other Asian countries. For instance, Mitsubishi set up textile manufacturing in Bangladesh. The net effect was a flying geese effect, with Japan diversifying and leading other Asian countries or tigers into manufacturing and development.

South Africa, with its advanced manufacturing base was well positioned to do that for Africa, but it missed the opportunity because of Apartheid. Here again, we had an era in which great minds like Adebayo Adedeji and Malawi’s Thandika Mkandariwe emphasised the need for manufacturing finished goods and market integration as the path to decolonisation and development. Instead, most African countries chose the Bretton Woods prescriptions of the Berg Report and the rabbit hole of the Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) that sought to discourage the global South from manufacturing and instead resign them to being net exporters of raw materials and agricultural products.

They understood that Africa could not develop without manufacturing finished goods and integrating its markets. Adedeji came up with the concept of the African Economic Community (AEC), the precursor to today’s African Continental Free Trade Area (AFCFTA). Beyond the advantage of manufacturing finished goods to improve terms of trade (otherwise more cashew nuts would be exchanged for the same tractor as societies

gentrify and increase their demand for manufactured goods), Mkandariwe reminded us that trade also includes selling things to acquire technology.

So, there are three ironies today: 1. The path to Pan-Africanism is through the continental free trade area. 2. As the father of capitalism Adam Smith once opined, “the free circulation of labour is the foundation of any free trade system.” 3. The AfCFTA is headed by a South African.

In closing, we have to also look at exogenous factors at play. Who funds March & March and Operation Dudala? Are the online hashtags that are serving as rallying points for anti-migrant sentiments organic or engendered from outside South Africa? South Africa was accused of racism towards white farmers when Nigeria was accused of the persecution of Christians. Are these a coincidence? The partnership of Nigeria and South Africa is too important for the continent’s future. When we worked together, we created NEPAD. And let us not forget that even in recent times, South Africa used its 2025 Presidency of the G20 to support Nigeria’s efforts towards joining the group. South Africa designated Abuja as the host of the Africa Outreach Meeting on Industry and Agriculture in November 2025.

I eagerly await Professor Lumumba’s keynote address.

Yusuf Maitama Tuggar was until recently Nigeria’s Foreign Affairs minister.

This is the text of remarks made as the Chairman of the Bridge Club’s 2026 Grand end-of-year event with the theme of xenophobia and Pan-Africanism.

World.title: Zamfara stands still as Gov Lawal hosts First Lady, Remi Tinubu for mega rally
World.content:
The First Lady of Nigeria, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, received a rousing welcome from thousands of residents and supporters during her visit to Zamfara State.

On Tuesday, the Zamfara State Government hosted the APC North-West Women’s Mega Rally and Empowerment Programme at the Trade Fair Complex in Gusau.

The event, led by Zamfara First Lady Huriyya Dauda Lawal, brought together former Zamfara governors, the first ladies of the North-West, ministers and other key All Progressives Congress stakeholders.

Before the rally, Senator Tinubu met with the Zamfara State traditional rulers to seek their blessings.

In her remarks, Mrs Tinubu described her visit as a powerful expression of solidarity and compassion, as well as a commitment to women’s welfare and advancement, especially for those facing insecurity, poverty and limited economic opportunities.

She said, “This is the happiest day of my life. Except for Zamfara, I have been in all 36 states of Nigeria, including the FCT. I have always wanted to come to Zamfara, and today I have fulfilled that. Because it is now easy to come, this is just the beginning; I am coming back again. Mr President is also coming.

“Before I start, I want to commiserate with you all for all the lives that were lost; they are very precious to us. May God forgive them, grant them Al-Jannatul Firdaus, and continue to be with us.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Today is Juma’at; we have to be fast; we have empowerment to give to women. This is the only party that empowers during the campaign, and it is not about the campaign; we have been empowering from day one. And that is why it is not politics.

“Earlier, I was also given a title in Zamfara, the ‘Jagaban Matan Arewa’ by the Chairman of the Zamfara State Council of Chiefs and Emir of Anka, Alhaji Attahiru Muhammad Ahmad. I thanked all the Emirs.

“I love Zamfara. I am happy to be here. Mr President said I should tell you he will continue working for you. Nigeria will continue to prosper, in sha Allah.”

Earlier, Governor Dauda Lawal thanked Senator Tinubu for her continued support through the Renewed Hope Initiative, including its Food Outreach Programme.

“Your Excellency, Mother of the Nation, your presence today represents more than an official visit. You have set a record in the history of our dear Zamfara State.

“Your Excellency, Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, in Zamfara State, we firmly believe that empowering women is not only our responsibility as a government; it is a needed and bankable investment in social and societal morality, economic prosperity, family stability, and sustainable peace.

“I assure Your Excellency that Zamfara’s government and people unwaveringly support Mr President’s second term. With the women here and the men supporting them, Zamfara and the North West will deliver for Mr President come January 2027.”

World.title: Finance must break developing countries from ‘debt and disaster’ loop – UN climate chief
World.content:
The executive secretary of UN Climate Change, Simon Stiell, told the ministers at COP31 that climate finance must be redesigned to lift developing countries out of a cycle of debt and disaster, adding that meeting a headline figure will not do it.

“Meeting a financial target does not always meet countries’ needs. To do that, we need to look at how finance is delivered,” Mr Stiell said on Friday at the opening of a high-level ministerial dialogue on climate finance in Antalya, Turkey.

Countries agreed at COP29 that developed nations would lead in providing $300 billion a year by 2035, as part of a wider effort to raise $1.3 trillion annually from all sources.

Mr Stiell said the roadmap for reaching those sums “must become reality”, but that the terms of the money mattered as much as the amount.

“Many developing countries are trapped in a downward loop of debt, disaster, and devastating capital costs,” he said. “The threat of floods, fires, storms and droughts hangs over them, pushing up the price of borrowing even before disaster strikes.”

He stated that the terms of finance should reflect each country’s debt position.

“Private finance, loans and guarantees are essential to achieving our collective goals. But grant-based and highly concessional finance will remain critical, particularly for Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States and other very vulnerable economies,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, broader action on debt is also needed to prevent countries from being forced to choose between repayments and resilience.

International climate finance for developing countries reached about $137 billion in 2024, and almost 70 per cent of it came in the form of loans, according to a UN Women flagship report released on Tuesday in Antalya.

Countries in sub-Saharan Africa paid more than twice as much in external debt service between 2021 and 2023 as they received in climate finance, according to an analysis published by the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

The analysis found that interest payments consumed more than 10 per cent of government revenue in 27 African countries in 2024.

The chair of the African Group of Negotiators, Nana Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, has said that a transition could not be called just if poorer countries have to “mortgage their futures” to pay for it.

The group lost a bid on Monday for a separate agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. It now wants the target prioritised in the summit’s cover decision.

Nigeria is not on the UN’s list of least developed countries, which places it among the states the UN climate chief expects to rely more on loans, guarantees and private capital.

It needs about $337 billion between 2026 and 2035 to implement its climate commitments, according to the National Council on Climate Change.

Omotenioye Majekodunmi, the agency’s director-general, said more than 80 per cent of that will have to come from private investment, commercial debt, and international carbon finance.

About $2.5 billion a year went to climate action in Nigeria in 2021 and 2022, counting domestic and international sources, according to the Climate Policy Initiative’s tracking.

The dialogue was the last in a series that began in 2013, and its conclusions will go to COP32 in Ethiopia next year, Mr Stiell said.

World.title: North accounts for most of Nigeria’s recorded maternal deaths – Report
World.content:
Women in northern Nigeria continue to bear a disproportionate burden of maternal deaths, with the Northwest and Northeast geopolitical zones accounting for about three-quarters of reported fatalities in health facilities, according to the 2026 Joint Annual Review (JAR) Statistical Book.

The report also highlights significant disparities in maternal health outcomes between rural and urban areas, with rural women recording a maternal mortality ratio of 656 deaths per 100,000 live births, compared with 444 deaths per 100,000 live births in urban areas.

Produced by the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the report reviews the third year of implementation of the Health Sector Strategic Blueprint. It was presented at the third Nigeria Health Sector Joint Annual Review in Abuja on 10 November.

The findings highlight persistent inequalities in maternal healthcare access and outcomes, despite a reported decline in maternal deaths across health facilities nationally.

According to the report, Nigeria recorded thousands of maternal deaths in health facilities between January and September 2026, although the figures represent only deaths captured by the facility reporting system.

The ministry acknowledged that the figures could be underreported or overreported but described the data as reliable for monitoring trends in the health sector.

Maternal mortality remains high

Maternal mortality refers to the death of a woman during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days of the termination of pregnancy from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Most maternal deaths are preventable through timely access to quality antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric services and appropriate postnatal care.

Despite the reported improvements, Nigeria’s maternal mortality ratio remains a major public health concern.

The JAR Statistical Book puts the country’s maternal mortality ratio at 572 deaths per 100,000 live births, significantly above the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of fewer than 70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030.

The burden is particularly concerning given Nigeria’s contribution to global maternal deaths.

In its 2023 report, titled “Improving Maternal and Newborn Health and Survival and Reducing Stillbirths: Progress Report 2023”, the World Health Organisation (WHO) estimated that Nigeria recorded 82,000 maternal deaths, 181,000 stillbirths and 277,000 neonatal deaths in 2020.

The combined 540,000 deaths accounted for 12 per cent of global maternal, stillbirth and neonatal deaths, despite Nigeria contributing only six per cent of global live births.

The report ranked Nigeria second after India among countries with the highest combined burden of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths.

Reported maternal deaths decline

The JAR data indicate a downward trend in facility-reported maternal deaths over the review period.

The country recorded 5,391 maternal deaths in health facilities in 2024, compared with 4,455 in 2025.

The figure declined further in 2026, although the exact total requires confirmation against the final statistical table. The quarterly data also indicate improvements.

Following a peak in the second quarter of 2024, maternal deaths and the maternal mortality ratio generally declined. By the third quarter of 2026, the maternal mortality ratio had fallen to 128 deaths per 100,000 live births, representing a reduction of about 46 per cent from the earlier peak.

Maternal deaths during the same period also declined by approximately 40 per cent to 947.

However, these improvements have not been evenly distributed across the country.

Northern states bear the burden

According to the report, maternal deaths over the past three years were heavily concentrated in the Northwest and Northeast geopolitical zones.

By 2026, the two zones together accounted for approximately three-quarters of all documented maternal deaths in health facilities.

The five northern states with the highest maternal mortality burden were Kano, Borno, Jigawa, Yobe and Katsina.

While the national figures showed a downward trend, maternal deaths reportedly increased across the two northern zones, contrasting with reductions recorded in southern parts of the country.

In most southern states, fewer than 50 maternal deaths were reported. The states with the lowest recorded numbers included Osun (four deaths), Abia (five), Enugu (eight), Ekiti (nine), and Bayelsa (nine).

Maternal morbidity

Beyond deaths, the report also highlights the burden of maternal morbidity, including complications that can have lasting effects on women’s health, wellbeing and livelihoods. In 2026, approximately 3,060 women were diagnosed with vesicovaginal fistula (VVF), compared with 4,350 in 2025.

VVF is an abnormal opening between the bladder and vagina that can result in continuous, involuntary leakage of urine, often following prolonged or obstructed labour.

Of the women diagnosed in 2026, 1,737 underwent surgical repair, representing 56.8 per cent of those diagnosed. This was lower than in 2025, when 2,564 women (59 per cent) underwent repairs.

The Northwest and Northeast again recorded the highest burden, with 1,420 and 982 cases, respectively, in 2026. The figures underscore the need to strengthen access to emergency obstetric care, timely referrals and surgical treatment, particularly in underserved communities.

World.title: COP31: White paper urges governments to invest in water-based energy storage
World.content:
A new international white paper launched at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, has urged governments to prioritise pumped-storage hydropower as strategic infrastructure to strengthen energy security and support the expansion of renewable electricity.

The paper, developed with input from more than 60 governments and international agencies through the Global Alliance for Pumped Storage (GAPS), outlines seven policy recommendations for accelerating investment in the technology, which can store electricity for extended periods and release it when demand increases.

It was presented at a high-level roundtable organised by GAPS, as countries consider how to strengthen electricity systems amid growing energy demand and the expansion of renewable energy.

Pumped-storage hydropower uses surplus electricity to pump water from a lower reservoir to an upper reservoir. When electricity demand rises, the system releases stored water through turbines to generate electricity.

Unlike conventional battery technologies, the system can store large amounts of energy for extended periods, while also providing services that help maintain electricity grid stability.

The white paper argues that the technology could help countries reduce dependence on imported energy resources and strengthen domestic energy systems because it relies primarily on water, suitable geographical locations, and local labour, rather than imported or processed critical minerals.

It also notes that projects can be developed using existing reservoirs, lakes, hydropower infrastructure and former mining sites.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Seven recommendations for governments

The paper identifies seven priority areas for governments seeking to accelerate pumped-storage development.

These include assessing national energy-storage needs and incorporating them into electricity planning, recognising pumped storage as strategic national security infrastructure and establishing clear legal definitions for energy storage.

It also recommends identifying and preparing suitable sites, simplifying permitting and licensing procedures, creating an enabling investment environment and ensuring that pumped-storage operators are adequately remunerated for the services they provide to electricity systems.

According to the paper, significant upfront investment, lengthy development timelines and site-specific preparation requirements have continued to limit the development of pumped-storage projects despite their established capabilities.

It argues that governments must create the necessary policy, regulatory and market conditions to attract investment while ensuring that projects meet environmental and social sustainability standards.

Energy security, renewable expansion

The launch comes amid efforts to expand electricity access and increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption.

Under the COP31 Global Electrification Pledge, countries are seeking to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption from about 23 per cent currently to 35 per cent by 2035.

Achieving this target will require electricity systems that can accommodate growing renewable energy generation while maintaining a reliable supply, the paper states.

It identifies pumped storage as one of the established technologies that can provide long-duration energy storage alongside other grid services, including frequency and voltage control, operating reserves, and black-start capabilities, which allow electricity systems to restart after a major outage.

President of the International Hydropower Association (IHA), Malcolm Turnbull, said countries seeking greater energy security and faster electrification could not afford to overlook the infrastructure required to support reliable electricity systems.

Mr Turnbull said pumped storage represented a long-term investment in national energy security and sovereignty, adding that the white paper provided governments with recommendations to translate the technology’s potential into projects, investment and more resilient electricity systems.

“As countries seek to become energy secure and accelerate electrification, we cannot afford to overlook the infrastructure that makes these systems work,” he said.

The paper also highlights the potential economic benefits of pumped-storage projects, including employment opportunities through domestic resources and local labour.

It argues that their long operational lifespans could make them important infrastructure investments for countries seeking to strengthen their electricity systems over generations.

World.title: Prophet who claimed he could resurrect Toluwanisings remanded
World.content:
A court has remanded a self-styled prophet, Moses Idowu, following allegations that he filmed the remains of gospel singer Olayemi “Toluwanisings” Bolaji while claiming he could resurrect him.

The Oyo State Police Command also arraigned content creator Oladapo Dunminimnun in a separate case over videos containing unsubstantiated allegations about the singer’s death and members of his family.

The command’s spokesperson, Ayanlade Olayinka, disclosed the developments in a statement on Friday. He said the two defendants were arraigned before courts of competent jurisdiction over separate publications linked to the controversy that followed Toluwanisings’ death.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the gospel singer slumped and died at his Ibadan residence in October. His death subsequently triggered disagreements among his relatives, wife and associates over the circumstances surrounding it and where he should be buried.

The dispute intensified after his paternal family opposed plans by his wife, Elizabeth, and some associates to bury him in a cemetery. Following police intervention, the parties reached an agreement, and the singer was buried at his residence on 9 November.

Alleged resurrection attempt

Mr Olayinka said Mr Idowu visited the morgue where Toluwanisings’ body was kept and claimed to possess the spiritual power to resurrect the dead.

During the visit, the police alleged he recorded the singer’s remains and circulated the footage on social media without obtaining permission from the family.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“In the course of the incident, the suspect recorded a video of the deceased’s body and subsequently circulated the footage on social media without the consent or authorisation of the deceased’s family, thereby subjecting the remains to indignity and causing further distress to the bereaved family,” the police spokesperson said.

The police further accused Mr Idowu of publishing claims that implicated the singer’s widow and personal assistant, Babadunmi Gbolabo, in his death without providing evidence.

He was consequently arraigned on four counts relating to the alleged unlawful recording and publication of false information, publication of defamatory material, indignity to a dead body and conduct likely to cause a breach of public peace.

The court ordered his remand at a correctional centre and adjourned the case until 2 December for further proceedings.

Content creator arraigned

In a separate case, the police arraigned Mr Dunminimnun on Thursday over videos he allegedly produced and circulated during the dispute surrounding Toluwanisings’ death and burial.

Mr Dunminimnun had interviewed members of the singer’s paternal family as the disagreement over his burial arrangements unfolded.

According to the police, he subsequently published videos accusing some of the singer’s relatives and associates of involvement in his death.

Mr Olayinka said the publications continued despite police warnings and an undertaking signed by the parties to end public exchanges that could escalate the dispute.

“Investigation revealed that the suspect proceeded to produce and circulate videos containing unsubstantiated allegations concerning the deceased, his wife and other family members,” he said.

The police spokesperson added that the publications were made despite repeated cautions against circulating unverified claims about the case.

Mr Dunminimnun faces allegations of spreading false information on Facebook, unlawfully publishing defamatory material and engaging in conduct capable of disturbing public peace.

The court adjourned his case until 11 December for further proceedings.

Police caution social media users

The police expressed concern about the circulation of unverified allegations and sensitive images involving deceased persons on social media.

Mr Olayinka said freedom of expression remained constitutionally protected but must be exercised within the boundaries of the law and with consideration for bereaved families.

“The command cautions members of the public, social media users and content creators against using digital platforms to spread false information, circulate sensitive images of deceased persons or make reckless allegations against individuals without credible evidence,” he said.

He urged the public to respect the dignity of the dead and allow investigators and the courts to determine issues arising from suspicious deaths.

The Commissioner of Police in Oyo State, Abimbola Olugbenga, also advised social media users to verify information before publishing it and avoid content that could disrupt public peace.

World.title: Nigeria poised to lead new era of health system transformation — WHO
World.content:
By Sola Ogundipe

Reform of the global health architecture is now being driven by a Member State-led process established by the 79th World Health Assembly in May 2026.

Hosted by the World Health Organisation (WHO), it brings together UN agencies, Gavi, the Global Fund, the Pandemic Fund, the World Bank and regional health organisations to develop a more coherent, country-led system with clearer mandates and financing aligned with national priorities.

The reform options will go before participating institutions’ governing boards between late 2026 and February 2027, ahead of recommendations to the World Health Assembly in May 2027. The process is linked to the UN80 reform initiative and Africa’s Accra Reset, which promotes health sovereignty. In this interview, the World Health Organisation (WHO) Representative and Head of Mission, Nigeria, Dr. Pavel Ursu, reflects on the Global Health Architecture Reform from the country level perspective.

Excerpts:



What the reset means for health outcomes in Nigeria



The first point is that the reset is a Member State-driven process. As institutions and partners in global health, we respect that process and look forward to its outcomes and the decisions of Member States on how we should focus and adapt our work. The structural questions being considered are important, and the reshaping of the global health architecture should follow this process. However, if you ask what this should ultimately mean for Nigerians, my perspective is pragmatic. The reset itself will not change health outcomes in Nigeria, certainly not in the short term. What matters is whether the changes it produces help countries translate resources, partnerships and technical capacity into stronger services and better health outcomes. For a mother in Sokoto or a child in Borno, the global health architecture is quite distant. What matters is whether it strengthens the services people depend on: primary healthcare, functioning supply chains, surveillance and laboratory systems, and adequately equipped and supported health workers.



Countries do not have to wait for the global process to accelerate progress. When governments invest domestic resources through national plans, strengthen accountability and align partners behind national priorities, they build the foundations that any future global health architecture should support. Nigeria already has important foundations through the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and the Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp). These offer opportunities to strengthen country ownership, partner alignment and accountability. The Joint Annual Review, alongside quarterly performance reviews, should go beyond assessing progress to identifying bottlenecks, correcting course and accelerating measurable results.



The Lusaka Agenda and Africa’s Accra Reset reinforce this direction towards greater country leadership and stronger alignment of global health initiatives with national priorities. Nigeria has an opportunity not only to accelerate its own progress but also to demonstrate what country-led transformation can achieve. Ultimately, the test of the reset will be whether it enables countries such as Nigeria to lead more effectively, mobilise sustainable domestic financing, coordinate partners behind national priorities and translate these efforts into better health outcomes.

Role of country capacity in achieving impact



National capacity is the pillar on which the others rest. Sustainable progress depends on countries being able to plan, finance, deliver, measure and continuously improve health services. International support is most effective when aligned with national priorities, systems and accountability mechanisms. I would assess any proposal, whether it involves merging agencies, pooling funds or setting timelines for reducing external aid, against one question: will it leave Nigeria’s health system more capable five years from now than it is today?

Where results should show: Polio and immunisation



Nigeria was certified free of wild poliovirus in 2020, a remarkable national achievement that many once considered impossible. However, variant poliovirus continues to circulate. According to the Global Polio Eradication Initiative’s October 28, 2026 update, Nigeria had reported 36 type 2 variant cases this year, down from 66 in 2025, alongside 15 type 3 cases, up from eight. The August IHR Emergency Committee noted that Nigeria remains the largest contributor to the global variant poliovirus caseload.



The priority now is improving delivery and making better use of limited resources. Transmission is concentrated in a number of local government areas in the North-West, where campaign quality, access and routine immunisation remain weak. We are working with NPHCDA and state governments to address each of these LGAs as a specific delivery challenge, with clearly assigned responsibilities, weekly performance reviews and a focused set of indicators. Rather than applying uniform national measures, interventions must respond to local realities. A better-aligned global health architecture can help by providing predictable funding for targeted interventions, but Nigerian programme managers must lead implementation on the ground.

Where routine immunisation stands



This is where polio will ultimately be won or lost. WHO and UNICEF estimates put Nigeria’s zero-dose children at approximately 2.2 million in 2025. National administrative data often show higher immunisation coverage than surveys and modelled estimates. That discrepancy highlights the need to improve data quality and population denominators. The surveillance systems, microplanning structures and community networks built around polio must increasingly support routine immunisation and primary healthcare. Making that transition is one of Nigeria’s most important health system capacity challenges.



Making global funding instruments work for malaria, TB and HIV



External investments have saved millions of lives globally and remain important. However, their effectiveness must be measured against the disease burden. WHO’s World Malaria Report 2025 estimates that Nigeria accounted for 24.3 per cent of global malaria cases and 30.3 per cent of deaths in 2024, representing approximately 68.5 million cases and 185,000 deaths. Nigeria therefore carries the largest share of the global malaria burden.



A country facing this level of burden needs malaria funding to do more than procure commodities. It must also strengthen surveillance, disease stratification and subnational management to ensure that bed nets, chemoprevention and vaccines reach the populations where they can have the greatest impact.



The tuberculosis control programme demonstrates what is possible. National notifications increased from approximately 107,000 in 2018 to 459,000 in 2025, against WHO’s estimated annual burden of about 510,000 new cases. This progress is largely attributed to improved diagnostics, private-sector engagement and active case-finding. The remaining detection gap and low enrolment for drug-resistant TB treatment are now key priorities.



HIV presents a more urgent transition challenge. Nigeria’s response has relied heavily on external funding, with PEPFAR historically supporting much of the treatment programme. The National HIV and AIDS Strategic Plan 2026–2030 and the government’s US$346 million co-financing commitment for HIV, TB and malaria in 2026 are important signals.



The priority now is ensuring that these commitments are released on time and that services are integrated into primary healthcare and health insurance without disruption.

What would make global funding instruments more effective?



Three things are important. First, investments must align with national health priorities, plans and annual operational frameworks, while strengthening country systems and accountability. Second, funding must predictably support the shared capacities on which all programmes depend, including health information systems, supply chains, the health workforce and primary healthcare. Third, governments and partners need joint transition plans with clear milestones to ensure that domestic financing increases as external support declines, rather than after funding gaps emerge.

Nigeria’s domestic financing and response to declining external funding



Domestic financing is critical to sustainability. Nigeria has established important policy foundations. The 2022 National Health Insurance Authority Act made health insurance coverage mandatory, while NHIA reports that enrolment had risen to more than 22 million by mid-2026. This represents progress from the low coverage levels that persisted for nearly two decades before the Act.

However, it still covers only about one in 10 Nigerians, leaving most people exposed to out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Enrolment alone does not guarantee financial protection or quality care. The next phase must extend coverage to informal-sector workers and poorer households while tracking not just who is registered but also what people pay and the quality of services they receive.

Effect of the reset on maternal mortality



Reducing maternal mortality remains one of Nigeria’s most important health priorities. UN inter-agency estimates put the country’s maternal mortality ratio at approximately 993 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2023



However, national and other estimates differ considerably, sometimes by almost half. For instance, the 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study (NVASA) puts the ratio at 572 deaths per 100,000 live births.



We are working with the government and partners to improve measurement. But the response requires action across the continuum of care, from family planning and antenatal services to skilled delivery, emergency obstetric care and effective referral systems. The 2023–24 Demographic and Health Survey found that only about 15 per cent of married women used a modern contraceptive method, while approximately one in five had an unmet need for family planning.

Helping women avoid unintended pregnancies, space births and prevent unsafe abortions can reduce high-risk pregnancies before obstetric care is even required. This must be complemented by quality antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric services, access to blood and functioning referral systems. These are health system investments, not isolated programme interventions. They are precisely the kinds of services that health insurance, the Basic Health Care Provision Fund and the SWAp are designed to support.

Requirements for a reset to translate into better outcomes: Where does primary healthcare fit?



Primary healthcare is the foundation of universal health coverage. It is where immunisation, maternal care, malaria services, HIV, tuberculosis and other essential health interventions reach communities. Nigeria has approximately 31,800 primary healthcare facilities, representing about four in five of all health facilities. However, many were non-functional for years. The government’s plan to establish at least one fully functional PHC in every political ward, covering approximately 17,600 facilities, with Basic Health Care Provision Fund resources flowing directly to facilities, provides an important framework.

NPHCDA reports that about 8,000 PHCs are functional, with approximately 3,000 upgraded. While encouraging, these are administrative figures. The next step is to verify functionality through joint facility assessments, ensure states access and utilise available funds, and demonstrate improvements in service utilisation and quality. Integrating disease-specific programmes into this platform, rather than running them alongside it, is also essential to managing the transition from external funding without disrupting services.

How serious is the health workforce gap?



Health workers are the backbone of the health system, and shortages remain one of its most binding constraints. Government figures put Nigeria’s doctor density at approximately four per 10,000 people nationally, while the 2025 workforce report shows that some northern states have as few as 0.5 doctors per 10,000 people. Emigration has accelerated, and states with some of the highest burdens of maternal deaths, malaria and zero-dose children often have the fewest health workers. Nigeria is responding through its National Policy on Health Workforce Migration, expanded training intake and the retraining of tens of thousands of frontline workers. With WHO support, it has also developed a National Health Workforce Registry and country workforce profile. The priority now is retention and equitable deployment. Midwives, nurses and community health workers must be available in the wards and states that need them, supported to remain there, and enabled to provide more services through appropriate task-sharing. Internationally, the WHO Global Code of Practice and managed migration arrangements should encourage destination countries to support the training pipelines on which they depend.

How should progress towards UHC be judged?



Progress should be measured by outcomes for people, not simply by inputs. WHO’s UHC service coverage index for Nigeria remains below the regional average, while out-of-pocket payments account for approximately 70–75 per cent of health expenditure. Functioning PHCs, an adequate workforce, reliable medicines and health insurance are the means. The real test is whether essential service coverage improves and fewer households face catastrophic health expenditure. There are, however, reasons to expect progress. Government investments and policy reforms at federal and state levels are increasingly focused on the foundations of UHC: stronger primary healthcare, a fit-for-purpose workforce, reliable access to essential medicines and expanded financial protection through health insurance. If implemented consistently and at scale, these reforms should translate into more people accessing essential services, fewer inequalities between states and population groups, and fewer families pushed into financial hardship by healthcare costs. Ultimately, that is the improvement Nigerians should expect and what the government and its partners must be held accountable for.

How will Nigeria measure the effect of the reset on health outcomes?



Strong data and analytics are essential. Countries need reliable information to track progress, identify gaps, allocate resources and improve outcomes. On maternal mortality, Nigeria has national figures, UN inter-agency estimates and IHME estimates that do not agree. Each uses different data and methodologies, and each is defensible on its own terms. However, policymakers need reliable figures for planning, while the public needs confidence in the data. We are supporting the government to harmonise these efforts through a technical working group on mortality estimation involving WHO, UNFPA, IHME and agencies working on HIV, TB, malaria and injuries.

This includes working with WHO headquarters to strengthen national and subnational analytical capacity, as well as improving civil registration and vital statistics, including maternal and perinatal death surveillance. The objective is to reduce reliance on periodic surveys and build more reliable national data systems. This is what we mean by an impact focus: using data to monitor progress, identify bottlenecks, solve problems and mobilise the resources and partnerships needed to achieve results. The quarterly performance reviews and Joint Annual Review under the SWAp provide opportunities to put this into practice. Better data will make those assessments more meaningful and help drive corrective action.

Why sub-national capacity matters



National averages can conceal significant inequalities in a country as large and diverse as Nigeria. States and local government areas make critical decisions on polio, malaria chemoprevention and obstetric care. State teams must therefore be able to analyse their own data, reconcile administrative and survey estimates, and use the findings to guide interventions. That capacity will remain long after individual grants expire, and we believe strengthening it is one of the most enduring contributions WHO can make.

Where do digital solutions and artificial intelligence fit in?



Digital transformation in health is not primarily about technology. It is about building stronger, more equitable and people-centred health systems, with technology serving as an enabler. Data and digital transformation is one of the six pillars of WHO’s cooperation with Nigeria for this reason. The ambition is not simply to expand digital health but to build connected systems that use technology to deliver measurable improvements. Too often, countries end up with multiple disconnected platforms, each funded by a different partner and unable to communicate with the others. Telemedicine, electronic health records and reporting tools should be integrated into primary healthcare, referral networks and the national health information system, rather than operating alongside them. Artificial intelligence also offers significant opportunities to support health workers, strengthen surveillance, improve decision-making and enhance service delivery. However, AI should complement, not replace, professional judgement.

Its application must follow WHO guidance on ethics, governance, equity, transparency, accountability, privacy and human rights. Successful deployment depends on strong digital foundations, including quality data, interoperability, cybersecurity, appropriate regulation and a well-trained workforce. Its value should ultimately be measured by improvements in health outcomes, service quality and equity. For Nigeria, three priorities matter. First, governance, standards, interoperability and digital architecture must be treated as national public goods, owned and led by government. Second, digital investments should be judged by their impact on service delivery and health outcomes, not the number of platforms launched. Third, AI should be pursued responsibly, guided by ethics, evidence, safety, national regulation and priorities, with data sovereignty protected and benefits extended to rural communities, women and people with limited digital access. This is also part of the global health architecture debate. Partners, philanthropies and technology companies should invest through Nigeria’s national digital health architecture, not around it.

What does the reset mean for WHO?



There have been concerns that WHO country offices have sometimes assumed substantial operational responsibilities, particularly during disease eradication efforts and public health emergencies. In some contexts, this was necessary to sustain critical public health functions and support national priorities. However, such arrangements are not intended to replace sustainable national capacity and leadership in the long term. Our role is evolving in three directions. First, we are increasingly focused on helping countries lead and sustain public health functions by strengthening institutions and systems to independently plan, implement, monitor and improve health programmes. Second, we are shifting from individual projects towards strengthening the health system through norms, guidelines and technical advice that improve multiple programmes. Third, we are moving from reporting activities to demonstrating accountability for outcomes we can reasonably influence. WHO remains fully committed to supporting a nationally led, demand-driven and less fragmented approach.

How do you demonstrate WHO’s contribution?



We have to be precise. WHO rarely causes a national result on its own. Governments, communities and many partners contribute to the work. What we can demonstrate is our contribution: a guideline adopted, a surveillance gap closed, a state team equipped to analyse its own data or a policy decision informed by better evidence. We are aligning our country plan around a smaller set of national outcome indicators, each with a clear description of WHO’s role and the assumptions behind it. Honest attribution builds more trust than inflated claims.

What should the reform process deliver for Nigeria, and what should Nigeria do?



The reform process should be judged by what changes in countries. It should deliver fewer parallel plans, reports and coordination meetings, and more funding and reporting through a single national plan, budget and accountability framework, such as the SWAp already provides. It should also support predictable investment in shared health system foundations, including data, the workforce, supply chains and primary healthcare, alongside clear and jointly agreed transition timelines.

Nigeria, for its part, must release domestic financing commitments on time, ensure partners channel their funding and reporting through the SWAp, and hold the health system accountable for outcomes rather than activities. If both sides deliver, Nigerians should see fewer children missed by vaccines, fewer deaths from malaria and childbirth, and less money paid out of pocket for healthcare. That is how the reset should ultimately be measured: in lives improved and saved.

I am cautiously optimistic. Nigeria has demonstrated that it can deliver difficult public health interventions at scale, from ending wild poliovirus transmission to vaccinating more than 100 million children through integrated campaigns and significantly expanding TB detection. The capacity exists, although it remains uneven and requires consistent support. WHO’s role is to strengthen that capacity, clearly demonstrate its contribution and step back as national institutions take over and sustainably perform these functions. That transition is the real measure of whether our time-limited support has built lasting capacity. If we get it right in Nigeria, the reforms agreed by global health institutions will have greater meaning and deliver more lasting results.

World.title: PRIVATE JETS: Calls grow for tougher sanctions against erring operators
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

Experts in the aviation sector have called for stricter oversight of private and charter aircraft operators in the country and urged relevant agencies to strengthen flight surveillance, improve information-sharing and impose stiffer sanctions on operators found violating aviation regulations.



The experts raised concerns over regulatory enforcement following two recent serious incidents involving private aircraft: a private jet, registration number N989BC, operated by VMO Aero Ltd, which landed on a road in the Ogwashi-Uku area of Delta State, and a Challenger 604 aircraft, registration number T7-SEI, operated by Triton Aviation, whose crew reported that a door had opened in flight



They particularly questioned the handling of the Asaba incident and raised concerns about the absence of a final investigation report and the enforcement actions taken against the pilot and the company responsible for managing the aircraft. One of the experts also queried the regulatory oversight of foreign-registered private jets operating in Nigeria, alleging that some operators might be exploiting their connections to influential individuals to evade regulatory requirements.



Speaking to Vanguard, General Secretary of the Aviation Safety Round Table Initiative, ART, Mr Olumide Ohunayo, expressed concern that months after the Asaba incident, the authorities had yet to provide a comprehensive account of the investigation and the actions taken.



“The DSS stepped in, the Ministry of Aviation, the NCAA, even the accident investigation body, yet nobody has come to tell us what they have done. Yes, there was a preliminary report, but I think we want to know what happened to that pilot. Are they not supposed to prosecute the pilot? What about the organisation that managed that aircraft?

“I don’t think we should panic (both incidents).



There is no red flag as far as I am concerned. There is this distinction between private and commercial operations. Yes, worldwide, commercial operations are stricter. There are more levels and layers of safety and certification that are compulsory before you can fly, compared to private operations.

I think these incidents, which are also serious incidents, are meant to strengthen the regulations and processes in place.”

Also speaking, aviation security expert, Group Captain John Ojikutu, retd, questioned the enforcement of regulations governing foreign-registered private aircraft operating in the country.

He said: “How many of those aircraft are Nigerian-registered? They are all foreign-registered. What is the enforcement of regulation on them? One big man will get the aircraft, and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, NCAA, will not want to get too involved because of the big man or whoever has it, or if the person has contact with the political officeholders.

“After the Asaba incident, what has been the report? The regulation says they (charter operators) must have security clearance. But why are they flying from one airport to the other? Are they commercial services? If it has to move from one place to another airport, it needs a security clearance. And that security clearance must be attached to the flight plan before the Air Traffic Controller, ATC, can clear.

“Look at the one that claimed it was going to Asaba, but didn’t go to Asaba and dropped people. The aircraft’s ladder was down, so what did it do with the ladder? Those are the things that should concern the security agencies. That is also the concern of the NCAA.”

Meanwhile, former Rector of the Nigerian College of Aviation Technology, NCAT, Capt Sam Caulcrick, said private jets had historically faced a different level of regulatory scrutiny from commercial airlines because of the distinction between the two categories of aviation.

He identified the regulatory framework and funding structure of aviation agencies as factors behind the difference in oversight.

According to him, commercial airlines were subject to stricter requirements because they transport fare-paying passengers, who depend on operators and regulators to ensure that aircraft maintenance and pilot qualifications meet prescribed standards.

Caulcrick, however, noted that the NCAA had increased scrutiny of private jet operations, including the examination of passenger manifests to determine whether aircraft approved for non-commercial use were being deployed for charter services.

He said: “Historically, private jet operations have faced less intensive regulatory oversight than commercial airlines. A primary structural driver for this difference in the aviation industry is the funding model of regulatory bodies like the NCAA.

“Commercial airlines heavily subsidise regulatory agencies through mechanisms like the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge, TSC, and Cargo Sales Charge, CSC. Because private jet operators do not transport fare-paying public passengers, they do not generate these specific revenue streams for regulators, leading to a traditional framework that treats private operations with a different regulatory philosophy.”

He, however, said aviation authorities like the NCAA had drastically increased scrutiny on private jet operations, adding that “regulators now aggressively audit the passenger manifests of private flights to ensure non-commercial owners are not running illegal charter businesses.

“Suspensions and policy enforcement have gone as far as suspending the Permit for Non-Commercial Flights, PNCF, for operators found violating these rules, signalling that the era of minimal oversight for private operations is coming to a close.”

World.title: Air Peace-Ethiopian deal offers alternative to foreign carriers’ dominance
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

Excitement is growing in the aviation sector over the bilateral interline agreement signed by Africa’s leading aviation group, Ethiopian Airlines, and Nigeria’s leading carrier, Air Peace.



In aviation, an interline agreement is a formal partnership between two or more airlines that allows passengers to travel across multiple carriers on a single ticket, with their luggage transferred to their final destination and their connections protected in the event of delays.



With Ethiopian Airlines operating 53 weekly flights into Nigeria through five major airports, including Lagos, Abuja, Kano, Enugu and Port Harcourt, many are eager to see how the agreement will strengthen connectivity between Air Peace and Ethiopian Airlines while expanding travel options for passengers.



Observers in the aviation sector have said the deal will be beneficial for the industry, saying it could offer a better alternative to allowing foreign carriers multiple entry points and frequencies into the country.



In fact, some said if government cannot restrict the operations of foreign airlines to one of the country’s major airports, domestic carriers such as Air Peace should explore interline partnerships with them.



When the agreement was signed a few days ago, the management of both airlines expressed optimism about its potential, saying it as a step towards bringing Africa closer to the rest of the world.



Group Chief Executive Officer of the Ethiopian Airlines Group, Mr Mesfin Tasew, said “We are delighted to partner with Air Peace, a leading carrier in Nigeria, through this strategic interline agreement. This collaboration reflects our shared commitment to enhancing connectivity, improving customer convenience, and supporting the growth of air travel across the African continent. By combining our strengths, we are creating more travel opportunities and bringing Africa closer to the world.”



For his part, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Air Peace, Allen Onyema, also said: “This partnership with Ethiopian Airlines represents another significant milestone in our commitment to strengthening Africa’s aviation connectivity and bringing the continent closer together. By combining Air Peace’s extensive domestic, regional network, and our growing international network with Ethiopian Airlines’ global reach, we are creating greater opportunities for seamless travel in and out of the African continent. Beyond expanding travel options, this collaboration reflects our shared vision of fostering stronger economic, commercial and cultural ties across Africa and beyond. At Air Peace, we remain committed to building strategic partnerships that enhance passenger convenience, broaden connectivity and position African aviation as a formidable force in global air transport.”

The agreement has also generated reflections within the country’s aviation sector, particularly over its implications for domestic airlines and the country’s ambition to develop a stronger aviation hub. Sharing his thoughts on the issue, incoming Country Manager of Uganda Airlines in Nigeria, Gbenga Onitilo, in a statement titled: ‘Air Peace and Ethiopian: Who Really Wins the Interline?,’ said a few years ago, few people in the country would have bet on seeing the two airlines partner.



The former Managing Director of Travelden stated that Ethiopian Airlines was the strategic partner lined up for Nigeria Air, the proposed national carrier project that domestic operators challenged in court and opposed publicly until it collapsed in 2023. Air Peace, he stated, was among the loudest voices in the opposition.

He said: “My advice to Air Peace is to treat this interline as a first step rather than a destination. It should use the booking data to argue for special prorate terms on key city pairs and, in time, a codeshare with shared revenue upside. It should build a protected connection product at Lagos, with guaranteed connection times, a dedicated transfer desk, and enforceable service levels with its handlers. With four hub carriers now competing for its feed, it should negotiate from strength rather than accept standard terms, and it should protect the routes it flies with its own aircraft through carve-outs and fare floors. Above all, it should invest relentlessly in punctuality and disruption handling, because in a partnership reputation is shared but blame is not.



“Government has homework too. Nigeria needs a genuine domestic-to-international transfer experience at Murtala Muhammed, firm reciprocity in its air services agreements, clear rules on passenger rights when interline journeys go wrong, and a coherent national position on the Single African Air Transport Market.



Policy should reward Nigerian carriers that build connecting traffic through Lagos, not merely those that feed it elsewhere. The handshake between Ethiopian and Air Peace is a good thing. It connects people, cities, and markets that were too far apart for too long. Whether it becomes a great thing for Nigeria depends on whether we use it to build our own hub or settle for feeding someone else’s.”



Aviation analyst, Mr Olumide Ohunayo, also added: “This is better than just collecting entry points and frequencies from the Ministry. Thank You Air Peace and ET.”

World.title: US Flight Ground Stop: What we know about disruption
World.content:
The United States has lifted a nationwide flight ground stop that lasted more than four hours, marking the longest shutdown of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) attributed Friday’s disruption to what it described as “extraordinary circumstances” arising from a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres across the country.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the incident resulted from an attack, assuring that passengers and aviation personnel were safe throughout the disruption.

Here are the major details of the incident.

How many flights were affected?

The ground stop resulted in more than 8,500 flight delays and nearly 8,000 cancellations on Friday, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware.

The FAA initially announced the restriction at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (20:54 GMT), directing that all departing flights within the United States remain grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the order was issued. While some were diverted to alternative airports, others continued to their intended destinations.

Several hours later, the FAA began allowing limited departures, including flights from San Francisco International Airport.

The agency officially reopened US airspace at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (01:15 GMT on Saturday).

What happened to international flights?

The disruption also affected international aviation, with flights bound for the United States from countries within the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, known as Eurocontrol, suspended at the FAA’s request.

Eurocontrol confirmed on its website that the suspension was due to technical problems affecting US aviation operations.

The organisation has 42 member states, including European Union countries, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, Turkey, Israel and Morocco.

Sydney Airport, Australia’s largest international airport, also grounded all US-bound flights pending further notice.

Air Canada equally cancelled flights between the United States and Canada.

When will normal flight operations resume?

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that the disruption would have consequences for airline operations over several days, even after the ground stop was lifted.

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” he said at a news conference on Friday night.

Duffy disclosed that tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports across the country, with many uncertain about where they would spend the night.

Major airlines announced different recovery plans following the reopening of US airspace.

Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations, while American Airlines said it was working to operate as many remaining flights as possible that evening.

JetBlue Airways announced that it would resume flights on Saturday morning.

What caused the ground stop?

Duffy attributed the disruption to an overloaded legacy telecommunications system used by the country’s air traffic control network.

He explained that the system’s analogue switches and routers became overwhelmed by data, resulting in failures that affected communications and radar operations.

“So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down,” he said.

The Transportation Secretary argued that the incident demonstrated the urgent need to overhaul the country’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure, estimating that the modernisation would cost about $50 billion.

“It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned.

Meanwhile, Mullin said investigators had found “zero evidence” that the incident was caused by a cyberattack.

He also ruled out any connection with the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday, saying the introduction of some new technology into an ageing air traffic control system had overwhelmed the existing infrastructure.

Both officials maintained that aviation safety was not compromised during the shutdown.

When was the last nationwide flight ground stop?

Friday’s incident was only the second nationwide flight shutdown since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when authorities grounded aircraft across the country following the hijacking of commercial planes by al-Qaeda operatives.

A previous nationwide grounding occurred in January 2023 after a technical failure affected the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system.

The system provides pilots with essential safety information, including potential hazards, airport facility changes and other operational notices.

Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify that Friday’s disruption was the worst since September 11, although he noted that the scale was not comparable to the 2001 attacks.

He recalled that the 2023 shutdown lasted one hour and 52 minutes, delaying approximately 9,500 flights and resulting in about 1,300 cancellations.

The earlier disruption occurred because the failure of the NOTAM system prevented the publication of essential aviation safety notices, forcing authorities to ground flights until the system was restored.

Friday’s shutdown, however, lasted considerably longer, further highlighting concerns about the reliability of the United States’ ageing air traffic control infrastructure.

…BBC

World.title: Ageing US air traffic equipment triggers repeated flight disruptions
World.content:
The nationwide grounding of departing flights across the United States on Friday was the second such shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks, highlighting recurring problems with ageing air traffic control equipment and communications infrastructure.

The latest disruption, which affected air traffic control centres across the country, is part of a series of technical failures that have repeatedly disrupted flight operations in the US over the past three years.

Although Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ageing air traffic control systems and recruit more controllers, the Trump administration is seeking an additional $30 billion to complete the modernisation programme.

Recent incidents have exposed vulnerabilities in the country’s aviation infrastructure, with communications outages, data-link failures and automation problems causing widespread delays and cancellations.

Major disruptions in recent years

November 13, 2026: Nationwide ground stop

The FAA grounded all departing flights across the US after air traffic control centres experienced a communications outage.

According to flight-tracking service FlightAware, airlines cancelled more than 1,000 flights and delayed nearly 10,000 others.

September 21, 2026: East Coast disruption

The FAA suspended flights to airports in New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Washington for eight hours after the primary and backup data links at the Philadelphia regional air traffic control facility failed.

The incident resulted in about 9,500 flight delays and cancellations across the country.

The disruption coincided with the arrival of 130 world leaders in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.

Dallas and Denver disruptions

A data service outage at the FAA’s Dallas Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), which manages aircraft movements between airports and higher-altitude airspace, forced the agency to impose ground stops at two airports in the Dallas area.

More than 1,800 flights were delayed, while hundreds were cancelled.

The FAA subsequently said contractor L3Harris had failed to ensure that backup systems were in place.

However, L3Harris told NBC 5 in Dallas that the outages were preventable and resulted from inadequate US government investment in replacing outdated analogue telecommunications circuits that had reached the end of their operational life.
