A day before the Dallas incident, a separate automation failure in Denver forced the FAA to slow flights into Denver International Airport, resulting in average delays of between 30 and 45 minutes.

April-May 2025: Newark and Philadelphia

Several telecommunications outages over a number of weeks at the FAA’s Philadelphia TRACON repeatedly disrupted flight operations at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey.

A 90-second outage early on May 9 alone resulted in 380 flight delays and 141 cancellations, according to FlightAware.

During the disruption, an air traffic controller reportedly told a cargo aircraft pilot that radar screens had gone blank again, urging passengers and industry stakeholders to pressure airlines to address the recurring problems.

January 11, 2023: Nationwide ground stop

The FAA ordered the first nationwide flight ground stop since the September 11 attacks after contractors accidentally deleted files, disrupting the agency’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) messaging system.

The system provides pilots with important information about potential hazards, airport facility changes and other developments affecting flight operations.

The shutdown lasted about 90 minutes, with more than 10,000 flights delayed or otherwise disrupted.

The recurring incidents have intensified calls for investment in modernising US air traffic control infrastructure to prevent further disruptions to the country’s aviation network.

…Reuters

World.title: US resumes flights after nationwide air traffic failure
World.content:
The United States has reopened its airspace after a nationwide ground stop triggered by a communications failure at air traffic control centres disrupted thousands of flights and left tens of thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the country.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the restriction on Friday, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announcing that US airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT on Saturday).

However, Duffy warned that flight operations would resume gradually, adding that airlines would need time to restore normal schedules.

“It’s going to be slow,” he told reporters at the White House.

According to flight-tracking platform FlightRadar24, more than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, while another 1,500 flights had already been cancelled for Sunday.

Aviation analysts warned that the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline operations for several days.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports nationwide following the disruption.

He disclosed that he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump at the Oval Office to discuss the incident.

What caused the disruption

Duffy said the problem began at 3:36 p.m. when air traffic control centres experienced instability in their radar and communications systems.

According to him, switches and routers became overloaded with data, resulting in inconsistencies in information transmitted through the network and prompting authorities to shut down the affected system.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” he said.

He maintained that authorities never completely lost radar or communications capabilities and were able to land thousands of aircraft safely.

Duffy said the immediate technical problem had been resolved and that flying was safe, but stressed the need for a comprehensive upgrade of the country’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure.

FG seeks $50bn for aviation overhaul

The Transportation Secretary blamed inadequate congressional funding for delays in modernising the country’s air traffic control system, calling for $50 billion to overhaul the infrastructure.

Earlier on Friday, before the disruption, the White House and the Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion for upgrades to the nation’s ageing airports and air traffic control infrastructure.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said.

“Give us the money to fix it.”

Meanwhile, Mullin said there was no evidence so far that the incident resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue artificial intelligence system, although investigators had not ruled out either possibility.

“It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we’re still looking,” he said.

He added that the National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation.

Two airline officials said the disruption appeared to have affected a telecommunications network operated by L3Harris Technologies, which handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots.

The company had yet to respond to a request for comment.

Passengers face prolonged disruption

Despite the lifting of the ground stop, passengers continued to face uncertainty as cancellations and delays mounted at airports across the country.

From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, travellers crowded departure halls and airline service desks as aircraft remained parked at airport gates.

Among those affected was 50-year-old Edward Kargbo, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, who was scheduled to travel on a 9 p.m. Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lomé, Togo.

Following the disruption, he said he would spend the night at the airport ahead of a rescheduled 6 a.m. Saturday departure.

“I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.”

Also affected was 47-year-old Louise Maher, whose British Airways flight from Newark to London was caught up in the disruption.

“I might cry at some point but not yet,” she said.

US airlines will not be required to compensate affected passengers because the disruption resulted from an FAA system failure rather than circumstances within the carriers’ control.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the September 11, 2001, attacks occurred in January 2023, when the FAA suspended domestic departures for about 90 minutes following an outage involving its Notice to Air Missions system.

The latest disruption also weighed on airline stocks, with shares of American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines falling between one and two per cent in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about three per cent.

American Airlines said it was prioritising flights to smaller cities outside its major hubs, as well as international destinations, to reposition aircraft and crews and accelerate the recovery of its operations.

…Reuters

World.title: US grounds all departing flights over communication failure
World.content:
Photo by Peter Xie on Pexels.com

US aviation authorities on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights following a communication failure affecting air traffic control centres, causing disruption and confusion among travellers across the country.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the order was issued after a technical problem affected communications across all Air Route Traffic Control Centres.

In a statement, the agency said its technicians were investigating the problem.

“The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” the agency said.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The nationwide grounding is relatively rare, as similar restrictions in recent years have generally been limited to individual airlines and lasted a few hours or less.

In January 2023, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop following an outage involving its Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which provides pilots with critical information about hazards, changes to airport facilities and other developments that could affect flight operations.

The disruption lasted just under two hours and was considered at the time to be the first nationwide flight grounding since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Friday’s incident came a day after US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy formally requested $30.1 billion from Congress to upgrade and modernise the country’s air traffic control system.

In a letter to lawmakers, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought described the proposed investment as essential to strengthening the nation’s aviation infrastructure.

“This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure,” they wrote.

The impact of the grounding was already being felt at airports, with passengers at Las Vegas airport reportedly informed by Southwest Airlines check-in staff that no flights would be taking off for 24 hours.

…Canadian Affairs

World.title: 2027: Aaro Meta urges Kwara South APC to back Danladi
World.content:
By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin

A political pressure group in Kwara South, Aaro Meta, has urged aggrieved members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the district to set aside their grievances and support the party’s governorship candidate, Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, Rt. Hon. Yakubu Salihu Danladi, ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The group also backed the emergence of a governorship candidate from Kwara North, arguing that equity, fairness and political balance informed the need for a shift in power to the district.

The group’s Coordinator, Engr. Adebayo S. Daramola, made the appeal on Friday while addressing journalists at the News Keg organised by the Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) in Ilorin.

Aaro Meta said it played an active role in the 2018 O to Ge movement, which contributed to the emergence of the APC-led government in the state in 2019, adding that its position was informed by the need to sustain the party’s political fortunes and promote fairness among the three senatorial districts.

The group recalled that during the 2019 governorship election, it supported the emergence of an APC candidate from Kwara Central, despite its base in Kwara South, in consideration of the prevailing political circumstances.

That decision, it noted, resulted in the emergence of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who won the 2019 election and secured a second term in 2023.

It urged APC members in Kwara South to demonstrate a similar spirit of political accommodation by supporting Danladi, who hails from Kwara North.

“Why can’t we also have a free mind like we did in 2019 to rally support for any candidate that emerged from the Kwara North Senatorial District, rather than having a preferred candidate?” the group queried.

Aaro Meta acknowledged that Kwara South had aspired to produce the APC governorship candidate but maintained that political power should be distributed fairly among the three senatorial districts.

It argued that since 1999, Kwara South had produced a governor for eight years, while Kwara Central would have accounted for 20 years in office by the time AbdulRazaq completes his tenure in May 2027.

The group said supporting a candidate from Kwara North would provide the district an opportunity to produce the state’s next governor.

It particularly appealed to aggrieved APC members in Kwara South and members of the G-15 political bloc to embrace reconciliation and work for the success of Danladi and other party candidates in the 2027 elections.

“We cannot afford to be a party to the destruction of the house and family we have all toiled to build and nurture all these years, but to always learn to forgive one another when we offend ourselves,” it said.

The group warned that internal divisions could give opposition parties an opportunity to gain political advantage, urging APC members not to abandon the party because their preferred aspirants failed to secure its tickets.

On security, Aaro Meta commended President Bola Tinubu and Governor AbdulRazaq for efforts to address banditry and kidnapping in Kwara South, particularly in Ifelodun Local Government Area.

It said insecurity had reduced considerably in the region but identified the Oro Forest corridor, stretching from Oro-Ago and Oreke Road towards Egbe, Okoloke and Lade, as a major security concern.

The group also commended the establishment of military bases in Oro-Ago and Babanla, as well as the recent establishment of the 184 Battalion in Omu-Aran, describing the military presence as strategic to tackling banditry and kidnapping.

It urged APC members to prioritise reconciliation, forgiveness and collective responsibility, maintaining that party unity was important to its electoral prospects in 2027.

World.title: Lagos Thugs, London Protesters and the Chaos Before the Ballot.
World.content:
By Adeola Akinremi

On Thursday, November 12, two incidents with red flags for the 2027 elections emerged. In London, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan was detained in his car by a group of protesters. In Lagos, thugs invaded a meeting venue, where supporters of the National Democratic Party (NDC) gathered for a town hall.



The Lagos and London incidents are not the same, but together they portend an increasingly fraught electoral season. They are early indicators of where we are headed if nothing is done to arrest them. The grievance in London concerned duplicate entries, AI-generated photographs and fake polling units in INEC’s preliminary voters’ register. For this, the protesters circled Amupitan’s car and prevented him from leaving Chatham House, where he had gone to give a presentation. They got what they wanted: an election umpire embarrassed on a foreign stage.



The irony is that Amupitan had already conceded much of their case. On November 9, he disclosed that the commission had removed 1,608,660 invalid registrations and identified 54 people across ten states for possible disciplinary action or prosecution. At Chatham House, he also acknowledged that transmission glitches in the 2023 elections had eroded trust in the commission.



I’d say that Amupitan’s candour deserves applause. But a commission that discovers more than 1.6 million invalid entries in its own register has handed its critics a case, and the distrust that follows does not stay confined to demonstrations outside think tanks. The danger is that when citizens doubt the count will be fair, some will conclude that the contest must be settled by other means. That is where London ends and Lagos begins.



The kind of political violence Lagos witnessed on Thursday has happened so often that it has become a motif of our existence in this country: an enduring injury, a simmering sadness, an ambient terror. As supporters of the NDC gathered for their town hall, thugs descended on them, destroying property and hunting down those in attendance. As long as this continues, the Nigeria of our dreams will remain a mirage.



We have been here before. The 2011 general elections produced one of the deadliest outbreaks of post-election violence in the country’s history. After Goodluck Jonathan defeated Muhammadu Buhari, who would later become president, rioting erupted across major northern cities. Machetes and guns were freely used, and reports put the toll at more than 200 killed and 40,000 displaced. In February 2023, Oyibo Chukwu, the Labour Party’s senatorial candidate in Enugu East, was killed when his convoy was attacked days before the national election.



The catalogue is lengthening. The African Centre for Security, Governance and Development counts 70 election-related attacks and 27 deaths so far in 2026. The Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room, drawing on the CLEEN Foundation’s threat assessment, also reports 27 deaths in the first ten months of the year and names campaign rallies and party offices as principal targets. The counts differ in method, but they agree on direction.



Nigerians, to their credit, still want to vote. A September survey by Yiaga Africa found that while 84 per cent of Nigerians of voting age are keen to vote in 2027, about 61 per cent worry about their safety because of the risk of election violence. That gap between wanting to vote and fearing to is the first real cost of normalised violence, and it is paid before a single ballot is cast.



The course can still be reversed, but only if we stop treating the thug as a freelance nuisance. Researchers who have studied Nigeria’s thug networks link them to elected officials, political financiers and armed groups. Thugs, in other words, have backers, and backers have names.



First, the state’s response must be firm and even-handed. It must go beyond the tired quarrel over whether a party obtained a permit for its rally, meeting or town hall. When campaign events become dangerous, turnout on election day falls, because voters who fear the rally will also fear the polling unit.



Second, the police must act before the violence, not after it. Those who profit from violence learn that it works, and what works escalates. Political actors are already testing their strategies for 2027, thugs included, and the police must sharpen their intelligence to anticipate them rather than merely count the casualties.



Third, accountability must reach the sponsor, not stop at the implementers. Every election season, a handful of young men are paraded before cameras while the men who paid them return to their campaign councils untouched. The National Assembly has toyed for years with an electoral offences commission and has never found the urgency to establish one. Until those behind the violence answers in court for the mayhem the bankrolled, violence will remain what it has long been in our politics: a cheap and dependable campaign expense.



Fourth, INEC must win back the argument the London protesters won. Removing 1.6 million invalid entries is a beginning; publishing the cleaned register in a form that citizens and parties can audit, polling unit by polling unit, is the end. Trust does not return through press conferences. It returns when voters can check for themselves that the ghosts are gone and the phantom polling units have been struck off.



The two incidents of November 12 must be read together because they feed each other. A register that cannot be trusted makes violence look rational to the desperate; violence that goes unpunished makes a clean register irrelevant to the frightened. Break either link and the cycle weakens. Leave both intact, and 2027 may be settled by those other means, long before INEC announces a single result.



Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving global businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: adeola@hintells.com

World.title: Elumelu to Deliver Keynote at WOC Justice Summit on Rule of Law, Economic Growth
World.content:
Wale Igbintade

Renowned entrepreneur and investor, Mr Tony Elumelu, will deliver the keynote address at the 2026 edition of the WOC Justice Summit, where he is expected to examine the role of the rule of law in promoting private sector growth and economic transformation.

According to a statement by Wole Olanipekun & Co., Elumelu’s keynote address is titled, “The Rule of Law as a Catalyst for Private Sector Growth and Economic Transformation”.

Elumelu, a prominent investor and philanthropist, is the immediate past Chairman of United Bank for Africa Plc, Chairman of Heirs Holdings and Transcorp Hotels Plc, as well as Chairman-designate of Seplat Energy Plc. He is also a recipient of the national honour of Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic (CFR).

With investments spanning financial services, power, energy, hospitality, technology and healthcare, Elumelu is expected to examine the relationship between the administration of justice, the protection of economic rights, the prosperity of private enterprises and Nigeria’s broader economic development.

His address will form part of the summit’s broader examination of future possibilities against the backdrop of established legal precedents, as well as the role of lawyers and the justice sector in shaping the nation’s future.

The summit, scheduled for November 19, 2026, at the Body of Benchers’ Complex, Abuja, will also feature the unveiling of a six-volume publication titled Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases by President Bola Tinubu.

With the theme, “From Precedent to Possibility: The Lawyer’s Role in Shaping the Next Fifty Years of Justice, Democracy and Public Trust”, the summit will bring together eminent speakers to examine the evolving role of the legal profession in protecting commerce, strengthening democratic institutions, advancing justice and safeguarding the rule of law.

The event is expected to attract leading policymakers and decision-makers across the three arms of government at both federal and state levels.

An initiative of Wole Olanipekun & Co., the WOC Justice Summit is conceived as a platform for generating ideas and fostering discussions on ways to strengthen justice delivery.

The six-volume publication, Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases, features analyses and commentaries on landmark cases involving the firm’s founder, Chief Wole Olanipekun, CFR, SAN, spanning his 50-year legal career since his call to the Nigerian Bar in 1976.

World.title: Meet Gloria: Glo Café 3.0 And Dawn of New Digital Civilisation
World.content:
Louis Ibeayoka

What happens when artificial intelligence acquires a distinctly human voice, telecommunications transcends its conventional boundaries, and an expansive universe of digital possibilities finds expression within the intimate convenience of a mobile application? What emerges when technology ceases merely to respond to human needs and begins to anticipate, interpret and accommodate them with remarkable intelligence?

The answer is Glo Café 3.0. And at the heart of this unfolding digital experience is Gloria, the personable artificial intelligence companion whose presence is redefining the interface between technological sophistication and human convenience.

“Hello! I am Gloria. How may I make your digital experience more rewarding today?” There is something disarmingly gracious about this introduction. Yet, beneath its conversational simplicity resides a compelling technological proposition: an intelligent digital companion conceived to transform how telecommunications subscribers interact with their network, access services, conduct transactions, discover entertainment and navigate the increasingly intricate landscape of contemporary digital living.

Meet Gloria. She is considerably more than an automated voice programmed to dispense information or respond to routine enquiries. She is the artificial intelligence-powered conversational personality of Glo Café 3.0, Globacom’s upgraded digital lifestyle and customer-engagement ecosystem. In her, technological intelligence acquires an approachable human dimension; through her, the otherwise intimidating complexities of digital innovation become accessible, intelligible and remarkably convenient.

In Gloria, technology discovers its voice; in Glo Café 3.0, that voice finds an expansive universe in which to resonate. Her linguistic versatility is particularly significant. Communicating in English, Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, French and Spanish, Gloria embodies an understanding that genuine digital inclusion must transcend linguistic limitations and geographical boundaries.

Through voice and text interactions, she assists subscribers in navigating services, obtaining information, making enquiries and discovering relevant offerings. It is an acknowledgement of a fundamental principle of technological advancement: innovation achieves its noblest purpose when it speaks the language of the people it exists to serve.

But Gloria is only the personable ambassador of a much larger digital enterprise. Glo Café 3.0 is, simultaneously, a digital marketplace, customer-service centre, entertainment boulevard and personal telecommunications assistant, ingeniously consolidated within a single application. Its redesigned interface, intuitive navigation and three-click transaction philosophy represent a deliberate departure from the cumbersome digital journeys that frequently frustrate consumers. The objective is elegantly straightforward: eliminate unnecessary procedural detours, simplify access and make essential transactions achievable with considerably less effort.

From purchasing airtime and subscribing to data plans to borrowing airtime or data, gifting data, managing subscriptions, examining transaction histories and settling postpaid bills, the application places an extensive range of services within convenient reach. Subscribers can equally recharge other Glo accounts, receive notifications and explore available offerings without negotiating an unnecessarily elaborate labyrinth of menus.

Its integrated payment architecture further enlarges this universe of convenience. Through supported debit and credit cards, bank transfers, USSD and other payment options, including MoneyMaster, subscribers enjoy greater flexibility in completing transactions. The underlying philosophy is unmistakable: convenience should not be an ornamental feature of digital technology but an indispensable component of its architecture.

Yet, perhaps where Glo Café 3.0 makes its most compelling commercial statement is in the generosity of its value proposition. Eligible first-time registrants are welcomed with an impressive 100GB introductory data benefit, comprising 75GB credited immediately and an additional 5GB monthly over five months. Subscribers who recharge through the application enjoy a 100 per cent recharge bonus, while eligible data subscriptions attract an additional 10 per cent data benefit.

Its Café Special Bundles further reinforce the proposition of affordability and purchasing power, with offerings including 750MB for 200, 1.5GB for 300, 2.5GB for 500 and 10GB for 2,000, subject to applicable validity periods and offer conditions.

These are not merely promotional figures assembled to excite the marketplace. They constitute a deliberate commercial philosophy, predicated upon extending the purchasing power of subscribers and ensuring that every naira committed to connectivity yields greater value, satisfaction and utility. In an economy where consumers increasingly scrutinise the relationship between expenditure and benefit, such considerations possess considerable competitive significance.

A senior Globacom management executive, reflecting on the philosophy underpinning the application, observes:

“Glo Café 3.0 represents our determination to move beyond the traditional boundaries of telecommunications. We are building a digital environment in which connectivity, intelligence, convenience and value converge to enrich everyday living. Our ambition is to ensure that subscribers do not simply consume telecommunications services but enjoy an integrated experience that anticipates their needs, simplifies their choices and rewards their loyalty.”

Beyond the conventional frontiers of telecommunications, the application opens an expansive window into entertainment and contemporary lifestyle experiences. Music, videos, games, radio, news and other engaging content transform the platform into a digital leisure destination. Here, communication and recreation inhabit the same technological address, allowing subscribers to migrate effortlessly between their essential telecommunications requirements and their personal interests.

It is, in effect, an attempt to dissolve the artificial boundaries separating connectivity from content, utility from entertainment, and transactional convenience from lifestyle enrichment. Equally commendable is the attention devoted to customer empowerment. Network speed testing, coverage checking and network-issue reporting provide subscribers with practical instruments for understanding, evaluating and managing their connectivity experience. Integration with Glo Fibre-to-the-Home self-care extends the application’s usefulness beyond mobile telecommunications, while Do Not Disturb management affords customers greater control over promotional communications.

Security, an indispensable consideration in the contemporary digital economy, also occupies an important place within the application’s architecture. Biometric authentication, PIN-protected transactions, two-factor authentication and other protective mechanisms provide additional layers of security for customer accounts and financial transactions. For subscribers who prefer direct human engagement, live chat offers access to customer-service representatives, ensuring that the march towards automation does not diminish the enduring value of human assistance.

Another senior Globacom management executive offers this perspective: “Our understanding of customer value must continually evolve. It is no longer sufficient to provide network connectivity and leave customers to navigate the rest of their digital lives independently. Glo Café 3.0 brings together services, entertainment, intelligent assistance and practical convenience within one ecosystem. It is another expression of our belief that customers deserve more, and that we must continually raise the standards of what we deliver.”

The significance of Glo Café 3.0 becomes even more compelling when situated within the broader context of Globacom’s technological infrastructure and enterprise capabilities. Its international Glo-1 submarine fibre-optic cable, fibre-to-the-home services, enterprise connectivity, cloud services, colocation and data-centre capabilities, managed business connectivity and public-sector solutions constitute important components of an expansive digital infrastructure portfolio.

These are the technological arteries through which Globacom continues to participate in Nigeria’s expanding digital economy. Beneath the apparent simplicity of a mobile application lies an extensive infrastructure of connectivity, technological investments and enterprise capabilities. Glo Café 3.0 provides an accessible, consumer-facing expression of this larger ambition, translating the company’s technological investments into practical experiences that resonate with the everyday aspirations of its subscribers.

For the consumer, however, the most persuasive endorsement of technological innovation is ultimately the experience it delivers.

A delighted Glo subscriber, Fortnatus Abioye, a technology entrepreneur resident in Jos, offers an enthusiastic assessment:

“I have used telecommunications applications before, but Glo Café 3.0 has made managing my Glo line considerably more convenient. I particularly appreciate the ease of purchasing data, the bonuses, the entertainment options and the assistance available through Gloria. I no longer have to approach every transaction as a separate exercise.

Everything is conveniently brought together. It makes me feel that Glo genuinely wants its customers to enjoy more for what they spend.”

Ultimately, Glo Café 3.0 is much more than another addition to the crowded catalogue of telecommunications applications. It is an expression of Globacom’s evolving relationship with its subscribers, bringing artificial intelligence, connectivity, entertainment, security, convenience and commercial generosity into a unified digital environment conceived around the customer.

And Gloria? She is the engaging intelligence at the gateway, the personable digital companion who lends a welcoming voice to this expansive technological universe. She represents an important psychological and experiential dimension of the platform: the humanisation of technology, through which sophisticated digital capabilities become less remote, less intimidating and more responsive to individual needs.”Thank you for choosing Glo. Your world of possibilities is only a few clicks away.”

Indeed, in an increasingly competitive telecommunications marketplace, where the contest among operators extends beyond subscriber numbers to encompass relevance, customer experience, loyalty and the coveted privilege of becoming indispensable to everyday living, Globacom is advancing a proposition that deserves considerable attention.

For existing subscribers, Glo Café 3.0 offers an opportunity to discover a richer, more rewarding dimension of the Glo experience. For customers currently patronising competing networks, it presents an attractive invitation to reconsider the destination of their telecommunications loyalty.The underlying proposition is both compelling and difficult to ignore: why settle for connectivity alone when intelligence, entertainment, convenience and exceptional value can coexist within one digital universe?

With Gloria as its conversational ambassador, Glo Café 3.0 as its digital gateway and Globacom’s technological capabilities as its formidable foundation, the invitation is unmistakable.Come into a world where possibilities are enlarged, experiences are enriched, convenience is redefined and greater value is brought within easier reach.

A world in which technology does not merely connect people to networks, but connects them to possibilities.

Globacom. Never Settle for Less.

Ibeayoka is a Communications Consultant, Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

World.title: Okoigun’s Mantra on Opportunities, Wealth, Economic Security
World.content:
Nduka Nwosu

Engr Dr. Alfred Okoigun, GMD/CEO of ARCO Plc, is a scholar, a teacher, and a patriot whose love for the nation is expressed on how, when, and where he invests his time and wealth.

As a scholar, Okoigun’s admission into the prestigious Government College Warri was significant in announcing his quest for knowledge, combined with service to the nation. The whole idea of ending up as a pioneer student at the Petroleum Training Institute (PTI) Warri was driven by love for the fatherland, which was to be counted among the pioneers of nation builders in the emerging oil and gas driven economy. But even at that, his exposure very early in the day within the ecosystem of the oil and gas business, whether in Warri or Italy, and France, told him there was need to dig deeper if we must make the best use of what the economy could offer.

His carried a one-man crusade to stop wasting the natural gas God has given to the country. That was when his organisation now ARCO Plc, hosted the country’s first international conference on gas re-injection, which deliberation was concretised in Lagos a few years later at a seminar chaired by the erudite economist Pius Okigbo. The communmique went to Dodan Barracks and was part of the backbone in the establishment of the Nigerian LNG Limited (NLNG).

The scholar in Okoigun is best appreciated through his educational foundation, which has mostly benefited hundreds of students in the oil and gas discipline and other multidisciplinary programme students. His commitment to institutional growth manifests itself in his huge contributions to the physical and intellectual sustenance of the PTI and GCU. Beyond these two, he has been active in promoting the standard of higher education in the country, leading to recognition and awards, something he is not easily taken to. Despite his shyness and tendency to stay away from these numerous awards coming to add value to his already festooned cap of achievements, three institutions stand out for mention-the University of Lagos, the Federal University of Technology Warri, and the Nigerian Academy of Engineers from where he had an investiture of fellowship. The University of Lagos, through its Engineering Society, designated or tagged Okoigun a Role Model in recognition of his philanthropy and scholarship awards to deserving students of the institution and the development and progress of the university. Again, because Okoigun would rather be the one recognising talents and giving awards

As a scholar, Okoigun keeps updating himself to keep abreast with modern trends and developments with exposures at the Lagos Business School (LBS), where he completed the Owner Manager Programme (OMP4), the Executive Education programme for the Owner/President Management Programme (OMP41) at the Harvard Business School, a certificate in Leadership Competences from the IESE Business School in Barcelona and at the IMD in Lausanne Switzerland.

With this type of background, is it any wonder Okoigun over the years has become an advocate of knowledge power over resource power urging policy makers whether in government or Corporate Nigeria to lay emphasis on knowledge over resources, the same way he led the change campaign advocacy in gas re-injection in 1982 and the early1990s.

Part of Okoigun’s tradition is to pay tribute to scholars who work through research and development. He launched the Nigerian Excellence in Science and Technology (NEST), which was initiated in recognition of outstanding Nigerian scientists who have excelled in their fields of endeavour locally and overseas. Two-time minister and professor of Robotics Barth Nnaji and computer guru Philip Emeagwali as well as Dr Henrietta Ukwu who was recently listed in the prestigious Marguis Who’s Who, what Okoigun described as “a testament to decades of intellectual rigour, ethical leadership and professional excellence in a very demanding and consequential field,” were honoured with awards at Dorchester Hotel London in 2001.

While Okoigun keeps tab with the ARCO Alumni, they in turn carry and wear his excellence mantra like a pair of a workman’s overall anywhere they go.

Dr Adedoyin Adeleke, co-chair of the United Nations Independent Group of Scientists and Executive Director Green Growth Africa, fits into this bill. An ARCO Alumnus, Adeleke had this to say about his former boss and mentor: “From a modest beginning, you built not just a company but an institution. Through courage, perseverance, discipline, and an unwavering belief in possibilities, you have shaped ARCO into a resilient enterprise that has stood strong for 46 years.

“Today, your vision sustains more than a thousand families. As one of Nigeria’s earliest indigenous oil and gas servicing companies, and among the few that survived and scaled, ARCO stands as a testament to your foresight and national impact.” Adeleke is just one among scores of the alumni that passed through the trajectory for which ARCO is known-a stickler for professionalism. There is Mrs. Funke Amobi who is an executive director at IBTC Bank and Vincent Ozoude managing director and chief executive of the Transafam Power Limited what Okoigun, a regular speaker at the LBS, defines as ARCO’s badge of honour and distinction, a placement of premium on talent, which it hones through training and exposure of its staff in highly recognised institutions, corporations and work stations in different parts of the world.

In the 1990s, ARCO Plc took a team of journalists and civil service executives for a fact-finding mission on why the Asian Tiger countries were galloping from the category of third world countries to the middle-income economies on the cusp of industrialisation.

Okoigun was also in the team of industrialists, bank CEOs, et al, who President Ibrahim Babangida delegated to the same Asian Tiger countries under the leadership of Chief MKO Abiola and Finance Minister Chu S P Okongwu on what lessons that could be learnt as well as economic collaborations that could be forged. Their reception back home and brief at Dodan Barracks signalled a new era of economic development for the country.

On a personal and corporate level, Okoigun has sustained this culture of Presidential briefing using the ARCO Plc platform and its progression for each incumbent Nigerian President in office with the exception of one or two, to date.

Okoigun, in recent times, has been partnering with NiDCOM, in recognising and rewarding diaspora and local talents. He has sponsored a football and tennis foundation, which discovered local talents for export.

And only recently in his regular lecture series, he had an update when the commandnt of the National Institute for Security Studies (NISS) JO Odama, invited him to deliver a lecture to the students with emphasis on entrepreneurship and national development through the creation of wealth, economic opportunities and the strengthening of economic security.

Well, his opening and basic argument was that entrepreneurship and national development may seem to be poles apart in terms of context. One, he said, focuses on investment and wealth creation while the other is all about the protection of life and property, institutions, and national interests. “However, I believe they are deeply connected,” Okoigun surmised.

The details flowed with revealing and convincing sub-heads:

“A nation cannot achieve lasting security without economic strength, and it cannot achieve economic strength without building its own productive capabilities. This is the central message I would like to share with you today.” he added.

“Drawing from my personal experiences and (with) more than four decades of building businesses in Nigeria, I would like to share with you today how entrepreneurship can help our country develop indigenous capabilities,” he added.

Entrepreneurship Lessons From Building ARCO

Entrepreneurship is often understood as starting a business. In reality, starting is only the beginning. Entrepreneurship involves identifying opportunities, solving problems, taking calculated risks and creating value. Sustaining an enterprise requires persistence, adaptability, discipline and the determination to build lasting competence. My journey with ARCO has taught me three important lessons.

It has involved investing in people, equipment, partnerships and professional standards. It has also taught me that local participation is not the same as local capability.

A company may win a contract without acquiring the expertise needed to execute similar work independently. Our objective must be to ensure that participation results in lasting competence.

Second, adaptability is essential.

Markets change, technology advances and customer expectations evolve. Yesterday’s achievements do not guarantee tomorrow’s relevance. Entrepreneurs must continually assess emerging needs and develop the capabilities required to remain competitive.

Third, we must build institutions, not businesses that depend entirely on their founders.

A company may begin with the vision and determination of one individual, but its long-term survival depends on professional management, governance, accountability, succession planning and strong systems.

Our ambition should be to build enterprises that preserve knowledge, sustain employment and continue contributing to the economy across generations. The objective must be to transfer not own capability.

Many of us have travelled abroad and observed how people live in other parts of the world. Such experiences can inspire us to think differently about what is possible in Nigeria. When we compare living standards in developed economies with those in many African countries, we carship.

Turning Nigeria’s challenges into opportunities means that we must not ignore the considerable challenges that remain because these challenges also present opportunities.

Consider education, healthcare, housing, transportation, water supply and electricity as examples. In many communities, access to these essential services remains inadequate.

Each gap represents a problem that needs solving.

And each problem presents an opportunity for entrepreneurs who can develop practical, affordable and sustainable solutions The important question is not simply why these problems exist. It is: What can we do to solve them? We must also recognise that solutions developed elsewhere cannot always be transferred directly to Nigeria. We should learn from successful economies, but adapt useful ideas to our own circumstances, resources and needs.

Nigeria has enormous potential in agriculture, manufacturing, energy, technology and infrastructure. Our task is to convert our resources into products, our knowledge into services and our opportunities into sustainable enterprises.

The Dangote experience

The experience of Aliko Dangote illustrates how entrepreneurship can move beyond trading into large-scale industrial production. Manufacturing creates additional value through factories, technical skills, employment, suppliers and supporting industries.

For Nigeria, the ambition must go beyond producing successful businesspeople. We must build competitive industries capable of meeting local needs and competing internationally.

ARCO and the power of local content

For Nigerian entrepreneurs, the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act of 2010 was an important milestone. It helped create opportunities for indigenous businesses to participate more meaningfully in the oil and gas industry.

However, our experience at ARCO taught us that policy alone is not enough. We must prepare people and build capabilities before opportunities arise.

Let me share two experiences.

Our experience in marine operations

When we entered the marine business in 1998, we had to employ expatriates because they possessed the experience and qualifications required to captain vessels serving multinational oil companies.

We recruited personnel from countries including Australia and the Philippines because Nigerian professionals were not being given adequate opportunities in these roles.Then came the Niger Delta crisis in 2007. As security conditions deteriorated, many expatriates had to leave the region. We were compelled to deploy Nigerians to pilot our vessels.

The opportunity emerged from a crisis, but we were able to respond because we had already begun developing local capacity.

This experience reinforced an important lesson. Sometimes an opportunity becomes visible only when circumstances change. The entrepreneur who has prepared for change is better positioned to respond.

Our experience in maintenance and engineering:

We experienced something similar through our subsidiary, ARCO Maintenance & Engineering Limited, formerly ARCO Petrochemical Engineering Company. As the Nigerian representative of a multinational Original Equipment Manufacturer, our initial responsibility was largely to supply equipment, while the principal provided the technical manpower.

We invested considerable time and resources in training Nigerian engineers and technicians at the manufacturer’s facilities so that they could eventually maintain and service the equipment themselves.

It was expensive, but we were looking beyond the immediate situation. We were preparing for the future.

Again, during the Niger Delta crisis in 2007, expatriate technical personnel had to leave the region. A gas plant maintained by our principal still needed to operate.

Our trained Nigerian engineers and technicians were called upon to take responsibility. For six months, they successfully maintained the plant to the satisfaction of our major client. This was a defining moment for us.

It demonstrated that Nigerians could perform highly specialised technical work when given the training, responsibility and opportunity.

However, the experience also created an unexpected challenge.

Our success affected our relationship with the foreign principal, and nineteen of our employees, including engineers, technicians and other critical personnel, were subsequently recruited away from ARCO.

The loss of these employees created a serious challenge for the business and, at one point, threatened its survival.

The situation became so difficult that members of the security community were involved in helping to resolve it. But the experience reinforced my conviction that Nigeria possesses intelligent, capable and committed professionals who can support the development of sustainable indigenous enterprises.

What is often required is vision, preparation, persistence and the willingness to invest in people before the benefits become obvious.

For me, this is the real power of local content.

It is not merely about awarding contracts to Nigerian companies. It is about developing the people, skills and systems that enable Nigerian businesses to deliver independently and competitively.

Developing and building lasting institutions

Our experience has also reinforced the importance of investing in science, technology, engineering and professional development. Over the years, we have sought to contribute to these areas through training, partnerships and initiatives that recognise excellence.

In 2001, we sponsored the Nigerian Excellence in Science and Technology Awards in the United Kingdom, recognising Nigerians who had distinguished themselves in science and technology. Among those honoured were Professor Barth Nnaji and Dr Henrietta N. Ukwu. Professor Nnaji subsequently served as Nigeria’s Minister of Power and went on to establish Geometric Power Limited, contributing to electricity supply in Aba and its environs.

His journey illustrates how technical expertise and entrepreneurship can be applied to address critical national challenges.

More recently, ARCO Maintenance & Engineering Limited was selected as one of three Nigerian companies to participate in an initiative sponsored by Nigeria LNG Limited to promote Kaizen, the Japanese philosophy of continuous improvement.

Representatives of participating companies travelled to Japan to learn from the Toyota model and explore ways to improve productivity, quality, efficiency and competitiveness. This is particularly important because developing local capability is not simply about acquiring technical knowledge. It is also about improving how businesses operate so they can compete to international standards.

In 2014, Lagos Business School also prepared a case study on our company titled Arco Petrochemicals: Climbing by Merit.

We consider this an opportunity for students and business leaders to learn from our experience and draw lessons that may help them build successful enterprises.

These initiatives reflect an important principle.

Entrepreneurship is not merely about making money. It is also about developing people, sharing knowledge, encouraging innovation and creating opportunities for others.

The impact of a business should therefore be measured not only by its financial performance, but also by the capabilities it develops and the contributions it makes to society.

World.title: Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A Rare  Gift of Generosity, Mentorship
World.content:
When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso.

As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty.

April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office.

He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied.

“When will you resume work?” he asked.

I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life.

“Tomorrow, sir,” I answered.

That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso.

When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. True to his word, when The Nation newspaper launched on July 31, 2006, I continued working with him as a 16-year-old boy.

One quality that set him apart from the very beginning was his uncommon, almost instinctive generosity. I remember one particular week when he repeatedly asked whether I had eaten. Each time, he would give me some money for food. As time passed and his instinctive generosity continued, I grew uncomfortable and began answering, “Yes, sir, I have eaten.” Not because I had suddenly become rich, but because I did not want him to think I was turning hunger into a business strategy.

That is Mr. Omotoso. His kindness is never calculated; it flows naturally.

His generosity was never limited to me. I recall a difficult period when the newspaper’s salaries were delayed for months. The newsroom was dampened, heavy with frustration. Sensing and discerning the quiet despair of his colleagues, he reached into his own pocket and gave everyone money to ease the hardship. That single gesture taught me a lesson I have never forgotten: true leadership is not about occupying an office; it is about lifting others when life weighs them down.

Beyond feeding my body, Mr. Omotoso fed my dreams. He encouraged me to keep studying while working and never once treated my academic ambitions as an inconvenience. During one management meeting, when questions were raised about my qualifications, he defended my potential and appealed for patience while I worked toward becoming a graduate.

I was determined not to disappoint him. In 2014, I graduated from the then Lagos State Polytechnic with a Distinction. He celebrated the achievement, then immediately urged me to aim higher. With his continued support, I went on to Caleb University, Imota, Lagos, where I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science in 2019, graduating with Second Class Upper honours and a CGPA of 4.36. For someone who had started as an errand boy, this was more than academic progress. It was living proof that when someone believes in your potential, your circumstances need not determine your destination.

Mr. Omotoso’s fatherly role extended far beyond the professional and academic. When I married in 2018, he provided a Honda Pilot and a personal driver to take me around all day, ensuring the occasion was memorable.

On August 20, 2019, he was appointed Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. Before leaving The Nation, he ensured my contributions were recognised with a promotion to Web Officer.

A month into his new assignment, he invited me to join him at the Ministry of Information and Strategy. That invitation opened yet another significant chapter in my career.

Since then, I have had the privilege of serving closely with him as his Personal Assistant and Programme Analyst within the Lagos State Government.

His commitment to my progress did not end there. He played an instrumental role in my appointment into the Lagos State Civil Service on December 31, 2024, personally presenting my credentials to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for consideration and approval.

How does one adequately thank a man who has consistently opened doors, sometimes long before one even knew those doors existed?

Yet my story is only one among countless testimonies of his compassion. Over the years, I have watched him discreetly pay hospital bills for people with whom he shares no family ties, sponsor the education of children whose parents could not afford school fees, and quietly rescue others from difficult circumstances.

He does not need a camera to demonstrate kindness, nor does he wait for applause before helping others. Behind his serious editorial background and the demands of public office is also a man blessed with a remarkable sense of humour.

An accomplished journalist, columnist and writer, Mr. Omotoso has a gift for satire. His humorous observations can turn even tense moments into shared laughter. And then there is table tennis.

Anyone who has faced him across the table knows that losing is not exactly his favourite pastime. He approaches every game with the intensity of an editor scrutinising a controversial front-page headline. Every point matters, every rally is a battle, and every defeat deserves a detailed explanation.

At 65, I suspect his opponents will still need more than youthful energy to defeat him. As I celebrate this remarkable man, I see far beyond the professional titles and accomplishments. I see a compassionate father figure, a bridge-builder, a generous leader, and a man whose quiet influence continues to transform lives.

Sir, on your 65th birthday, I pray that Almighty God grants you long life, sound health, renewed strength, divine protection, and enduring peace. May the years ahead be filled with greater accomplishments, happiness, and the joy of seeing the many lives you have touched continue to flourish. May God reward every sacrifice you have made for others, replenish every resource you have so freely and generously shared, and surround you with love, honour and abundant blessings.

May your pen never run dry, your wisdom never diminish, your laughter never cease, and may you continue winning your table tennis matches, even when your opponents believe they deserve a chance!

For more than 22 years, I have experienced your kindness firsthand. I may never be able to repay all you have done for me, but I will forever remain grateful.

Happy 65th birthday, my boss, my mentor, my father figure, and my God-sent benefactor.

The world may know you as Gbenga Omotoso, the accomplished journalist and Commissioner. I know you as the man God used to rewrite the story of a fatherless boy. And for that, I will remain eternally grateful.

Uwemedimo is a Programme Analyst and Personal Assistant to the Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy

World.title: Unlocking More Barrels: From Recovery to National Renewal
World.content:
Olu Verheijen

Last year, I asked this gathering to judge our progress by four things: reserves, revenues, reliability and responsibility. Those tests still stand. Today, I want to put a larger question before us. What will Nigeria build with its next era of oil and gas production?

We have celebrated discoveries before. We know the excitement of announcing what lies beneath our soil. The harder task is to change what is possible for the people who live above it. That is the ambition I bring to “Unlocking More Barrels”: turning investment recovery into national productive strength. The next barrel must help build more than our production numbers. It must help build our country.

Consider the IMA gas field. Discovered in 1973, it reached a final investment decision in September 2026. More than half a century. A child born when that gas was discovered could have finished school, entered the workforce and raised a family before the decision to develop it was taken.

The gas did not suddenly appear in 2026. The conditions for investing in it changed. For too long, Nigeria asked excellent geology to compensate for weaknesses elsewhere in the investment proposition: uncertain responsibilities, slow contracting, uncompetitive economics and unreliable routes to paying customers. Under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s leadership, we have set about changing that proposition. The President provided the mandate and political backing. Our team’s work began with the reform blueprint and continued through fiscal design, negotiations and implementation, alongside ministries, regulators, NNPC, operators and investors. We examined actual projects, benchmarked Nigeria against competing destinations and worked to remove the obstacles preventing investment decisions.

The fiscal principles were deliberate: reward production, protect existing revenues, keep the rules workable and tailor incentives to the resource. Time-bound eligibility encouraged investors to bring Nigerian projects forward in their portfolios. In gas, fiscal reform and commercial negotiation had to move together. Incentives could support development; access to customers and prices that justified investment could make it financeable. That is why opening opportunities for third-party gas supply to NLNG mattered.

Policy earns its value by changing a decision and enabling something real to proceed.

Ubeta and Bonga North reached final investment decisions in 2024. Since we last gathered, IMA has joined them. These decisions move projects into execution, commit capital and begin the work that will support future production. Our responsibility is to carry them through while improving output from assets already operating.

We have begun to change the investment story. We must now change the production story, and through it, the economic story. This year’s theme gives us three practical responsibilities: exploration, local capability and adaptive technology. First, we must replenish the opportunity. A country cannot produce tomorrow what it does not discover, appraise or develop today. Nor can it sustain growth by celebrating the same discoveries for another generation.

We need reliable geological data, credible exploration programmes and development plans that account for infrastructure and markets from the outset. Better reservoir understanding, infill drilling and improved recovery can deliver nearer-term gains. But those gains must finance ambition, not replace it. Mature fields and the next generation of developments must advance together.

To operators, my challenge is straightforward: bring forward the programmes that replenish your portfolios. Identify the government decisions needed to unlock them. And demonstrate the capital, people and execution plans behind your proposals.

Second, we must build capability worthy of our ownership. The rise of Nigerian independents creates an opportunity to drive near-term onshore and shallow-water growth, while international companies concentrate on deepwater and integrated gas. Success depends on what each owner does with those assets. It requires sound governance, strong balance sheets, technical competence and obligations honoured to workers, communities and the environment.

Local content should leave Nigeria more capable after a project than before it began. It should mean engineers who can lead the next development and fabrication companies that can win work beyond our borders. It should give a young Nigerian the chance to master difficult work, not simply stand beside someone else doing it. We should be proud of Nigerian ownership. We should be ambitious enough to demand Nigerian excellence.

Third, we must use technology to change performance. Better seismic interpretation can reveal what an older model missed. Reservoir modelling can improve recovery. Digital monitoring can reduce downtime and losses. Methane measurement can help preserve valuable gas. The test is what changes in the field: uncertainty reduced, costs lowered and operations made safer.

Artificial intelligence will expand what our professionals can do. It will not remove the need for good data and sound judgement. NAPE connects knowledge across companies and generations. Use that reach to deepen the skills this next phase requires.

These responsibilities matter far beyond the upstream sector. Investors have choices. New developments in Guyana and across Africa remind us that Nigeria must compete through the quality of its proposition. A disruption elsewhere may create an opening.

It cannot be our business plan. Our projects must remain competitive when prices fall and new supply arrives.

Our greatest opportunity is larger than the next cargo. It is a more productive Nigeria and a more industrialised Africa. Energy poverty is also an industrialisation problem. Factories cannot compete without dependable power. Farmers cannot realise the full value of their harvest without processing, storage and transport. Young people cannot find enough productive work in an economy constrained by unreliable energy.

This is why oil, gas and power belong in one national strategy. Oil can strengthen export earnings and public finances. Gas can supply industry, electricity and export markets. But a gas field is only as bankable as the customer at the other end of the pipe.

Resolving legacy power debts, improving metering and targeting support to vulnerable consumers are therefore part of the same economic task. Suppliers need confidence they will be paid. Consumers need accurate bills and credible service.

Alongside renewables, stronger networks and greater efficiency, these reforms can build an energy system capable of supporting our ambitions.

We should manufacture more of what we consume, process more of what we produce and supply more of what our neighbours need. We should be able to trace the connection from a well to a business that grows, from a project to a skill that endures, from public revenue to public value.

A family struggling with the cost of living cannot spend a forecast. A business cannot run on a policy announcement. Nigerians are entitled to ask when reform will make their lives better. We owe them honest answers and sustained delivery.

President Tinubu’s mandate has opened the way for difficult changes. Government and industry must now make them endure beyond any one officeholder or investment cycle. Last year’s tests still apply: reserves, revenues, reliability and responsibility. Let us meet them through the projects we execute and the service our economy receives.

More than half a century separated the discovery of IMA’s gas from the investment decision to develop it. The young professionals here should not wait a working lifetime to see their country’s promise put to work. Let them inherit more than a catalogue of resources: an industry with the competence to develop them, institutions with the discipline to steward them, and an economy in which their talent has a future.

Let us unlock more barrels, and with them, a greater future for Nigeria.

· Text of address delivered by Special Adviser to the President on Energy, Verheijen at the 44th NAPE annual international conference and exhibition

World.title: BBR: The Road that Ended Bonny Island’s Isolation
World.content:
After decades of dependence on boats and ferries, the commissioning of the Bodo-Bonny Road has ended Bonny Island’s isolation, opening new opportunities for connectivity, trade and economic development across Rivers State, writes Blessing Ibunge

For as long as most people can remember, getting to Bonny Island meant crossing water. Residents, traders, workers and visitors had little choice but to rely on ferries, speedboats and barges to move between the island and the Rivers state mainland. The journey was a way of life, but it often came with delays, high costs and the uncertainties of weather and tide.That reality has now changed.

With the completion and the recent commissioning of the Bodo-Bonny Road, BBR, Julius Berger Nigeria Plc has turned a long-held dream into reality, delivering a permanent road link between Bonny Island and the mainland for the first time in history. What generations only talked about is now a road people can drive on.For an Island that hosts some of Nigeria’s most strategic energy assets, including facilities operated by Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas, NLNG Limited, the new connection is about much more than convenience. It opens the door to faster movement of people and goods, greater investment opportunities and stronger economic ties between and among the communities with the rest of the country.

But perhaps its greatest significance is what it means to the people of Bonny themselves. For residents who have spent a lifetime crossing creeks to access schools, hospitals, markets and opportunities on the mainland, the road is more than infrastructure. It is a symbol of inclusion, progress and possibility. After decades of waiting, Bonny is no longer an island apart. It is finally connected. That era has now ended.

With the completion and formal commissioning of the Bodo-Bonny Road and its accompanying bridges across the Opobo Channel, Julius Berger Nigeria Plc has delivered one of the most ambitious and technically complex infrastructure projects ever undertaken in the Niger Delta, permanently connecting Bonny Island to mainland Nigeria for the first time in history.

The landmark project represents far more than a road. It is a transformative economic corridor, a symbol of engineering resilience and a catalyst for regional development.

Constructed through challenging marshlands, tidal waterways and swampy soils, the approximately 39-kilometre road project includes major bridge crossings over Afa Creek, Nanabie Creek and the Opobo Channel. The undertaking demanded sophisticated engineering solutions capable of withstanding the demanding environmental conditions of the Niger Delta.

According to project officials, the road and bridge works were completed in 2026, with ancillary works such as landscaping, street lighting installations and finishing elements following thereafter. Despite the complexities associated with construction across wetlands and waterways, the project was delivered within approved budgets.

The project was financed through a unique partnership between the Federal Government of Nigeria and Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), demonstrating how public-private collaboration can deliver nationally significant infrastructure.

The commissioning of a national assetThe official commissioning by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu marked the culmination of years of planning, investment and construction. During the ceremony in Port Harcourt, the President formally declared open the Bodo-Bonny Road and bridges across the Opobo Channel, recognising the project’s significance to national development and regional connectivity. The commissioning attracted government officials, traditional rulers, community leaders, business executives and residents who viewed the project as a historic breakthrough for the Niger Delta.

A historic milestone

For the Managing Director of Julius Berger Nigeria Plc, Dr. Peer Lubasch, the project’s completion represents the fulfilment of a vision that had remained unrealised for more than four decades.

Speaking on the sidelines of the commissioning, Lubasch described the delivery as a defining moment for both Rivers State and Nigeria, saying, “today marks a historic milestone, not only for the people of Rivers State, but for Nigeria as a nation. For the very first time, Bonny Island is permanently connected to the mainland by road infrastructure.”

He further noted that the project traverses both Bonny and Gokana Local Government Areas, providing a vital transport link capable of unlocking new economic opportunities and improving the quality of life for residents.

The statement reflects the broader significance of the project. Beyond the concrete, steel and asphalt lies a new chapter in mobility, trade and investment for an island long regarded as one of Nigeria’s most economically important destinations.

Umahi announces expansion

Minister of Works, Engr. David Umahi, has consistently praised the quality and strategic value of the Bodo-Bonny Road.

During inspections and at the commissioning ceremony, Umahi described the highway as a strategic national asset capable of enhancing regional connectivity, improving security and stimulating economic activities throughout the Niger Delta. Perhaps even more significantly, the Minister disclosed that President Tinubu had approved an extension of the project to link the corridor directly to the East-West Road, further strengthening integration with Nigeria’s national transport network. The approved extension covers an additional 8.9 kilometres of dual carriageway.

Umahi also highlighted the scale of investment required to deliver the project, noting the extraordinary engineering demands associated with the extensive bridge infrastructure.

Hope, opportunity and growth

Reactions from stakeholders have been overwhelmingly positive.

For businesses, especially those operating in the oil and gas, logistics and maritime sectors, the road creates new opportunities for supply-chain efficiency, workforce mobility and investment.

Community leaders and development stakeholders have also welcomed the project as a catalyst for tourism, industrialisation and job creation across Bonny, Gokana and neighbouring communities. The permanent road connection is expected to increase commercial activity while opening previously difficult-to-access areas for development. According to a teacher that work in a community school on the route, Ifediaye Bonny, “this road has changed everything for Bonny. It has broken the water barrier. Julius Berger has delivered a very historic mainland link road.”

An indigene of Gokana Local Government on the Road retorted thus, “the commissioning of this road marks the end of Bonny Island’s isolation; it is a story of how Julius Berger linked Bonny to the mainland where other companies before them failed.” And for residents of Bonny Kingdom, the road represents easier access to healthcare, education, commerce and government services.

The reduction in dependence on boats and ferries is expected to improve safety and lower transportation costs for thousands of people.

Industry observers have similarly pointed to the project as evidence of what sustained infrastructure investment can achieve in historically challenging terrains.

More than a road

The Bodo-Bonny Road is ultimately more than a transportation project. It is a bridge between communities, a connection between industry and opportunity, and a demonstration of Nigerian engineering capability at its best. By successfully delivering one of the country’s most complex road-and-bridge projects, Julius Berger Nigeria Plc has added another landmark achievement to its infrastructure legacy.

As vehicles now travel seamlessly between Bonny Island and the mainland, what was once a decades-long aspiration has become a tangible reality, one that will shape the economic and social future of Rivers State for generations to come.

World.title: Temitope Ajayi @ 50: An Omoluabi to Behold
World.content:
Raheem Akingbolu

Temitope Ajayi’s career has taken him through journalism, public relations, political communication and public service. His ability to work across these fields has shaped a professional journey marked by adaptability and a sound understanding of the communication business. As friends, colleagues and admirers continue to celebrate his 50th birthday, the unveiling of Omoluabi, a book in his honour, offers an opportunity to reflect on the man and his journey because his story gives fresh meaning to the Yoruba philosophy of the concept.

Some milestones are too significant to be confined to a single day. A fragrance lingers long after the flower has been admired, just as a memorable song remains in the mind long after the music has ended. Tope Ajayi’s golden jubilee belongs in that category. The birthday marked an important moment, but the values and accomplishments it celebrates continue to resonate.

Among the Yoruba, there is a popular saying: “Omoluabi to mo owo we lo le ba agba jeun.” Literally, it means that “a well-brought-up person who is well cultured can dine with elders.” Beyond its literal meaning, it speaks to character, humility, respect and the capacity to earn the confidence of those whose wisdom and experience command admiration. Few descriptions capture Tope Ajayi more accurately.

Perhaps this explains his enduring relationships with people considerably older and more experienced than himself. Over the years, he has built friendships with respected figures such as Dele Alake, Tunji Bello, Bayo Onanuga and Tunde Rahman, among others. His ability to relate comfortably across generations reflects respect for experience, a willingness to learn and an appreciation of meaningful conversations.

These qualities predate his current role in the Presidency. Before joining the team that helped shape President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s media and public engagement strategy ahead of the 2023 presidential election, Tope had already established himself in political communication. An important chapter was his involvement in the communication effort surrounding the 2019 Lagos governorship election, working alongside Segun Fafore and Gboyega Akosile, now Special Adviser on Media and Publicity to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. The assignment deepened his understanding of media relations, public perception and message discipline.

What has always stood him out to me, however, is the combination of newsroom experience and public relations expertise that Tope brings to his work. I first met him at Soulcom, the public relations subsidiary of SO&U, owned by Sir Udeme Ufot. We connected almost immediately, largely because of our shared affection for Ekiti State and pride in our cultural heritage. Beyond that common bond, I recognised a professional with a valuable understanding of both journalism and strategic communication.

His newsroom background gave him insights many public relations practitioners spend years trying to acquire. He understood deadlines, editorial judgement and the importance of presenting accurate and credible information. More importantly, he understood what makes a story relevant to the audience it seeks to reach. That appreciation of the newsroom has remained an important part of his approach to communication.

He also appreciated that effective media relations go far beyond issuing press releases or securing media coverage. It is built on trust, credibility and mutual respect. Having worked on both sides of the media divide, he developed a balanced perspective that has served him well in strategic communication. This blend of experience is one of the qualities that distinguishes his professional contribution.

His academic journey deserves equal recognition. Following his formative years at Annunciation College, Ikere, Tope attended Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, where he studied Literature in English. He later earned a master’s degree in the same discipline from the University of Lagos in 2005. His early professional experience at The Punch provided an avenue to translate academic knowledge into practical journalism.

The connection between literature, journalism and strategic communication is often overlooked. Yet all three disciplines require clarity of thought, sensitivity to language, an understanding of human behaviour and the ability to communicate ideas effectively. For someone whose career would revolve around narratives, public perception and stakeholder engagement, this combination provided a strong intellectual foundation.

Another aspect of Tope’s life that deserves attention is his understanding of relationships and the responsibilities that come with an extensive professional network. The true value of his network lies not simply in the prominence of the people he knows, but in his ability to understand people, connect them where necessary and use those relationships to help solve problems.
