Defenders: Ahmed Fatouh, Rami Rabia, Hossam Abdelmaguid, Mohamed Hany

Midfielders: Mohanad Lasheen, Nasser Maher, Marwan Attia

Forwards: Omar Marmoush, Mohamed Salah, Mahmoud Hassan “Trezeguet”

World.title: Slight rise in temperatures across Egypt on Friday
World.content:
On Friday, the Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) released its weather forecast and rainfall map, announcing a slight rise in temperatures across most regions.

Mild to warm autumn weather will prevail during the day across most areas, turning hot in southern Upper Egypt, while becoming cool to cold at night and during the early morning hours across most parts of the country.

Temperatures in Cairo are forecast to reach a high of 26°C with an overnight low of 16°C.

There are chances of light to occasionally moderate rain (approximately a 30 percent probability) at intermittent intervals over parts of Halayeb and Shalateen, alongside weak chances of light rain (around a 20 percent probability) over parts of the Northern Coast and northern Lower Egypt (Delta).

Low-lying clouds will also form over scattered areas of southern Lower Egypt, Greater Cairo, and the Suez Canal cities.

Satellite imagery detected intermittent wind activity reaching speeds of 30 to 35 km/h across most regions.

World.title: Republicans’ lame-duck dash to confirm judges is already hitting speed bumps
World.content:
The Democrats’ coming takeover of the Senate has kickstarted a scramble to confirm two dozen of President Donald Trump’s judicial nominees before Republicans turn over the gavel in January.

The mad dash included a November 4 call from Republican Sen. Ted Cruz to a top lawyer in Trump’s Justice Department to solicit the lawyer’s interest in filing a seat in Texas, after the state elected James Talarico, a Democrat who will have veto power over district court nominees. Trump formally announced the nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel, less than a week later.

But the compressed timeline has also heightened clashes between the White House and Republican senators over the president’s choices.

The stalemates already forced a switcheroo this week of Trump’s choice for an appeals court seat, potentially slowing down the timeline for filling it, while at least one other district court nomination in Oklahoma may be imperiled because of the resistance of a Republican home state senator.

Trump’s remaking of the judiciary – from the Supreme Court on down in his first term – could arguably be the longest-lasting legacy of his presidency. Right-leaning judges could continue to serve as a check on Democrats, by striking down their policies, if they expand their power in Washington in 2028 and beyond.

In his second term, Trump has not been able to match the record-breaking number of judicial confirmations he achieved in his first administration, particularly on influential appeals courts, as he returned to the White House with far fewer vacancies to fill than the start of his first term. Now, Republicans are anticipating the possibility that Democrats won’t allow any of his nominees to be confirmed once they take Senate control, raising the stakes for getting every possible judge approved in the next month and a half.

With little time to spend for negotiation over who the president selects, tensions are flaring within the conservative legal community over how local politics are getting in the way of confirming judges with the bona fides they prefer.

“Trump has set precedents where he will roll over for the state senators,” said Joshua Blackman, a South Texas College of Law professor and a conservative who has written extensively about judicial nomination battles. “And we have the picks who probably are not the best picks as a result.”

Republican leaders are juggling this infighting with the threats of Democratic procedural maneuvers that will jam up the process of confirming Trump’s nominees.

The Senate Judiciary Committee has set an aggressive calendar to push the remaining nominees through the pipeline – prompting Democratic accusations that the GOP is breaking Senate norms – while leadership is charting out a path for moving the nominees along on the Senate floor along with other priorities.

“We’re going to make every second count, and that means all these judicial appointments,” Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the Republican whip, said Tuesday. “We’re going to do everything we can to get every single one of them confirmed.”

GOP infighting over Trump’s choices

The first post-election Judiciary Committee meeting Tuesday kicked off with sparring between its chair, Iowa GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley and Sen. Dick Durbin, its top Democrat, about the lengths Republicans were willing to go to speed Trump’s nominees through.

But soon after, it became clear that the calendar was not the only problem.

Plans to for the committee to vote Tuesday on two nominees to Oklahoma’s federal court were derailed by the opposition that one of the nominees, Zachary West, faces from the junior senator from the state, Republican Sen. Alan Armstrong, according to a source familiar with the nominations process.

Supporting Armstrong in his opposition, according to the source, is North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, meaning that West would struggle to get out of the committee, which Tillis serves on.

So far, the White House is standing by Trump’s choice, with an official telling CNN Wednesday that the “President has selected two highly qualified nominees for the district court in Oklahoma, and we are confident they will be confirmed.”

But the White House on Tuesday night had to reverse course on a nomination for an Arkansas seat on the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals, after the home state senators balked at the choice over their preferred candidate.

The canned nominee, US District Judge Lee Rudofsky, was widely celebrated by the conservative legal movement for the decisions he has issued from his current perch on the trial-level federal court in Arkansas. Rudofsky had already had his hearing and would have been primed for a vote out of the Judiciary Committee by next week.

The 8th Circuit already has a deep right-lean, but the seat had significance for Trump-aligned legal advocates because filling it will mean that he appointed a majority of judges on that court.

Now, Republicans will go back to square one and schedule a new hearing from the freshly announced nominee, Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland.

“The committee is carefully vetting Hiland’s nomination,” a committee spokesperson told CNN. “As chairman, Senator Grassley has discretion to set the committee’s schedule and is working to efficiently process President Trump’s pending judicial nominees.”

That conservative legal world was already grousing about the current nominee for a Mississippi seat on the 5th Circuit Trump is trying to fill this Congress, who has the support of the senior Republican senator from the state, Sen. Roger Wicker, but is not seen as a reliable vote for the right’s most cherished causes.

According to Blackman, the movement would have preferred a candidate like Mississippi Solicitor General Scott Stewart, who argued successfully at the Supreme Court for overturning nationwide abortion protections. The current nominee, Todd Butler, is a former clerk for the retiring 5th Circuit judge he is set to replace, and according to his application paperwork, he received outreach from Wicker before the vacancy was publicly announced.

“They’re jamming (the White House) up, and I think Trump is just going along with it because he has other stuff he’s worrying about,” Blackman said.

Like Texas, Mississippi flipped a Senate seat, with Democrat Scott Colom projected to beat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Colom, a local district attorney, ran for the seat after Hyde-Smith blocked his nomination to a judgeship by President Joe Biden).

When Trump announced Gaiser’s nomination on Tuesday, he also rolled out nominations for another judicial vacancy in Texas – choosing a Texas Supreme Court justice who just lost his reelection for that seat – and in South Carolina, which elected Democrat Annie Andrews to the Senate.

Democrats have speculated that local politics could get in the way of confirmation of Gaiser, and Texas Sen. John Cornyn, a retiring Republican who also sits on the Judiciary Committee, told the AP he had concerns about how the White House has tried to “air-drop” somebody into the vacancy.

The attorney did not go through the usual process Texas senators use to vet nominees, and Democrats have zeroed in on his limited ties to Texas, which they say amount to just a clerkship in Houston while spending the rest of his career in Ohio or Washington, DC.

Race against the clock

To push through, Grassley has previewed an all-gas-no-breaks approach in his committee – an approach he said Tuesday was justified by signals that Democrats could block any nominee Trump tried to put forward next Congress.

“They’re planning to stonewall a president’s ability to appoint judges – now that is what is unprecedented,” Grassley said at Tuesday’s committee meeting. “So yes, I’m working. I’m going to work hard to get judges confirmed quickly during the lame duck session.”

Under the normal Senate timelines, nominees will need to get their confirmation hearing before the committee by next week if Republicans want to get them on the Senate floor by mid-December, before lawmakers leave for the holidays.

Democrats argue that Grassley is violating procedures in how he is orchestrating that final push. They’ve pointed to norms around having judicial hearings at least two weeks apart (a plan for a November 18 hearing comes after a confirmation hearing on November 10) and giving the Senate committee at least 28 days to review the paper applications – known as Senate Judiciary Questionaries – that are submitted with their nominations.

“Don’t be surprised if some of these violations have now become routine enough to be followed in the future,” Durbin, who is retiring after this year, warned Tuesday.

Grassley countered with examples of Democrats also violating those rules when they held the gavel. Regardless, once Republicans get the nominees out of committee and on to the Senate floor, Democrats have leverage in slowing down the process. Unless Republicans can reach a deal with Democrats, the Senate must devote 30 hours of floor time for appeals court nominees. Only two hours of floor are necessary for district court nominees, but even that could be a burden while the Senate also tries to pass a significant piece of permitting reform legislation.

Thune took a step towards navigating those competing interests on Wednesday, by laying the groundwork for the Senate to stick around through Friday – an uncommon work day for a chamber that usually wraps up by Thursday early afternoon – for opening votes that would start the floor clock on a tranche of district court and appellate nominees.

Democrats have the ability to make the floor process “excruciating” for Republicans, said John P. Collins, a professor at George Washington Law School who focuses on judicial nominations.

Historically, the parties have been able reach deals at the end of a Congress, when senators are eager to get home for the holidays, that allow for the quick confirmation of some nominees in exchange for leaving others behind.

But, Collins said, Republicans have also traditionally been more impassioned about judicial confirmations than Democrats.

“They might be more willing to stay up late in the night to hold all these votes in a way that Democrats were not.”

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer contributed to this report.

World.title: House Agriculture Committee Lauded for Intervention in Contentious Executive Order 166
World.content:
Monrovia, November 13, 2026 – A prominent rubber planter has commended the House of Representatives, through its Committee on Agriculture, for taking a bold step to bring all stakeholders together to examine the controversial Executive Order 166.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Mr. Charles Bamakpeh, Chief Executive Officer of Meawon Liberia Incorporated, said the Committee’s decision to convene series of roundtable discussions was a welcome intervention that could pave the way for better understanding and a recommendation to the President for a positive reversal of the order.



Since the issuance of Executive Order 166, local rubber farmers across the country have cried foul, arguing that the order disadvantages them while giving leverage to bigger farmers and concessionaires. Many smallholder farmers have expressed frustration on ground that the policy has made it difficult for them to compete and survive in the sector.

Bamakpeh indicated that the House’s intervention is timely and shows that lawmakers are listening to the plight of local farmers.

“This is a bold step by the House of Representatives. Bringing all stakeholders to one table to ascertain the facts surrounding Executive Order 166 is the right thing to do. It will lead to better conversation and a recommendation to the President,” Bamakpeh told legislative reporters at the Capitol Building.

The latest meeting, however, ended prematurely due to the absence of several key stakeholders, including representatives of big concession companies, regulatory authorities, and the Ministry of Agriculture.

According to Committee, the hearing could not properly proceed because of the absences and other irregularities observed. The Committee said it does not want to keep pushing the matter down without proper verification and stressed the need for all relevant parties to be present to ensure a fair and transparent process.

A new date for the hearing is expected to be announced once all parties have been duly notified.

Despite the postponement, Bamakpeh is somewhat excited for the step taken by the House.

“This action should be lauded, though it’s the first step forward.”

He called on the august body to exert further and speedy action to bring the situation to a successful and conclusive end.

“As I said, we appreciate the House for starting this process. We now call on them to act swiftly so that this matter can be brought to a successful and conclusive end for the benefit of all Liberian rubber farmers,” he added.

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai signed Executive Order No. 166 on June 24, 2026, banning the export of unprocessed natural rubber indefinitely, effective July 1, 2026. The order defines unprocessed rubber broadly such as natural latex, coagulum, cup lump, tree lace, bark scrap, ground scrap, and any rubber not subjected to industrial processing.

The government pointed out that the ban is intended to strengthen local processing, create employment, increase domestic value addition, and ensure Liberian rubber farmers benefit more directly from the industry.

But this has somewhat proven indifference, as local farmers believe that it’s an unjust way of taking them from the industry.

World.title: AfDB, World Bank Urge Liberia to Strengthen Institutions to Unlock More Development Financing
World.content:
CPIA workshop identifies weak governance and unreliable data as key barriers, as YEIB-MANCO CEO calls for establishment of National Data Center

By Charles G. Lamadine

Monrovia- The African Development Bank (AfDB) and the World Bank have called for stronger institutional performance, improved governance and reliable national data as critical measures to help Liberia secure increased concessional development financing.



The call was made during a one-day high-level Country Policy and Institutional Assessment (CPIA) workshop hosted on Wednesday by the AfDB Liberia Country Office in collaboration with the World Bank Liberia Office.

The workshop brought together deputy ministers from the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Public Works, alongside senior officials of the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL), technical representatives of both development institutions, the Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), and other government institutions and development partners.

The meeting focused on helping government officials understand the CPIA assessment process, examine Liberia’s current performance and identify reforms needed to improve the country’s ratings and access to concessional financing.

The workshop was moderated by AfDB Senior International Consultant, Dr. James Francis Davis, who described the CPIA as an important instrument for measuring the quality of a country’s policies and institutions in promoting economic growth and reducing poverty.

Dr. Davis explained that the assessment forms the foundation of the AfDB’s Performance-Based Allocation (PBA) system, which determines how a significant portion of the African Development Fund’s (ADF) concessional resources is distributed among 37 eligible African countries.

He noted that countries with stronger policies and institutions generally receive greater access to concessional financing, making the CPIA more than a technical assessment exercise.

According to him, Liberia’s performance under the assessment directly influences the volume of development financing it can access and also serves as an important reference for bilateral donors and international development partners.

Liberia’s CPIA Performance Under Review

Presentations during the workshop highlighted the differences and similarities between the AfDB and World Bank assessment frameworks.

While both institutions use nearly identical CPIA methodologies, they independently assess countries to determine their respective concessional financing allocations.

The AfDB presented its assessment methodology and recent scores for Liberia, explaining the relationship between the country’s performance and its allocation under the ADF.

The World Bank, meanwhile, outlined its assessment framework and explained how the ratings influence financing available to Liberia through the International Development Association (IDA).

The CPIA measures the quality of a country’s policies and institutions on a scale of one to six, with one representing the lowest performance and six the highest.

The AfDB framework comprises six clusters and 18 criteria, including an additional cluster on Regional Integration. Unlike the World Bank, which conducts its assessment annually, the AfDB carries out its CPIA assessment every two years.

Data presented at the workshop showed improvements in Liberia’s economic management, particularly in monetary policy, whose AfDB score increased from 3.5 in 2020 to 5.0 in 2025. Fiscal policy maintained a score of 4.0.

However, governance and other institutional performance indicators remain below regional averages, requiring further reforms and sustained government attention.

The World Bank’s assessment placed Liberia’s overall CPIA score at 3.0, with Public Sector Management and Governance recording the weakest performance at 2.6, compared with 3.3 for Economic Management.

Presenters emphasized the financial implications of these ratings, noting that a 0.1-point improvement in Liberia’s overall CPIA score could increase the country’s IDA allocation by approximately 10 to 13 percent.

The workshop also highlighted developments in Liberia’s Debt Sustainability Assessment (DSA), which has indicated an improvement in the country’s debt-carrying capacity from weak to medium.

However, participants were informed that two consecutive positive assessments are required before the improvement can be formally confirmed.

Workshop Recommends Inter-Ministerial Committee

To improve Liberia’s performance, the workshop recommended the establishment of an Inter-Ministerial Committee to coordinate and lead the national CPIA process.

It also called for the preparation of a detailed action matrix covering each CPIA cluster, with measurable targets, clearly assigned institutional responsibilities and implementation timelines.

The proposed committee would be required to report progress monthly or every two months to the Minister of Finance and Development Planning.

Another major recommendation was increased investment in institutions responsible for producing national statistics and ensuring that reliable, up-to-date information is accessible through official government websites.

Participants identified weak data collection, documentation and accessibility as significant obstacles to Liberia’s performance in international assessments.

Rwanda was cited as an example of a country that has made the CPIA an integral part of routine government performance management, contributing to stronger institutional ratings.

YEIB-MANCO CEO Calls for National Data Center

Meanwhile, the Chief Executive Officer of the Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), Joseph Fatorma Sando, has called for the establishment of a National Data Center to strengthen Liberia’s data collection, verification and management systems.

Delivering the institution’s statement, Mr. Sando urged the AfDB and World Bank to support the Government of Liberia in establishing a coordinated national data management system that would improve the timely collection and accessibility of credible information across ministries, agencies and public institutions.

He argued that the absence of reliable and verifiable data could negatively affect Liberia’s performance in international institutional assessments, regardless of the progress being made by government institutions.

“A Data Center Coordinator in every ministry, agency and parastatal will minimise the challenges currently affecting the country’s rating, which has a significant impact on economic decisions and investors’ attraction,” Sando stated.

He explained that a coordinated data management system would help Liberia improve its institutional ratings, strengthen its eligibility for concessional financing from the ADF and IDA, and build a stronger investment profile.

“Liberia is doing a lot, but if what we are doing is not documented, verified and made accessible in a timely manner, it will not count in these assessments,” he emphasized.

Sando further maintained that improved data management would strengthen government accountability and provide development partners and investors with credible evidence of the country’s progress.

Why the CPIA Matters to YEIB-MANCO

The workshop also holds strategic importance for YEIB-MANCO, which receives financing from the AfDB under the Program for Advancing Youth Entrepreneurship Investment (PAYEI).

According to the institution, improved CPIA performance could create greater opportunities for development financing and support the expansion of its three principal funding windows: the Investment Fund, Credit Guarantee Fund and Technical Assistance Fund.

YEIB-MANCO also noted that its institutional performance, particularly in procurement, disbursement, auditing and governance, contributes to the broader assessment of Liberia’s AfDB-supported development portfolio.

The institution said its growing database, which includes 1,124 applicants, information on women-owned businesses, financing requirements and employment creation, could provide useful evidence of progress in the country’s youth entrepreneurship sector.

It further highlighted its contribution to regional integration through support for businesses engaged in cross-border trade.

As a non-bank financial institution licensed by the Central Bank of Liberia, YEIB-MANCO said it recognizes the importance of maintaining strong standards of transparency, accountability and fund management.

YEIB-MANCO Pledges Support for Government Reform Efforts

Speaking at the close of the workshop, Sando reaffirmed the institution’s commitment to strengthening its internal governance, operational performance and data management systems to support Liberia’s broader development objectives.

“The CPIA shows clearly that the strength of our institutions determines how much development Liberia can attract. At YEIB, we will continue to strengthen our governance, delivery and data systems so that we contribute to better scores and unlock more financing for young Liberian entrepreneurs,” he said.

He also expressed YEIB-MANCO’s readiness to support any government-led CPIA coordination initiative, including serving as a pilot institution and data partner for private-sector and youth entrepreneurship indicators.

About YEIB-MANCO

The Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO) is a non-bank development finance institution licensed by the Central Bank of Liberia and financed by the African Development Bank.

Through its Investment Fund, Credit Guarantee Fund and Technical Assistance Fund, the institution provides financing and business development support to youth-led micro, small and medium-sized enterprises across Liberia, with a stated target of reaching 30,000 young entrepreneurs.

World.title: Liberia: Kemayah, Co-Defendants Appeal 10-Year Prison Sentences to Supreme Court
World.content:
As Criminal Court ‘C’ Denies Motion for New Trial Before Sentencing Convicted Officials in US$500,000 Saudi Rice Case

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and other defendants convicted in Liberia’s controversial US$500,000 Saudi Rice case have announced an appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia following Criminal Court ‘C’s denial of their motion for a new trial and subsequent imposition of prison sentences.



The announcement of the appeal came Friday, November 13, 2026, shortly after Criminal Court ‘C’, presided over by Judge Ousman Feika, denied the defense’s request for a new trial and proceeded to sentence the convicted defendants at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia.

Kemayah and some of his co-defendants were sentenced to 10 years in prison, while other convicted defendants received five-year prison terms, according to information from the court proceedings.

The decision marks another significant development in one of the most closely watched corruption-related prosecutions arising from the administration of former President George Manneh Weah.

With the motion for a new trial rejected and sentences imposed, the defense has now turned to the Supreme Court, seeking appellate review of the convictions and the proceedings that resulted in the guilty verdicts.

Defense Takes Fight to Supreme Court

The defense team’s decision to appeal follows its unsuccessful attempt to persuade Criminal Court ‘C’ to set aside the October 9 jury verdicts and order a fresh trial.

The motion for a new trial, which was heard on November 6, challenged the outcome of the proceedings involving 13 defendants accused of various offenses connected to the alleged diversion of humanitarian rice donated to Liberia by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The defense had maintained that the jury’s findings were inconsistent with the weight of evidence presented during the trial, which lasted more than 40 days.

However, Criminal Court ‘C’ declined to grant the requested relief, clearing the way for the court to proceed with sentencing.

The defense has now announced its intention to pursue an appeal before the Supreme Court, Liberia’s highest judicial authority.

The appeal is expected to place the trial proceedings, the jury’s findings, the denial of the new-trial motion, and the resulting sentences under further judicial scrutiny.

For Kemayah and his co-defendants, the Supreme Court represents the next available judicial avenue to challenge the outcome of the prosecution.

From Jury Verdict to Prison Sentences

The latest development follows the October 9, jury verdict, which produced mixed outcomes among the 13 defendants.

Eight defendants were found guilty, three were acquitted, while the jury failed to reach unanimous verdicts on two others.

Among those convicted were Kemayah, former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, and other former government officials.

The convictions arose from allegations involving the handling and distribution of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice donated by the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center in April 2023.

The donation was intended to assist disaster victims and vulnerable communities in Liberia.

Prosecutors alleged that 25,054 bags of the donated rice, valued at approximately US$425,918, were diverted from their intended humanitarian purpose.

The defendants faced charges including theft of property, economic sabotage, misuse of public office, criminal conspiracy, and misapplication of entrusted property.

The prosecution argued that the humanitarian donation was improperly handled, while the defense consistently challenged the allegations and the evidentiary basis of the case.

The October 9 verdicts subsequently resulted in the sentencing proceedings now being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court Review Could Become Another Major Legal Battle

The announcement of an appeal introduces another important phase in the Saudi Rice prosecution.

Under Liberia’s criminal justice framework, defendants convicted of criminal offenses have the right to seek appellate review of their convictions and sentences in accordance with applicable law and procedural requirements.

The Supreme Court will be expected to examine the issues properly raised in the appeal and determine whether the proceedings complied with the applicable legal standards.

Among the questions that could arise are whether the trial court properly applied the law, whether the evidence supported the jury’s findings, whether any prejudicial procedural errors occurred, and whether the denial of the motion for a new trial was legally justified.

The appellate proceedings will also provide an opportunity for the defense to formally present its objections to the convictions and sentences.

Depending on the arguments and the court’s findings, the Supreme Court may affirm the lower court’s decision, reverse all or part of the judgment, or grant another legally appropriate remedy.

However, the filing or announcement of an appeal does not automatically invalidate the convictions or sentences.

The defendants must pursue the appeal through the prescribed judicial process.

For the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, AREPT, and the Ministry of Justice, the convictions and sentencing represent a significant stage in the prosecution’s pursuit of accountability.

For Kemayah and his co-defendants, however, the rejection of their motion for a new trial has made an appeal to the Supreme Court their next major legal undertaking.

The three defendants acquitted by the jury remained distinct from those convicted and sentenced, while the two defendants against whom the jury could not reach unanimous verdicts remain subject to separate judicial proceedings.

As the matter moves toward the Supreme Court, the central legal question will no longer be limited to the prosecution’s allegations but will also encompass whether the convictions and sentences can withstand appellate scrutiny.

The Supreme Court’s eventual determination could have implications for the defendants and the broader administration of criminal justice in Liberia.

The Saudi Rice case, therefore, enters a new chapter, from the jury’s guilty verdicts, through the denial of a new trial and prison sentencing, to an impending appeal before the Supreme Court of Liberia.

World.title: COP31 Climate Finance Debate Highlights Liberia’s Funding Gap and Delayed Projects
World.content:
COP31 President Murat Kurum speaks at the Antalya Leaders Summit. Photo:UNFCCC

leaders at COP31 called for predictable climate finance, but reports show that much of the funding available to developing countries comes as loans, adding to debt pressures.

Liberia had received about US$213 million of the US$573 million identified in its previous climate plan by December 2024, while key projects, including its US$10 million Climate Information System and Monrovia’s coastal protection project, remain delayed.

Questions remain over whether climate finance will reach vulnerable communities. Experts argue that adaptation needs grants rather than loans, as debt repayments continue to limit the resources available for public services.

By Aria Deemie | Climate and Environment Reporter

African leaders at the United Nations climate conference in Türkiye have called on developed countries to deliver promised climate finance, warning that vulnerable nations cannot continue shouldering the growing costs of climate change.

For Liberia, the debate has immediate consequences. The country has identified hundreds of millions of dollars in climate financing needs, but much of that funding remains undisbursed. Meanwhile, projects intended to improve weather forecasting and protect communities from coastal erosion remain unfinished or delayed.



At the November 11–12 COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya, heads of state and government discussed climate adaptation, clean energy and finance. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed warned that the cost of climate damage was competing with investment in essential services.

“The more we spend coping with climate damage, the less we have to invest in schools, healthcare, and opportunity for our young people,” he said.

Liberia’s previous climate plan identified about US$573 million in financing. By December 2024, about US$213 million had been disbursed, leaving roughly US$360 million outstanding. This represents the difference between financing identified and money reported as disbursed. It does not mean all the funding had been approved and withheld.

Liberia is not alone. Across Africa, governments face mounting climate risks while struggling to finance and implement their climate plans.

At COP31, Côte d’Ivoire’s Vice President Tiemoko Meyliet Kone said unpredictable seasons were threatening agricultural production, household incomes and families’ futures. Seychelles Vice President Alix Sébastien Pillay called for climate finance commitments to be translated into actual resources, describing climate disasters as a major burden for small island nations.

Rwanda’s Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva said implementing the country’s latest climate plan would require US$12 billion in investment. He called for projects in developing countries to be assessed on their merits rather than their location. Zimbabwe’s Vice President Constantino Chiwenga also urged developed countries to provide measurable finance, including greater support for adaptation and loss and damage.

The experiences of other African countries show the scale and complexity of the challenge.

In Zambia, implementing the country’s climate plan across 11 priority sectors is estimated to cost about US$17.2 billion between 2023 and 2030, according to an International Monetary Fund assessment . The report identifies limited financing, technical capacity and coordination as constraints.

Malawi faces a different but related pressure. Its 2025/26 climate financing budget relies heavily on donor support, with 61 percent of on-budget donor development financing coming through blended arrangements involving loans and grants, according to a UNICEF budget brief . The brief warns that these loans add to the country’s already unsustainable external debt burden. The World Bank says interest payments alone absorb nearly half of Malawi’s domestic revenue , leaving less for social services, infrastructure and resilience spending.

Mozambique offers another perspective. Its National Directorate for Climate Financing says the country mobilized more than US$1.3 billion for climate projects between 2012 and 2024. About US$245 million came directly from international climate funds, with the remainder provided through co-financing. The projects cover coastal adaptation, food resilience and green infrastructure. The directorate also acknowledges technical and coordination challenges in accessing climate funds.

These examples show that countries face different obstacles, from raising money to implement climate plans to accessing international funds and managing the debt associated with borrowing.

A major concern is the form in which climate finance is provided. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, countries agreed that developed nations would take the lead in providing at least US$300 billion annually by 2035 to support climate action in developing countries, including efforts to reduce emissions, adapt to climate change and strengthen resilience. The agreement also called for finance from all sources to reach at least US$1.3 trillion annually by that year.

Mohamed Kamal of the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives , an international network working on environmental justice and zero-waste solutions, said the US$300 billion target fell short of what developing countries had demanded.

“The request at that time was a trillion dollars or $1.3 trillion just for the targeted annual climate finance to be provided,” he said.

Kamal criticized African negotiators who accepted the lower figure as a compromise.

“Some African negotiators decided back then that it’s better to take something instead of nothing. And that’s quite problematic,” he said.

He also questioned the reliance on loans to finance climate action, arguing that countries should not have to repay money for projects that protect people and ecosystems but do not generate revenue.

A November 10 report by CARE International adds to concerns about the debt burden. Its report, The Climate Finance Boomerang , found that 67 percent of public climate finance was provided as loans in 2024. It estimated that US$20.1 billion in repayments on climate loans fell due that year, compared with US$6.9 billion in 2020. The report warned that annual repayments could exceed new climate lending by 2036 if lending continued at its 2024 level and loan terms remained unchanged.

ActionAid Liberia’s September 2026 brief, Who Bears the Cost? Debt, Climate and the People Who Pay the Price , highlights the pressure debt repayments place on Liberia’s public finances. It reported that public debt reached US$2.84 billion by June 2026, up 317.5 percent from 2014. Debt servicing absorbed 18.65 percent of domestic revenue in 2025.

ActionAid warned that debt payments leave less room in the public budget for healthcare, education, water and social protection, even as climate disasters create additional demands on government spending.

For Kamal, loans are particularly unsuitable for adaptation projects, which help countries prepare for climate impacts but often do not generate income.

“Liberia’s needs are probably not mitigation. They are probably adaptation-oriented projects,” he said, pointing to forest protection.

“So why am I having to pay back a loan for them?”

At the Liberia Pavilion on November 12, Bushuben Keita, the President’s legal adviser, reiterated the government’s call for more accessible and predictable climate finance. Speaking on behalf of President Joseph Boakai, he called for faster adaptation funding and support for loss and damage, referring to climate-related harm that cannot be avoided through emissions cuts or adaptation.

“Vulnerable countries should be able to protect their people without deepening unsustainable debt,” Keita said.

The difficulties of turning climate finance into completed projects are already visible in Liberia. A FrontPage Africa investigation published in April 2025 documented years of delays to a US$10 million Climate Information System project intended to improve weather forecasting and provide early warnings to vulnerable communities. In its 2023 annual performance report, the African Development Bank, which oversees implementation, attributed some delays to the former Environmental Protection Agency’s administration failure to follow recruitment procedures and respond promptly to requests. The Bank also acknowledged that its own due-diligence review delayed the appointment of a project manager. Wilson Tarpeh, who headed the EPA under former President George Weah, disputed the Bank’s account, defending the recruitment process and saying the Bank’s internal procedures also contributed to the delays.

The ClimSA/PUMA2025 satellite weather-monitoring system, installed by the Liberia Meteorological Service at Roberts International Airport in October 2025 to support weather monitoring and forecasting in Liberia. The installation is separate from the US$10 million Climate Information System project discussed in this story. Photo: Liberia Meteorological Service.

A subsequent 2025 annual performance report , submitted by the Bank in July 2026 and still under review by the Green Climate Fund, identified further delays linked to differences between the Bank’s disbursement procedures and Liberia’s financial and tax regulations, the departure of the project’s procurement officer and the limited availability of government staff assigned to the project. The Bank said corrective measures agreed in December 2025 included recruiting a new procurement officer and improving coordination with the Ministry of Finance. Although the report recorded progress in project planning, financial management and staff training, it did not indicate that the early-warning system was operational. The Fund’s project page lists the project as under implementation, with completion estimated for October 2027 and US$4.17 million disbursed from the US$10 million grant.

A separate project to protect Monrovia’s coastline is also behind schedule. The US$25.6 million Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project includes plans for a 1,050-metre coastal defense structure at West Point, where erosion threatens homes and livelihoods. In a November 8 update , the Environmental Protection Agency reported that construction had not started by the end of October because contract negotiations were still ongoing. About US$2.07 million had been spent from US$21.37 million in cash commitments.

Aerial view of West Point, a coastal community in Monrovia, Liberia, vulnerable to coastal erosion and flooding. Photo: Yale News.

Accessing international climate funds presents another hurdle. Kamal said governments can work through institutions such as the United Nations Development Programme or the World Bank when they lack nationally accredited institutions to access funding directly. But this does not remove the difficulty of preparing proposals that meet the funds’ requirements.

Liberia’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution, its official climate plan, targets a 64 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035. Achieving that target depends substantially on international financial and technical support. The country also faces flooding, coastal erosion and changing rainfall patterns, with limited infrastructure and resources to respond.

African governments have also struggled to secure agreement on some of their negotiating priorities. At the start of COP31, the African Group sought a separate agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. The proposal did not secure consensus and was not included as a standalone item on the official agenda, although the COP31 presidency said the issue could still be discussed elsewhere.

The African Group also pushed for discussions on climate-related trade measures and an assessment of funding needs for the Green Climate Fund.

Kamal believes African countries need to use their collective political influence more forcefully.

“We are the continent in the most need for adaptation. There’s no question among it,” he said.

“We’re not going to get anywhere if we’re not more confrontational, if we’re not more direct.”

He suggested African governments could use political meetings beyond COP negotiations to strengthen their common position.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership ,a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia: Seven Charged And Forwarded To Court Over Assault on Police Officer in Sinkor
World.content:
Officer Reportedly Suffers Eye Injuries as Attackers Allegedly Seize Police Radio, Cap and US$150

Monrovia-The Liberia National Police, LNP, has arrested and forwarded seven individuals to court over the alleged assault of a police officer and obstruction of law enforcement personnel performing their official duties in Sinkor, Monrovia.

By:Willie N. Tokpah

The suspects, identified as Yokie Johnson, Rachel Johnson, Obediah Yorkor, Anthony Hallie, Spencil Z. Gaye, Prince Sackie and Harris Clomo, are facing multiple criminal charges arising from an incident involving officers responding to a situation on 26th Street, behind ERA Supermarket.



According to an official police statement issued Thursday, November 12, the incident occurred when Police Officer Sedeke K. Kammara, accompanied by two officers of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, LDEA, responded to a reported situation in the area.

However, the police alleged that while the officers were attending to the situation, they were attacked by a group of individuals from the beachside.

The LNP statement further disclosed that the two LDEA officers reportedly left the scene during the confrontation, leaving Officer Kammara behind, where he was allegedly assaulted.

The officer reportedly sustained injuries to his right eye during the incident.

Beyond the physical injuries, the attackers allegedly took his police-issued communication radio, face cap, and US$150 in cash.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged departure of the two LDEA officers during the confrontation were not immediately explained in the police statement.

Following an investigation, the LNP arrested the seven suspects and forwarded them to court to face prosecution.

Multiple Criminal Charges

The suspects are facing charges of Aggravated Assault, Hindering Law Enforcement, Physical Obstruction of Government Functions, Theft of Property and Disorderly Conduct.

The charges were brought under Sections 14.20, 12.4, 12.1, 15.51 and 17.3 of Liberia’s Revised Penal Law.

If proven in court, the allegations could expose the defendants to criminal penalties under the applicable provisions of the law.

However, the suspects remained entitled to the constitutional presumption of innocence, and the prosecution will be required to establish the allegations against each defendant through the judicial process.

Police Warns Against Attacks On Officers

In its statement, the Liberia National Police condemned violence against police officers and other law enforcement personnel performing their lawful responsibilities.

The police maintained that no individual has the right to assault, threaten, or obstruct officers in the execution of their official duties.

The institution also reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining public order, protecting lives and property, and ensuring that individuals suspected of violating the law are held accountable through due process.

The incident has again drawn attention to the safety of law enforcement personnel operating in communities across Monrovia, particularly when responding to confrontations involving groups of individuals.

Meanwhile, the prosecution of the seven suspects is expected to provide an opportunity for the court to examine the circumstances surrounding the confrontation, the injuries sustained by Officer Kammara and the alleged disappearance of his police-issued equipment and personal cash.

World.title: Liberia: Was Cllr.  Benedict Sannoh A Victim of Chicanery, Betrayal and Ingratitude?
World.content:
Counsellor Benedict Sannoh

MONROVIA – An independent assessment conducted in the case involving Counsellor Benedict Sannoh and two complainants in which a six months’ suspension was recommended against him has uncovered what appears to be a chicanery , betrayal and ingratitude against him.

By Augustus D.R Bortue-augustusd.rbortue@frontpageafricaonline,com

Following a series of hearings, the committee asked that he be suspended for alleged misconduct. But an independent probe has shown a more detailed information about what really transpired, how and why .



Cllr. Sannoh was approached by Madam Jallawleh Kollie to help them receive every benefit for a group policy of her late father, which he held with John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company when he worked for the Massachusett Bay Transport.

It was established by our assessment that this matter dates back to 2002 and was initially looked into by the Ministry of Justice.

On July 19, 2024, Madam Kollie again built a 160 thousand dollars case against Cllr. Sannoh, claiming he had negotiated on their behalf to receive such amount .

However, this was on the contrary again when Madam Kollie drew in Cllr. Varnie Sherman who she said had promised to give her 50 thousand on behalf of some relatives against said amount but she declined. It is not known whether the issue of the 160 thousand was taken before the committee.

A statute of limitation in the law says once a matter is not brought before the court after three years such matter is barred from being heard especially when those involved are in the country. It is more than twenty years since this issue came to the fore, our investigation has established.

World.title: Liberia’s City Streets in Limbo
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — In Liberia’s county capitals, paved streets have been promised many times. This year, the money was finally set aside. The pavement has not followed.

By Rodney D. Sieh

By September 30, the government had recorded more than $10 million against 15 city street projects, in towns from Buchanan on the Atlantic coast to Zwedru near the Ivorian border. The figures appear in the Ministry of Public Works’ pages of the draft national budget for 2027. On Thursday, the ministry said not one contractor had been paid.



The money, it said, is caught in the paperwork of the Ministry of Finance, at the purchase-order stage, a step short of the vouchers that release cash. Contractors will not move equipment onto sites until advance payments arrive. The ministry expects the work to be substantially complete by March 2027.

In Liberia, public money passes several gates before it reaches a contractor.

The Legislature approves it. The PPCC, the procurement regulator, clears the contract. The Finance Ministry releases an allotment, a purchase order commits it to a named firm, and only a payment voucher releases cash. The ministry says most city streets money is stuck at the fourth gate.

The budget book suggests the money may run out before the asphalt arrives. Liberia’s fiscal year ends December 31. In the draft budget for 2027, every city streets line under Public Works is blank.

For a country of about 5.5 million people, where most roads outside the capital are unpaved and many turn to mud in the rainy season, city streets are among the most visible promises of President Joseph Boakai’s government. Public Works Minister Roland Layfette Giddings has called November and December critical months, as the dry season opens the best window to build.

A statement, and numbers that match

The ministry’s statement, headlined “MPW Sets the Record Straight,” followed local media reports that $10.1 million had been disbursed. It urged the public to do due diligence before publishing information about its work.

On its central claim, the government’s own figures support the ministry. Fourteen projects, it says, have cleared Liberia’s procurement watchdog, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC). All 14 show money recorded: $9.12 million of $13.2 million budgeted. The 11 projects still waiting for the commission’s sign-off, known as a “No Objection,” show nothing.

Most of the cleared projects sit close to 70 percent of their budgets.

That is the pattern of a fixed tranche set aside, not of bills paid for work done.

Where the account frays

Not every figure fits. Two projects are recorded in full: $300,000 for streets in Ganta, a trading hub near the Guinean border, and $200,000 for a road to the Duport Road/Soul Clinic community outside Monrovia. The ministry describes all of its allotments as partial. It did not explain the difference.

Then there is Kakata, a market town about 50 kilometres from the capital. The full $950,000 budgeted for its streets is recorded. The ministry says Kakata is a separate, older contract on which paving has begun, but did not say how much the contractor has received. In March, residents complained that work had stood still since November 2025.

Buchanan, the port city that carries the largest allocation at $2.5 million, raises a sharper question.

At a November 3 briefing, Giddings listed it among projects already underway. Nine days later, his ministry said the Buchanan contractor had not been paid and would mobilise only after an advance.

The delays are not new.

In October, Giddings acknowledged the programme was behind schedule. It had been drawn up with legislators, he said, so engineers had to gather data in the field before tendering could begin. He expected the contracts to be finalised with the Finance Ministry within about a month. Six weeks after the September tally, the money still had not moved.

A race against the calendar

The deeper problem is time. Roughly $4.1 million budgeted for the cleared projects has not been set aside at all. The 11 projects still awaiting clearance, worth $4.35 million, range from Greenville and Cestos, whose tenders closed only on October 23, to Sanniquellie, Yekepa, Tappita and the Gibi road in Margibi County. None has a line in the 2027 draft.

Unless unspent balances are carried over, or lawmakers restore the lines before passing the budget, towns could be left with signed contracts and no money to honour them. The same budget page raises wider questions about the ministry’s spending.

A programme to buy road-building “yellow machines” had recorded $8.57 million against a $5.97 million budget, $2.6 million over, and the 2027 draft proposes $14.2 million more. Street lights and two other lines show money recorded with nothing budgeted at all.

Larger projects fared better than the streets. The $26 million St. Paul Bridge and Bo-Waterside roads and the $5 million ELWA–RIA road are recorded in full. Across all its capital projects, the ministry had recorded $80.65 million of $115.4 million, or 70 percent, by September 30.

It is unclear whether the budget’s “year to date” figures record cash paid or money set aside, and whether unspent balances will carry into 2027. It also raises questions as to how much the Kakata contractor has received, and why Ganta and Duport Road are recorded in full.

The ministry closed its statement with a rebuke to its critics: the call for accountability, it said, must come from a position of transparency. In a dozen county capitals, residents will judge that by what is on their streets when the rains return.

World.title: What Benoni Urey’s Role on Dangote’s ECOWAS Business Council Means for Liberia
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three decades ago, Liberia needed West Africa’s soldiers to help end its civil war. Today, it has a chance to help shape the region’s economic future.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Benoni W. Urey, a Liberian businessman best known as a founding shareholder of the mobile network Lonestar Cell MTN, has been named Liberia’s representative on the ECOWAS Business Council. The council is a new advisory body chaired by Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, and is meant to give the private sector a direct line to the presidents of West Africa.



The appointment comes at a delicate moment. The regional bloc has lost three members, its trade ambitions have stalled, and its energy map is being redrawn by one giant Nigerian oil refinery.

Whether Liberia’s new seat delivers anything for ordinary people — cheaper fuel, easier border crossings, steadier electricity, a bigger market for Liberian goods — will depend on how the council works, whose interests it serves, and how hard Liberia’s representative fights for a small country in a room full of giants.

A Bloc Under Strain

The Economic Community of West African States, or ECOWAS, was founded in Lagos, Nigeria, in 1975. Liberia was one of its founding members.

For many Liberians, though, ECOWAS means peacekeeping more than trade. Its military force, ECOMOG, entered Liberia’s civil war in 1990, and ECOWAS mediators helped broker the 2003 peace agreement in Accra, Ghana, that ended 14 years of conflict.

Fifty years after its founding, the bloc’s economic promise remains largely unfulfilled.

It has also shrunk. In January 2025, the military-led governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formally walked out and formed their own Alliance of Sahel States. That left ECOWAS with 12 members and cost it roughly a fifth of the levy revenue that funds its institutions. In October 2026 the two blocs agreed to set up working groups to manage their relationship, but there is no sign of a reunion.

Trade among members remains thin. Less than 15 percent of the region’s trade happens between ECOWAS countries, held back by tariffs, red tape, roadside checkpoints and poor roads. A long-promised single currency, the Eco, has been postponed again and again; leaders now say it will launch in 2027, starting with the countries that meet its economic targets.

The bloc also has new leadership. General Birame Diop of Senegal now heads the ECOWAS Commission, succeeding Dr. Omar Alieu Touray of The Gambia.

For Liberia, a country of about five million people, the stakes are practical. It trades heavily with neighbouring Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, imports almost all of its fuel, and depends on regional power lines and road links that ECOWAS helps plan and fund.

Long Promised, Just Starting

The ECOWAS Business Council is not quite as new as it appears. ECOWAS ministers created it on paper in 2021, and its launch slipped from December 2024 to September 2025. Dangote was finally named its first chairman by the bloc’s foreign ministers in Abuja in December 2025, and West African heads of state later endorsed him.

The council’s job is to advise ECOWAS leaders on trade, investment and industrial policy, and to help clear the barriers that stop people, goods, services and money from moving freely across the region’s borders.

Each member state gets one representative, and Nigeria, the region’s largest economy, gets two more. Regional business associations also have a voice. Dangote’s team says his two-year term will focus on energy corridors to ease the power shortages that choke business, as well as ports and logistics, with funding to be sought from lenders such as the African Export-Import Bank and the Africa Finance Corporation.

The council is still finding its feet. By mid-2026 only a handful of national representatives had been confirmed, and its first meeting was planned for late October or early November, with further approvals due at a ministerial meeting in December.

The risk is familiar. Business councils across Africa have often become talking shops. This one will be judged on results — fewer roadblocks, faster customs clearance, power projects that actually get built — and on whether its members speak for market traders and young companies, not just the region’s biggest conglomerates.

Dangote at the Helm

Choosing Aliko Dangote sends a clear signal about how ECOWAS sees its future: industrial, energy-driven and led by large regional investors.

No single business has done more to change West Africa’s fuel market in recent years. Dangote’s refinery outside Lagos, built at a reported cost of about US$20 billion, reached its full design capacity of 650,000 barrels a day in February 2026 and is aiming for 700,000. It now supplies most of Nigeria’s fuel, and according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Nigeria’s fuel exports to other African countries rose to nearly 120,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026. Analysts estimate the refinery has cut West Africa’s imports of refined fuel from outside the region by close to a quarter. When the conflict involving Iran disrupted supplies from the Gulf and Europe this year, Dangote stepped in with more gasoline exports across the continent.

The company markets its cleaner, European-standard fuel as an end to the days when West Africa served as a dumping ground for low-quality imports.

For Liberia, which imports nearly all its fuel and where pump prices have often run higher than in neighbouring countries, a major refinery a few days’ sail away could mean shorter supply chains, more reliable deliveries in a crisis, and cleaner fuel.

But there are real concerns.

The first is concentration. A region that trades its dependence on Europe and the Gulf for dependence on one private refinery gains proximity but may lose competition. And the council advising presidents on energy and trade policy will be chaired by that refinery’s owner.

The second is conflict of interest. Dangote’s empire spans cement, sugar, fertilizer and petroleum — all sectors shaped by tariffs, import rules and industrial policy. Dangote has long argued that Africa should produce what it consumes and has championed protection for local manufacturers. Regional protection can help West African industry grow, but small, import-dependent economies like Liberia can end up paying more for everyday goods.

The third is Nigeria’s weight. With three seats and the chairmanship, Nigerian business interests will carry outsized influence in the council’s decisions.

None of this means the council cannot serve the whole region. Dangote has publicly urged governments to protect private investment, back local investors and keep their policies consistent — messages that resonate with business owners in Monrovia. The real test is whether the council produces rules that open markets or rules that protect those already on top.

The Record Urey Brings

Urey’s career spans several of the sectors the council has made its priorities.His biggest business success is in telecommunications. Through his company PLC Investments, he was a founding shareholder of Lonestar Communications Corporation, which launched in 2001 in partnership with South Africa’s MTN Group. Lonestar grew into one of Liberia’s two main mobile networks and a major provider of mobile money. That experience matters: ECOWAS wants payment systems that work across borders, and cross-border mobile money may be the most direct way regional integration reaches traders and families who send money to relatives in neighbouring countries.

He also knows shipping. From 1996 to 2003, Urey headed Liberia’s Bureau of Maritime Affairs, which oversees the country’s international ship registry. Liberia, despite its size, flags one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, making the registry one of the country’s few globally significant economic assets. With ports and logistics high on Dangote’s agenda, that background could prove useful.

On energy, Urey once served as a deputy director general at the state-owned Liberia Electricity Corporation. Power is the council’s headline priority, and Liberia remains one of the least electrified countries in the region. Urey could press for faster completion of the regional power lines linking Liberia with Côte d’Ivoire, Sierra Leone and Guinea.

He also runs commercial farms in Konola and Careysburg, outside Monrovia, that supply the local market — relevant in a country that still imports much of its staple food, rice.

And he knows politics. Urey served as mayor of Careysburg and founded the All Liberian Party, running for president in 2017. That gives him a feel for how policy plays out on the ground, but it also raises a question: how will a political party leader keep party interests separate from a regional business role?

What Liberia Should Ask For

A well-connected representative could push hard on the issues that matter most to a small economy. Among them: ending harassment and illegal fees at busy border crossings such as Bo Waterside, on the Sierra Leone border, and Ganta, on the Guinea border; securing regional fuel supply on fair terms; speeding up power links; making mobile payments work across borders; and opening regional financing to Liberian small businesses.

Urey has said he wants Liberia’s entrepreneurs and young companies to have a clear voice in regional policy. That promise is the yardstick by which his tenure should be measured.

What to Watch

Three questions will shape how this appointment is judged.

Business interests. The council will advise on telecoms, digital finance, agriculture and trade — sectors in which Urey has commercial stakes. Lonestar’s competition with rival Orange Liberia is one example. The council should publish a clear conflict-of-interest policy for all its members.

Selection. The press statement announcing the appointment says Urey was chosen after consultations across the region and that membership is by invitation. It is not clear whether Liberia’s government, its Chamber of Commerce or its business associations had a say.

Accountability. Liberian businesses will need a way to bring their concerns to their representative, and a way to hear back from him.

The Bottom Line

Liberia has gained a voice in a body that, if it works, could influence how fuel, power, money and goods move across West Africa. Dangote’s chairmanship gives the council financial muscle and direct access to presidents. It also concentrates influence in the hands of the region’s most dominant industrialist.

For a small country with limited bargaining power, the value of Urey’s seat will be measured in concrete results: lower costs at the border, reliable fuel and electricity, and real opportunities for Liberian entrepreneurs. Anything less, and the appointment will be just another title.

World.title: PRESIDENT HICHILEMA ENGAGES SOUTHERN PROVINCE TRADITIONAL LEADERS ON DEVELOPMENT
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on traditional leaders in Southern Province to encourage their subjects to reserve adequate maize stocks ahead of the 2026/2027 farming season, which is projected to be affected by El Niño weather conditions.

‎And the Head of State has reaffirmed the government’s commitment to sustaining development gains achieved during his first term, including investments in free education.

‎Mr Hichilema was speaking in Choma today when he addressed traditional leaders during a celebratory community engagement following his re- election in the August 13 general elections.

‎ President Hichilema assured traditional leaders that the government will work closely with them to ensure the successful implementation of various development programmes.

” We are grateful that the public trusted us by ensuring UPND emerged victorious. They elected us into office to serve the Zambian people therefore we pledge to ensure that we deliver on our developmental promises,” He explained.

President Hichilema also called on traditional leaders to help fight early marriages and keep young girls in school so they can benefit from the Free Education Policy.

He implored traditional leaders to engage headmen and other community leaders to heighten public awareness against the vice.

“As a government we have invested in the free education policy that ensures all children have an opportunity to go to school. I implore you all to sensitize your subjects about the need to ensure all children go to school. Education is one-way girls can be safeguard from early marriages” He added.

Meanwhile, Southern Province Council of Chiefs Chairperson, Chief Nalubamba, has pledged the traditional leadership’s continued support for Government programmes aimed at advancing national development.

World.title: MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND MEDIA PS ANNOUNCES LAUNCH OF THE 2027 SADC MEDIA AWARDS COMPETITION
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana has announced the launch of the 2027 Southern African Development Community (SADC) Media Awards competition.

The competition is open to journalists in four categories: Photojournalism, Print Journalism, Television Journalism and Radio Journalism.

To be eligible for the competition, entries must comprise journalistic works that were published or broadcast between 1st January and 31st December 2026 and only works published or broadcast within this eligibility period will be considered for the 2027 Awards.

Mr Kawana said the competition underscores the important role of the media in informing citizens about SADC’s activities and achievements, while providing a platform for journalists to bring regional issues closer to communities across the region.

The Permanent Secretary noted that through quality, accurate and impactful journalism, media practitioners play a critical role in strengthening public awareness, enhancing the visibility of SADC and promoting greater citizen participation in the regional integration process.

“Under the 2027 competition, the first-prize winner in each of the four categories will receive US$2,500, while the runner-up in each category will receive US$1,000. The winners will be announced during the Opening Ceremony of the 47th SADC Summit of Heads of State and Government, scheduled to be held in Zambia,” Mr Kawana revealed.

He has since encouraged journalists across the country to participate in the competition and take advantage of the opportunity to showcase their journalistic talent, creativity and professionalism while contributing to greater public awareness and understanding of SADC’s regional integration agenda.

Established in 1996, the SADC Media Awards recognise outstanding journalistic work that contributes to the dissemination of information about SADC and promotes greater public understanding of the regional integration agenda.

The Awards seek to recognise journalists who demonstrate excellence, originality, accuracy, depth of research and impact in reporting on SADC programmes, policies, initiatives and matters relating to regional cooperation and integration.

Interested journalists can obtain further information and entry forms from the SADC National Media Coordinator at the Ministry of Information and Media or through the Ministry’s website: www.mim.gov.zm.

Completed entry forms, with all required information duly typed, must be submitted to the SADC National Media Coordinator at the Ministry of Information and Media no later than 28th February 2027.

World.title: CHIPOLOPOLO FORCED TO SHARE SPOILS WITH BURUNDI
World.content:
Senior Chipolopolo coach George Lwandamina has expressed disappointment after Zambia was held to a 1-1 draw by Burundi in the 2027 Africa cup qualifier game at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on the Copperbelt.

Speaking during the post-match press briefing, Lwandamina said the team lacked proper coordination during the match.

‎”It is a bad day,” Chicken George Lwandamina said.

‎He, however, expressed confidence that the players will bounce back in the next encounter against Burundi on 17 November next week.

‎Zambia took the lead in the 64th minute through Edward Chilufya, whose low shot beat Burundi goalkeeper Jonathan Nahimana following a good pass by Albert Kangwanda.

‎However, Burundi responded through Jean Claude Girumugisha, who found the back of the net to restore parity and secure a point for the visitors.

The first half ended goalless, with Burundi showing greater dominance during the opening 45 minutes.

‎Meanwhile, Burundi national team coach Patrick Sangwa praised his players for their performance and that they did a good job against a tough Zambian side.

‎”As expected, we knew we would face a tough game, but credit to my players, they have done a good job,” he said.

‎Sangwa said his team will continue preparing for the return fixture in Bujumbura, Burundi.

World.title: UPND GAINING POPULARITY COUNTRYWIDE SAYS PRESIDENT HICHILEMA
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) has continued to gain popularity across the country, with its growing support reflected in the over three million votes he secured in the August 13 general elections and the party’s performance in the recently held 14 by-elections.

Speaking during a UPND thanksgiving community engagement at Choma Sports Club in Southern Province, President Hichilema called on party members to remain united, protect the party and continue expanding its support base to make it the party of choice across all ten provinces.

He challenged councillors and party officials to intensify mobilisation, urging them to reach out to communities and strengthen party structures down to polling station level.

“Councillors, let us go out there and mobilise our people. Let us start from our constituencies, our wards and right down to every polling station. We must make sure that our people are mobilised,” Mr Hichilema said.

The President said party mobilisation was important in sustaining the development programmes being implemented by his administration.

“If we want to continue enjoying the different developments we are enjoying, let us mobilise for the party because it is the party that delivers,” he said.

Mr Hichilema thanked the people of Southern Province for giving him a second mandate, assuring them that his administration remained committed to delivering development and improving the lives of citizens.

He reaffirmed his government’s commitment to free education, saying the policy remained central to expanding access to education for children across the country.

The President also directed teachers who had deserted their rural stations to immediately return to their original places of deployment or risk being replaced.

Meanwhile, UPND alliance partner Highvie Hamududu and former Minister of Transport and Logistics Frank Tayali called on the people of Southern Province to continue supporting President Hichilema and his development agenda.

The thanksgiving community engagement attracted thousands of people from across Southern Province, including party supporters, alliance partners, local leaders and residents who gathered at Choma Sports Club to interact with the Head of State.

World.title: ENGINEERS CERTIFYING POOR-QUALITY PROJECTS FACE DISMISSAL
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary Milner Mwanakampwe has called for the dismissal of engineers who certify substandard works that fail within five years of completion.

Dr Mwanakampwe said substandard works are a burden on the government, stressing that contractors responsible for such projects should be blacklisted, while government engineers who certify the defective works should be dismissed.

He was responding to Chibmbo District Commissioner Lloyd Kayeka who said a whole classroom block at Shifwankula Primary School was last week blown off following a heavy downpour, barely three years after it was built.

The Permanent Secretary indicated during a courtesy on the District Commissioner that a number of newly built structures across the province continue to experience damage while those built in the Kaunda era are still standing saying the quality of the works should be questionable.

“There must be a quality audit after so that all those involved in the construction and certification of the works are identified after which necessary punitive measures should be taken,” said Dr Mwanakampwe.

Earlier, Mr Kayeka announced that a number of schools had their roofs blown off following last week’s heavy rains, with Shifwankula being the worst hit.

He stated that the infrastructure was constructed by a well-wisher about three years ago.

Mr Kayeka said a team of engineers was sent to assess the extent of damage and to quantify the materials needed for the blown off classrooms.

He said the affected schools require urgent rehabilitation works before the rains intensify.

World.title: GOVERNMENT REAFFIRMS COMMITMENT TO CREATING AN ENABLING BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
World.content:
The Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) has hosted the 2026 IDC Group Directors’ Forum to review the institutional performance of its subsidiary and investee companies and to develop strategies that will strengthen the Group’s contribution to Zambia’s national development agenda.

Minister of Industry Noel Nkhoma who officiated at the forum, urged all public and private sectors to play a leading role in driving the Grow Zambia Agenda through increased production, investment and value addition.

Mr Nkhoma said the government has made significant progress in stabilising the economy and assured that it is investing in creating an enabling environment to drive its development agenda, ensuring that these efforts go beyond mere rhetoric and translate into tangible investments, job creation, and economic growth.

He further reaffirmed the government’s commitment to safeguarding local industries and called on businesses to honour their tax obligations, stressing that the attainment of the country’s economic goals depends on enhanced collaboration between the Government and key stakeholders across all sectors.

Meanwhile, IDC Board Director and Chairperson of Investment and Portfolio Management Committee Beatrice Nkanza emphasised the importance of collaboration and partnerships among businesses, boards and stakeholders in achieving Zambia’s national development objectives, noting that organisations must move away from working in isolation and instead coordinate their efforts towards a common goal.

Mrs Nkanza urged businesses to complement one another, saying collaboration is key to achieving the set objectives.

She implored boards to rethink their strategies by embracing investment, taking calculated risks, and fostering partnerships to address challenges such as limited financial resources, technological constraints, and shortages of skilled manpower.

World.title: Zambia Police to go digital
World.content:
Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security Clement Andeleki has disclosed that Government plans to digitalise Zambia Police Service operations to strengthen crime prevention, detection and national security.

Dr Andeleki says this will involve the deployment of surveillance cameras in strategic public places, enabling the Police to respond to crime more effectively.

He was speaking at the 2026 Lusaka Division Superior Officers’ Annual Ball, held under the theme “A Peaceful Nation, Our Shared Responsibility”.

The Minister also commended Police officers for their professionalism in maintaining law and order and ensuring a peaceful electoral process during the 2026 general elections.

Dr Andeleki said the planned digital transformation forms part of the government’s broader development agenda aimed at modernizing public institutions and improving service delivery.

And speaking earlier, Lusaka Province Police Commissioner Ronald Zaambo pledged to intensify efforts to reduce crime levels in 2027.

Mr Zaambo added that security remains critical to national development and attracting investment.

He reaffirmed the Police Service’s commitment to supporting the government’s efforts to maintain law and order, safeguard life and property, and foster national unity.

Mr Zaambo has also urged officers to uphold integrity, discipline and professionalism while executing their duties.

Meanwhile, Lusaka Province Minister Obvious Mwaliteta who was also present at the event urged Police officers to always maintain professionalism as they discharge their duties.
