World.title: YOUTHS IN SOLWEZI PLEDGE TO WORK WITH THE LOCAL AUTHORITY
World.content:
The United Party for National Development (UPND) in North-Western Province has pledged to work with the Solwezi Mayor in fostering development in the district.

Speaking when UPND Provincial Youth Chairperson Bruce Kanema paid a courtesy call on Solwezi Mayor Evans Lubelenga today, Mr Kanema said the youths are ready to work closely with the office of the Mayor to address challenges being faced in the district.

He has appealed to the Mayor to embrace everyone and serve people equally regardless of their political affiliation, adding that his office is meant to serve every community member in Solwezi.

“We want people to freely come to your office to access services and information on programs the government is implementing for its people,” said Mr Kanema.

Meanwhile, Solwezi Mayor Evans Lubelenga says he is committed to working closely with President Hakainde Hichilema in achieving his vision of serving all Zambians equally and ensuring that development reaches all members of the community.

World.title: Former mine director loses reinstatement bid
World.content:
FORMER Botha Gold Mine managing director, Themba Hlongwani, has suffered a major High Court setback in his bid to reclaim his job at the Bindura-based mining operation.

In a 15-page judgment issued on November 11, Justice Samuel Deme struck Hlongwani and former board chairman Augustine Manyau’s urgent application from the urgent roll with costs, citing significant weaknesses in their case.

The two had challenged resolutions passed at the company’s extraordinary general meeting on October 20, which endorsed their expulsion and appointed Munyaradzi Nzarayapenga as interim board chairman.

World.title: Muguti was out of order: Charamba
World.content:
PRESIDENTIAL spokesperson George Charamba, has publicly rebuked former Local Government and Public Works permanent secretary Tafadzwa Muguti saying he was fired for going “out of order”.

Charamba’s remarks came a day after Muguti was fired from the influential government post, barely two months after his appointment. .

World.title: Minister orders ZIMDEF to deliver results, not just collect money
World.content:
Local News

Valentine Maya · November 12, 2026

HIGHER and Tertiary Education minister Frederick Shava has reminded the Zimbabwe Manpower Development Fund (ZIMDEF) that its success will be measured by the skills it imparts on students and the jobs it supports, not by the money it collects or disburses.

Officially opening the 2026 ZIMDEF strategic planning workshop in Mutare this Thursday, Shava said, “ZIMDEF must remain focused on interventions that deliver tangible value to the economy, within its statutory mandate and the Ministry’s policy priorities.”

Shava said the retreat must produce a comprehensive assessment of 2026 performance against the strategic plan; clearly defined corrective measures for outstanding commitments and implementation challenges; and a realistic, costed and prioritised 2027 annual work programme and budget aligned with the government’s long-term plans.

He also said the workshop’s outcomes must be an evidence-based assessment that demonstrates what has been achieved, what remains outstanding and what must be done differently to improve delivery.

“Last year, ZIMDEF developed its 2026–2030 strategic plan, aligned with the Second National Development Strategy (NDS2). Our task today is to take stock of implementation during 2026, identify areas requiring improvement and agree on strategic priorities for 2027,” he said.

He urged delegates to approach the exercise with openness, objectivity and a clear focus on results.

The Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education, Innovation, Science and Technology Development, ambassador Frederick Shava, receives a token of appreciation from ZIMDEF vice chairperson colonel Siwinile Tauya at the ZIMDEF 2026 Strategic Planning Review Workshop in Mutare.

Pictures: MHTEISTD Communications and Advocacy Officer Kudakwashe Hunda

On the 2027 budget, Shava said resource allocation must be guided by strategic priorities, available resources, demonstrated needs and the readiness of proposed projects for implementation.

“Particular attention must be given to completing ongoing projects and ensuring that previous investments generate their intended benefits,” he said.

Shava also called for tighter revenue collection.

“I wish to emphasise the importance of strengthening revenue mobilisation and compliance and ZIMDEF must sustain engagement with contributing employers, improve the efficiency of collections and pursue outstanding obligations consistently and professionally, within the applicable legal framework,” he said.

The minister also tied the fund’s work to the ministry’s heritage-based education 5.0 philosophy.

“Within this framework, ZIMDEF has a critical responsibility to support the development of a skilled, competent and productive workforce that responds to the needs of our economy,” he said.

He acknowledged the ZIMDEF board and management’s continued commitment to strengthening the fund’s contribution to skills development and human capital formation in Zimbabwe.

World.title: Ambition without means is inadequate, says VP Chiwenga
World.content:
VICE-PRESIDENT Constantino Chiwenga has told world leaders at the COP31 Leaders’ Summit that developed countries must turn their climate finance pledges into transparent and measurable financial flows, warning that ambition without means is inadequate.

Speaking on behalf of President Emmerson Mnangagwa in Antalya, Turkiye, Chiwenga said the commitment to mobilise at least US$300 billion annually under the Paris Agreement must be honoured, with developed countries taking the lead.

“Commitments must be honoured and measurable,” he said.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - After The Historic Achievement, The Challenge of a Lasting Legacy for Africa
World.content:
The first Youth Olympic Games held on the African continent, the Dakar 2026 YOG, concluded on November 13th with a record praised by leaders of the Olympic movement. Beyond the organizational success and popular enthusiasm, Senegal and its partners now face a major challenge: transforming this historic first into an engine of sporting, economic, and social development. Youth training, job creation, infrastructure development, and the emergence of new talent are the main priorities for the post-Games period.

Senegal is preparing to close a historic chapter in world sport. For two weeks, from October 31 to November 13, 2026, Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly hosted the first Youth Olympic Games (YOG) organized in Africa, placing the continent at the center of attention of the international Olympic movement.

With approximately 2,700 young athletes representing 204 National Olympic Committees, 25 competitive sports, ten engagement sports and 153 medal-winning events, this fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympic Games was an exceptional showcase for Senegal and, beyond, for the entire African continent.

But behind the sporting performances, the ceremonies and the popular mobilization, a question now arises: how to make Dakar 2026 more than just a successful event and ensure its lasting impact on the development of Africa?



This question was a major theme of the joint press conference of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the Organising Committee of the Youth Olympic Games (COJOJ), held on November 12 in Diamniadio.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry hailed the event as a "100% organizational success," stating that expectations had been exceeded. She particularly encouraged the continent to build on this experience.

"My wish is that Africa and the continent become fully aware of their potential. It is now up to us to make it a reality," she said.

A message that sums up the challenge of the post-Dakar 2026 era: to transform the international recognition acquired during the Games into concrete prospects for new African generations.

An Olympic first that changes the way we see Africa

By hosting an Olympic event of this magnitude, Senegal has taken a symbolic step in the history of African sport. Long absent from the map of host countries for Olympic competitions, the continent has demonstrated its ability to mobilize infrastructure, skills, and human resources around a major international event.

For the IOC's executive director of the Olympic Games, Christophe Dubi, one of the most striking elements of this edition will remain the welcome given to foreign delegations and the enthusiasm of the Senegalese people.

From Dakar to Saly, via Diamniadio, the mobilization of the public helped to give these Games a popular dimension, beyond just the competition venues.

This success also sends a signal to other African countries that aspire to host major international sporting events.

However, this does not mean that all organizational and financial obstacles have been removed. The Senegalese experience will need to be analyzed to identify financing, governance, and infrastructure management models that could be replicated elsewhere on the continent.

The stakes thus go beyond mere symbolic recognition: it is about making Dakar 2026 a reference for the organization of future sporting events in Africa.

New talents and disciplines to develop

From a sporting perspective, the Youth Olympic Games provided an international platform for a new generation of African athletes, while also allowing the Senegalese public to discover disciplines that are still underdeveloped in the country.

The chairman of the IOC Coordination Commission for Dakar 2026, Humphrey Kayange, particularly emphasized the interest generated by the sporting activities organized on the Corniche of Dakar.

These discovery spaces have allowed many young people to try out different sports and consider new opportunities for involvement.

But this enthusiasm will need to be maintained.

For Humphrey Kayange, national sports federations now have an essential role to play in order to extend this momentum, structure emerging disciplines and facilitate their access for young people.

The issue of talent identification and support is another major challenge. Kirsty Coventry pointed out that approximately 15% of participants in the Youth Olympic Games go on to compete in the Olympic Games.

This proportion highlights the role that the Youth Olympic Games can play in preparing future generations of elite athletes.

For Africa, where many young athletes still face difficulties accessing equipment, qualified coaches and funding, the continuity of training programs will be crucial.

The true sporting success of Dakar 2026 will therefore not be measured solely by the number of medals won, but also by the ability of African countries to support the talents revealed during the Games.

Training and employment: the economic legacy takes shape

Beyond sport, one of the most promising achievements of Dakar 2026 concerns the development of professional skills.

The Dakar 2026 Learning Academy, set up to prepare young professionals for jobs related to the organization of major events, has trained more than 300 participants, from 21 African nationalities, according to information provided by the IOC.

This program is a concrete example of how an international sporting competition can contribute to strengthening human capital.

Event management, operational coordination, communication, logistics and sports organization represent all areas in which the skills acquired could be valued after the Games.

The challenge now is to transform these training programs into sustainable career opportunities.

The president of the COJOJ, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, notably mentioned discussions with the World Bank regarding employment prospects and integration of young people.

Presented in Washington before the Games, the Learning Academy reportedly attracted the interest of the international financial institution, particularly for its potential in terms of training and employability.

In this context, closer ties have been envisaged with the World Bank's regional SIRA program, dedicated to skills development and access to employment.

These discussions, however, have yet to be finalized. No definitive funding has been announced at this stage.

For Senegal, the sustainability of this type of program could contribute to developing a pool of African professionals capable of intervening in the organization of sporting, cultural and institutional events on an international scale.

Infrastructure to be valued beyond the Games

Another central question of the Olympic legacy: the future of the sports facilities mobilized or modernized for Dakar 2026.

Organizing the Youth Olympic Games required investments in infrastructure and reception facilities, particularly in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly.

While this equipment has met the requirements of the competition, its future use will represent a real test for public authorities and sports federations.

International experience shows that the legacy of major sporting events largely depends on the ability of host countries to ensure the maintenance, financing and accessibility of facilities after the competitions.

For Senegal, several perspectives could be explored: development of training centers, organization of regional competitions, hosting of international internships and opening of infrastructure to schools and sports associations.

The development of these facilities could also contribute to the development of a local sports economy, by promoting training activities, event services, sports tourism and related jobs.

These potential benefits will, however, need to be accompanied by appropriate management mechanisms and a long-term financing strategy.

Sport as a response to the social challenges facing youth

Beyond infrastructure and performance, Senegalese officials also want to inscribe the legacy of the YOG in a social perspective.

Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye thus mentioned a project to create sports academies in several coastal localities, including Saint-Louis, Kayar and Rufisque.

This initiative aims to offer young people new opportunities for training, guidance and integration through sport.

It takes on a particular dimension in areas facing youth unemployment, economic insecurity and perilous departures by sea.

The ambition would be to make sport a tool for support and opening up towards professional prospects, possibly involving public actors, federations and development partners.

The project remains at a design stage and will need to specify its financing arrangements, its operating model and the target audiences.

Its success will also depend on its ability to combine sports practice with education, vocational training and access to employment.

Because while sport can play an important role in social inclusion, it cannot, on its own, address the structural difficulties faced by African youth.

A legacy to be built on a continental scale

The organization of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games finally raises the question of African sports cooperation.

Close 

By bringing together athletes, coaches, officials and professionals from different countries, the Games have created opportunities for exchange and collaboration that can continue after the competition.

This dynamic could promote the sharing of expertise between federations, the implementation of regional training programs and the development of partnerships around emerging sports disciplines.

The participation of young professionals of several African nationalities in the Learning Academy already illustrates this continental dimension.

But to produce lasting effects, these initiatives will need to be part of coordinated sports policies, supported by long-term institutional funding and commitments.

Africa has significant demographic and sporting potential. However, its development requires regular investments in local infrastructure, coach training, athlete support, and the professionalization of sports-related jobs.

Dakar 2026 could thus serve as a starting point for a broader reflection on the place of sport in African development strategies.

After the celebration, the test of the results

As the first Youth Olympic Games held in Africa come to a close, Senegal can boast of international recognition and popular mobilization that have marked this edition.

But the Olympic legacy is not decreed at the end of a closing ceremony. It is built over time, through public policies, sustained investments and programs capable of producing measurable results.

How many young people trained by the Learning Academy will find employment? How will the sports facilities be used? Will the disciplines discovered during the Games find a place in national federations? Will the sports academy projects actually come to fruition?

These are all questions that the coming years will need to answer.

Dakar 2026 will have demonstrated that Africa can host a major international Olympic event. The next challenge will be to prove that such an event can also contribute sustainably to the economic, social, and sporting transformation of the continent.

Only under this condition will the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games be able to transcend its status as a historic first and become a true legacy for future generations.

This article was originally published in French

World.title: South Africa: Africa's Waste Pickers Demand Recognition in Climate Action
World.content:
As COP31 puts zero waste on the climate agenda, waste pickers across Africa say the continent's circular-economy transition cannot succeed without the people who already recover and recycle much of what it throws away.

Waste is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions, accounting for nearly 20% of the global total, yet the sector remains underfunded and inadequately monitored.

The UN Environment Programme estimated that municipal solid waste reached 2.1 billion tonnes in 2023 and will be at 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), improved waste management, through a circular economy and better treatment technologies, has the potential to make a substantial contribution to reductions in national GHG emissions.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Under its Global Climate Action Agenda, COP31 is championing the Zero Waste initiative, which seeks to unlock the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular economy solutions. The initiative is focused on preventing food waste, moving towards circular economy solutions that turn waste into resources, and encouraging countries to include waste-related methane reductions in their updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The aim is to prevent emissions at source and make waste management an integral part of national climate strategies.

The need is greatest in low-income countries, where 97% of waste is openly dumped or burned. Uncontrolled dumpsites and open burning threaten communities, contaminate water and release climate pollutants, and without knowing where these sites are, how much waste they receive and what they emit, effective intervention is extremely difficult. As COP31 pushes countries to include waste methane in their climate plans, some African investors say the continent has a chance to turn waste into an economic resource.

Waste pickers say they must be part of that shift.

Across Africa, waste pickers and reclaimers collect, sort and recover recyclable materials that would otherwise end up in landfills, rivers or the environment. Many still work with limited formal recognition, social protection, and decent working conditions. Their inclusion is therefore emerging as a key question in discussions about Africa's zero-waste future. A transition to more sustainable waste management systems, advocates argue, must build on the knowledge and contribution of existing waste workers rather than exclude them.

For the International Alliance of Waste Pickers (IAWP), the success of such initiatives will depend in part on whether the people already driving recycling and resource recovery are recognised as essential partners in their implementation.

In an interview, Eva Mokoena of South Africa's African Reclaimers Organisation (ARO) discusses the role of waste pickers in climate action, the opportunities presented by the Zero Waste Districts initiative, and the changes needed to secure their place in Africa's transition to a circular economy.

Waste is often seen as an environmental and sanitation problem, but it is increasingly recognised as a major climate challenge. Why does tackling waste matter for the fight against climate change, and what role can zero waste play in reducing emissions?

Waste is a climate issue because what we throw away does not disappear. Organic waste buried in landfills and dumpsites rots without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in the short term. Open burning of waste adds black carbon and toxic smoke to the air our communities breathe. Every item that is landfilled or burnt also means new materials must be extracted, manufactured, and transported to replace it.

Zero waste addresses all of these at once. When materials are separated at source, recovered, reused and recycled, and when organic waste is composted or turned into biogas, methane from landfills falls and the demand for virgin materials drops. This is one of the fastest and most affordable ways to reduce emissions.

The key to making it work is already on the ground. Waste pickers and reclaimers are the people removing waste from landfills, rivers, and streams every day. With proper recognition, equipment, and collaboration from governments, municipalities, and residents, they can multiply the climate impact they already deliver.

Waste is often overlooked in climate talks, yet food waste and landfills are major sources of greenhouse-gas emissions, especially methane. What practical policies and local actions would most effectively reduce food waste and keep organic waste out of landfills?

The most effective policies are the ones that recognise and include waste pickers and reclaimers. They are the frontline educators of their communities: they already teach residents to separate and recycle what they buy and eat. Governments and policymakers should write waste pickers into waste and climate legislation, so that this work is formally recognised, supported and paid for.

In practice, this means separation at source, in households, markets and businesses before it reaches the landfill, with waste pickers leading door-to-door awareness and collection.

In logistics, waste picker organisations need access to land, storage facilities and transport, so that organic material can be collected, stored and processed close to where it is generated. Local processing of food waste should be turned into compost, manure and biogas through community-run facilities, creating useful products and income instead of methane.

Investment in people is also important. Incubating reclaimer cooperatives, with full access to logistics and infrastructure, is what turns good policy into results.

If we continue to ignore the people on the ground, we will keep struggling. If we invest in them, organic waste can become a resource for our communities.

How can African governments make waste reduction and the circular economy a more central part of their national climate policies?

Governments can start by recognising who already runs Africa's circular economy. Waste pickers and reclaimers are unrecognised heroes: many spend their own time and resources recovering materials and cleaning public spaces without pay or protection. Bringing them into national climate policy means three things.

First, recognition in law. National climate plans, including Nationally Determined Contributions, and waste management legislation should name waste pickers as essential service providers and set out their rights, their role and how they will be paid.

Second, a seat at the table. Waste picker organisations should take part in designing, implementing and monitoring these policies. When waste pickers help shape the rules, the rules work on the ground, and waste pickers gain the recognition and confidence to expand their work.

Third, real support. Recognition has to come with resources: equipment, infrastructure, social protection and fair payment for the services waste pickers provide to cities and to the climate.

Looking at initiatives such as Zero Waste Districts and the 1x100 campaign, how can these programmes translate into tangible benefits for African communities, from cleaner cities and reduced landfill waste to decent jobs and better livelihoods for waste pickers?

These programmes deliver real benefits when everybody works together: governments, municipalities, residents, the private sector and waste picker organisations. Waste pickers are already on the ground, in every neighbourhood and in every landfill. What makes the difference is giving them space, resources and a central role.

Education is the most important key. With educational tools, training and empowerment, waste pickers can lead awareness campaigns, help households separate their waste, and recover a much wider range of materials at once. The result is cleaner streets, less waste reaching landfills and rivers, and recycling that actually works.

For waste pickers, the benefit must be decent work: formal contracts, fair payment for collection and recovery services, safe working conditions and social protection. When district programmes are built around existing waste picker cooperatives, the jobs and income they create stay in the community.

Two African nations that have joined the Zero Waste Districts programme are Ghana and Kenya. What are the biggest waste management challenges these countries are hoping to address, and what makes the district-level approach different from previous efforts?

What makes the district-level approach different is that it starts from the community and from the organisations that already exist, rather than from large, centralised projects designed far away from the people who manage waste every day. Our affiliates in both countries describe it in these terms.

In Ghana, the Green Waste Pickers Cooperative Society Limited and the Kpone Landfill Waste Pickers Association are supporting community-led circular initiatives that build on existing cooperatives. These cooperatives drive the process of diverting waste at source, adopt measures to pre-process materials, and lead environmental campaigns in their communities.

In Kenya, the Nakuru County Waste Pickers Association is advancing zero waste through waste reduction, reuse, recycling and waste picking, alongside community-led initiatives, progressive policies and the promotion of a circular economy.

In both cases, the district becomes the unit where waste pickers, residents and local authorities can work side by side, and where results can be seen and measured.

Many African cities are still grappling with poor waste collection, overflowing landfills, and very limited recycling. What kind of investment and what kind of partnerships are required to build effective waste management and recycling systems across the continent?

Close 

The investment that works is investment in the people already doing the job. Instead of expensive systems that bypass or displace waste pickers, African cities should incubate reclaimer and waste picker cooperatives and give them full access to what they need.

In infrastructure, sorting centres, storage space and land can help make the work safer. In logistics, vehicles and equipment to collect and move materials efficiently are needed. Processing capacity with facilities to recycle materials and to turn food waste into compost, manure and biogas is necessary. Fair contracts are also a key issue to provide payments from municipalities for the collection and recovery services waste pickers provide.

The partnerships that work are inclusive ones. Municipalities, national governments, producers, funders and residents should partner directly with waste picker organisations, as equals and from the design stage. If we keep ignoring the people on the ground, cities will keep struggling with the same problems. If we invest in them, Africa can build recycling systems that are effective, fair and locally owned.

Given that COP31 is placing such a strong emphasis on zero waste, what specific commitments should African countries be demanding in order to ensure that waste reduction actually becomes a measurable element of climate action rather than just another one of the international promises?

African countries should demand commitments that reach the ground, not only the negotiating rooms. In particular, direct funding for equipment and machinery that allows waste pickers and reclaimers to recover and recycle more materials, including food waste.

Educational tools must also be designed with waste pickers and be easy to use for both reclaimers and residents, so that separation at source becomes everyday practice in every household.

Formal recognition of waste pickers in national climate plans and waste policies, with a guaranteed role in their implementation and measurable targets for diverting organic and recyclable waste from landfills, monitored with the participation of waste picker organisations, are commitments that promote long-term climate solutions.

Waste pickers are good at what we do, and we make sure that everyone we work with understands our livelihoods on the streets and in the landfills, and the important role we play. Climate commitments on waste will only become real when they are built with us.

World.title: Nigeria: Index Ebola Case - Swiss Diplomat's Wife Recovers, Discharged From Hospital
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

Abuja — Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said that the Nigeria's Ebola index case- Swiss diplomat's wife has recovered and discharged from hospital in Switzerland.

The disease intervention centre had confirmed the infection on October 20, 2026 after the patient's blood samples tested positive at the Abuja Reference Laboratory.

After receiving preliminary treatment at an undisclosed private hospital in Abuja, she and her husband were subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland with an air ambulance on October 26, 2026.

Addressing journalists in his office in Abuja on Friday, NCDC Director General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the Swiss authorities had announced the recovery and discharge of the woman after testing negative.

He said index case tested negative after receiving treatment in an isolation facility in Switzerland.

World.title: South Africa: Joburg Turns Up the Heat As Residents Wait for Relief
World.content:
Outdoor workers should take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

Cooler weather and thunderstorms are expected over the weekend, offering some relief from the heat.

Johannesburg residents face another scorching day on Friday, with emergency services urging people to drink water, take breaks and stay out of the midday sun.

The City of Johannesburg's Emergency Management Services says extremely hot conditions are expected to continue across much of the city. Outdoor workers have been urged to take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

The South African Weather Service's heatwave advisory issued earlier this week included southern Gauteng, with persistently high temperatures expected until Friday, 13 November.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But some relief could arrive over the weekend.

Weather service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said cooler conditions, accompanied by thunderstorms and thundershowers, are expected over the weekend.

Until then, residents have been urged to protect themselves from the heat.

"Residents are urged to stay hydrated, drink lots of water, avoid direct sunlight especially between 11h00 and 15h00 in the afternoon," Johannesburg emergency services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi said earlier this week.

For street traders, gardeners, construction workers and others spending hours outside, regular breaks in a cool or shaded place are especially important.

The World Health Organization says older people, babies, outdoor workers and people with existing medical conditions face greater risks during hot weather. Residents should also check on relatives and neighbours who live alone.

Keeping cool does not have to mean switching on an air conditioner. The organisation recommends loose, light clothing, cool showers and wetting the skin with a damp cloth. Drink water regularly and avoid alcohol.

Never leave children, dependent adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even while running a quick errand.

Parents have also been warned to watch children seeking somewhere to cool off.

Mulaudzi urged families to keep young children away from dams and river streams to prevent drownings.

Heat illness needs prompt attention. Dizziness, weakness, intense thirst and headaches are signs to move into a cool place and drink water.

Confusion, seizures or a loss of consciousness require urgent medical help. Move the person into shade or a cool room and use cold, wet cloths to help cool them while waiting for assistance.

Close 

For life-threatening emergencies in Johannesburg, call 011 375 5911. The city says this number connects residents to emergency assistance, including ambulance and fire services.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak - Armed Groups Unrest Hold Back Response
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread amid repeated and ongoing deadly attacks on civilians and frontline health workers by armed groups that are obstructing efforts to stop transmission, UN responders said on Friday.

In an update, the UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, stressed that more people are being killed by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in recent days.

And yet the attacks on "tens of villages all across the south of Ituri and North Kivu (provinces) goes unnoticed", Mr. Harneis maintained. "People are scared, people are furious at the lack of action on this."

Up to 500 infections per week



Echoing that message, the UN World Health Organization (WHO)'s Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director of WHO's Health Emergencies Programme, said that despite much progress in containing transmission within eastern DRC, about 400 to 500 cases of infection are still being identified every week.

This trend is linked to the emergence of cases in rural and hard-to-reach areas.

In more positive developments, the WHO official noted that prevention efforts have led to "a significant reduction" in transmission in previous hotspots, in particular Bunia, Mongbwalu, Rampara and Nizi, all in Ituri province in eastern DRC.

Nonetheless, the violent unrest across the vast area impacted by Ebola creates huge challenges for responders.

"We've seen so many attacks on healthcare, attacks on communities as well, attacks on people providing care, and people losing their lives, nurses in burials," Dr Ihekweazu explained. "So, we need to keep working with the community, and this is very important. And working with the specific groups instigating these attacks."

Disease threats in addition to attacks

Communities are already facing outbreaks of diseases, malnutrition and displacement driven by decades of violent unrest fuelled by dozens of armed

groups that remain active in the resource-rich region.

Earlier this week, WHO condemned attacks against frontline healthcare workers and community awareness officers, including in Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians including three health workers. Three health facilities were also looted.

Two weeks ago, a nurse was also killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province.

Tedros appeal

Other attacks have included an arson attempt on a treatment centre and stones thrown at a vehicle used for conducting safe and dignified burials, an indication of the need to continue to build trust with extremely vulnerable communities.

"We cannot focus only on Ebola. Some people in the affected communities have said told me personally that Ebola is a lesser evil compared to some of the other threats they face," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stressed earlier this week.

A massive humanitarian emergency

The DRC Ebola outbreak was declared in May and has since become the largest yet as it continues to spread faster than any previous outbreak in the vast country's east and northeast provinces.

To date, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed and more than 5,000 people have died.

In a related development, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that nearly 29 million people in the DRC face acute food insecurity, with most in the conflict and Ebola-affected eastern and northeastern provinces. That number is likely to continue to increase, said Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP Director of Food Security and Nutrition Analysis.

Briefing journalists via video in Geneva, Mr. Bauer stressed that conflict is driving the hunger crisis, in addition to the Ebola outbreak.

Close 

"What we need right now is access, and we need resources to avoid the situation becoming more difficult in the DRC," he said.

Hunger emergency

Latest UN-backed food insecurity expert assessments indicate that between January and June 2027, 30.3 million people will be in crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse, with 4.2 million of this number experiencing "emergency levels" of hunger and the most acute needs in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces "driven by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement".

Mr. Bauer noted that Ebola is just one of many disease outbreaks in DRC, but that it is compounding the hunger crisis for communities already struggling to eat.

"Families are being displaced, they're being cut off from their farms, from their livelihoods," he explained. "Food prices are rising, making affording a meal quite complicated for too many households."

World.title: Rwanda: Kigali Wetlands Will Protect 220,000 People From Floods, Says PM
World.content:
Rehabilitation of five wetlands in Kigali will reduce flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities, Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva said at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

ALSO READ: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva makes case for green industrialisation

With national and international partners, approximately $195 million has been invested in flood-risk reduction, informal settlement upgrading, the construction of access roads and, more recently, the rehabilitation of five urban wetlands covering nearly 500 hectares in Kigali, the Prime Minister said.

ALSO READ: VIDEO & PHOTOS: Inside Kigali Wetlands Park

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"These investments are reducing flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities. Nature-based solutions can deliver resilience at scale," he said.

Rwanda is committed to extending this model to secondary and satellite cities, in line with the third version of its climate action plan, known as NDC 3.0.

However, he said, achieving this requires financing.

"Developing countries will need more than $300 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, up to 14 times the current support," he noted.

ALSO READ: COP31: What issues are on agenda as UN climate summit begins?

Rwanda has welcomed Türkiye's Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative introduced under the COP31 Action Agenda.

The facility is intended to help cities turn climate objectives into investable projects, secure financing and deliver investments.

Another model of climate resilience

Prime Minister Nsengiyumva also cited the Green Gicumbi project in Gicumbi District, supported by the Green Climate Fund, which aimed to strengthen the resilience of about 249,000 people, nearly two-thirds of the district's population.

ALSO READ: What's at stake for Rwanda as COP31 approaches?

"Communities terraced hillsides, protected watersheds and moved vulnerable families into climate-resilient homes. Its independent evaluation confirms that climate-smart practices have spread, food security has improved and households are better able to withstand shocks," he said.

Achieving these ambitions requires addressing the barriers that have constrained investment, he noted.

"Good plans do not automatically become bankable projects."

Reducing carbon emissions

Delivering Rwanda's statement at the high-level segment for heads of state and government at COP31, the Prime Minister said national action alone cannot deliver the transformation required.

Close 

"Under our third Nationally Determined Contribution, Rwanda has committed to reducing emissions by 53 per cent by 2035, relative to the business-as-usual scenario."

Achieving this target requires $12 billion in investment, 80 percent of which is conditional on international support, he said. Rwanda needs predictable, accessible and adequate financing for adaptation and mitigation to meet these targets.

"We must also remove the barriers that prevent capital from flowing into viable projects in developing countries. As President Kagame observed at the recent Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, the perception that 'there are higher risks for investments in the South than in the North' is misplaced. Investments should be judged on their merits, not on their location."

He said governments and the private sector must work together to make viable projects investable, deepen markets and mobilise capital on terms that developing economies can afford, without adding to unsustainable debt.

"Rwanda stands ready to cooperate with all nations. As we assume the chairmanship of the G77 and China in 2027, we reaffirm our commitment to strengthening solidarity among developing countries and completing the outstanding work under the climate negotiations, including work on Global Goal on Adaptation indicators relating to financial needs and financial provision," he said.

World.title: Nigeria: 2027 Lagos State Governorship Debate - How the Candidates Fared
World.content:
The Lagos State governorship candidates fielded questions on the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, flooding, and other areas where the state faces challenges.

The debate among the candidates of the leading political parties for the 6 February 2027 governorship election was held last Sunday. The debate, organised by the Nigeria Debate Consortium, featured Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Obafemi Hamzat of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) who is the incumbent deputy governor of the state, Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and Adedeji Doherty of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

The debate, broadcast live on Sunday, 8 November, was moderated by Seun Okinbaloye of Channels Television and Nifemi Oguntoye of TVC News.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The candidates were asked how they would solve challenges affecting Nigeria's economic capital and largest city by population, such as the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, and flooding. PREMIUM TIMES monitored the debate and here is our review of how each of the candidates fared at the debate.

Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour

Due to the alphabetical arrangement of the names of the candidates' political parties on the podium, Mr Rhodes-Vivour of the ADC was asked most of the questions first. Dressed in a plain while kaftan with a hat to match, Mr Rhodes-Vivour, who was the runner-up in the 2023 governorship election when he ran on the platform of the Labour Party, started by saying that his desire for Lagos was one that is better, safer, cleaner and economically viable. He explained that his desires are the same as those of every Lagosian.

He stated that the misgovernance of the ruling APC is the reason the state is bedeviled with a lot of seemingly insurmountable problems. (The political hegemony that makes up the APC in Lagos has been in power in the state since 1999, when Nigeria's incumbent president, Bola Tinubu, who is generally considered as the political godfather of the state was elected governor under the banner of the Alliance for Democracy. Since then, his political proteges have governed the state under two other political banners - Action Congress of Nigeria and currently APC.)

He claimed he has a track record of siding with the people unlike the APC, which he claimed is elite-centred. To buttress his claim that his government would be people-centred, he immediately promised to build 100,000 housing units within four years to reduce the creeping housing shortages in the state.

The Lagos State Government estimates a housing deficit of 3.3 million in the state. This acute shortage has contributed significantly to arbitrary increases in rent and other sharp practices in the real estate sector.

During debates, politicians often struggle with the "how" of implementing their promises. Mr Rhodes-Vivour appeared to have thought through his implementation strategy. He said he would achieve his housing plan from funds to be derived from a luxury tax. He, however, did not give details of the nature of said luxury tax.

He said, if elected, his government would pass a law that would require landlords to give tenants at least a six-month notice before increasing rent. He said the law would also peg the percentage rent can be increased within a given time.

He said he would develop the Eastern Foreshore area of the state - around the Ibeju-Lekki axis while decentralising development in the state.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour plan of developing the Ibeju-Lekki area of the state leaves one wondering about his claim of decentralising development in the state.

The Ibeju-Lekki area is already one of the fastest growing areas of the state with a growing residential and industrial hub championed by facilities like the Dangote Refinery, the Lekki Free Trade Zone and the Lekki Sea Port.

With the pace at which developments in Ibeju-Lekki are moving, it is near impossible for other areas of the state such as Badagry, Ojo, and the densely populated Alimosho to keep up with that axis in the nearest future.

He promised to adopt a private sector driven approach to solving some of the persistent problems of the states such as transportation. Mr Rhodes-Vivour said he would ensure that the state is safer by removing street urchins and prioritising skill acquisition.

He said he would solve the perennial flood problem of the state by adopting a wetland policy. He said instead of just sand filling wetlands, which blocks the absorption of excess water he would introduce and encourage the adoption of technology that would not hinder the right of way of water.

When asked to respond why the state appears to be rich while its residents are poor, Mr Rhodes-Vivour admonished the government for being elite-focused rather than people-focused. He said during the campaign towards the 2023 election, Mr Hamzat promised the inhabitants of Makoko, a sprawling slum in Yaba, of developing their community only to turn around to demolish their homes and forcibly evict them.

He said while Lagos is wealthy on paper, most residents are not benefiting from that wealth.

On traffic management, Mr Rhodes-Vivour said urban planning should be decentralised. He said he would depart from the approach of building long and expensive bridges to connect parts of the state and would rather use short bridges of a few kilometres to connect communities within the state. He said he would revisit the proposal of using cable cars, improve water transportation, create cycle lanes and develop inner roads within towns and local governments.

On the metro rail, he chided the government for building the project on its balance sheet rather than welcoming private sector investment for the speedy completion of the project that has been on-going for more than 20 years. He alleged that corruption and avoidance of transparency were the reasons the project is being built on the state's balance sheet rather than through private investment.

On health, he promised to create emergency rehabilitation centres across the state to reduce the travel time of patients in need to critical and urgent care.

He also said if elected, his government would depart from what he claimed is the current pick-and-drop waste disposal policy of the state, which he blamed for the foul smell in many parts of the state. He said he would encourage capable private sector participation in waste management that would prioritise recycling and creating wealth from waste.

VERDICT: Mr Rhodes-Vivour displayed a relatively deep understanding of the problem facing the state and his responses showed that he had thought through the solutions to the problems. In many cases he explained how these problems will be solved and how his approaches at tackling the problem differ from what the incumbent administration is doing. His ideas are fresh, innovative, and in many cases reasonable alternatives to the approaches of the incumbent administration.

However, his idea of decentralising Lagos appears to be contradictory and heavily focused on the provision of transportation infrastructure without considering other means of decentralisation such as expanding of commercial and industrial hubs to other parts of the state, provision of recreation centres and entertainment facilities, which will reduce the travel time and distances across the state.

SCORE CARD: 8/10.

Obafemi Hamzat

He started by saying he considered the debate a job interview and Lagosians as his employers. He said he would bring his experience as a seasoned administrator in the United States and in Nigeria (he was the state's commissioner for science and technology under the administration of the then-Governor Bola Tinubu and was retained in the position by Mr Tinubu's successor, Babatunde Fashola).

He listed the Lekki-Ikoyi Link Bridge, the first cable bridge in West Africa and the second in Africa as one of his achievements as the commissioner for science and technology. He said his plan for Lagos will be hoisted on seven pillars, which he said formed the acronym PROMISE. He said P stands for the people, R for renewal, O for opportunities, M for machinery of government, I for inclusion, S for system and E for economic development. When asked why many Lagosians are poor but the state is rich on paper, he did not answer the question directly but went ahead to reel out some of the achievements of the incumbent government and his plan if elected as the governor of the state.

Mr Hamzat said that his government would work toward completing the metro rail line therefore creating a better and hassle-free connection of parts of Lagos. He said his government would prioritise mass movement of people by providing 4,000 CNG-powered BRT buses. He said BRT lanes would be created to connect major towns in the state like Badagry. He also promised to introduce electric ferries to improve water transportation.

He listed the housing projects that are being built by the government in areas like Ajara in Badagry. He said the government already enacted a law - the Lagos Real Estate Registration Agency Law, to deal with sharp practices in the housing sector and encourage Lagosians to report erring landlords and realtors for better enforcement of the law.

He acknowledged that the housing shortage in the state is more severe in lowbrow areas of the state, saying he intends to solve that by encouraging developers to build in less desirable parts of the state as they build expensive houses in highbrow areas like Ikoyi and Lekki. He however did not explain how this will be done.

He blamed perennial flooding in the state to increase rainfall and climate change. He acknowledged that the state is demolishing structures built on wetland or obstructing the flow of water. When challenged about the flooding in communities along the coastal roads, which was blamed on the lack of environmental impact assessment before the road was constructed, he said that contrary to the claim, an environmental impact assessment was done during his tenure as commissioner for science and technology.

On healthcare, he said, the government intends to expand the Ilera Eko health insurance programme to capture more users. Mr Hamzat said the state government is building or expanding several general hospitals across the state and that it plans to establish a university of medicine.

VERDICT: As expected, Mr Hamzat put up a spirited defence of the policies of the incumbent administration, while trying to also project that he was his own man. Refreshingly, he did not use the word "continuation" as many potential successors of ruling parties in the country are wont to do. He tried earnestly to explain the policies of the current government and what has been achieved. His responses suggested that he was aware that the job is nowhere near being done and that some of the policies require fine tuning and expansion.

However, some of his responses are hard to understand and he did not bother to explain how they would be achieved. For instance, his suggestion that property developer would be made to build houses in cheaper areas of the state sounded strange as he did not explain how he would go about doing this, the incentives to make developers or private businesses whose aim is to maximise profit use resources to develop properties in poor areas where such properties would not bring the same profit as those built in highbrow areas.

His claim about the flooding along the coastal road and how helpless the state government was with demanding that a proper impact assessment was done by the federal government sounded unconvincing. There are several areas where state governments have collaborated with the federal government for a proper development of infrastructure.

SCORE CARD: 7/10

Funsho Doherty

Mr Doherty said Lagos is operating below its potential and blamed this underperformance on bad governance. He said bad governance has made life increasingly difficult for many Lagosians. He said residents of the state are not getting the worth of the taxes they pay. He said it was time to change the political hegemony that has governed the state for the past 27 years because they have had all the time to fix the problem but have failed to do so.

He said he would prioritise affordable housing and plans to build 150,000 housing units in the first four years of his tenure, if elected. He promised to create an ombudsman to deal with sharp practices and arbitrary increases in the rent in the state, saying a situation where Lagosians use a large chunk of their salaries for rent is not sustainable.

He added that the government has to be the driver of social housing. He berated the state government for stepping back and allowing the sector to be almost fully run by the private sector, a situation, he said, is bad for many Lagosians.

The NDC governorship candidate promised to focus his attention on other areas including small businesses and the environment, while also vowing to run an honest and accountable government.

He also said his government will be people-centred as he drew a connection between the wealth of the place to the wealth of the people living therein.

He stated that, if he is elected, his government would be more involved in the provision of affordable social amenities such as transportation, healthcare and education.

He promised to make education truly free and that, if elected, his government would provide one affordable meal to children in schools. He said his idea is to enable people to prosper.

On the recurrent flooding in the state, he said, the problem is a symptom of a long failure in governance. While admitting that Lagos is a coastal state thus, exposed to flooding, he said, the government should raise the bar in tackling the problem as seen elsewhere. He advocated for the protection of wetlands. He said the practice where people are allowed to build on wetland for such properties to be demolished years later is not the solution that Lagos needs.

He claimed that no environmental impact assessment was done on the coastal road before it was constructed, hence, the unprecedented flooding experienced in the corridor this year. He said even if the road was a federal road, it was the responsibility of the state government to insist that things are done properly.

He also chastised the state government for deliberately refusing to modernise its transportation system. He said the state is stuck with the old transportation system, which is mainly run by rickety buses known as danfo, because persons in the government have vested interest. By this he was suggesting that the state government has no political will to remove street urchins and touts, popularly called agbero, representing road transport unions collecting tolls from commercial motorists. He said it is an eyesore for a city like Lagos to have its transportation system still in the hands of miscreants. He said, if elected, he would modernise transportation infrastructure in the state.

He said healthcare under his government would be made totally free for the poor. He argued that the government-run health insurance scheme, Ilera Eko, was either inadequate or not the way to go and said the government has to play a more participatory role in healthcare provision.

On waste management, he said it was too centralised, and that if elected, he would encourage local governments to play more role in the collection, recycling and disposal of waste.

Close 

VERDICT: Mr Doherty easily picked holes in the shortcomings of governance in the state. He was clear-headed about what needed to be done. However, maybe due to time or the way the questions were structured, he could not explain, for instance, how he intends to fund the one free-meal for school children and his idea of a totally -free primary healthcare provision.

One would have loved to hear how he intends to modernise the transportation infrastructure and system in the state and how he plans to rid the state of agberos.

Score Card: 7/10

Adedeji Doherty

Adedeji Doherty spent the time allotted to him to introduce himself and his plan for the state, talking about how he is a man of the people and a loyal member of the PDP.

Interestingly, he used almost a minute of his allotted three minutes to pay homage to Mr Hamzat, and Musiliu Obanikoro. a former governorship candidate of his party, who has since joined the ruling APC.

He said he has a 10-point agenda but could not list all in the time remaining.

On tackling the housing shortage in the state, he said unlike the other contestant, he has no plan to build 150,000 housing units in the state, saying that he does not control the price of building materials and cannot tell developers how to sell or rent their houses. "There is no government that can control landlords," he said. He, however, mentioned that if elected he would form a research team to look into the housing problem in the state, but again could not fully explain the role of this research team before he ran out of time.

Strangely, he said to end sharp practices in the housing sector and end arbitrary rent increases, the state government will rent houses from landlords and sublet them to Lagosians. He did not explain how this idea would be achieved or how feasible it was.

When asked why Lagosians are not reaping the benefits of its seemingly wealthy government, he blamed it on the debt burden of the state government. He said the government uses N20 billion to service debt.

He, however, promised to run a small government to save up funds for other developmental projects adding that the state currently has over 160 ministries and agencies and maintaining them was not sustainable.

He said there was nothing the state government could do about flooding and blamed the yearly flooding of the state to global climate change and that flooding is experienced all over the world. He said credit should be given to the state government for what it is doing to manage flooding in the state.

On traffic management, he said, if elected, he will build long bridges connecting far-flung parts of the state like from Berger (Kara) to Lagos Island, And another to Badagry. He wondered why the government had yet to build the 4th, the 5th and the 6th mainland bridges to deal with traffic congestion.

VERDICT: Most of Mr Adedeji Doherty's responses were trained towards either excusing the inadequacies of the policies of the incumbent government or to suggest that there was little he would do to change the status quo. This leaves one wondering about his reasons for contesting for the position if all he wants to do was rehash the ways things are being done.

He also proposed some strange policies like how his government would rent houses from landlords and then sublet them to residents. His idea of solving the traffic problem of the state by building long bridges that traverse one end of the state and another appeared not to have been given a proper thought. Of all the contestants at the debate, he was clearly the least prepared.

SCORE CARD: 3/10

World.title: Namibia: MPs Weigh in On Income Tax Amendment Bill
World.content:
Members of Parliament (MP) have backed up the proposed Income Tax Amendment Bill, while raising concerns about its impact on ordinary taxpayers, government revenue and access to tax justice.

During a debate in the National Assembly on Wednesday, MPs welcomed proposed tax relief measures and the establishment of an independent Tax Court but called for improved taxpayer education, transparency and affordable dispute-resolution processes.

The contributions highlighted the need to ensure that the proposed reforms benefit workers and small businesses without compromising Government revenue or making it difficult for ordinary citizens to challenge tax assessments.

Lukato: employee tax deductions

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Martin Lukato welcomed the proposed tax relief measures, including deductions for retirement contributions and education policies, saying they could improve employees' disposable income and encourage long-term savings.

He also supported the proposed reduction of corporate income tax for qualifying small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to 20%, saying it could encourage business formalisation and economic activity.

However, he raised concerns about the taxation of retirement benefits and restrictions on employees offsetting losses from secondary businesses against their salary income. Lukato further questioned the proposed arrangements for employee tax refunds, warning that employers facing cash-flow difficulties could struggle to refund workers following retrospective tax adjustments. He called for more accessible tax services, particularly for workers outside major towns, and cautioned that penalties of up to 200%, together with interest, could place a heavy burden on taxpayers who fail to declare their income or fringe benefits correctly.

Atshipara: clarity on revenue implications

Modestus Atshipara supported the proposed reforms, particularly the establishment of a dedicated Tax Court and tax incentives aimed at supporting businesses and improving Namibia's investment environment. He highlighted several proposed changes, including increasing the tax-free retirement fund lump-sum commutation limit from N$50 000 to N$375 000, introducing an annual cap of N$400 000 on housing benefits and reducing the corporate income tax rate for non-mining companies from 30% to 28%.

However, Atshipara questioned whether government had assessed the revenue implications of the proposed tax reductions.

He warned that reducing corporate tax rates without properly calculating the potential revenue losses could affect Government's ability to fund public services adding that Government must ensure that efforts to attract foreign investment do not discourage local shareholders, pension funds and small investors.

Atshipara also called for adequate funding, judicial capacity and accessible procedures for the proposed Tax Court, stressing that taxpayers outside Windhoek should not be disadvantaged.

Lutuhezi: tax education and affordable justice

Lilian Lutuhezi supported the Bill but called for stronger taxpayer education, particularly among informal traders, young entrepreneurs and small business operators. She focused on three areas, namely taxpayer education, access to justice, independency and transparency of Tax Court.

She said many people operating businesses, including those selling goods through social media, might not understand their tax obligations, record-keeping requirements and customs procedures.

She urged NamRA and Ministry of Finance to provide simplified information through different media platforms and indigenous languages, as well as conduct outreach programmes in rural communities.

Lutuhezi also questioned whether ordinary taxpayers would be able to afford legal representation when challenging tax assessments before the proposed Tax Court.

She raised concerns about provisions limiting appeals to grounds stated in the initial notice of objection, warning that taxpayers without professional assistance could lose opportunities to raise legitimate arguments. She further questioned provisions relating to court costs and the non-public nature of court proceedings, calling for transparency and safeguards to protect taxpayers' rights.

Busch: Tax Court must be operational without delay

Sharonice Busch supported the establishment of an independent Tax Court, describing it as a necessary intervention following the 2021 High Court judgment that declared the previous Special Tax Court arrangements unconstitutional.

She said taxpayers had been left without a specialised court to hear income tax and value-added tax disputes following the judgment.

Busch described the proposed reform as long overdue and urged Government to ensure that the court becomes operational without further delays once the legislation is enacted. She said the institution must be accessible, affordable, efficient and independent, warning that prolonged tax disputes could affect businesses' cash flow, investment decisions and employment.

Close 

She also called for adequate judicial capacity and reasonable turnaround times to ensure that taxpayers receive timely decisions.

Thomas: Calls for relief from the tax burden

Festus Thomas supported the establishment of an independent Tax Court but argued that the Bill should also address the financial pressure taxation places on ordinary Namibians. He described the combination of Pay As You Earn deductions and Value Added Tax as a double tax burden, saying workers are taxed on their earnings and again when spending their remaining income.

Thomas called for an increase in the tax-free income threshold, arguing that the current N$50 000 threshold had not kept pace with inflation and the rising cost of living.

He also proposed zero-rating essential goods and services, including basic food, electricity, water and sanitary products, to provide relief to low-income households.

Thomas further called for a review of taxes affecting employment and small businesses, saying excessive taxation could discourage formal employment and business development.

World.title: Mike Evans ruled out, Trent Williams questionable as NFC-leading 49ers' injury concerns persist
World.content:
The San Francisco 49ers will be without wide receiver Mike Evans for a third straight game Sunday after ruling him out against the Dallas Cowboys as he continues to deal with Achilles tendinitis.

Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether standout left tackle Trent Williams will suit up after injuring his shoulder in practice this week.

Injuries are an unavoidable part of the NFL, but few teams have dealt with them as consistently as the San Francisco 49ers have in recent seasons. Their injury report has become a weekly storyline.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Evans and Williams were not the only concerns for San Francisco this week. Coach Kyle Shanahan said cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green were also on the injury report. Both missed practice Wednesday and Thursday after suffering injuries in last week’s game against Las Vegas, but they were limited participants Friday.

Linebacker Dre Greenlaw was also listed as questionable after hurting his knee at practice Thursday, while cornerback Nate Hobbs (adductor), defensive back Upton Stout (shoulder, neck) and defensive tackle C.J. West (knee) were also questionable.

At 38, Williams remains a 12-time Pro Bowler playing at a high level, making his availability significant for San Francisco. He left practice early Thursday and did not participate Friday, but Shanahan remained hopeful the veteran tackle would feel well enough to play Sunday.

RAVENS FINALLY REVEAL LAMAR JACKSON'S OFFICIAL RETURN TIMELINE AND QB COULD MISS REST OF REGULAR SEASON

Vederian Lowe would likely start if Williams is unable to go, but replacing the longtime standout would be a major challenge for the 49ers.

"The left tackle in general is always huge. Then a guy of Trent’s caliber is huge," Shanahan said. "Just the way he plays out there, down in and down out, what he means to the team, just his presence, the type of person he is, and just what he brings on game day. He’s a captain for a reason, and everyone knows Trent Williams is one of the best players in this league."

San Francisco will have more help at receiver this week with Deebo Samuel set to return after missing the past three games with a hamstring injury and Keenan Allen set to make his debut for the 49ers after being acquired earlier this week in a trade from Indianapolis.

But they will be missing Evans again after he left a Week 6 game against Washington early with the injury. He missed the next two games and has been unable to practice since then but is making progress. Shanahan said there’s a chance Evans could play next week in Mexico against Minnesota.

The 49ers enter Sunday’s game with an NFC-best 7-1 record.

World.title: Kentucky needs buzzer-beating three to survive Northern Arizona's upset bid at Rupp Arena
World.content:
The Kentucky Wildcats have one of the most expensive rosters in college basketball. It didn't look like money well spent for 39 minutes and 58 seconds on Friday night.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Kentucky needed a last-second three-pointer from Alex Wilkins to beat winless Northern Arizona 78-77 at Rupp Arena. NAU, which entered the game as a 30.5-point underdog, had every opportunity to pull off a massive upset in the closing minute. The Lumberjacks had a 77-73 lead with just 22 seconds remaining.

Kentucky cut the deficit to two on a basket by Mason Williams, then had to intentionally foul Northern Arizona. Max Majerle, son of former Phoenix Suns All-Star Dan Majerle, missed the front end of the one-and-one, but a Kentucky player knocked the ball out of bounds in the scramble for the rebound.

CBB WITH DANNY Z: KANSAS, TENNESSEE AND USC LEAD ANOTHER HUMAN POLLS VS. ANALYTICS ARGUMENT

Once again, Kentucky had to foul. Northern Arizona got the ball in the hands of Chris Komin, an 82% free throw shooter last season. But like Majerle, Komin missed the front end of the one-and-one. The Wildcats grabbed the board with 7 seconds left, moved the ball into the frontcourt on a pass from Mason Williams to to Wilkins, and Wilkins hit the game-winner.

CBS Sports puts Kentucky’s roster in its $20 million-plus spending tier. The team it barely beat Friday had lost its first three games by an average of 24 points.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

When Northern Arizona went to the line with a chance to go up four, I wondered how far back I’d have to go to find a Kentucky loss as a 30-point favorite. I couldn’t find one. The Wildcats were favored by 25 when Evansville won at Rupp Arena in 2019 and by 26 when Gardner-Webb won there in 2007.

So how did Kentucky get that close to losing? The same problem I brought up before the Kansas game. The Wildcats had given up 80 points to James Madison, and I wondered whether they could get enough stops against the Jayhawks. Kansas scored 89 and won by 20.

Then Northern Arizona came into Rupp, having scored an average of 62 points in their two losses to New Mexico and No. 12 Arizona, and shot 13-for-26 from 3 en route to 77 points.

Kentucky shot 56.4% and turned the ball over just four times Friday. If you’d told me that before tipoff, I would’ve figured the walk-ons were getting a few minutes.
