World.title: Cowboys owner Jerry Jones updates timeline for NFL's 18-game schedule, floats preseason reduction
World.content:
The NFL expanded from a 16-game schedule to 17 games in 2021. Since then, speculation has persisted about whether the league will eventually add an 18th regular-season game.

Such a change would require negotiations over roster sizes, player salaries, the preseason schedule and the timing of the Super Bowl. The NFL Players Association would also have to approve the plan before it could move forward.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But Jerry Jones, one of the NFL’s most high-profile and outspoken owners, offered a timeline Friday for when the league could add another regular-season game. "I don’t think we’re far away from it," Jones told Dallas sports radio station 105.3 FM.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jones suggested the league could move to an expanded regular season as soon as 2027.

"I don’t know what is far away — next month, next year, maybe. Next year, maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players. But it’s in everybody’s best interest."

Interest in potentially adding another game to the schedule for each of the NFL’s 32 teams has been fueled by the league’s growing popularity and expanded international schedule. This season features a record nine games played outside the U.S.

A 10-game international slate has been approved for 2027.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has been a vocal supporter of many owners’ push for an 18-game schedule. Jones suggested the preseason could be shortened if the change becomes reality, with teams using the early weeks of the regular season to ramp up.

"You’d cut back on the preseason games, you’d have teams more developed in the first few games, the type of thing you were trying to get done in the preseason. It’s in everybody’s interest, and it certainly is in the players’ best interests, in my mind."

Jones’ comments suggest an ambitious timeline.

The NFL Players Association has expressed mixed feelings about expanding the regular season. In March, NFLPA executive director JC Tretter told The Athletic that the union was determined to "defend our players and their health."

ROGER GOODELL DETAILS NFL EXPANSION POSSIBILITIES AND A TIMETABLE FOR A FULL SEASON OF INTERNATIONAL GAMES

"There are things that are not good for our players that we need to make sure we’re protecting them from," Tretter said. "And as of right now, those are all subjects of bargaining. The league can’t expand past 10 international games. The league’s at 17 games in the CBA. That is where we’re at, and we’re going to make sure we defend our players and their health and safety because our guys feel they know what this feels like."

Tretter, a former offensive lineman, spent eight seasons in the NFL and last played for the Cleveland Browns in 2021.

"I understand what it felt like when I played 16 (games) and then moved to 17," Tretter said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I understand the toll that takes on the body … I understand the same thing with international. I played an international game. I understand the timeline and how tough it is to recover, how tough it is to turn around and get on the flight on the way back and then get ready for the next week. That is not easy."

The Washington Commanders and New York Giants opened Week 10 of the 2026 season. The Commanders defeated the Giants 24-21.

World.title: NBA star Dejounte Murray requests trade after Pelicans clash, public frustration spills onto social media
World.content:
The apparently strained relationship between Dejounte Murray and the New Orleans Pelicans took another turn Friday.

Representatives for the All-Star guard at Klutch Sports requested a trade, prompting the team to say it would evaluate potential opportunities. "Today, Dejounte Murray’s representatives informed us of his request to be traded," the Pelicans said in a statement. "We will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Murray, 30, was ruled out Friday night against the Memphis Grizzlies due to a left ankle sprain. Pelicans coach Jamahl Mosley said Murray was not at Smoothie King Center.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"He’s not in the building, from what I’ve been told," Mosley said.

The Pelicans acquired Murray in a June 2024 trade with the Atlanta Hawks in exchange for two first-round picks, Dyson Daniels, Larry Nance Jr. and E.J. Liddell.

David Griffin, then serving as the Pelicans’ executive vice president of basketball operations, viewed Murray as a defender and playmaker who could provide ball-handling help for Zion Williamson, but he never approached the play that had earned him All-Star honors in 2022.

DEJOUNTE MURRAY ACCUSES NEW ORLEANS PELICANS OF INSIDE 'SABOTAGE' IN DELETED SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

Murray’s tenure with the Pelicans was dogged by injuries. He broke his hand in the 2024 season opener and then suffered a season-ending Achilles injury in January 2025.

Over the last three seasons, Murray has played just 54 games with New Orleans, averaging 16.6 points, 6.6 assists and 5.9 rebounds. The Pelicans have gone 1-8 with him in the lineup.

Murray's salary is reportedly $32.8 million this season. He has a player option for $30.8 million next season. He recently made his frustrations with the team clear through several critical social media posts.

After one social media reporter mentioned the Pelicans were 3-0 without him in the lineup, Murray wrote back: "From what’s going on INSIDE, this sounds like someone hit you to say this! THE ‘SABOTAGE’ IS REAL!"

The tweet was deleted shortly after.

The timing of Murray’s trade request drew some scrutiny, as it surfaced while the Pelicans were on a four-game losing streak. Nevertheless, Mosley said his focus remained on the players available to him and maintaining the team’s standards.

"How well we play is very important to me, and making sure that we keep up that standard," Mosley said. "That’s why it’s so glaring when we don’t, because I know what this team has shown during training camp, what it has shown during the preseason."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Mosley also said the Pelicans need to return to the style of play they showed earlier this season.

"The first couple games didn’t go on the win column, but the way we played, we did a lot of good things. … As the leader of this group, how we’ve been playing these last three games have not been a representation of this organization, the city, of the way we said we were going to play. That’s been my focus over this last day or so. How do we get back to that style of basketball that we know represents this organization the right way?"

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: ADF seeks to defend Washington girls' sports measure, argues state cannot fully represent female athletes
World.content:
Alliance Defending Freedom filed a motion on behalf of Female Athletes United to defend Washington’s voter-approved girls sports initiative against an ACLU-backed lawsuit, arguing that the state cannot adequately represent the athletes’ interests.

The Nov. 13 motion asks King County Superior Court to allow Female Athletes United to join the case as a defendant to defend Initiative 638. The request seeks the court’s permission to participate; it is not an order granting intervention.

"We’re asking to be allowed to step in and help the state of Washington defend the validity of the law so that I-638 goes into effect on December 3rd, just like the voters in the state of Washington asked for," ADF attorney Hal Frampton told Fox News Digital.

WASHINGTON AG'S OFFICE INDICATES IT WILL DEFEND GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE AFTER ACLU SUES TO BLOCK IT

The initiative would prohibit students who are biologically male from competing in school athletic competitions designated for female students. It also requires participants in girls’ competitions to provide verification of their biological sex from their personal healthcare provider as part of the sports physical process.

The lawsuit challenging it includes parents, TransFamilies and the Washington Education Association as plaintiffs. They argue the measure violates Washington’s constitution, including privacy and equal-rights protections, by excluding transgender girls and imposing sex-verification requirements on participants in girls’ sports that do not apply to boys’ sports.

Asked whether he trusted Washington Attorney General Nick Brown to defend the initiative, Frampton pointed to the athletes his organization represents.

"We trust female athletes to defend the law on behalf of the state of Washington," he said. "That’s why we’re seeking to intervene and make sure that their perspective is part of the, part of the picture and part of the process."

The motion argues that Washington’s previous defense of transgender participation in girls’ sports could prevent it from advancing all the arguments Female Athletes United wants the court to consider.

"While the State may defend its law as a permissible policy choice, FAU will argue not only that the Initiative is valid but that the U.S. Constitution, Title IX, and Title IX’s regulations require Washington to have female-only sports teams, as do pre-existing state laws," the motion states.

SEATTLE MAYOR BACKS EFFORT TO BLOCK GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE THAT PASSED IN 36 OF WASHINGTON'S 39 COUNTIES

Those assertions are the organization’s legal arguments, which the motion asks the court to consider.

Brown announced Nov. 12 that he had appointed outside law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner to defend I-638 on the state’s behalf. He said the arrangement would allow the initiative to be defended while his office continued its work protecting transgender rights.

"My personal views do not dictate what laws get defended or the strength of that defense," Brown said in his announcement.

Frampton said ADF was prepared to work with anyone defending the measure. Asked during the interview whether ADF had contacted the attorney general’s office, he answered, "Not that I’m aware."

"What I know is that we will mount a vigorous defense for Initiative 638 on behalf of female athletes and that we will do everything in our power, make every argument available to us to ensure that democracy prevails and that fairness and safety for women reign in Washington," he said.

The motion draws on accounts from athletes who describe competing against transgender athletes and, in some cases, considering leaving their school teams if the initiative is blocked.

WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR'

The motion cites declarations from five Female Athletes United members: Soleil Hoefer, Charlie Garrett, Sierra Retzlaff, Elise Bierer and Ahnaleigh Wilson.

In a separate declaration, FAU board chair Kristine L. Brown describes the organization as a coalition of prospective, current and former female athletes, coaches, family members and other supporters. She says its work includes legal advocacy and protecting athletes’ privacy in locker rooms and other intimate spaces.

Brown says the organization does not engage in election campaigning, but individual members advocated for or voted for I-638. She identifies Washington athletes whose school sports opportunities the group seeks to protect.

Hoefer, who joined Frampton for the interview, said her experience in high school track helped motivate her advocacy.

"In my personal experience, I was made to run against a boy at state track, and my teammates had run against him the year prior," she said.

Her declaration says she graduated from Prosser High School in 2025 and now attends Walla Walla Community College on a soccer scholarship. She also points to her younger sister, who plays high school volleyball and basketball, as a reason she supports the initiative.

Hoefer said the election result carried personal significance.

"I think it’s a matter of the voters seeing that they didn’t need to vote red or blue. It was voting for women and for our safety and our protection in sports," she said.

Garrett, a Skyview High School runner, describes in her declaration walking off the starting line with teammate Retzlaff at a September meet involving a transgender runner from Camas High School.

Garrett says she later competed against the Camas athlete at postseason meets. According to her account, she finished third behind the athlete’s second-place finish at districts, and eighth behind the athlete’s seventh-place finish at regionals.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

"Standing up for what I believe is right has been isolating and difficult," Garrett says in her declaration. "But it will all be worth it to protect girls from unfair competition and to protect girls’ safe spaces and opportunities."

She says she might run for a club instead of her school this spring if a court blocks the initiative.

Retzlaff makes a similar statement in her signed declaration, dated Nov. 13, saying she might choose club running over school competition next year if I-638 does not take effect.

"It would break my heart if a court blocked Initiative 638," Retzlaff says. "I have been fighting for it the last few months, and it has been one of the hardest things I have ever done."

Bierer, a Battle Ground High School runner, describes in her declaration walking off the starting line alone at districts rather than competing against the Camas athlete.

"When the starting gun went off for the varsity race, I walked off the line with tears in my eyes," her account says. "I was the only runner who did."

Bierer says she will not return to the cross-country team next year if she must continue racing against biologically male athletes.

Wilson, an Eastmont High School runner, describes in her declaration supporting I-638 through public advocacy and signature gathering. She says she traveled around Washington gathering signatures and asking adults to vote for it.

"If a court blocked Initiative 638, it would be devastating to me," Wilson says. "It would feel like my two and a half years of advocating for girls and the mental toll it has taken on me were a waste."

Several of the athletes also address the verification requirement challenged in the lawsuit. Hoefer, Garrett, Retzlaff and Wilson say in their declarations that they would be comfortable having their doctors verify their sex for athletic eligibility.

Frampton said the athletes’ future participation is central to ADF’s effort.

Arians served as the Indianapolis Colts' offensive coordinator and then interim head coach, stepping in for Chuck Pagano, who stepped away from the team to undergo treatment for leukemia.

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented  meeting on the sidelines of APEC, officials say
World.content:
President Donald Trump will meet with the leaders of China and Russia on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen, China’s tech hub, next week, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.

“President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People’s Republic of China and the president of the Russian Federation,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a call with reporters Friday night. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”

It is not anticipated that any sort of agreement will come from the trilateral meeting, according to a senior U.S. official, who described the session as an “entry point” and “the first conversation,” pointing to the reduction of nuclear arsenals as a key topic.

“We do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the senior U.S. official said about the issue of nuclear weapons.

Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.

The three-way summit with Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin comes at a complicated moment in relations for the three countries.

Trump intends to discuss the Iran war with the two leaders, but not the war in Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that discussions about the war in Ukraine are a separate “track” that China is not part of so it would not be “appropriate.”

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.

Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.

There is no bilateral with Putin scheduled, but the two leaders will appear at events and the trilateral meeting together, according to a senior U.S. official.

There are no plans for Trump to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to a senior U.S. official.

Separately, Elon Musk will be the only business leader who is part of the president’s delegation, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that other U.S. business leaders will attend the summit in their own capacity but there is no official U.S. business delegation.

Musk will not be part of any official meetings, according to a senior U.S. official.

Two senior U.S. officials said that they don’t think Trump will raise the espionage investigation focused on Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence agent who allegedly had a romantic relationship with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, with China.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip. In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls,” a senior U.S. official said. “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration and interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.”

Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit

By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.

For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.

“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.

More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.

“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.

The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years

Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”

Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.

Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.

As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.

In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.

Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.

Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.

“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”

World.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
World.content:
The federal government on Friday announced a six-month delay in enforcing a Medicaid work requirement — a central provision in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” that experts said would lead millions of Americans to lose health coverage.

The requirement still technically starts on Jan. 1, but under new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, states that choose not to enforce it won’t be held accountable until at least July 1.

The move is a striking turn for an administration that has spent months defending the policy against criticism from state officials and healthcare advocates who warned that the rollout was moving too quickly and that people who should be eligible for Medicaid would lose coverage because of the additional red tape and paperwork.

CMS called the six-month window a “hold harmless” period, and the delay is optional. States that choose to take advantage of this period will still start checking on Jan. 1 whether Medicaid enrollees are working, volunteering or in school or whether they qualify for an exemption. But until July, no one in those states will lose coverage for failing to meet the requirements.

“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term,” said Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at CMS.

The White House declined to comment.

00:00 00:00 How Democrats intend to deliver on their big campaign promises 03:12

Some states have already moved forward with implementing the work requirements. In Nebraska, which launched the work requirements May 1, over 1,000 people have lost coverage or been denied benefits because of the new rules, according to state figures through August.

The Medicaid work requirement was a cornerstone of Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” a massive tax and spending package that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy through tax breaks while slashing the social safety net for vulnerable Americans. Millions of Americans are expected to lose health coverage and food assistance as a result of the law, the signature domestic legislation of Trump’s second term.

The law requires many able-bodied adults under the age of 65 to prove they work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours a month to keep Medicaid, which provides health coverage for low-income and disabled Americans. The Trump administration argues the requirement and other provisions in the law encourage work, reduce waste and protect government benefit programs for those who need them.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work requirements alone would leave 5.3 million more people uninsured by 2034 and would save the federal government $317 billion, part of nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts in the law.

Pressure on the administration to delay the requirement had been building for months. Five Democratic governors last month asked Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to postpone the implementation, saying that state agencies weren’t ready. And a federal judge last month blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a portion of the requirement related to medically frail people, saying it could lead some to wrongly lose coverage.

The delay comes a little more than a week after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on a promise to reverse the GOP’s cuts to healthcare and food assistance.

“Millions of people’s health care is at risk because of the Republican reconciliation law’s work requirement, as states scramble to implement on a rushed timeline & respond to shifting federal requirements,” Sarah Lueck, vice president for health policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said in a post on X. “Today’s news lets states delay the harm.”

World.title: U.S. measles deaths rise to 10 after new reports in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin
World.content:
Total measles deaths in the United States this year rose to 10 on Friday, a grim milestone in an outbreak that has seen a record number of infections and prompted state and local health departments to ramp up vaccination efforts.

Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each reported a new measles-associated death on Friday. The Wisconsin Health Department said a child had died, but declined to release more information, citing the family’s privacy. The Pennsylvania Health Department said its latest death was an unvaccinated resident of Montour County who had tested positive for measles.

The virus, the most contagious known to humans, can lead to deadly complications, like pneumonia or swelling of the brain, in unvaccinated people.

So far this year, Pennsylvania has reported seven measles-associated deaths, Wisconsin has reported two and New York has reported one. Prior to those deaths, none of the states had seen a measles death in more than 30 years.

As of Thursday, around 5,400 measles cases have been recorded in the U.S. — more than double last year’s count and the highest since 1991. Public health experts attribute the outbreak to a sharp decline in measles vaccination rates coupled with a global resurgence of the virus.

Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning it was no longer continuously spreading, though there can be occasional outbreaks. The country now seems poised to lose that designation: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a group within the World Health Organization, met this week to determine whether the U.S. can still be considered measles-free. Their decision is expected to be announced on Tuesday.

At the center of PAHO’s deliberations is whether there has been ongoing transmission in the U.S. for a full year. Canada lost its elimination status last year after the agency determined that the virus had been spreading there for at least 12 months.

Measles is already spreading widely enough in the U.S. to threaten infants who aren’t eligible for their first shot. At least four deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated. In response to their outbreaks, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are recommending an early dose for infants ages 6 to 11 months who live in areas with high case counts.

The first dose is usually given around a child’s first birthday and the second at 4 to 6 years. Two doses are 97% effective.

Nationwide, 75% of counties and jurisdictions with measles vaccine data fall below the 95% vaccination rate needed to prevent outbreaks, according to an NBC News investigation.

The share of kindergartners who had been vaccinated for measles fell from 95% during the 2019-20 school year to 92% during the 2025-26 school year.

World.title: Rep. Lauren Boebert, conservative firebrand from Colorado, loses her race for re-election
World.content:
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., a conservative firebrand who was caught up in several headline-grabbing controversies during her six years in Congress, has been defeated by Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, NBC News projects.

Laubacher is a retired Navy rear admiral and Afghanistan war veteran who served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration.

“Integrity matters. Character matters. Truth matters, and public service should always be about what you can do for other people, not what you do for yourself,” Laubacher told supporters on election night, according to The Colorado Sun. “Those things were worth fighting for when we started.”

Boebert, who won re-election in Colorado’s 3rd District by just 546 votes in 2022, shifted to the much redder 4th Congressional District in 2024 and won re-election more easily.

But that shift proved no match for the anti-Trump blue tsunami that washed over the country in these midterm elections, sweeping her and many other GOP incumbents out of office.

“There was a lot of money dumped on my head,” Boebert said after the election, while also blaming the Senate for failing to pass many House-approved Republican bills.

Eileen Laubacher thanks her supporters on election night. Hyoung Chang / Denver Post via Getty

Before her political career, Boebert was a gun-rights activist and owned Shooters Grill in Rifle, Colorado. She upset Rep. Scott Tipton, R-Colo., in the GOP primary in 2020 and became a vocal defender of Donald Trump in Washington.

But their relationship soured more recently. In November 2025, Boebert was one of four Republicans who joined Democrats in signing a discharge petition to force a vote to release the Justice Department’s Jeffrey Epstein files, against Trump’s will.

When Trump vowed to unseat Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., for leading the Epstein files push, Boebert sided with Massie and campaigned with him this May. Trump lashed out, calling her “dumb” and “weak-minded,” and threatened to rescind his endorsement of her, though he never did.

Boebert was known on Capitol Hill more for her controversies and clashes with fellow lawmakers than for legislative savvy.

In 2021, she apologized after video emerged of her suggesting that fellow Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was mistaken for a terrorist in an elevator both were riding in the Capitol. Omar said Boebert’s description of the two riding an elevator never happened.

At the State of the Union address in 2022, Boebert and then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., stood up and heckled President Joe Biden throughout his speech, including trying to start a “build the wall” chant. The two conservative women later had a very public falling-out, with Greene calling her colleague “a little b----” on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert and her date were escorted out of a performance of the “Beetlejuice” musical in Denver. They were alleged to have been vaping, taking photos and engaging in other disruptive behavior.

World.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights
World.content:
A rare nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights that lasted several hours Friday has been lifted, and flights are resuming, the Federal Aviation Administration said. Officials said the issue stemmed from a "telecommunication outage."

"At 8:15 tonight, Eastern time, we've opened up the airspace," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during a news briefing Friday night. "Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It's going to be slow. So if you're watching, you're at an airport, check with your airline."

In a social media post following the briefing, the FAA said that "before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours.

Duffy attributed the ground stop to outdated air traffic control technology and routers overloaded by data.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said during the news conference. " ... Our routers actually got overloaded with data and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down."

"The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming," the FAA confirmed in a social media post following the briefing. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

An update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage, multiple sources told CBS News earlier Friday. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Friday's briefing that new security patches introduced into the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers.

Duffy said the FAA would try to move as many flights as possible Friday night depending on crew capacity.

"If not, we're going to start tomorrow [Saturday] morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft. But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.

There were more than 10,000 delays and over 4,000 cancellations listed Friday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.

Duffy said he thinks flights will be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel" during the Thanksgiving holiday later this month.

Mullin told reporters in an earlier briefing outside the White House Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."

"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."

Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global Microsoft outage.

"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said during the news briefing with Duffy. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."

He also said flights will be able to land safely.

Passengers wait at San Francisco International Airport during a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights on Nov. 13, 2026. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images

"We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that's going to be in the air, that's currently on the plane, the loved ones, as I said, we're going to get you on the ground and we're doing it in a safe manner," Mullin said.

Federal agencies are all working together on the situation, Mullin added.

"I don't want to say that this is a crisis, but it is because we're ... we had to do a nationwide ground stoppage," he said.

According to the flight tracking site Flightradar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began.

Delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."

On Friday night, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

"But you will have more of these," Duffy said during the news conference. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."

Mullin argued that the incident demonstrated why he believed piecemeal modernization was insufficient and said the Trump administration wants a complete replacement of the air traffic control system, at an estimated cost of $50 billion.

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, known as FTI, is the communications backbone that connects air traffic control centers and other FAA facilities. It supports the transmission of essential voice communications and operational data used to manage air traffic.

The FAA awarded Harris Corp., the predecessor to L3Harris, a contract to modernize, operate and manage the network in July 2002, more than 24 years ago.

A November 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review described the FTI network as obsolete and said it depended on an older communications technology known as TDM.

The review also warned that the technology was no longer supported by the telecommunications infrastructure on which it relied and that an unexpected failure could leave individual FAA facilities, or even an entire regional air traffic control center, disconnected from the broader network.

In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.

World.title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
World.content:
A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water.

Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.

The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark.

In a news briefing late Friday afternoon, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said.

New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port NOLA.

Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by a tanker ship in the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Gerald Herbert

Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Nearby boats reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water.

Emergency responders, including Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, conducted rescue and response operations, Port NOLA said. Moreno said that along with local and federal agencies, private vessels that happened to be on the river at the time responded "as volunteers to try and get people out of the water."

Moreno described the successful rescue operation as a "miracle on the Mississippi."

One witness, Jamie Holford, told CBS News he saw the American Heritage hit the dock after the collision. He described seeing people hurrying off the boat. Then, as it rolled over, some were climbing over the railings of the boat, he said.

"It looked like something off the Titanic," he said.

Asked what the collision sounded like, Holford said, "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like."

U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Coast Guard investigators were on scene working to determine what caused the tanker to lose control.

"The investigation is still ongoing, there seems to be some kind of a loss of steering," Burnham told reporters. "The exact reason why, we don't know that."

The National Transportation Safety Board said in a statement that it was sending a "Go Team" to the scene Saturday to begin its own investigation into the cause. However, in a follow up social media post, the NTSB clarified that because of the nationwide ground stop earlier Friday that canceled and delayed thousands of flights, it would no longer be sending one of its board members to the scene, and its team of investigators would be driving instead of flying to New Orleans.

Burnham also noted that she was working to reopen the river, which the Coast Guard had closed when the collision occurred.

"We're going to start evaluating how to reopen it as soon as possible," Burnham said.

In a Truth Social post, President Trump praised the response of the Coast Guard and other law enforcement agencies for "doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana."

The American Heritage was built in 2015 and is operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The Associated Press reports that the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. The tanker specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semisolid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

CBS News has reached out to the tanker's owner for comment.

World.title: How "Banana Man" took a small Indiana town by storm
World.content:
In Linton, Indiana, there have been reports and sightings of a superhero of sorts, "Banana Man."

"Just boom, like a yellow streak goes by," one Linton resident said. "... And everybody is like, 'It's the Banana Man.'"

"Little bitty legs and tights on," stated another.

Banana Man began popping up around town a few months ago. Videos that also began circulating on social media appeared to show a boy, about middle school age, biking all over town in a banana suit.

"Banana Man" rides his bike in Linton, Indiana. November 2026. CBS News

So CBS News came to Linton to investigate and find out who and why, but it wasn't easy.

Because Banana Man's other trademark is that he doesn't ever talk. In fact, by all accounts, he has never spoken a word publicly. That is, until now.

In an interview, CBS News disguised his voice to protect his identity.

"So my mom bought a banana costume from Goodwill, and I put it on and rode my bike as a joke," Banana Man explains as to how his alter ego took shape. "And I saw that it made a lot of people smile, and I like making people smile."

Banana Man said that when he was younger, he dreamed of being a superhero.

"But I didn't expect to be a banana," he said.

But as a banana, he has so much more appeal. Linton residents have now thoroughly embraced the legend, and many even dressed up as him for Halloween.

A local girls cross country team did a run in his honor. Some people are even wearing Banana Man T-shirts.

"People honk and yell and wave," one Linton resident said of Banana Man sightings.



In gratitude to his legions, Banana Man hands out autographed cards, which have become quite the collector's item in Linton.

What started out as a joke has now made a serious difference. Banana Man has brought the town together.

"Yeah, feels good. I feel proud," Banana Man said. "And I'm just going to keep doing the same thing that I've been doing."

World.title: SpaceX launches first-of-its-kind Starship test flight
World.content:
SpaceX launched its huge Starship rocket on the program's 15th test flight Friday, a 22-hour mission that was meant to feature planned launch pad catches of both the booster and the Starship's upper stage.

However, after the booster sent the Starship on its way to orbit as planned, a problem of some sort prevented a return-to-the-launch-pad capture. Instead, the rocket made a splashdown off the Texas Gulf Coast, exploding in a spectacular fireball moments before hitting the water.

SpaceX managed to catch a Super Heavy booster during three previous test flights, using giant mechanical arms on the launch gantry to snag the rockets as they descended tail first on the power of three of their 33 Raptor engines. But the flight plans always include a splashdown option if an issue crops up preventing a safe capture.

It was not immediately known what triggered the diversion Friday or the explosion before splashdown.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launches from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, on Nov. 13, 2026. Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty Images

It was a disappointment for SpaceX workers who had hoped the Super Heavy-Starship rocket's 15th test flight would be the first to demonstrate full reusability in an orbit-class rocket. The company still plans to attempt its first-ever launch pad catch of a Starship upper stage Saturday at the conclusion of the mission.

Loaded with 8 million pounds of supercold liquid oxygen and methane fuel, the rocket's 236-foot-tall first stage, powered by 33 methane-burning Raptor engines, roared to life and majestically propelled the booster away from SpaceX's "Starbase" launch site on the Texas Gulf Coast at 5:47 p.m. ET.

Arcing away to the southeast, the Super Heavy booster propelled the rocket out of the thick lower atmosphere before falling away about 2 minutes and 20 seconds after liftoff.

Technical problem forced SpaceX to divert booster to Gulf Coast

While the 171-foot-tall Starship continued the climb to space using six Raptors of its own, the booster flipped around and fired up a set of Raptors to reverse course and head back to the launch site.

But a little more than 6 minutes after liftoff, flight controllers ordered a diversion to a Gulf Coast splashdown because of a technical problem. Long-range cameras captured the big booster slowly descending to the Gulf, shrouded in steam and then a fireball as residual propellants ignited.

The Starship, meanwhile, followed a suborbital trajectory, ensuring a safe ocean splashdown in case of problems, while giving SpaceX flight controllers time to assess its health before committing to a final push to orbit.

But no issues were found and after an 18-minute coast, a single Raptor reignited for a short 10-second burn to push the craft into its planned orbit. Eight and a half minutes after that, the first of 26 upgraded version 3 Starlink internet satellites was expected to be pushed out into space to fly on its own.

For the rest of the flight, controllers planned to closely monitor the Starship, periodically assessing its health to make sure it could be safely de-orbited in case of problems that might prevent a safe return-to-launch-site capture at the same pad where it launched Friday atop the Super Heavy booster. It will be SpaceX's first attempt to get a Starship back to its pad for possible refurbishment and relaunch.

"During this prolonged coast phase, flight control teams have several options to end the mission early and return Starship to pre-cleared areas of the Pacific Ocean if needed," SpaceX said in a blog post. "These locations include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission splashdown opportunity several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. These precleared areas ... provide a safe place to land Starship if any conditions arise that may preclude the ability to perform a safe reentry."

Starship's upper stage slated to reenter Earth's atmosphere and land at Starbase on Saturday

One hour after a final "return check" Saturday, a single Raptor is expected to fire at 3:21 p.m. Eastern time to lower the far side of the Starship's orbit deep into the atmosphere for a 56-minute belly-first reentry and return to the Texas Gulf Coast.

"During reentry, Starship can alter its flight path by moving its four control flaps," the company said. "This will permit Starship to maintain a safe and known trajectory while guiding itself with high precision control toward Starbase."

As it descends, the Starship will carry out "a series of small turns in its trajectory to intentionally fly over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas," SpaceX said.

Starship will avoid major cities in the Rio Grande Valley and pass to the north of South Padre Island before heading "out over the Gulf of America as it makes its final turn south towards Starbase."

Nearing the launch pad, the 171-foot-tall Starship will fire three Raptors to flip upright. Once the maneuver is complete, one Raptor will be shut down as the rocket descends between the gantry's mechanical arms. Finally, with just one engine firing to slow the rocket to a near stop, the mechanical arms will move in to snag the spacecraft.

But all of that depends on a problem-free descent. If any problems develop that might lead to an uncontrolled landing, flight controllers can ensure a vehicle breakup before it has any chance to reach a populated area.

"During reentry, flight controllers will have several options to end the reentry early and safely by intentionally tumbling Starship to ensure that it breaks up in the atmosphere before reaching land," SpaceX said. "There is also a late-reentry option to send Starship into the Gulf ... if any of its systems or the tower itself encounter an issue after reentry that would preclude a safe catch at Starbase."

SpaceX calls development of a fully reusable rocket "the holy grail of rocketry," opening the door to airplanelike cadence where a vehicle flies again rapidly.

NASA is counting on a variant of the Starship to carry Artemis astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it is also open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready.

World.title: Lutnick agrees to testify as Bessent blames him for chip sales
World.content:
Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.

GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department.

"Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."

Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

World.title: Man whose wife, son were injured in building collapse wants answers
World.content:
The world crumbled around Anderson Velez's family on Wednesday when the multi-use Brooklyn building where they resided collapsed.

Video from a baby monitor showed his terrified sons and wife, Joanna, inside their third-floor apartment as the walls broke open and crashed. CBS News also obtained surveillance video capturing the apartment building and storefront crashing down.

Eight people, ranging in age from 9 to 31, died in the collapse, including two children. Another 18 were injured.

Joanna Velez remains hospitalized, as does their 9-year-old son, Pablo Alvarez, who is recovering from surgery for a severe head injury. Miraculously, their 2-year-old son Joseph Alvarez survived with barely a scratch.

Anderson Velez, who was not home at the time, told CBS News his fear when he heard of the collapse was that his children had "lost their lives."

The building where the Velez family resided collapsed into an adjacent construction site and also tore off the side of another building in the process.

Now, the search for answers and accountability is underway, as the Brooklyn District Attorney's Office has launched a criminal investigation into the incident.

The collapsed building had 98 open violations, according to records from the New York City Department of Buildings.

The same agency had also earlier this year ordered a contractor to stop demolition work that was underway at the adjacent construction site. When the contractor continued the demolition work despite the stop-work order, the buildings department issued a violation in April.

In May, though, the violation was addressed and the stop-work order was lifted, the buildings department said.

That contractor, Townhouse Builders, has been sued at least 67 times since 2012, according to court records reviewed by CBS News.

"Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failures," Farah Louis, a member of the New York City Council, said in a news conference Friday. "Especially when records show a building with nearly 100 open violations sitting next to an excavation site cited for violating a stop-work order."

Anderson Velez believes that construction taking place in the site next door led to the collapse.

"The building had no reason to fall on its own," he said.

Asked about his thoughts when he sees the video of the collapse, Anderson Velez responded, "Honestly, I still watch it and tears come to my eyes."

CBS News has reached out to the owner of the collapsed building for comment but has not heard back.

World.title: Small Indiana town gets its own superhero, a kid known as "Banana Man"
World.content: Meet Indiana's "Banana Man" A boy became a local legend in Linton, Indiana, for regularly riding his bike in a banana costume, earning him the nickname "Banana Man." Steve Hartman has the story. More

World.title: DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop
World.content:
DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke to at the White House on Friday afternoon after the FAA issues a total ground stop. NPR was there for the briefing.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Travelers across the country are now stranded in airports and sitting on runways after the FAA issued a total ground stop this afternoon. There are very few details about why Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made that call. All we know at this time is that it's being attributed to communication difficulties. Here is Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaking at the White House just a few minutes ago.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We're getting a ton of calls saying, is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack? Everybody's safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones, if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that.

PFEIFFER: NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram was there listening to Mullin when he talked to reporters, and she's with us now. Deepa, what can you tell us about what's going on?

DEEPA SHIVARAM, BYLINE: Yeah. So this all happened in the span of the last 30 minutes, I would say. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin came out to brief reporters just outside the White House, and he started off by saying that there is not a threat to the U.S., and they believe that this whole situation boils down to a telecommunications issue.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MULLIN: There was no prior indication. There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It is just a telecommunication outage as of right now.

SHIVARAM: He was asked about his wording there, as of yet, when he said that there, you know, wasn't any indication that this was a nefarious attack. He said that they're not ruling out anything. They're still looking into the details, and they're not at a point where they can rule anything out, hence his wording, as of yet. He said that all flights are accounted for, and he was very emphatic multiple times that this was not a 9/11 situation.

MULLIN: Out of abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for. As incoming flights, either internationally or the flights that are currently still in the air - we'll be dealing with those case by case.

SHIVARAM: The secretary also said that he does not think this is affecting other countries. He did have some information that was a little unclear, though. He added that there are two places in the U.S. that were not affected by this outage, this communications outage, but he couldn't quite share more details about that. So that part of this is a little bit unclear and, I think, underscores that there's still a lot of information that's coming in.

PFEIFFER: Interesting. I guess we'll find out later whether he means continental U.S. or otherwise. We'll try to answer that question for our listeners later. Did he give any details about what steps are underway to try to resolve this?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So he said the first thing officials are working on is trying to restore communications to the full extent, make sure that all flights are on the ground. But no specific timeline was given here, Sacha. He was asked if this whole process was going to be, you know, a matter hours. Are people going to be stuck on tarmacs? Is it going to take days, months? He didn't really have an exact answer to that. All he said is that it's going to take some time. And he said this isn't going to be turned around within the hour. It's just going to take some time, and that part is still a little bit unclear as well.

PFEIFFER: Deepa, as I've been reading about this over the past 30 minutes, I saw some reporting that said there was some new system, possibly an AI-driven system, that was rolled out earlier this week by the FAA. Do you know anything?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So at at this stage, the secretary said that this outage today is not connected to this AI system, and I'll just explain that really quickly. The FAA rolled out an AI air traffic tool nationwide earlier this week, and that tool is built to help assist with air traffic management. It was already piloted in D.C., actually, in September, and then this week, it was applied nationwide. The secretary said, though, that at this stage, they don't think those two things are connected. He also was asked about the Microsoft outage that happened yesterday and if there was any possible connection to that and what's going on today. And he said he didn't see any reason to connect those two situations.

PFEIFFER: Has President Trump weighed in on this at all?

SHIVARAM: We have not heard from the president yet. I have been refreshing his social media feed to try and see if we will hear from him imminently. He has been briefed on this, and the secretary said that, you know, everybody's involved with this right now. It takes the FAA, obviously. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has been speaking with the president, the State Department. He called the situation unprecedented when you have something like this going on. I will say, in terms of Trump's travel plans, he is expected to stay in Washington this weekend, so no imminent travel for him, but he is planning on Monday to depart for Asia, where he'll be going to the Philippines and China for two summits.

PFEIFFER: You know, Deepa, I am supposed to fly tonight. I'm now bracing...

SHIVARAM: Oh.

PFEIFFER: ...Myself for probably not being...

SHIVARAM: My goodness.

PFEIFFER: ...Able to fly tonight. So I have so many questions. And I have a few I want to ask you that you actually may not know. Please feel free to say, I don't know.

SHIVARAM: Yeah.

PFEIFFER: We know they're grounded, and you touched on this, but do we know if planes that are actually in the air are going to be brought down, they have to get out of the air? Or that's a case-by-case situation?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So that's, like, kind of a split ticket right now. The secretary did say that they're working on getting all flights grounded. So I think that's something that's in the process of happening. The split ticket that I referred to, I think, when it comes to international flights that are incoming - that is being treated as a case-by-case basis.

PFEIFFER: And in terms of where the planes who might have to come down quickly have to go, that's...

SHIVARAM: Yeah.

PFEIFFER: ...Just the challenge that air traffic controllers deal with. How do we get them down? Where do we put them?

SHIVARAM: Yes. So when they talk about this communications outage, I believe that the secretary said they're still able to communicate with certain planes that are in the air and things like that. And so the process of getting everybody on the ground sounds like it's obviously very complicated. The specifics on which communications elements here are, you know, up in the air, for lack of a better word and unclear - that part is sort of just broadly being spoken as a widespread telecommunications issue.

PFEIFFER: So I imagine a lot of people stuck in airports, a lot stuck in tarmacs. If people are trying to decide whether to go to the airport, maybe call your airline, but I'm sure they're overwhelmed by calls right now.

SHIVARAM: Yes. It sounds like the information is a little unclear, especially when it comes to grounding flights versus departing flights. I don't think there's been guidance that's been issued on that quite yet.

PFEIFFER: Thank you for that. That's NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram.

SHIVARAM: Thank you.

World.title: Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences
World.content:
Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences

Passengers stuck on airplanes on tarmacs across the country during the FAA ground stop on Friday share their stories.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

When today's FAA ground stop was announced, thousands of planes at airports across the country were on the tarmac with passengers on board. We spoke with one of them, Regina Heirlig (ph).

REGINA HEIRLIG: I am at the Dallas Fort Worth airport right now, and I'm trying to go to San Diego. I flew out of BWI in Baltimore this morning and connecting in Dallas Fort Worth, trying to go to San Diego. I'm trying to help a family member who had an emergency, and so I need to get there, and I hope it's today, but I'm not feeling really optimistic about it at this point.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

We also heard from Gillian Karen (ph).

GILLIAN KAREN: I'm at O'Hare, and I'm going to LaGuardia. We boarded normal time, everything normal, sat on the tarmac for quite some time. And then flight attendant comes over the speaker saying there's a nationwide grounding.

DETROW: Allison Frankel (ph) said she was in a bit of an information vacuum.

ALLISON FRANKEL: You know, it's hard sitting here without information, so we're all looking for information and guidance from the government and for as much information as we can from news reporters. But at the end of the day, you know, we all want to stay safe, so grateful, at least, to be on the ground and safe.

PFEIFFER: And as we were talking to Gillian Karen, she got some news.

KAREN: Oh, wait, sorry. There's - hold on, they're...

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Inaudible). Turn off seatbelts.

KAREN: Oh, OK. We are at the gate.

DETROW: Good news - better to be in the terminal than on the tarmac all night.

World.title: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
World.content:
What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop

The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The U.S. air travel system is slowly getting back off the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the rare nationwide ground stop it issued earlier today, citing telecommunications failure. That grounded thousands of planes at airports across the country, stranding millions of passengers. NPR's transportation correspondent Joel Rose is here. We've been talking all afternoon and evening trying to sort this out. Joel, now we have a little bit of a resolution, but not really. What's the latest?

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Yeah. We just heard from the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, that, as you said, the airspace has reopened. The ground stop is lifted. But it's going to take some time to get this hourslong - to get through the backlog of canceled and delayed flights. And it's going to take even longer to figure out, apparently, what happened here.

During the news conference, Duffy said that investigators are still trying to understand exactly what the problem was. Duffy blamed the - Duffy cited intermittent communications, intermittent radar and blamed this on outdated air traffic control equipment that was overloaded with data. We have old switches, old routers, he said. It's an old system that went down. It got overloaded. Here's more of what Duffy said.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We're getting very little information. Our pilot's been great and has been giving us updates every 15 minutes, which has been really helpful and reassuring.

DETROW: I think we had the wrong tape there, Joel. But...

ROSE: That's the wrong cut. Well, you got...

DETROW: Yeah, yeah, keep going.

ROSE: I'll tell you more about Secretary Duffy.

DETROW: Sure.

ROSE: So he spent a lot of this press conference blaming old gear that failed. But when reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong today, he wasn't able to give them a whole lot of specifics. He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic control system, which has been a big priority for this administration but was - we just don't - we still have only Duffy's word that this was the old gear that failed. We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was at this press conference too. He said, there's no indication that this was a cyber attack, but he could not rule that out entirely - also started the press conference by saying that this outage is not related to the Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and some other services yesterday.

DETROW: Yeah, I feel like I had a lot of questions watching that briefing, as did many other people. And meanwhile, there's people all over the country trying to get home. Our reporter at Washington National Airport, Ava Berger, says she is hearing announcements that the hold's has been lifted, but the announcements are saying - urging people to please be patient. About half the board there is red with canceled flights. But she said people are now starting to optimistically slowly go back to their gates to see if their plane's ever going to leave. I mean, Joel, what is the situation like on the ground at other airports around the country?

ROSE: This is a mess, and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, we've canceled - airlines have canceled thousands of flights. Thousands more are delayed. Planes are out of position. Crews are out of position. This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once.

DETROW: Ooh.

ROSE: You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled, and it's going to take days, optimistically...

DETROW: Yeah.

ROSE: ...Before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.

DETROW: We've got about 10 seconds left. Remind us how rare something like this is.

ROSE: Very unusual. This is the second nationwide groundstop since September 11. The most recent was in 2023, and that one only lasted less than 2 hours. So this now appears to be the longest nationwide groundstop since September 11 of 2001.

DETROW: NPR's Joel Rose, thanks so much.

ROSE: You bet.
