World.title: International News Briefs for Friday, November 13, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen Will Challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader

Nov 13, 2026

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday he will challenge New York’s Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader when Democrats retake control of both chambers of Congress in January. This follows historic gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. They’ll now control at least 255 seats in the House of Representatives and 55 in the Senate. This is Senator Van Hollen speaking on MS NOW.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen: “And it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty. It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people and that’s fueled by a corrupt political system. And the call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Van Hollen is the first Democratic senator to launch a leadership challenge since 1994. His bid was quickly endorsed by Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders.

Youth Climate Activists Protest in Chuck Schumer’s Office to Demand New Senate Leadership

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: Sunrise Movement

More than 50 young activists with the Sunrise Movement were arrested Thursday after hundreds of protesters staged a sit-in inside Senator Chuck Schumer’s Washington, D.C., office. Activists are pushing for new Democratic leadership in the Senate after nearly a decade under Schumer. They also want Democrats to abolish the Senate filibuster. Children also participated in the action Thursday as many of the protesters held signs that read “The filibuster kills,” “Stop the climate crisis,” and “Schumer: Step up or step aside.”

Sunrise Movement activist 1: “Chuck Schumer and establishment Democrats are more scared of the voices of young people than of the climate crisis.”

Grace: “The American public is tired of the same old politics, and we’re ready for real change.”

Sunrise Movement activist 2: “Chuck Schumer would rather listen to billionaires than young people.”

Sunrise Movement activist 3: “Chuck Schumer doesn’t listen to us. He listens to corporate money, specifically coming from AIPAC. Over $400,000 have been invested into him.”

Jamie: “I chose to do this because when I was in high school, I saw the places I love burn to the ground because of the climate crisis. As I’ve grown older, I’ve seen American tax dollars go to burning and bombing Gaza.”

Grace: “I think everybody, including young people the most, can see the writing on the wall at this point, right? And we’re all saying the ship needs to be going in this direction.”

Nvidia’s Colette Kress to Serve as Interim CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Scandals

Nov 13, 2026

Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned. The chip maker says its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia’s board of directors searches for a permanent replacement. Huang stepped down as Reuters reported he’d had an intimate relationship with a second employee, whom Reuters did not name. That follows reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials claim was spying for Beijing as part of a Chinese intelligence operation seeking to acquire advanced computer chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. Huang reportedly helped the alleged spy acquire at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips for China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before House lawmakers in a closed-door hearing later this month. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market capitalization since its all-time high in early October. We’ll have more on this story after headlines.

Microsoft Outage Disrupts Communications for Millions Across 74 Countries

Nov 13, 2026

In more technology news, Microsoft is scrambling to fix a major outage that’s disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries since Thursday morning. The outage has cut off access to Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot.

Iran Says It Blew Up U.S. Early-Warning Radar as Trump Declares, “We Don’t Need a Deal with Iran”

Nov 13, 2026

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. Officials also claimed four attacks on oil tankers in ​the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, following strikes on a pair of supertankers one day earlier.

Iran’s attacks came as President Trump on Thursday sidelined Vice President JD Vance as the top U.S. negotiator with Iran. Trump said in a social media post he’d directed Vance to instead focus on fighting what Trump called “corruption and crime” in Democratic-controlled cities and states. Trump wrote, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Houthis Claim Fresh Attacks on Saudi Oil Facilities Including East-West Pipeline

Nov 13, 2026

Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis, has claimed fresh attacks on oil infrastructure and an air base in Saudi Arabia. A Houthi spokesperson said targets included the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea, an Aramco facility in Riyadh and a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline, which is Saudi Arabia’s main route for shipping oil past Iran’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Arab League warned Thursday that a Houthi siege of the southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz is leading to a humanitarian disaster, with “acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies.”

Russia and Ukraine Continue Deadly Strikes as U.S. Envoys Meet Putin and Zelensky

Nov 13, 2026

Russia and Ukraine traded drone and missile attacks overnight, despite a diplomatic push by the Trump administration that’s purportedly seeking an end to the conflict. The violence came after President Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, followed by a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a prisoner swap that Zelensky called the largest since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Zelensky has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of once again restricting service to Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink internet satellite constellation, which Ukraine uses for drone attacks.

Infant Dies of Hypothermia in Gaza as Calls Grow for Israel to Allow Imports of Winter Supplies

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: Deutsche Presse-Agentur GmbH

In Gaza, a Palestinian infant has died from hypothermia after Israeli attacks left his family displaced and living in a tent in Khan Younis. Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was just 9 months old. His death came as Israel continued to impose severe restrictions on imports of fuel and winter supplies into Gaza. U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher says 150,000 tents remain stuck in warehouses at Gaza’s borders, even as some 350,000 displaced Palestinians face heavy rain, flooding and plummeting temperatures. On Thursday, a group of 49 nations issued a joint call for Israel to ease restrictions on shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies to Gaza. The United States did not sign the statement. This is Britain’s ambassador to the U.N., Sarah MacIntosh, speaking from U.N. headquarters.

Sarah MacIntosh: “As winter sets in, far too many people in Gaza are still without adequate shelter and risk exposure to hypothermia, respiratory infections, waterborne diseases and other preventable illnesses. Constraints on the entry of critical shelter items and other life-saving supplies continue to prevent humanitarian organizations from responding at the scale required.”

In more news from Gaza, a Palestinian was killed by Israeli gunfire east of Gaza City earlier today. That followed an Israeli strike on a car near the gate of Al-Shifa Hospital which killed one person and left several others critically wounded. That attack came as Palestinians in Khan Younis held funerals for a ​surgeon, a teenage boy and four other Palestinians killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted southern Gaza’s Nasser Hospital complex. We’ll have more on that attack, and the latest from Gaza, later in the broadcast.

ICE Detention of USF Professor Draws Protests and Demands for Her Release

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: University of San Francisco

In California, community members are demanding the release of beloved nurse and University of San Francisco professor Ann Lawani, who was detained by ICE nearly two months ago. Lawani is originally from Nigeria and has lived in the U.S. since 2007. She was reportedly at home in Lodi, still wearing her pajamas, when ICE agents showed up at her door in early September, taking her to a local holding facility. Then she disappeared from ICE’s database for three days, with her older brother telling The New York Times, “It was the worst time of my life, knowing she had been siphoned into an abyss and there was nothing I could do about it.” Lawani is now being detained thousands of miles away at an ICE jail in Basile, Louisiana.

Protesters in San Diego Demand ICE Release 8-Year-Old Haitian Boy to Relatives

Nov 13, 2026

Hundreds of protesters, including teachers and elected officials, rallied outside San Diego’s federal building Thursday, calling for an 8-year-old Haitian boy to be reunited with his relatives. He was taken into federal immigration custody after a check-in last week. The boy is a third grader at a local elementary school. His family and advocates say they do not know his whereabouts.

23 Immigrants Died of Medical Neglect in ICE Custody in First Year of Trump’s Second Term

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: GEO Group

Nearly two dozen immigrants died in the custody of ICE during the first year of President Trump’s second term due to medical neglect. That’s according to findings by the San Francisco Chronicle, which obtained internal ICE investigations into the 29 deaths that occurred in 2025. ICE’s own documents admit immigration jails failed to provide emergency medical care. In some cases, ICE jail staff even mocked or ignored people who requested help and who later died.

At least 62 immigrants have died in ICE custody since Trump’s return to office. In response to the abuse, immigrants jailed across the nation have staged hunger strikes and other peaceful actions. This week, the publication L.A. Taco reported at least 24 people detained at the Adelanto ICE jail in California’s Mojave Desert started another hunger strike — the second so far this year. Meanwhile, another hunger strike at the Northwest ICE jail in Tacoma, Washington, is also ongoing. Hunger strikers at both facilities have reportedly faced threats, including being transferred to other ICE jails across the country. Both Adelanto and Northwest are operated by the for-profit prison company GEO Group.

NYC Mayor Mamdani Orders Inspections at 100 Sites After Deadly Building Collapse in Brooklyn

Nov 13, 2026

Here in New York, tenant advocates are demanding justice after what they described as the preventable collapse of an apartment building in Brooklyn that killed at least eight people, including two children, and injured at least 23 others Wednesday. Among the victims were two construction workers from Ecuador and Guatemala; a food delivery worker and Amazon worker, who were relatives from Guinea in West Africa; and two young cousins from Colombia.

The publication amNewYork reports the collapse may have been caused by corner-cutting by subcontractors and developers working on an adjacent construction site where crews were digging a pit for a new massive, multi-story development. In the wake of the collapse, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said five contractors and developers connected to the disaster are associated with about 100 other sites across New York, and that the Department of Buildings would immediately begin inspecting those sites.

The executive director of NYS Tenant Bloc, Sumathy Kumar, said in a statement that the tragedy “stresses the urgency of taking buildings out of the hands of bad landlords who are looking to make quick profits at the expense of people’s safety” and “highlights the need for dignified, high quality housing built with union labor, which is why we are fighting for social housing across the city and state.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: I Had Fun Killing My Protagonists!
World.content:
When Christopher Columbus landed on Cuba’s northeastern coast in 1492, it was probably near Gibara, where I took this photo.

By Jenny Cressman

HAVANA TIMES – In my first three diary columns, I did a lot of reminiscing about my early trips to Cuba. Now, however, I think it’s time for something different. Since I concluded my last column with comments about reincarnation, I’ll start there.

The short stories in my latest book, Kat of Nine, are linked by reincarnation, although that isn’t revealed until the fourth story in the nine-tale collection. As I began writing these stories, I did not initially intend to link them. In fact, I hadn’t even planned on writing a collection! It was just an interesting activity to occupy me during COVID.

I wrote the first story because I’d read a lot about Cuban history and one thought kept rumbling around in my mind: What would native inhabitants of the island have thought when they witnessed Christopher Columbus arrive? I’ve ruminated on this in other books and articles I’ve written but, this time, I decided to delve into the concept more fully. And, because it was the time of COVID, I had time to ride that train of thought.

Since I’d written a trio of romance-adventure novels from the perspective of the protagonist, it seemed natural to write in the first-person narrative style again. I put myself in the head of a young woman watching from shore as Columbus’ trio of ships sail into view. The first paragraph in her story summarizes her recollections. Then, the story shifts to present tense, as she experiences the initial arrival of Spanish sailors.

From there, her tale leaps forward to key moments that occurred at later times in her life. Eventually, she meets Hatuey, an iconic figure in Cuban history; his story always intrigued me! The end of the story is, essentially, her end. This scene is set soon after the protagonist witnesses Hatuey being burned.

Because the stories are linked by reincarnation, I don’t think I need to declare a “spoiler alert” when I point out that all but the last protagonist had to die. In writing these short stories, I enjoyed the challenge of finding different ways to kill off my beloved characters! But, I must admit, I cried as I wrote about the demise of each Kat of Nine heroine.

When I read excerpts at book events, I sometimes provide “trigger warnings” regarding violent incidents. I don’t like violence but, in this case, my desire for authenticity superseded my own way of living. Cuba’s past was not a pony ride through the park. Spanish conquistadors were brutal, as were many who came later in the island’s centuries of domination.

I commissioned Cuban artists to provide illustrations for each of the stories in Kat of Nine. This dramatic piece by Manuel Olivera Alvarez (MOA), is aptly entitled “The Conquest.”

But, let’s get back to “1492,” the first story in Kat of Nine. Here’s an excerpt:

…My memory of that day, that time, is a little jumbled. I was just a girl then; now, I am a woman. I recall feeling anxious and excited as we gathered on the beach and watched the ships approaching. Their white sails flapped like the wings of a bird that is settling to roost for the night. We waited impatiently. Finally, a small boat was dropped from one of the big boats and we could see movement, black shapes against the sun.

The small boat began to come toward the shore. When it arrived on the sand, amid the waves, some men from our group ran forward to help them. Together, their men and ours dragged the boat up onto the beach so that their leader would not get wet when he stepped out. We could tell immediately who their leader was. Even if he had not been wearing a big hat and a coat with shiny buttons, we would have been able to tell. He had the bearing of someone in charge. He waved his hand to command action and his men jumped.

Our leader did not have a fancy hat and did not behave like that, but he stood tall when he stepped forward to greet these peculiar people. He calmly spoke our customary words of welcome. I don’t remember exactly what was said but I remember the feelings. Excitement fluttered in my chest. I was eager to get close and find out who these strangers were, where they came from and why they were here, but I was timid and nervous. I stayed back a little, off to one side, with some of the other young girls.

These men – there were no women – looked very different from us, and even smelled different. They had on many layers of clothing and I could tell they were hot. The beads of sweat popped out on their foreheads and slowly slid down their faces, causing their skin to glisten. They were not smiling. They looked very uncomfortable. Were they afraid of us? I had the impression they might be, at first. But, soon, I think they understood that we were not dangerous. We were just curious…

While our leader tried to communicate with theirs, the rest of us coyly looked each other over. We tried to be careful in our visual assessment because we did not want to cause offence, but one of my friends was a little more bold. She crept closer to a pair of men at the edge of their group who were sitting on a log, so I followed. When these men noticed us near them, they become interested. They sat up straighter and looked directly at us. But, they didn’t just look at our faces. Their eyes ran up and down our bodies. One said something to the other and licked his lips. I didn’t understand the words but I knew what he was thinking. I grabbed my friend’s arm and whispered that we should go back to our families now.

After those first men left, we did not see any big boats for a long time. We had not expected them to return….

The back cover of my book, Kat of Nine, gives you a brief summary of what the nine stories in this collection are about.

[Watch for my next column in approximately two weeks. If you like my writing here, you’ll probably enjoy Kat of Nine / Kat de Nueve – all text is in both English and Spanish. You can find it on Amazon or at locations in Muskoka, my ‘hood.]

Read more from the diary of Jenny Cressman here on Havana Times.

World.title: US Immigration Judge Denies Asylum to Stateless Nicaraguan
World.content:
Former political prisoner Jairo Lenin Centeno Ríos. Photo: Carmen Aguirres / Nicas Libres Ya

Javier Centeno, one of 222 Nicaraguan political prisoners banished to the US in 2023, was denied asylum on the basis of Ortega-Murillo’s bogus drug charges.

By 100% Noticias

HAVANA TIMES – On November 10, 2026, a US immigration judge denied Jairo Lenín Centeno Ríos the right to political asylum. Centeno was one of 222 political prisoners the Ortega regime exiled to the United States in February 2023 and subsequently stripped of their citizenship. Stateless, he now faces the threat of deportation back to Nicaragua or to a third, unknown, country.

The court’s decision was announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, during a hearing held via video call from the Folkston D. Ray Detention Center in Georgia, where Centeno remains in immigration custody. Javier now fears being sent back to the country where he was imprisoned and from which he was expelled.

Meanwhile, he remains in an ICE detention center, leaving his four minor children in Nicaragua without the financial support he provided them.

Decision the result of baseless drug charges filed in Nicaragua

The Nicaraguan, originally from León, claims that the decision was based on a drug trafficking conviction handed down in Nicaragua, even though a United Nations report declared his detention arbitrary.

In statements to the Nicaraguan newspaper LA PRENSA, on Wednesday, November 11, the former political prisoner explained that the judge rejected his request for protection, given the criminal record resulting from his imprisonment in Nicaragua. The judge termed him a danger to the United States due to the crimes for which he was convicted by Nicaraguan authorities, despite the attempts of his defense team to explain the circumstances of his imprisonment in Nicaragua and subsequent exile.

Centeno maintains that the Nicaraguan regime’s drug charges were bogus, used by the regime to politically persecute him. He is now in a state of uncertainty, as he has already received a deportation order that he has refused to sign, and is waiting for his attorney to file an appeal.

From Exiled Political Prisoner to ICE Detainee

Centeno was arrested by the Ortega regime on September 14, 2018, during the period of repression that followed the outbreak of massive anti-government protests. He was released on December 30, 2019, under the regime’s unilateral Amnesty Law, but was recaptured on February 26, 2020 in a manner the Nicas Libres Ya website termed: “arbitrarily and illegally, and without a warrant in a raid at his grandmother’s house.”

Centeno remained in a Nicaraguan prison until February 2023, when he was among the 222 political prisoners the Nicaraguan authorities released and transferred to the United States under an agreement with the Biden administration. Almost immediately afterwards the Ortega-Murillo regime ordered all members of that group to be stripped of their citizenship. Centeno, like many of the others, remains stateless.

Arrested and detained by ICE despite the conclusions of the UN Working Group

After arriving in the United States, Centeno tried to rebuild his life. He began working in the construction industry as a welder.

However, on July 27, 2026, he was once again arrested – this time by agents of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while he was at a beach in Maryland, spending a day off with his partner, Conny Martinez. He was subsequently transferred to Georgia, where he remains in detention.

One of the most significant aspects of the case is that Centeno’s detention in Nicaragua was examined by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention. In its Opinion 69/2023, adopted during the session held from November 13 to 17, 2023, the international body analyzed the situation of 23 individuals imprisoned in Nicaragua, including Jairo Lenín Centeno Ríos.

The document concluded that his detention was arbitrary and contrary to the guarantees recognized in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. In its analysis, the Working Group also identified serious violations of the guarantees to a fair trial in the case of Centeno and other individuals included in the opinion.

This conclusion constitutes a documented international precedent regarding the irregularities of his imprisonment in Nicaragua. Unfortunately, the United Nations’ ruling does not automatically lead to the granting of asylum in the United States. The immigration decision depends on a separate procedure, subject to US law, within a US political administration that has moved to deport as many immigrants as it can.

According to Centeno, his attorney presented to the judge both the political nature of his imprisonment and the fact that he was stripped of his nationality, but neither of these arguments were given the weight he had hoped for.

Detention leaves his Nicaraguan children without economic support

Beyond his immigration status, Centeno faces the anguish of being unable to financially support his four minor children, who remain in Nicaragua. Before his arrest, he worked as a welder in construction and, as he explained to LA PRENSA, was the children’s primary financial provider.

Since his arrest by ICE in July, he has stopped sending them money.

In the interview, he expressed concern about his children’s needs and the possibility of remaining in detention for a longer period. He is particularly concerned for how his Nicaraguan family can sustain the costs associated with their studies if he continues in detention. This is the dilemma of many in ICE detention: while he fights to obtain legal protection in the United States, he leaves his children without economic support.

Fears Being Sent to Nicaragua or to a Third African Country

According to a report published by LA PRENSA, on Tuesday, November 10, Centeno received a deportation order that calls for his return to Nicaragua or the possibility of sending him to a third country in Africa.

The former political prisoner stated that he has not signed the document because he fears the consequences of returning to Nicaragua, where he was imprisoned for reasons he considers political.

He also expressed his opposition to the possibility of being transferred to an African country, given the difficulties he already faced in adapting to a new life after several years of imprisonment.

His concern is compounded by the revocation of his Nicaraguan citizenship, a measure that has affected numerous opponents and critics of the Ortega-Murillo regime.

The existence of a deportation order does not necessarily mean that his expulsion has already been carried out or that the transfer will be immediate. The situation will depend on pending legal proceedings and the appeal decisions of immigration authorities.

In this case, Javier’s defense team will seek to overturn the court’s decision while he remains in custody in Georgia. He is currently seeking support from human rights organizations and bodies that could help resolve his situation.

Centeno’s situation raises questions about the legal options available to people who were expelled from their country, lost their nationality, and now face deportation proceedings in the United States. It also raises questions about whether convictions handed down by governments accused of political persecution should be considered valid evidence in immigration proceedings.

In Javier Centeno’s case, there is a United Nations ruling documenting the arbitrary nature of his imprisonment, but it is not yet publicly known whether that information was fully considered in the U.S. immigration decision.

The Nicaraguan reiterates that he did not arrive in the United States on his own initiative, but rather as part of a group of political prisoners transferred from Nicaragua in February 2023.

The fear of returning to Nicaragua, the uncertainty surrounding his immigration status, and concern for his four children are all part of a situation that, as he told LA PRENSA, has deeply affected him.

The outcome of his appeal will determine whether he can continue to seek protection in the United States or whether he will face new deportation proceedings.

Seven of the 222 Nicaraguan ex-prisoners revictimized by ICE

According to a September 18th article in the Nicaraguan news site Confidencial, seven of the group of 222 have been newly detained by ICE. One was released, one has been ordered deported to Ecuador, and – at the time of the article – the others, including Centeno, were awaiting resolution of their cases.

First published in Spanish by 100% Noticias and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure
World.content:
US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure

14th Saturday, November 2026 - 00:53 UTC Full article

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday ordered a halt to all flights departing from the country’s airports “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed and hundreds of thousands of passengers were stranded. The government has so far ruled out an attack.

The order took effect at around 4 p.m. US Eastern time (6 p.m. in Montevideo) and was extended until at least 11.30 p.m. Eastern time, according to TheStreet. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA said, attributing the problem to a “temporary telecommunications outage” and saying it halted flights out of an abundance of caution. Aircraft already airborne continued to their destinations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating. According to an internal Alaska Airlines message cited by CNBC, the problems affect communications and radar.

“There was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, though he said all possibilities were being examined. Mullin rejected comparisons with the 2001 attacks — “This is not the same as 9/11” — and warned that the problem “is not going to be resolved in an hour”.

The most affected airports were Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare and New York’s airports, according to FlightAware. Just over two million passengers fly domestically in the US each day, and the disruption comes less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, the busiest travel period of the year. United and American Airlines said international departures were also being handled case by case.

It is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a failure of the pilot notification system halted take-offs for hours, and before that since the September 11, 2001 attacks.

World.title: Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries
World.content:
Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:09 UTC Full article

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform

Microsoft said on Friday its services were recovering after a global outage that began on Thursday afternoon, European time, and for hours affected millions of users in more than 70 countries, including public bodies in Australia and Japan. The company ruled out a cyberattack.

The disruption hit Outlook email, the Teams work platform, SharePoint Online, the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, the OneDrive and OneNote cloud services and the Microsoft 365 suite, widely used by businesses and governments. “We’re seeing continued progress in recovery across affected regions,” the company said, warning that some users could still experience intermittent problems. “We know our customers rely on our services to do important work every day, and we’re sorry for the impact these outages had,” it added.

“At this time, I can confirm there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platforms, wrote on X. According to the company, several servers unexpectedly became unavailable and their load shifted to the remaining ones, in a domino effect that overwhelmed systems linked to Exchange Online, its email service. There is still no definitive analysis of what happened.

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke activated a clause in the digital resilience agreement signed with Microsoft in June so that the country would receive priority in restoring services. In Japan, government spokesman Minoru Kihara confirmed that the government’s IT infrastructure was also disrupted, with no incidents at health facilities. Problems were reported in public services in Singapore and the Philippines, and in Thailand four major banks temporarily suspended email-dependent services.

Complaints on the Downdetector platform peaked first on Thursday afternoon, European time, and a second wave came on Friday morning, before returning to normal levels in the afternoon. According to the company, Microsoft 365 has more than 450 million corporate users and 95 million consumers, and Teams more than 320 million.

World.title: Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands
World.content:
Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:06 UTC Full article

The Chilean-flagged Danstar aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years, carrying food, machinery and building materials as an alternative to supplies from Montevideo

Chile’s Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna has ruled out asking Argentina for authorisation for the voyage of the Chilean vessel Danstar, which plans to reopen the commercial route between Punta Arenas and the Falklands in December, invoking the right of innocent passage recognised by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. “Countries do not ask permission,” he said, according to Argentina’s La Nación.

“Chile believes in the right to free navigation, which is guaranteed, the right of free passage, innocent passage, as it is called in UNCLOS maritime law. And we trust that right will be respected,” Pérez Mackenna said. He was responding to his Argentine counterpart, Pablo Quirno, who said on Monday on the A24 channel that the vessel must request permission to cross Argentine jurisdictional waters. “Thousands of ships pass through the Strait of Magellan every year. There are thousands of ships that ask for authorisation to cross when they leave for the Malvinas,” Quirno said. Since 2010, Argentina has required by decree prior authorisation for ships sailing between the mainland and the islands or crossing Argentine waters towards them.

The Danstar, a 72-metre Chilean-flagged cargo ship operated by Easter Island shipping company, aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years with a cargo of food, machinery and construction materials, as an alternative to the supplies that arrive regularly from Montevideo. The private-sector initiative is promoted by the Falkland Islands Development Corporation and backed by Punta Arenas. “We want to be the islands’ big supermarket,” said its mayor, Claudio Radonich.

The Argentine government fears the route could provide logistical support to the Sea Lion oil project. Quirno recalled “the Chilean government’s commitment that this will not contribute logistically to the exploitation of natural resources” in the islands. According to La Nación, Chilean diplomats privately expressed “indignation” that Argentina has tolerated regular trade between the islands and Uruguay for years but concentrates its pressure on Chilean vessels. Argentina’s Foreign Ministry denies seeking to provoke an incident.

The exchange comes during a key week in the dispute over the islands. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion, after the hearings in Hamburg, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies is debating the sovereignty defence bill, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. In October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised with Chilean President José Antonio Kast London’s interest in the islanders’ right to self-determination.

World.title: Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”
World.content:
Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”

13th Friday, November 2026 - 02:58 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Yara Nardi

Pope Leo XIV met some 52,000 young people at Lima’s National Stadium on Thursday, according to El País, in the last event of his stay in the Peruvian capital before travelling to Chiclayo, the diocese he led as bishop. “Someone told me that Peru needs hope. You are the sign of hope,” he told them, to applause.

The young people came from the coast, the highlands and the jungle, many with parish groups and others on their own, and alongside Peruvian flags there were also Venezuelan and Chilean ones. The Pope entered the stadium track in the popemobile at around six in the evening, as the stands displayed signs asking for his blessing. The vigil included testimonies, a theatrical performance in which Peruvian saints came to the rescue of young people in crisis, music and scissor dancers, an Andean ritual.

At around half past seven, Leo XIV spoke with a message of comfort and encouragement. “Dear young people, when you suffer, turn to Jesus. Do not be afraid to speak to him sincerely. He knows our tears,” he said. “Be passionate about everything worthwhile. Cultivate your talents. Discover the richness of your culture. Do not settle for living according to what others expect of you.” He ended with an invitation to those who believe they are beyond redemption: “It is not too late to begin again.”

The Archbishop of Lima, Cardinal Carlos Castillo, recalled during the event Inti Sotelo and Bryan Pintado, the two young men of around twenty who were shot dead during the November 2020 protests. “In the recent history we have lived through in our country, young people often took to the streets to protest and in some cases several were shot. There are two martyrs: Inti and Bryan,” he said. Castillo said that after the crackdown many young people found in dance a form of expression that eventually reached the parishes. The testimonies included that of a young woman who lost a dozen relatives and of a nun who suffered abuse by a member of the Church.

Leo XIV, 71, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery, celebrates Mass on Friday at the Pampas de Pimentel, near Chiclayo, where nearly a million faithful are expected. On Saturday he will visit Cajamarca and Zaña, and on Sunday Cusco and Pucallpa, before returning to Rome on Monday, November 16.

World.title: British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982
World.content:
British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:01 UTC Full article

Aged 18, Andy Gatrick found two wounded Argentine soldiers, later captured, at Mount Harriet in June 1982 and kept one’s helmet, which bore a name: Hector. Photo: Mick Dawson

A former Royal Marine has travelled to Argentina to return to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took during the Battle of Mount Harriet in the 1982 Falklands War, in a reunion filmed for a documentary, BBC Sussex reported.

Andy Gatrick, who was 18 at the time of the war, came across two injured Argentine soldiers during the Battle of Mount Harriet, fought on June 11 and 12, 1982. Both were captured by the Marines. Gatrick kept the helmet of one of them, which bore a name: Hector. Now 63, he managed to track him down and on October 23 flew to Gualeguaychú, in Entre Ríos province, to return it in person to Héctor Pereyra.

“I put my weapon down and as I bent down to put the strap over my shoulders, I saw movement and a cloth which looked like a white handkerchief. My eyes adjusted and there was two Argentinians, I didn’t know they were badly injured. I dived to the floor, weapon up. There was lots of shouting and swearing, bedlam,” Gatrick, from Bolton in northern England, said in footage sent to the BBC.

He was joined by another Royal Marine veteran, Mick Dawson, 62, who filmed the meeting for a documentary called Hector’s Helmet. According to Dawson, the British kit was poor and the Marines fought in berets, while the Argentines had American helmets, so Gatrick “borrowed” Pereyra’s. “In a very emotional day, he handed the helmet back in person to the guy he could have just as easily killed that night,” Dawson told BBC Radio Sussex. The two veterans “embraced like long lost brothers”, he said.

Dawson interviewed Pereyra about the moment when, wounded, he saw Gatrick emerge from the darkness. “He said, ‘I knew this man had the power of life or death over me and he chose life’,” Dawson recounted. “He then showed me a picture of his nine grandchildren and four children that wouldn’t have existed if Andy made a different decision that night. It was just the most amazing thing to witness.”

Dawson hopes to release the documentary next year. The 74-day war in 1982 left 907 dead: 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British personnel and three civilian islanders.

World.title: Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election
World.content:
Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:02 UTC Full article

The visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will visit Madrid on Monday, November 16, to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, less than two weeks before the snap general election on November 29, in which Sánchez is seeking re-election. It will be Lula’s first visit to Spain since he won Brazil’s election on October 25.

According to the Spanish government’s official statement, the two will hold a bilateral meeting at the Moncloa Palace to discuss relations between the two countries and coordination of initiatives such as Democracy Always and the Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty. Lula will stop in Madrid on his way back from the UN climate summit, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, where he will also make a state visit to the Philippines.

According to the Spanish press, the visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it. Sánchez has presented Lula’s re-election and the Democratic victory in the US midterms as proof that the advance of the radical right can be halted.

CNN Brasil reported that Lula will be accompanied by congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback. The Spanish government and the Socialist Party insist that Janones is not advising Sánchez’s campaign and there are no plans for him to do so.

Polls show a slight recovery for the Socialists, so far insufficient to govern. A survey by 40dB for El País and Cadena SER shows the Socialist Party up almost two points, but the People’s Party and Vox would together win a comfortable absolute majority of more than 190 seats; 176 are needed to govern. The state-run Centre for Sociological Research shows a stronger Socialist recovery.

Neither Lula nor Sánchez attended the Ibero-American Summit held in Madrid last week. According to El País, Lula needed to rest and recover his voice after the campaign. Sánchez spoke by phone on Thursday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum about bilateral relations and the outcome of the summit.

World.title: Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation
World.content:
Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 11:20 UTC Full article

Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials

Paraguay’s Superintendent of Banks, Holger Insfrán, was arrested on Thursday as part of the investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has already led to the pre-trial detention of former President Santiago Peña and former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to prosecution sources cited by the EFE news agency. The charges against him have not been disclosed.

The Superintendency of Banks, part of the Central Bank, is responsible for supervising and regulating Paraguay’s financial institutions, including Ueno. Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials.

According to prosecutors, Ueno received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, including from five pension funds, while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, the Vázquez Group. The bank had 2.94 million customers.

Peña, removed by the Senate on November 6, is charged with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator, and could face a maximum sentence of 15 years, according to prosecutors. He says he is innocent. Carvallo, who headed the finance company from which the bank emerged before Peña appointed him to lead the Central Bank in 2023, is accused of breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration.

The Central Bank said on Wednesday that 100% of customers covered by the state guarantee have received an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121.8 million guaraníes or roughly US$19,600, under the emergency law passed by Congress. It has until Monday to complete repayments up to the guarantee ceiling of 75 minimum wages, about 228.3 million guaraníes or roughly US$36,600.

World.title: Leo XIV arrives in Peru, his “homeland”, defending international law and reconciliation
World.content:
Leo XIV arrives in Peru, his “homeland”, defending international law and reconciliation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 10:59 UTC Full article

Leo XIV will remain in Peru until Monday, November 16. On Friday he will celebrate Mass in Pimentel, near Chiclayo, the diocese he led from 2015 to 2023

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lima on Wednesday, the final stage of his South American tour, and in his first speech in Peru, the country where he lived for some twenty years and whose nationality he holds, called for diplomacy that “respects international law” in the face of wars and for the country’s past events “to be dealt with justice and sensitivity”.

President Keiko Fujimori received him at the foot of the plane, and thousands of people greeted him along the route from the airport. After meeting him at the Government Palace, the Pope addressed the authorities. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own history also belongs to you,” he said, referring to a country he regards as his homeland.

In the first international reference of his tour, Leo XIV said, without naming any country, that “the wars and tensions afflicting so many peoples demand patient diplomacy that keeps dialogue open, respects international law and seeks agreements that protect the life and dignity of people”. “Every nation has legitimate aspirations, but none can consider the fate of others alien to it,” he added, encouraging Peru to keep contributing to regional and international cooperation.

The Pope also referred to the country’s recent past. “Peru too has gone through difficult moments that have tested coexistence among its people. The events of the past deserve to be dealt with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow,” he said, adding that “democratic life means recognising that no one can be treated as a problem, but as a person with dignity”. Fujimori, who spoke before him, said “Peru needs to reconcile” and that “no country can live as a prisoner of its wounds”.

The Pope spoke alongside the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, the former president convicted of human rights violations, pardoned in 2017 and who died in 2024. According to El País, in 2017 the then Bishop of Chiclayo Robert Prevost criticised the former leader for apologising only in a “generic” way. On the eve of the visit, victims of state violence during the armed conflict of the 1980s and 1990s and of the crackdown on the 2022 and 2023 protests, in which at least some fifty people died, sent a letter alleging that “some people, from within the Church” are preventing their stories from reaching the pontiff. Former President Dina Boluarte, under whose government those deaths occurred, attended the speech.

Leo XIV will remain in Peru until Monday, November 16. On Friday he will celebrate Mass in Pimentel, near Chiclayo, the diocese he led from 2015 to 2023, where nearly a million faithful are expected; on Saturday he will visit Cajamarca and Zaña, and on Sunday, Cusco and Pucallpa, before returning to Rome.

World.title: Ready to host another World Cup? Mexico-US-Costa Rica-Jamaica joint bid for 2031 women’s tournament likely
World.content:
Mexico appears set to host another World Cup in less than five years after FIFA green lighted a joint hosting bid of which the Mexican Soccer Federation is a part.

FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, announced on Wednesday that the bid to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup submitted jointly by Mexico, the United States, Jamaica and Costa Rica “has a strong foundation” and will be voted on at the Extraordinary FIFA Congress on Nov. 23.

If approved (as the lone bid, it is expected to pass with little difficulty), it would mark the second FWWC to be hosted jointly after Australia and New Zealand co-hosted the 2023 tournament.

The Congress will also be considering the joint bid to host the 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup (FWWC) submitted by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Next year’s FWWC is to be hosted by Brazil and will feature 32 teams and 64 matches. The 2031 tournament will be expanded to include 48 teams and 104 games.

The joint 2031 bid proposes 20 host stadiums across the four countries, with 14 in the United States, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica. Mexico’s proposed host cities are Mexico City (Estadio Azteca), Guadalajara (Estadio Akron), Monterrey (Estadio BBVA-Bancomer) and Torreón, Coahuila (Estadio Corona).

Following a thorough assessment of the proposal, including inspection visits to the prospective host countries, FIFA published an evaluation report indicating that the bid exceeded its minimum requirements.

“While certain commitments require further engagement, there is a sound basis for confidence that continued dialogue and collaboration with the relevant government agencies should support the successful organization and delivery of the tournament,” FIFA said.

In endorsing the bid, FIFA acknowledged the success of this year’s men’s World Cup which Mexico and the U.S. co-hosted alongside Canada.

FIFA also praised Mexico’s “longstanding record as a FIFA host, having staged the FIFA World Cup in 1970 and 1986, the FIFA Confederations Cup in 1999 and multiple youth competitions, including the FIFA U-20 World Cup 1983 and FIFA U-17 World Cup 2011.”

The technical evaluation focused on “defined priority areas, including the event vision, infrastructure, services and commercial considerations” as well as FIFA Fan Festival sites, while the risk assessment considered “safety and security, sustainability, human rights and environmental protection.”

As co-host, Mexico’s women’s team would be participating in its fourth FWWC after qualifying for the 1999, 2011 and 2015 tournaments. The El Tri Femenil also participated in the unofficial 1971 Women’s World Cup hosted by Mexico. The first FWWC was held in 1991.

With reports from Reuters, Fox Sports, FIFA and ESPN

World.title: New faces and old favorites: Mexico’s 2026 Latin Grammy wins
World.content:
Mexican and Mexican American artists won in at least 10 categories at the Latin Grammys in Las Vegas on Thursday — from 22-year-old Xavi collecting his first two trophies to hitmaker Edgar Barrera becoming the awards’ most decorated winner ever.

Nominated in six categories, Silvana Estrada won one award with her song “Dime,” while Texan Bobby Pulido followed his election to Congress last week with his third Latin Grammy — then announced his retirement from music.

The 27th annual ceremony at Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena also featured a first win for Guadalajara-born mariachi singer Camila Fernández and a big centennial tribute to the late Mexican singer-songwriter and ranchera legend José Alfredo Jiménez.

Barrera, born in McAllen, Texas, to a Mexican family, converted a leading 10 nominations into two awards: producer of the year and best regional song for “No Capea.” The two wins brought his career total to 31, breaking the all-time Latin Grammy record he had shared with Puerto Rican rapper Residente.

Xavi, Grupo Frontera – No Capea (Official Video)

Watch this video on YouTube

Barrera, 36, shared the songwriting award with five co-writers, including Xavi and Grupo Frontera singer Adelaido “Payo” Solís III. The prize recognizes the writers, not every member of the performing group.

Xavi won both his nominations, also taking best contemporary Mexican music album for “Dosis.” Born Joshua Xavier Gutiérrez Alonso in Arizona, Xavi was raised largely by his grandparents in Nogales, Sonora, before moving to Phoenix at age 15 with his father.

Grupo Frontera, a Mexican-American band that formed in Texas in 2022, won best norteño album for “Lo Que Me Falta Por Llorar.”

Fernández won best ranchero/mariachi album for “La Fernández.” The 28-year-old is the daughter of ranchero star Alejandro Fernández and the granddaughter of the late Vicente Fernández, one of Mexico’s most famous entertainers of all time.

Edén Muñoz, 36, the former Calibre 50 frontman from Los Mochis, Sinaloa, won best banda album for “Piedras a la Luna.” He was also nominated for best regional song as the writer of “Osadía,” his duet with Cristian Castro.

Estrada, 29, recently named the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s first creative chair for Latin music, received six nominations, including album of the year for “Vendrán Suaves Lluvias” and record and song of the year for “Dime.”

Silvana Estrada — Dime (Video Oficial)

Watch this video on YouTube

The ballad about heartbreak and the liberating power of anger didn’t win in those two categories, but it did garner best singer-songwriter song. The native of Coatepec, Veracruz, now has two Latin Grammys, following her best new artist award in 2022.

Alejandra, Daniela and Paulina Villarreal — three sisters from Monterrey, Nuevo León, who make up the hard-rock trio The Warning — shared best rock song honors for “Ego” with three co-writers.

Mexico City singer Marco Barrientos shared best Spanish-language Christian album for “Eterno” with two others.

Pulido, who has Mexican heritage, won his third Latin Grammy, taking best Tejano album for “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol.2/En Vivo).”

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” Pulido said in Spanish while accepting the award. He missed the traditional group photo for incoming House members while traveling to Las Vegas, according to The Hill.

Afterward, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries congratulated his fellow Democrat in a social media post: “Felicidades and what a month for Congressman-Elect Pulido.”

¡Felicidades! @bobbypulido425 Mejor Álbum de Música Tejana 🎶👏👏👏 #LatinGRAMMY https://t.co/e39HDhTISH — The Latin Recording Academy / Latin GRAMMYs (@LatinGRAMMYs) November 12, 2026

Chilean Mexican singer Mon Laferte, who has a house in Tepoztlán, Morelos, performed “Femme Fatale” — a week after a concertgoer threw a cellphone that struck her in the face — but went winless in six categories.

Carín León lost both his nominations, for record and album of the year.

Arath Herce from the city of Veracruz went winless in four categories: best new artist, singer-songwriter album, singer-songwriter song and pop/rock song.

Spanish singer Rosalía won five awards, including album of the year for “LUX (Complete Works)” and song of the year for “La Perla.” Argentine singer Milo J took four, including record of the year for “Niño.”

Colombian singer Aria Vega won best new artist, besting a field that included Mexicans Herce, former street sweeper Macario Martínez and Sofía Monroy.

In all, Mexican and Mexican American artists won across all six regional Mexican categories, an umbrella grouping for styles including mariachi, banda and norteño. For the full list of winners, see Billboard.

With reports from Billboard, Uno TV, Infobae and Hola!

World.title: Mexico sets a new record for tourist arrivals and spending, even as growth slows
World.content:
Listen to this article

Despite increased travel costs, a decline in air arrivals and a lack of promotion, Mexico registered record figures in international tourist arrivals and spending during the first nine months of 2026.

Data compiled by national statistics agency INEGI through September indicates that foreign currency spending by travelers grew 1.4% year-on-year to nearly US $26.1 billion and the number of international tourists rose 3.8% to 35.97 million people.

However, rising travel costs are blamed for a drop in the segment of tourists arriving by air which experts link to the lower dynamism observed since these travelers represent 80% of tourism foreign exchange.

The INEGI report, released on Thursday, reveals that the 1.4% increase in tourism revenue is lower than the 6.1% growth recorded during the first three quarters of 2025.

Additionally, the International Travelers Survey (EVI) found that the 3.8% increase in international tourist arrivals (by air and by land) came in below the 6.4% rise registered during the same period last year.

After the release of the EVI and INEGI data, the Tourism Ministry on Friday lauded “the historic records both in the arrival of international travelers and in their spending.”

The private sector does not share this enthusiasm.

Humberto Molina, tourism analyst at Grupo Empresarial Estrategia, told El Economista newspaper that although the accumulated results are good, it’s clear that tourism “isn’t taking off,” lamenting the lack of a public policy to provide certainty of sustained growth in the short term.

“In addition to the lack of promotional campaigns, next year will be impacted by the 17.8% increase in the Non-Resident Tax paid by foreign tourists (1,158 pesos starting in January),” he said.

The private sector has also criticized the government’s lack of attention to the tourism sector, describing the 20 million pesos dedicated to tourism in the 2027 budget proposal as “clearly insufficient to promote the different destinations and segments of tourism in the source markets and in the national market.”

The decline in air arrivals is seen as the biggest challenge.

The INEGI figures reflect a cumulative decrease for two consecutive years in that indicator, unseen since records began, impacting the country’s three primary sun and beach destinations: Cancún, Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta.

The Center for Advanced Research in Sustainable Tourism (STARC) at Anáhuac University Cancún reported that, through October, the airports that service these three locations have seen a cumulative reduction of 1.9 million international passengers compared to 2025.

Still, spending by tourists arriving by air increased by 7.1% in September.

One reason cited for the September boost is the gradual recovery of business tourism, which had contracted due to this summer’s World Cup.

This could be good news for the tourism sector since the second half of the year is popular for Mexico’s meetings industry, with an increase in congresses, exhibitions and conventions.

With reports from El Economista, UnoTV and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico has delivered less than 1% of the water it owes to the US as border dams run low
World.content:
Despite recent agreements to resolve the situation, Mexico continues to have problems meeting its water-delivery commitments to the United States, having covered only 0.36% of the deficit it accumulated during the 2020–2025 water-sharing period.

According to the U.S. section of the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC), as of Oct. 24, Mexico this year had delivered only 3,159 acre-feet of the 865,139 acre-feet it owes from coming up short in the previous five-year period. It has until 2030 to pay off the rest, during which period it is also obligated to send north 350,000 acre-feet per year to meet its current obligations for the 2025-2030 period, which will total 1,750,000 acre-feet.

Mexico and the U.S. share water from the Río Bravo under the terms set out in a 1944 water treaty that establishes that Mexico must deliver to the U.S. a minimum of 350,000 acre-feet of water every year. But Mexico concluded the five-year cycle spanning Oct. 25, 2020 – Oct. 24, 2025, delivering only 884,861 acre-feet, resulting in a deficit of 865,139 acre-feet owed to the U.S.

In October, the two countries signed onto a plan that was meant to ease repayment with both agreeing to use less water from the Río Bravo (called the Rio Grande in the U.S). But compliance continues to drag.

A major factor hampering Mexico’s water delivery commitments has to do with reduced reserves, as international border dams La Amistad and Falcon remain at less than 30% capacity.

According to data from the Mexico section of the IBWC, as of Oct. 26, La Amistad dam, located on the Río Bravo along the border of Coahuila with Texas, stood at 28% of its capacity. Meanwhile, Falcon, located along the border of Tamaulipas and Texas, was at 17%.

Water deliveries from Mexico are stored in those dams.

Roberto Constantino, a researcher at the Metropolitan Autonomous University (UAM), told the newspaper El Economista that reduced availability in the Río Bravo and Colorado River basins threatens both compliance with binational agreements and the water supply on both sides of the border.

The expert suggested that the 1944 Water Treaty should be revised to better reflect current environmental conditions. However, he noted that bilateral tensions and the trade agenda make this an inopportune time to initiate such negotiations.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: El Jalapeño: Disgruntled Quetzalcóatl not recognized on his long-awaited return to Mexico
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

VERACRUZ — Quetzalcóatl, the Feathered Serpent, Lord of the Dawn and Creator of Mankind, expressed profound frustration Friday after making his long-prophesied cosmic return to the shores of Veracruz, only to discover that no one seemed to recognize him.

The deity, who descended upon the port city in a blaze of iridescent plumage, windstorms and celestial lightning, reported that despite checking every traditional physical requirement of the Mesoamerican return myth, locals merely asked if he had a reservation for the port tour or if he was part of a promotional campaign for a local craft brewery or something.

“I manifested on the exact promised date, riding a raft of interwoven serpents, wielding the wind of the four cardinal directions, and people just kept walking past me to get iced coffee,” said Quetzalcóatl, speaking to reporters while attempting to parse a laminated city map. “From time immemorial, it has been written that when a bearded figure arrives from the east, he’s coming to reclaim his throne. But apparently times have changed.”

According to municipal officials, the god’s arrival caused minor traffic delays along the malecón, but failed to trigger the existential awe documented in ancient texts.

“We had a gentleman in full ceremonial feathers claiming to control the cycle of Venus and the rebirth of the sun,” said Veracruz transit officer Roberto Morales. “He seemed very surprised when we asked him to move his serpent-raft out of the commercial loading zone. I told him that while we respect cosmic creators, the dock permit guidelines apply universally.”

Sources close to the deity confirmed he attempted several standard divine demonstrations, including summoning localized squalls and speaking in ancient Nahuatl verse, but was repeatedly directed toward the municipal cultural center’s administrative desk.
