World.title: Sheinbaum denies ‘friction’ in bilateral ties after US reportedly shelters a wanted Mexican official: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🔎 Sheinbaum asks Security Cabinet for information on Zuany: Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts.

Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts. 🇲🇽 🇺🇸 No friction expected with U.S.: Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t.

Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t. 📊 Gap between INEGI and SESNSP homicide data under review: Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers.

Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers. 🏍️ Drug lord’s motorbikes fetch 71 million pesos: INDEP director Mónica Fernández said the auction of Ryan Wedding’s luxury motorcycles raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million), about 11 million pesos above expectations. Fifty-seven of the 62 motorcycles were sold, and the remaining five will go up for auction in late November. Proceeds will go to the Office of the Presidency to fund social justice projects, including for the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and for Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo communities.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The New York Times’ reporting on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, was once again a topic of discussion at President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference.

The Times reported on Tuesday that Zuany had facilitated the operation of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency in Chihuahua and, in exchange, his U.S. visa — reportedly revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out” — was reinstated. At her Wednesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum described the report as “very interesting,” and said that it was “worth learning about” who Zuany is “and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies.”

On Thursday, the Times reported that Zuany — who is wanted by Mexican authorities — had fled to the United States.

The former prosecutor’s alleged cooperation with the CIA is part of a larger story that has remained in the headlines in Mexico for much of 2026. In April, CIA officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid alongside Chihuahua state forces without the authorization or knowledge of the federal government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials were killed in a car accident after the raid.

The CIA’s alleged participation in the operation has strained relations between the federal government and the Chihuahua government, which is led by Governor Maru Campos of the National Action Party, Mexico’s main opposition party. It also led Sheinbaum to accuse the U.S. government of interference in Mexico. The former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was taken into federal custody last month on a charge of treason related to the CIA’s alleged involvement in the drug lab raid.

Beyond the case involving Zuany and the CIA, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was homicide statistics.

A range of experts have expressed skepticism about the accuracy of the Sheinbaum administration’s homicide statistics, with claims that state-based Attorney General’s offices — which provide homicide data to the federal government — are fudging the numbers. There has been renewed focus on the accuracy of the data this week after the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported over 5,000 more homicides in 2025 than the federal government’s Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), the largest gap in more than a decade.

Sheinbaum: US collaboration with former Chihuahua prosecutor won’t cause friction in bilateral ties

A reporter asked the president about a report published by The New York Times on Thursday that states that Zuany “has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”

“The story about this character is long,” Sheinbaum said.

“I don’t want to talk about it here at this time,” she added.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” between Mexico and the United States.

She said she would ask the federal government’s Security Cabinet to provide all the information it has about Zuany, including anything it knows about his current whereabouts.

🚨Claudia Sheinbaum considera que el caso de Guillermo Zuany, exvicefiscal de Chihuahua señalado por presunta corrupción y vínculos con el crimen organizado, es relevante para la relación entre México y Estados Unidos. La presidenta pidió al Gabinete de Seguridad informar sobre el caso de Zuany, quien se encuentra en territorio estadounidense. 🗞️Israel Aldave | @Radio_Formula — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) November 13, 2026

“Hopefully the federal Attorney General’s Office or the Security Cabinet can provide information,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether “the situation” with Zuany could create “friction” between Mexico and the United States, the president responded:

“No, because it’s been spoken about with the U.S. government.”

Sheinbaum said in April that the U.S. government had agreed to comply with the Mexican Constitution and Mexican laws in bilateral security cooperation. She also expressed confidence that U.S. participation in a security operation on Mexican soil wouldn’t be repeated.

Sheinbaum says government is reviewing discrepancy between INEGI and SESNSP homicide numbers

A reporter asked the president about the discrepancy between INEGI’s 2025 homicide statistics and those of the SESNSP.

Sheinbaum said that the gap between INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) and that of the SESNSP (24,348) is “something we’re reviewing with INEGI.”

She stressed that the homicide statistics presented at her press conference on a monthly basis come from the country’s Attorney General’s Offices. Sheinbaum noted that INEGI looks at death certificates and records (among other information) when classifying deaths as homicides. She also noted that INEGI publishes preliminary and final data on homicides. Sheinbaum said that the upward revision in INEGI’s 2025 homicide count between its preliminary and final figures was larger than in previous years.

“We have a working group to look at why this situation occurred,” she said.

“And we’re also looking at the difference in each state between what the Attorney General’s Offices reported and what the civil registry later reported. This revision is done with INEGI,” Sheinbaum said.

The Security Ministry said in August that the difference between INEGI’s homicide numbers and those of the SESNSP is “expected” as “each institution performs different functions, uses different [data] integration procedures, has different collection, validation, and publication periods, and generates information for specific purposes.”

However, “both sources show the same trend with respect to the evolution of intentional homicide,” the ministry said.

INEGI’s final data shows that homicides declined 12.1% in 2025 compared to the previous year, whereas the SESNSP reported a significantly larger reduction of 21.2%.

Auction of drug trafficker’s motorbikes raises 71 million pesos

Mónica Fernández, director of the Institute to Return Stolen Goods to the People (INDEP), reported early in the press conference that the auction this week of a collection of luxury motorcycles formerly owned by Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million). That amount was around 11 million pesos above expectations.

“We sold 57 of 62 motorcycles,” Fernández said, noting that the motorbikes were seized by authorities and subsequently handed over to INDEP in July.

Wedding’s motorcycles were seized last December after authorities raided four properties in Mexico City and México state linked to the former Olympic athlete known as The King of Cocaine. Wedding turned himself into Mexican authorities in January after more than a decade on the run.

Fernández noted that there was a large turnout at the auction of the drug trafficker’s motorbikes, which was held in Mexico City.

She said that the five motorcycles that weren’t sold will be put on the block at another INDEP auction to be held in late November.

The resources obtained from this week’s sale of Wedding’s motorbikes and other seized assets will be allocated to the Office of the Presidency, and will be used to finance social justice projects, including actions benefiting the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and communities of the Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo peoples.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: El Tri is back in action Saturday in its first official match of the Rafa Márquez era
World.content:
After a winless start to the Rafa Márquez era, Mexico’s national soccer team has an opportunity to right the ship on Saturday evening in Kingston, Jamaica.

El Tri will take the field at Independence Park against underdog Jamaica in the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, making it Márquez’s first official match as Mexico manager.

Márquez, who succeeded Javier Aguirre after serving as his top assistant during the 2026 World Cup, has yet to win a match as Mexico’s top man. El Tri is 0-2-2 since he took over, including an embarrassing 3-0 loss to Team USA.

For this two-game stretch (the second leg will be played in Monterrey on Tuesday), Márquez summoned a more experienced squad than he did for the four friendlies during the September-October window.

Back with the team is forward Julián Quiñones, who was Mexico’s leading scorer during the World Cup. Also returning are winger Jesús Corona (a 33-year-old with experience in Europe) and fullback Rodrigo Huescas, who missed the World Cup after suffering a knee injury 13 months ago.

However, the team will be without top striker Raúl Jiménez, who underwent surgery to repair his medial collateral ligament last month.

Teen midfielder Gilberto Mora will be expected to direct the El Tri attack, while captain Johan Vásquez and Erik Lira form the backbone of the defense. All eyes will be on goalie Raúl Rangel whose two howlers against Team USA won’t soon be forgotten.

As humiliating as it was to lose to the U.S. in the manner they did, Mexico’s players realize that, as heavy favorites to advance to the semifinals, a loss to Jamaica would be even more devastating.

The defending Nations League champions are ranked 59 spots above Jamaica in the FIFA World Rankings (Mexico is No. 10, Jamaica No. 69), losing just three of 29 matches against The Reggae Boyz, while winning 21 and drawing five. And El Tri has outscored Jamaica 72-15 overall.

However, Mexico is only 3-3-1 in its last seven official matches against Jamaica, including a 1-0 loss in the 2017 Copa Oro semifinals.

Jamaica’s other two victories over Mexico were by identical 1-0 scores: in an Oct. 11, 2008, World Cup qualifier and in a Nov. 17, 1996, World Cup qualifier.

Still, The Reggae Boyz failed to qualify for this summer’s World Cup even though Concacaf had six slots in the tournament. Jamaica finished second to an upstart Curaçao side in the regional final group stage, then lost to DR Congo in an interconfederation playoff.

With reports from SBNation, ESPN and Soy Fútbol

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Pilgrimage preparations, ancient remains and delivery protests
World.content:
From preparations for one of Mexico’s largest annual religious gatherings to archaeological discoveries and transportation projects, Mexico City has plenty happening this November.

Authorities are gearing up to welcome millions of pilgrims to the Basilica of Guadalupe, while construction of a major passenger rail connection revealed an unexpected discovery. Meanwhile, a proposed licensing overhaul for motorcycle delivery workers hit a roadblock following protests.

Let’s get into it.

Authorities outline priorities for ‘Operation Basílica 2026’

Mexico City authorities have begun organizing a major security and public services operation ahead of Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe, the annual December celebrations honoring the Virgin of Guadalupe. Approximately 13 million pilgrims are expected to visit the Basilica of Guadalupe this year, which is on par with last year’s figures.

The Gustavo A. Madero borough, home to the religious complex, held its first interagency planning meeting earlier this month to coordinate the “2026 Operativo Basílica.” More than 30 federal and local government institutions are expected to participate in the effort.

The operation will cover public security, traffic management, emergency medical assistance, civil protection, sanitation and more. Participating agencies include the National Guard, Mexico City’s Citizen Security Ministry, the Navy, the National Defense Ministry, the Red Cross, the fire department and the city’s Metro and Metrobús systems.

Planning and coordination

Gustavo A. Madero Mayor Janecarlo Lozano said early coordination is necessary to manage crowds and ensure authorities can respond quickly to emergencies.

“Our responsibility begins with the planning stage and continues until the pilgrims begin their journey home,” Lozano said, according to Excelsior. “We want them to find guidance when they need it, assistance when they require it, and dignified treatment at all times.”

The holiday and pilgrimage honor an event in 1531, when an apparition of the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared to an Indigenous peasant named Juan Diego on a mountain above the holy site.

Last year’s operation provides a starting point for this year’s preparations. In 2025, the borough deployed 10,600 city workers, 250 law enforcement officers and 110 law enforcement vehicles. Authorities also installed 450 portable toilets, 26 hydration stations and two bike parking structures capable of housing 12,000 bicycles.

“We have years of experience and the opportunity to improve,” Lozano said, according to Milenio. “Let’s make each meeting a source of clear agreements and use all our institutional capacity to provide a timely response to the people. Because governing is about caring, we work together to live up to the trust of millions of people.”

INAH discovers possible pre-Hispanic ossuary during Mexico-Querétaro train works

Meanwhile, archaeologists have uncovered what may be an ancient ossuary containing human remains and artifacts at Mexico City’s Buenavista railway terminal, according to a news release from Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The discovery was made Sept. 17 during construction work on the Mexico City-Querétaro train line.

Researchers have so far identified nine human skeletons, five mandibles and several other bones, including ribs, femurs and pelvic fragments.

According to Secretary of Culture Claudia Curiel de Icaza, the discovery reveals new dimensions to the region’s pre-Hispanic funerary practices and how they honored their dead.

1 of 3

“A possible ossuary speaks not only of death: it raises questions about how the ancient communities of this territory treated and remembered their dead during a time of profound change,” Icaza said in a statement.

The burial deposit may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200-1519) or the early years of Spanish contact (1519-1535). Associated artifacts include domestic pottery, miniature spindle whorls, figurines and stone tools. Several obsidian blades may have originated in Hidalgo’s Sierra de las Navajas region.

“Taken together — bone fragments and ceramics — they could correspond to the final years of the pre-Hispanic period and the colonial era (1535-1821),” said José Manuel Cervantes Pérez, head of the Physical Anthropology Laboratory.

The recovered materials have been transferred to laboratories in Hidalgo for cleaning, restoration and further study.

“The associated materials offer clues to this encounter between different historical moments; it will be up to the INAH to study them rigorously and explain what they reveal,” Icaza said. “In this way, a history that lay hidden beneath the city can be incorporated into the knowledge of everyone.”

Mexico City-Querétaro train line construction is now 32% complete

Speaking of the Mexico City-Querétaro train line, construction has reached 32% completion, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Oct. 31 during a visit to a portion of the project in Polotitlán, State of Mexico.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Expansion (@expansionmx)

Additionally, Sheinbaum said 90% of the land rights needed for the project have been secured and that construction is progressing according to schedule.

At a cost of roughly 700 billion pesos, the approximately 230-kilometer railway will connect Mexico City with Querétaro, passing through the State of Mexico and Hidalgo. The journey is expected to take approximately two hours, with trains averaging 130 kilometers per hour.

The route will feature six stations: Buenavista in Mexico City, Huehuetoca and Teoloyucan in the State of Mexico, Tula de Allende in Hidalgo, and two stops in Querétaro.

Sheinbaum described the project as part of a broader effort to revive passenger rail services across the country, which in turn would offer an alternative to increasingly congested highways.

According to officials, 47 trains have been contracted and are currently being manufactured.

Mexico City suspends special license and commercial plate plan for delivery drivers

And now a win for the thousands of men and women who keep this city humming via Rappi, Uber Eats and countless other delivery services …

Mexico City authorities have suspended a pilot program that would have required motorcycle delivery workers operating through digital platforms to obtain special licenses and commercial plates, following protests over the proposed regulations.

The city’s Mobility Ministry (Semovi) reached the agreement Nov. 9 after Secretary Héctor Ulises García Nieto met with representatives of several groups to discuss their concerns. Both sides also agreed to establish additional working groups to review any revised proposals and develop an alternative regulatory framework.

The announcement followed several hours of demonstrations in western Mexico City, where app-based delivery workers blocked major roads in the Santa Fe area, causing traffic delays.

‘Unnecessary administrative hurdles’

Protesters argued that the proposed requirements would impose unnecessary administrative hurdles and additional expenses on workers who already hold motorcycle licenses. Some also complained about frequent police enforcement operations targeting delivery riders during their shifts, as well as unsafe working conditions.

“I mean, we already had a license, first the regular one, then they made us get another one for a motorcycle, and now a special one. It’s tough,” a delivery driver who did not give their name told La Gazzetta DF. “Besides, the police are around all the time on this side; there are operations, they keep driving their trucks around us, and now the National Guard is involved, they show up and everything. It’s like we’re criminals, and we’re not.”

Semovi said the initiative was intended to organize motorcycle-based delivery services and improve protections for workers in a sector that has historically faced precarious working conditions.

The program’s suspension leaves the proposed licensing and registration requirements under review, with further discussions expected between authorities and motorcycle delivery groups.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

Latin America ended Friday unsettled: a four-hour US flight halt grounded travel plans, and local money worries filled the quiet that followed.

The day across Latin America at a glance.

The Continent’s Mood Today – Grounded, and Counting the Cost

On Friday afternoon the US aviation authority, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), stopped every departing flight in the country for more than four hours. It blamed communication problems at several air route traffic control centres.

For Latin America, the US is the hub that holds travel plans together. Three airlines reacted: Brazil’s Gol warned about two flights bound for Brasília, Colombia’s Avianca let passengers move trips planned for 13 and 14 November, and Panama’s Copa warned of delays.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication as of yet” of anything nefarious. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old technology and routers overloaded with data, and the FBI is checking whether a software update caused it.

The scare passed, but it left a reminder of how much of the region’s daily life runs through systems it does not control.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico” Get the brief

Brazil – Tired Nerves and a Weakening Real

The real fell to its weakest level in a year on Friday. Our Morning Call linked it to worries about public debt, even as the Senate backed a fiscal plan by 45 votes to 31.

Brazilians are also bracing for a shorter work week. A justice kept the start date, the central bank flagged the change, and retailers say they are preparing for a shorter trading week.

There was good news and bad news about money. The digital bank Nubank posted a record profit of US$1.1 billion, while a Treasury leak exposed 4,000 Pix keys (addresses for Brazil’s instant payments) and a court gave President Lula three days to explain spending.

For foreigners, a weaker real makes dollars go further, but expect bank and shop-hour changes once the shorter week begins.

Mexico – Shopping Under a Shadow

El Buen Fin, Mexico’s big discount weekend, opened under a Trump tariff threat. BBVA is letting customers pay until March 2027 and offering up to 15% back, the kind of offer banks make when they want people to spend.

The US flight halt hit Mexican airlines from Mexico City’s airport outward, because flights bound for the US were told to stay on the ground. Families heading north for the holiday paid the price.

In Jalisco, an army clash left two dead and two hurt, a reminder that security never leaves the headlines. A federal audit also flagged pay going to dead workers.

For foreigners, expect crowds and card deals this weekend, and check US-bound flights before leaving for the airport.

Chile – Fuel Anger, Budget Fights

President José Antonio Kast’s government has just faced its first truckers’ strike, called on 10 November over rising fuel prices.

Calm is thin: deputies rejected three ministry budget lines as debate on the 2027 budget continued.

Chile’s old split between order and reform is back, this time in the budget debate. For foreigners, budget fights and a jobs focus matter more than headlines about the ministers, so watch fuel prices and tax signals.

Argentina – Prices Up, Pay Behind

October inflation rose to 2.2%, and Argentines noticed that pay is not keeping up. INDEC, the national statistics institute, said wages rose 1.3% in September while prices rose 1.9%.

The mood is a mix of fatigue and stubborn work.A gas blast near Buenos Aires killed one person and hurt more than 20. It rattled a country that lives with ageing infrastructure.

There was some lift.A Santa Cruz silver and gold mine may reopen with about 300 jobs, and Scaloni is reported to be staying as national coach until 2030. For foreigners, prices rising faster than pay means local costs keep climbing, so budget in dollars and expect shops to reprice often.

Colombia – Pride in Profits, Worry About Prices

Ecopetrol, the state oil company, is eyeing a 10-year gas deal with Venezuela. Retail sales rose 9.7% in September and factory output grew 1.5%.

For foreigners, the data show spending holding up, so expect busy shops, and check local security advice before you travel.

Peru – Faith, Quakes and Unfinished Business

Pope Leo returned to Chiclayo, the Peruvian city he called home, during his visit to Peru that runs until 16 November.A union also said dynamite was found at a Lima court site, and a court asked the Senate to pick six judges. Peru blocked two Lima mayors from staying on, adding to the sense of institutions being tested.

Meanwhile the trade surplus eased to US$3.95 billion in September. For foreigners, the Pope’s visit will bring crowds and tight security in Cusco and Chiclayo, so book early and keep documents with you.

The Shared Mood – Tired, Hopeful, Watching the Clock

Across the continent, people spent Friday doing sums: flights, prices, pay and the dollar. Black Friday sales began, and the mood was careful rather than carefree.

The flight halt was a small shock, but it matched a larger feeling that big systems can pause and leave ordinary people waiting. Latin Americans answered the way they usually do, with patience, jokes and a plan B.

Saturday brings football, a Pope in Peru, and bargains in Mexico. The undertone is a wish for stable prices and calm institutions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the US flight halt on 13 November 2026?

The FAA cited communication problems at several air route traffic control centres. Bloomberg reports the FBI is probing whether a software update caused it, and officials say there is no sign of an attack.

How did the flight halt affect Latin America?

Flights bound for the US from Mexico were told to stay on the ground, and Brazilian departures were also hit. Gol, Avianca and Copa warned of delays or offered rebooking.

Why is the Brazilian real weak?

The real hit its weakest level in a year, with worries about public debt weighing on it. The Senate backed a fiscal plan by 45 to 31 the same day.

01 Tech takes the hit

The S&P 500 closed at 7,562, down 0.40%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91% to 25,136. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.10% to 52,348.

That split tells the story. Investors sold growth stocks, whose profits lie far in the future and lose value when yields rise, and kept hold of older industrial names.

The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, rose 3.21% to 19.3. That is a nervous reading, not a panic.

02 Hot prices, higher yields

The US 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.145% on Friday, a level that makes bonds a real rival to shares. The dollar index gained 0.23% to 103.411.

Producer prices rose 0.3% in October against a consensus of 0.4%, and 6.5% from a year earlier against 6.6% expected. Both were a shade softer than forecast, but the annual rate is up from 6.3% in September.

Core producer prices, as listed in the RT economic calendar (RT), rose 0.3% on the month, in line with consensus, and 5.0% on the year. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics’ own core gauge, which also excludes trade margins, rose 0.5% on the month and 4.9% on the year.

That follows hot consumer inflation earlier in the week, which revived fears of a Fed rate hike. The next Fed meeting is on 8 to 9 December.

Gold slipped 0.16% to $3,874/oz as the firmer dollar and higher yields weighed on it.

03 Brazil holds the line

Brazil’s central bank held the Selic, its benchmark rate, at 13.75% on 4 November. The vote was unanimous and ended five straight cuts of 0.25 percentage point.

The minutes, published on 10 November, say rates must stay high for longer. Copom projects 2026 inflation of 5.6%, against a ceiling of 4.5%.

A US yield above 5% and a firm dollar are bad news for the real, because they pull money back to the US. That limits Brazil’s room to cut, even if growth slows.

Domestic data is not weak. Brazilian retail sales rose 1.7% in September from a year earlier, against 1.0% expected, and 0.2% on the month, against a forecast fall of 0.2%.

Colombia was stronger still. Retail sales rose 9.7% year on year against 8.7% expected, and industrial output grew 1.5% against a forecast fall of 0.8%.

US crude stocks rose 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million in the week to 6 November, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA, eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly). Gasoline stocks rose 1.8 million barrels and distillates 4.1 million, a cushion for consumers but a small drag for oil exporters such as Brazil and Colombia.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the Nasdaq fall while the Dow rose?

Growth stocks are most sensitive to rising bond yields, so the Nasdaq fell 0.91% to 25,136. The Dow rose 0.10% to 52,348 on firmer older industrial names.

How high is the US 10-year yield?

It ended Friday at 5.145%, up on the day. That makes Treasuries a serious rival to shares and pressures emerging markets.

Did US producer prices cool?

Slightly. October PPI rose 6.5% year on year against 6.6% expected, and 0.3% on the month against 0.4%.

What does this mean for the Brazilian real?

A firm dollar (index 103.411) and a 5%-plus Treasury yield pull money out of emerging markets. That leaves the real with little support while the Selic is 13.75%.

When are the next Fed and Copom meetings?

The Fed meets on 8 to 9 December and Brazil’s Copom on 9 December. Markets expect the Selic to stay unchanged.

World.title: Two Quakes Empty Ibagué Government Offices
World.content:
Ibagué, the capital of Colombia's Tolima department, seen from the hills above the city. (Photo: Duvanlopupa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · EARTHQUAKES

Two magnitude 4.2 earthquakes struck the Colombian department (state) of Tolima 18 minutes apart on Friday 13 November 2026, sending workers out of government offices in Ibagué, the regional capital. The Colombian Geological Service (SGC) recorded them at 2:43 p.m. and 3:01 p.m. local time (19:43 and 20:01 GMT), at shallow depths under 30 kilometres.

No damage or injuries had been reported by Friday evening, and the evacuations were precautionary. The shocks matter because Ibagué is part of a region of Colombia that has felt a long run of tremors since September.

Why a 4.2 Is Far Weaker Than a 5.6

Each whole step on the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy, so the 5.6 of 3 November released roughly 126 times the energy of a 4.2. That is why Friday’s evacuations were precautions rather than responses to damage.

Two shocks within 18 minutes still keep officials cautious. Buildings must be checked before staff return.

Whether the two shocks signal a larger quake is not known, and no damage assessment has been published. No date for further official updates on the Chaparral sequence has been announced.

World.title: Lula’s Party Wants More Posts, Lower Rates
World.content:
Photo: Josemar Gonçalves / Câmara dos Deputados / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Brazil’s Workers’ Party (PT), the party of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, backed his government’s fiscal package on Friday 13 November 2026 while demanding more posts in his next cabinet and lower interest rates. Its national directorate, the party’s top decision body between congresses, approved the resolution at a meeting after Lula beat conservative Flávio Bolsonaro in the 25 October runoff.

For US investors the message is that Lula’s own party wants cheaper money, even as the central bank’s benchmark Selic rate stands at 13.75% a year. That tension will shape how fast Brazilian borrowing costs can fall.

What Did the Party Decide?

The directorate backed the economic team’s measures even though several leaders said in speeches that nobody had consulted them. Anyone who accuses the government of an “electoral swindle” (estelionato eleitoral) acts in bad faith, the resolution says.

Why Is the Party Attacking the Central Bank?

The resolution says the benchmark interest rate is the biggest obstacle to growth and income policies, and that household debt eats into disposable income. In its words, “there is no justification for the Central Bank’s excessive conservatism”.

The Selic stands at 13.75% a year, and the central bank’s rate-setting committee, Copom, next meets on 8 and 9 December 2026. Lower rates would ease the state’s debt bill and household budgets, but they would also narrow the yield that draws foreign money to Brazilian bonds.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders price “no change” in the December Selic decision at 88.0%, a 25-basis-point cut at 7.3% and a 25-basis-point rise at 1.3%, with US$77,312 traded across all outcomes (as of 9:35 p.m. ET, 13 November 2026). These prices are bets, not polls, and a price is not a forecast.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Posts, Taxes and the Criminal Age

Directorate members asked the party to take more space in strategic areas of government, including the Cities Ministry, which the MDB, a centrist party, held in the previous government. They also argued that public accounts should be balanced by taxing the rich more, for example by ending tax exemptions on LCI and LCA, popular real-estate and agribusiness credit notes.

Silva said the measures have nothing to do with cutting social programmes. He added that the PT opposes lowering the age of criminal responsibility, which contrasts with Lula’s campaign position that under-16s accused of heinous crimes should answer as adults.

What It Means for You

Investors in Brazilian bonds or the real face a government whose own party wants cheaper money while the central bank, which sets the Selic independently, keeps rates high. The resolution is a political demand, not a decision.

Companies planning around Brazilian credit costs should watch the 9 December Copom decision. The party’s text is political pressure, not a change in policy.

What Is Not Known

The resolution’s full text and the vote count have not been published, and Lula has not said which posts the party will receive. The size and final content of the fiscal package are not confirmed here.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the PT back Lula’s fiscal package?

Yes. The party’s national directorate approved a resolution of support on Friday 13 November 2026, although several leaders said they were not consulted.

What is the Selic rate?

The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, set by the central bank’s Copom committee. It stands at 13.75% a year.

When is the next Copom decision?

Copom meets on 8 and 9 December 2026, with the decision announced on the second day. Traders on Polymarket price a hold at 88.0%.

World.title: US Brands Three Guatemalan Gangs Terrorists
World.content:
Rafts on the Suchiate River, seen from the border bridge between Ciudad Hidalgo, Chiapas, and Tecún Umán, Guatemala. (Photo: AlejandroLinaresGarcia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · CARTELS · SANCTIONS

The United States on Friday 13 November 2026 designated three Guatemalan crime groups as terrorist organisations, saying they help Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), two large drug-trafficking organisations, move drugs. The State Department named Los Lorenzanas a Foreign Terrorist Organization, while the Treasury sanctioned Los Huistas and Los Mendoza as Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGT).

For US readers the move reaches banks and businesses, because assets of the designated groups under US jurisdiction are blocked and Americans are barred from dealing with them. It also extends Washington’s terrorism label from Mexican cartels to their Guatemalan partners.

Effect Assets under US jurisdiction are blocked, and US persons may not deal with them.

Who Are Los Mendoza and Los Huistas?

Los Mendoza and Los Huistas are Guatemalan drug-trafficking groups that, Treasury says, work together as allies. It links both groups to the Sinaloa Cartel, and Los Huistas also to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG).

What Is New This Time?

Los Huistas were already sanctioned for drug trafficking in March 2022, under a US counter-narcotics order. Los Mendoza were added on Friday under both the narcotics and the terrorism authorities, according to reports of the Treasury notice.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Do the Designations Do?

A designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist blocks assets under US jurisdiction and bars US persons from transactions with the target, with limited exceptions. The Foreign Terrorist Organization label, applied to Los Lorenzanas, also exposes anyone who gives it material support to US criminal law.

The State Department describes Los Lorenzanas as one of Guatemala’s most powerful drug-trafficking clans and holds it responsible for violence against civilians, officials and soldiers. In February 2025 the Trump administration designated the Sinaloa Cartel and the CJNG, among others, as terrorist organisations.

Why It Matters

Treasury says the alliance helps move drugs across borders toward the United States and gives the two groups control over key segments of the supply chain. For US enforcement, that means targeting the middle of the chain, not only the Mexican groups at its end.

Each added name widens the net around the cartels’ logistics. That is the stretch between production and the US border, which designations of the Mexican groups alone did not reach.

What It Means for You

Companies with Guatemalan partners must now screen for the three names, a task for their compliance teams. The designations are not a travel warning for Guatemala.

What Is Not Known

Neither department has said how much money is affected by the blocking. No date for further US action has been announced, and Guatemala’s government response is not covered here.

Who are Los Mendoza?

A Guatemalan family-run criminal organisation founded in the 1980s. Treasury says it serves as an intermediary for the Sinaloa Cartel in Guatemala and Honduras.

What does a global terrorist designation mean?

It blocks the target’s assets under US jurisdiction. It also bars US persons from transactions with the target, with limited exceptions.

Which agency designated which group?

The State Department designated Los Lorenzanas. The Treasury designated Los Huistas and Los Mendoza.

World.title: Dollar Falls to a Record Low of 446 Colones in Costa Rica
World.content:
The U.S. dollar closed at its weakest level on record against the Costa Rican colón on Friday, falling to a weighted average of 446.10 colones on the country’s wholesale foreign-exchange market. The Monex close came in 0.72 colones below Thursday’s average of 446.82 and beat the previous low of 446.80, set on Sept. 17, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) trading data. On Thursday, the rate had sat just 0.02 colones above that record.

Friday marked the eighth consecutive session of decline, a slide that began on Nov. 4, when the average stood at 452.01 colones. Trades ranged between 445.80 and 446.30 colones per dollar, with $49.3 million changing hands in 228 operations. The BCCR’s reference rate for Friday stood at 442.74 colones for buying dollars and 448.37 for selling. The currency had already fallen to around 448 colones earlier this week.

The dollar has now lost 50.97 colones, or 10.3%, since the first trading session of 2026 on Jan. 2, when it opened the year at 497.07. After the September low, it recovered to 460.45 on Oct. 1, then fell 3.1% in a little over six weeks. Measured against its peak of 696.76 colones on June 21, 2022, the dollar has lost 36% of its value in Costa Rica.

In practical terms, every $1,000 converted at the Monex average now yields about 446,100 colones, roughly 51,000 fewer than at the start of the year. Bank and exchange-house rates sit on either side of the wholesale average, but they have moved in the same direction. The shift cuts both ways. Households and businesses that earn in dollars and pay their bills in colones receive less local currency for each dollar, while anyone who needs dollars, whether to pay a dollar-denominated loan or to import goods, needs fewer colones to buy them.

For people living on income from abroad, the squeeze comes as lawmakers weigh a bill that would tax residents’ foreign income at 15%. Dollar debt is a significant part of the picture. Data from the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef) through August show that 62% of foreign-currency loans in the financial system go to borrowers exposed to exchange-rate risk, meaning their income is not in dollars.

A strong colón lowers those payments for now. Sugef has warned, however, that if the exchange rate rises, the ability of a significant share of those borrowers to pay could be affected. Foreign-currency lending has also been growing faster than lending in colones. Sugef figures for September show dollar loans grew 6%, compared with 2.7% for colón loans.

The Central Bank has been buying dollars as the rate falls. Through Nov. 12, it had purchased $94.9 million this month in stabilization operations, bringing its 2026 total to $1.36 billion.

On Thursday alone, the BCCR bought $13.7 million for stabilization and another $11 million to cover the currency needs of the non-bank public sector. Stabilization purchases are meant to smooth sharp swings in the rate rather than to defend a specific level. Costa Rica has operated under a managed float since February 2015. Monex began operating in November 2006, which makes Friday’s close the lowest in the platform’s two-decade history.

Trading has been heavy in recent weeks. On Oct. 27, Monex recorded $153.4 million in transactions, the largest volume since its creation. Monex trading resumes on Monday, Nov. 16, when the market will show whether the slide extends to a ninth session.

World.title: Costa Rica Flights Caught in Only the Third Nationwide US Ground Stop Ever
World.content:
If you’re flying between the United States and Costa Rica this afternoon or tonight, expect delays and possible cancellations. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) stopped every departing flight across the United States on Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”

The order took effect shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern time, just before 3 p.m. in Costa Rica. It stays in place until further notice. Any flight scheduled to leave a U.S. airport for San José or Liberia is grounded for now. That includes flights from the Florida hubs that carry much of Costa Rica’s U.S. traffic, such as Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Orlando, as well as other major gateways.

Planes already in the air are being allowed to continue to their destinations. Flights from Costa Rica to the United States are less clear. The FAA said inbound international flights will be handled case by case. Even if your flight is cleared, it may still be late. Many U.S. airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same aircraft back, so a jet stuck on the ground in Miami or Houston means a late or canceled departure here.

The FAA hasn’t officially said what caused the stop. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue is affecting all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle planes flying between airports. Outages on radio frequencies used by controllers had been reported in parts of the country before the order was issued.

There’s no confirmed time for flights to restart. Some flight-tracking services listed 5 p.m. Eastern time, or 4 p.m. in Costa Rica, as the first point the order would be reviewed, but it could be extended. Delays will likely last well past the end of the stop, because planes and crews will be out of position. In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop of about 90 minutes, triggered by the failure of a computer system that sends safety notices to pilots, led to more than 11,000 delays and cancellations.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. The January 2023 one was the most recent. Before that, the only other was ordered after the September 11, 2001, attacks. Check your flight with your airline before you head to the airport. Airline apps and text alerts usually update before airport departure boards do.

Look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. During large disruptions, airlines often let you change your flight without a fee, which can be easier than waiting for a rebooking. If your flight is canceled and you decide not to travel, U.S. rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines aren’t required to pay for hotels or meals when the disruption isn’t their fault, so keep your receipts if you have travel insurance that covers delays.

If you’re connecting through a U.S. hub, you may miss your connection even after flights restart. Rebook through the airline that issued your ticket rather than each carrier separately. Updates on local flights are posted on the official social media channels of Juan Santamaría International Airport and Guanacaste Airport.

This is a developing story and will be updated as the FAA and airlines release more information.

World.title: Banks and Businesses in Costa Rica Must Accept Digital ID Starting January
World.content:
Starting January 1, 2027, banks, government agencies, businesses and other institutions in Costa Rica will be required to accept the Costa Rican Digital Identity (IDC), the smartphone version of the national ID card, for any transaction or procedure that requires identification. The Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) said the digital credential carries the same legal validity as the traditional plastic ID card. From that date, institutions will no longer be able to turn it away simply because it is presented on a phone.

The digital ID has been available since September 9, 2025, but until now institutions could decide whether to accept it. According to the TSE, 107,243 people had requested one as of November 1, 2026. The change could make everyday procedures simpler, from banking to administrative paperwork and any service that requires proof of identity. It does not replace the physical card, which will continue to be issued and accepted throughout the country.

Unlike the physical ID, which is free for most applicants, the digital version costs 2,600 colones (about $5.80) and is valid for four years. Senior citizens are exempt from the fee. The service is available only to Costa Rican citizens. Applicants need a valid physical ID card, a smartphone with an active phone line running iOS or Android, and no identity document waiting to be collected at the TSE.

People applying for their first Costa Rican ID must get the physical card before they can request the digital version. Applications are handled online through the TSE website at tse.go.cr/idc. Applicants enter their ID number, complete an identity verification step, provide a valid email address and pay with a Visa or Mastercard credit or debit card.

Once the application is approved, the credential is activated through the official IDC-Ciudadano app, available on Apple’s App Store and Google Play. It is protected by a personal PIN and facial recognition, which the TSE checks against the biometric data collected during the holder’s most recent physical ID procedure.

Citizens can still obtain or renew their physical IDs free of charge at the TSE’s headquarters in San José or at any of its 32 regional offices. A fee applies only when a person exceeds the annual limit on duplicate replacements. The January requirement applies to the institutions that must accept the credential, not to citizens. Getting a digital ID remains optional, and anyone who prefers the plastic card can keep using it.

World.title: Heavy Storms Could Drop Nearly 3 Inches of Rain on Costa Rica Today
World.content:
The rest of this Friday afternoon could bring short, heavy downpours and thunderstorms to the Central Valley, the northern zone and the Caribbean. If you still have to get somewhere today, plan your trip around them. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects intense storms lasting one to three hours, with 20 to 40 millimeters (0.8 to 1.6 inches) of rain in most affected areas. In the Central Valley, the Caribbean and the northern zone, totals could reach 70 millimeters (2.8 inches).

That much rain in a short window can overwhelm city drains and push creeks over their banks, especially in the Central Valley. If you live or park near a stream or on a street that floods, move your car early and don’t drive through standing water. Wind is the other risk. Isolated gusts could reach 80 kilometers per hour (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines. When a storm hits, get indoors and keep away from trees and fallen cables.

The mountains and the eastern and northeastern parts of the Central Valley have the highest chance of storms. Rain could also spread to the northern lowlands and the northern Caribbean. On the Pacific side, expect storms in the mountains of the Central and South Pacific. The Nicoya Peninsula and the southeast of the North Pacific should see less activity.

The storms come in bursts rather than as an all-day rain. If one hits while you’re on the road or about to drive home, it is usually safer to wait it out than to push through it. The reason for the change is the trade winds. They usually keep the Pacific side dry at this time of year, and earlier this week they were bringing strong gusts across the country. Now they have weakened, which lets sea breezes and westerly winds carry moist Pacific air inland. Warm temperatures then build storm clouds over the mountains by afternoon.

This back-and-forth is typical of the transition from the rainy season to the dry season, which has already begun in Guanacaste and the Central Valley. Unsettled weather continues into Saturday, with more chances of afternoon rain. From Tuesday, the IMN expects rising pressure over the Caribbean Sea to strengthen the trade winds again.

If you’re driving between the Central Valley and the Caribbean coast, keep an eye on Route 32. Heavy rain in the mountains is what brings rock and mud down onto the highway through Braulio Carrillo National Park, which has closed repeatedly this year. If Route 32 closes, the usual alternatives are Route 10 through Turrialba and Route 126 through Vara Blanca. Both are narrower and slower, so leave extra time.

Check the IMN’s website and social media for updated warnings before you head out this afternoon or on Saturday.

World.title: Salvadoran Troops Turn Haiti National Stadium Into Base After Retaking It From Gangs
World.content:
El Salvador will turn Haiti’s national soccer stadium into a forward base for its troops after Salvadoran and Haitian forces retook the Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince from armed gangs on Thursday, President Nayib Bukele announced. The joint operation took place in the early hours yesterday and involved the Haitian National Police, the Armed Forces of Haiti, a government-contracted security unit known as the Task Force, and Salvadoran special forces, according to Bukele and Haitian police. Bukele said it was carried out under a bilateral agreement between the two governments.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that its officers had taken full control of the stadium and its surroundings before handing security of the complex to the Salvadoran armed forces. More than 20 armored vehicles and trucks carrying Salvadoran military personnel were stationed inside the stadium after the operation, according to local media reports.

Bukele said troops found several human skulls inside the facility. Authorities have not announced any identification of the remains or said whether they will be examined. The Salvadoran president said his forces would use the stadium as a base to advance deeper into territory held by gangs, and that the allied forces now hold the advantage on the ground.

In a message addressed directly to gang members, he told them to leave the area before the next phase of operations begins and warned that those who stay to fight Salvadoran and Haitian forces will face the consequences. He did not give a start date. The stadium, home ground of Haiti’s national soccer team, had been held by gangs since early 2024. Its loss forced Haiti to play every one of its home qualifiers for the 2026 World Cup outside the country.

The recovery is the latest step in a rapidly expanding Salvadoran military presence in Haiti. El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 troops since October 18, when gangs ambushed an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran Air Force aviation technicians in Croix-des-Bouquets, northeast of Port-au-Prince. The Salvadoran military said the vehicle was struck by gunfire and explosives and caught fire, and that the four men got out before going missing.

The technicians were serving with the Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission authorized by the United Nations Security Council to support Haitian police against armed groups that control large parts of the capital and other areas. Salvadoran officials have described them as non-combat personnel whose main job was carrying out medical evacuations.

The Salvadoran government maintains that the four are alive, but their whereabouts remained unknown as of now. Bukele has previously offered to withdraw all Salvadoran forces from Haiti if the technicians are released unharmed. The Gang Suppression Force has distanced itself from the actions of the Salvadoran troops sent in after the ambush, which operate under the separate bilateral arrangement with the Haitian government. Bukele has said the contingent is focused on confronting the gangs responsible for the October attack and related violence.

The stadium operation came two days after Bukele said Salvadoran troops had destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang, an operation for which Haiti’s prime minister publicly praised the Salvadoran leader. Gang violence in Haiti has forced nearly 1.5 million people from their homes, and the international force sent to help contain it has so far deployed only a fraction of the 5,550 personnel the Security Council authorized.

World.title: Shakira Returns to Costa Rica in 2027 After More Than 15 Years
World.content:
Shakira’s world tour has added Costa Rica to its 2027 Latin American leg. It’s the strongest sign yet that the Colombian superstar will perform at the National Stadium in La Sabana on Sunday, January 31. It would be her first concert in the country since April 2011. The tour’s official accounts posted a graphic this week listing six countries for the new leg: Brazil, Venezuela, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico and Panama. The post gave no dates or venues for any of the stops.

The January 31 date comes from the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce (MEIC). In October it authorized a presale plan for the show. The authorization lists an 8 p.m. start at the National Stadium and lets the production company, Two Shows Ltda., sell 53,114 tickets through eticket.cr.

Ticket prices and the on-sale date have not been announced. The ministry requires a presale authorization before any large event goes on sale, to protect buyers, but it doesn’t mean tickets are available. Wait for an official announcement and buy only through the authorized seller.

There is a reason for caution. In September 2024, the ministry approved a presale of 51,446 tickets for a Shakira concert at the same stadium on March 27, 2025. That show never happened bug the difference this time is that the tour itself has named Costa Rica as a stop.

The show is part of the Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, named after her 2024 album, her first studio record in seven years. The tour opened in Rio de Janeiro in February 2025. Her production team says the tour has grossed more than $534 million and sold over four million tickets worldwide. Shakira recently closed a 13-show residency in Madrid that drew more than 700,000 people.

She has played Costa Rica twice before. She brought her Pies Descalzos tour to the Palacio de los Deportes in Heredia in 1995. She then performed at the National Stadium on April 3, 2011, shortly after the stadium opened. A full stadium on the last Sunday of January would also land in the middle of high season, when flights and hotels around San José are already busy.

Prices, seating sections and the sale date are expected once the producers make a formal announcement.

World.title: Finish Your Government Paperwork by Dec. 21 as Costa Rica Offices Close
World.content:
The government has ordered seven days of collective vacation for public employees: Dec. 22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30 and 31. With Christmas, New Year’s Day and two weekends in between, offices that work Monday to Friday will be closed from Tuesday, Dec. 22, through Sunday, Jan. 3. Staff return on Monday, Jan. 4, 2027.

President Laura Fernández signed the directive with Planning Minister Carla Morales Rojas and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla. The government announced it on Thursday, Nov. 12. It takes legal effect once it’s published in the official gazette La Gaceta. The tricky part is that not every public office follows the same calendar. If you assume everything closes, or that everything stays open, you could be caught out.

The directive covers the central and decentralized public administration, meaning the ministries and the agencies under them. Five groups set their own dates instead: the Education Ministry (MEP), the Office of the Attorney General (Procuraduría General de la República), the National Registry, police forces and emergency institutions. The leaders of each will decide based on what their services need.

Other branches of government don’t have to follow the order. The Legislative Assembly has already approved its own recess, from Dec. 21 to 31. The judiciary sets its own year-end closure under its 2026 vacation plan. In June it ruled that a similar government directive was not binding on the courts.

Autonomous institutions and municipalities also decide for themselves. When the government ordered a collective vacation week in July, the Social Security System (CCSS), the Comptroller General’s Office, the public universities and the judiciary all chose to keep working. Some services keep running no matter what. Every institution must keep essential services open and have staff ready for emergencies. Health care and public security must not be interrupted.

Each institution must also publish its holiday hours and say which service channels stay open. Most had not done so as of Nov. 13. Check the schedule for the office you need before you make the trip. Immigration is where an unplanned gap hurts most. If you have a residency application, a DIMEX renewal or another filing with the General Directorate of Migration and Immigration, finish it well before Dec. 21 and expect appointments to be in high demand. In past years, Migración has partly closed its main office in La Uruca over the holidays. In 2023 it also stopped accepting new filings on its digital platform until offices reopened.

Immigration control at airports and border crossings continues through the holidays because it is a security function. Some land border posts have changed their hours over the holidays in past years. If you plan to cross by land, check the hours first. If you’re buying property, registering a company or transferring a vehicle, the National Registry’s dates matter. The Registry will set its own schedule, so ask your lawyer or notary when it will stop receiving documents. A sale signed in late December may not be recorded until January.

One deadline does not move: the 2027 marchamo, the annual vehicle circulation fee, is due by Dec. 31. It’s collected by the National Insurance Institute (INS), not a ministry. You can pay it online, in banking apps or at authorized payment points. From Jan. 1, unpaid vehicles face fines, surcharges and possible removal of their plates.

If you need a Costa Rican criminal record certificate (hoja de delincuencia), request it early. The Judicial Registry issues these certificates. During last year’s judicial closure it shut for the first week and reopened with shorter hours in the second. Tax filings with the Finance Ministry are made online, but the ministry has not announced its holiday schedule. If a filing or payment deadline falls between Dec. 22 and Jan. 3, ask your accountant whether it moves. If you have a court case or a legal deadline, the judiciary’s calendar applies, not the government’s.

The state-owned banks compete with private banks, and in the past the government has only invited companies like them to join its collective vacations. Online banking normally runs through the holidays, but check branch hours before you go. The government says the closure will reduce the large backlog of unused vacation days in the public sector. It also expects savings on electricity, water, telecommunications and fuel. The seven days come out of each employee’s own vacation balance.

The directive also allows the Ministry of the Interior and Police to give public employees in central San José the day off on Dec. 31 for the city’s year-end civic festivities. The simplest plan: if a task needs a government stamp, signature or appointment, finish it by Dec. 21. Then check the published schedule of the specific office before heading out in late December.
