World.title: Two arrested for Prinsjesdag train sabotage
World.content:
Police have arrested two people in connection with the sabotage on the railway during Prinsjesdag, the public prosecution service (OM) announced on Friday.

A 49-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman from Drenthe were arrested on Thursday. According to the OM, the pair remain suspects but there was not enough evidence to keep them in custody.

Train services across the country were disrupted in September in what network operators described an act of coordinated sabotage. The attacks took place during Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in The Hague and one of the biggest days in the Dutch political calendar.

Steel pipes were attached to the tracks at multiple locations across the country, disrupting rail service nationwide.

It is not yet known who was behind the attacks. On the same day, tractor tires, hay bales, and pallets were lit on fire at various locations. Some of those incidents were tied to farmer activists.

The Farmers Defence Force, responsible for recent motorway disruptions, said it was not responsible but that “wild actions” by individual farmers had been expected on budget day.

The two suspects are the first to be arrested in the case.

World.title: The Hague is the tile “whipping” champion
World.content:
No city has done more to whip their gardens into shape than The Hague, which took home the Golden Tile prize for removing the most paving stones from its gardens, totalling a record 507,000 citywide, breaking the previous record by nearly 50,000.

The NK Tegelwippen, or Dutch National Tile Removal Championship, pits councils against one another to see who can free up the most green space.

According to the organisation, this makes neighbourhoods more attractive, combats flood and rising temperatures and gives children more areas for play.

“It is fantastic that we are still breaking records. It shows that perseverance pays off and that residents consider greenery in the city increasingly important,” Joris Wijsmuller, the director of Duurzaam Den Haag, said in a statement.

Some 150,000 tiles were taken out by residents, schools, sports clubs, and companies participated in the event, according to the council. The remainder were removed by the city in public spaces.

The Hague also won the title in 2021 and 2022.

World.title: Three’s a crowd: Will Jetten’s tax bill kill the cabinet?
World.content:
There is an old medical joke about a surgeon who declares: “The operation was a complete success, but the patient died.”

After months of chaotic, gruelling negotiations, Rob Jetten achieved a majority in parliament for his tax bill on Thursday night, but his coalition is in tatters. The right-wing liberal VVD were so incensed by the deal the other two partners, Jetten’s D66 and the Christian Democrats (CDA), struck with the left-wing Pro that they voted against the entire plan, which had been extensively drafted and redrafted by the VVD finance minister, Eelco Heinen.

The party’s leader, Dilan Yesilgöz, denounced it as “a bad deal for the Netherlands” and demanded a “fundamental reset” of the centre-right coalition. Essentially, she wanted the prime minister to switch his cabinet off and switch it on again.

The millionaires’ tax knife twist

Strikingly, the amendment that D66, CDA and Pro agreed on Wednesday afternoon was a milder version of one that the VVD had seemed willing to tolerate earlier in the week. Pro wanted to raise an extra €1.5 billion in wealth taxes in order to pay for an income tax cut for the lowest earners. D66 and CDA had negotiated the amount down to €1 billion and built in counterbalancing measures to protect people with modest savings – at an earlier stage one of the key concerns for the VVD. Its impact, even on the private investors it was aimed at, was marginal.

But none of that mattered. For the VVD, the deal was unacceptable because it crossed a red line – raising taxes on successful, hard-working entrepreneurs – and it was drawn up behind their backs between their coalition partners and Pro.

Jesse Klaver, the leader of Pro, then twisted the knife by describing the measure as a “millionaires’ tax”, a phrase that went down like cold gravel in the throats of not just the VVD, but CDA leader Henri Bontenbal.

The seeds of the crisis were sown around 10 days earlier, as a reconstruction in AD.nl has found, when the coalition parties agreed to enter what commentators immediately called an “open marriage”. After months of abortive attempts to strike a collective deal with a divided opposition that balanced the interests of left and right, the three parties would try to form separate majorities for their own priorities. It would allow D66 and CDA to pair up with Pro and Volt while the VVD could court the right-wing opposition block of JA21, the farmers’ party BBB and the orthodox Protestant SGP. As a last resort, they could even vote on opposite sides when the amendments were tabled in parliament, if it meant that the tax bill and the coalition survived.

Unagreed terms

The problem was, none of the parties had agreed on the terms of the open marriage. And what the VVD hadn’t reckoned with was that D66 and CDA would go all the way with Pro and produce an amendment that seemed calculated to hurt them. D66 and CDA protested that they had kept their partners informed throughout the negotiations and even invited them to the table. But the VVD’s whole reason for joining the coalition in the first place was to keep the left-wing Pro out of power, as D66 and CDA knew all too well.

For Yesilgöz, the amendment represented the very outcome that she had entered the partnership to avoid, and Klaver’s press conference and Instagram reel to celebrate the millionaires’ tax were simply rubbing salt into the wound. To extend the analogy, it was like agreeing to an arranged marriage only to see your partner immediately phone up the ex-girlfriend he told you was no threat and take her for dinner at the Ritz.

None of this should obscure the extent to which the VVD engineered their own downfall. The minority cabinet was built on unstable foundations because the VVD wanted to shut out the opposition party that would have the strongest hand in the upcoming negotiations. When the coalition agreement was published, they took out billboards to parade their achievements, such as retaining mortgage interest tax relief.

The final betrayal

From the outset the VVD have focused more on defending their red lines within the coalition than finding the opposition votes they need to pass their legislation. It allowed Pro to exploit the deadlock to torpedo key VVD policies such as the €6.5 billion of welfare cuts. The budget amendment was the final betrayal for the VVD, but it was also the inevitable outcome of a process in which the party had refused to build any kind of constructive relationship with Pro, while D66 and CDA had reached out to unlikely partners such as Gidi Markuszower’s far-right DNA. And when the VVD decided to reject its own budget deal, its partners delivered a final humiliation by salvaging it with the support of a pair of fringe parties on the left: Denk and the animal rights party PvdD.

What happens next is unclear. The VVD, stung by what they see as a deep betrayal, want the coalition to renew its vows. Jetten prefers to talk about a “restart”, the language usually used for businesses that have called in the receivers. Yesilgöz almost goaded the other parties to try their luck with Pro in a new combination, but that would leave the cabinet still nine votes short of a majority and a hostile opposition dominated by the right. Jesse Klaver may well have overplayed his hand with his “pick me” posts on social media.

But new elections are an equally risky option for three parties whose standing in the opinion polls has been further damaged by the tax plan saga. And if the coalition survives in its current form, it will be as a marriage of inconvenience. Not for the first time, politics and matrimony have turned out to be a toxic mix.

Nine people have been arrested in Rotterdam as part of a major drug dealing investigation, according to regional broadcaster RTV Rijnmond.

Raids were carried out on Monday and led to the seizure of cars, cash and drugs.

Eight of the men are Rotterdam residents and one is from The Hague; they are being charged with membership of a criminal drugs organisation and three are are also suspected of money laundering.

What types of drugs were involved has not been disclosed. All suspects are between 27 and 40 years old, and police have reportedly not ruled out further arrests.

World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A novel about a Dutchman living in Austria during the interwar period has been awarded the 2026 NS Public Prize.

Narcis by Judith Fanto follows Manno, who moves from Haarlem to Vienna following the death of his mother and finds a circle of friends, bonds that are tested as Hitler rises to power.

Fanto described the honour as “wonderful” during a ceremony on Thursday evening. “This appreciation from the readers is the exuberant culmination of years of work in silence,” she said.

She takes home €7,500 and a sculpture in recognition.

The award, now in its 25th edition, is a collaboration between the Foundation for Collective Promotion of the Dutch Book and Dutch railway operator NS.

More than 131,000 readers cast their votes and Narcis beat five other works, including The Superfluous by Herman Koch.

A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops. The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture. We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Huge thanks to: 🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk 🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC — Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026 “The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.” The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH). “The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general. “We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.” The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year. All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums. The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community. 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim. W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53 — Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026 The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending. “Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.” The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch. The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology. A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for. The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state. ❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL. Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab — Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees. Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised. Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026 On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed. Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury. “The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry. In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”. “It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.” Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters. Sąd w Brukseli uznał sprzeciw PAŻP wobec zajęcia komorniczego dokonanego na wniosek Pfizer za zasadny i uchylił postanowienie z 25 czerwca 2026 r., stanowiące podstawę zajęcia komorniczego. Rozstrzygnięcie jest zatem korzystne dla PAŻP, ale wyrok nie jest jeszcze prawomocny. — PANSA (@PANSA_PL) November 12, 2026 The dispute stems from Poland’s refusal in 2022 to accept and pay for COVID-19 vaccine doses ordered from Pfizer under European Union procurement agreements. In April 2022, the then health minister, Adam Niedzielski, invoked a force majeure clause following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 Poland, which by then had already sold or donated some of its surplus vaccines, argued the mass influx of Ukrainian refugees strained its public finances, while its cases of Covid infections had dropped. Romania later made a similar decision to not comply with the contract. In 2023, Pfizer sued both countries in Belgium, the country where the contracts were signed. Over the course of the case, Poland also argued that Pfizer had potentially abused its market position. A Belgian court has ordered Poland to pay US pharmaceutical giant Pfizer around €1.3 billion for Covid vaccines ordered by the European Commission on behalf of member states during the pandemic but which the Polish government later refused to receive https://t.co/1ZtPgl8Y3o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 But in April, a Belgian court rejected those arguments and ruled in Pfizer’s favour, ordering Poland to accept approximately 64 million vaccine doses and pay more than 5.6 billion zloty, plus interest and legal costs. Poland appealed against the judgment in August 2026. The health ministry said on Thursday it would not disclose details of its legal arguments or planned procedural steps while the proceedings remain ongoing. World.title: Temporary no longer: Ukrainian refugees in Poland confront the long term
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Leo Greenberg Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back. “We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said. Zelensky: We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026 Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return. A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority. This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty. A new reality sets in When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year. When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.” Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.” In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023 For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland. The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens. So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes. Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022 For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad. Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers. Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026. “Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited. Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return. Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May. ⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin. "This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0 — The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025 So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.” Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools. Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return. Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration. However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs. Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.” So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back. From welcome to wariness in Poland Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland. Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees. The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits. Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced. Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added. Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment. She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps. Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay. Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners. Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026 This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency. Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status. Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.” The citizenship question At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections. An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier. In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry. The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values. Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day. Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply. Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”. Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.” Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for. At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that. For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says. For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”. At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland dismisses Russia’s claim of breaking up Polish spy network as “disinformation”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”. On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland. It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”. The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia. The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency. In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day. He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”. Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB. However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said. Jako rzecznik ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych nie komentuję materiałów zamieszczanych w sieci przez rosyjskie służby. 🛑 W dniu Narodowego Święta Niepodległości traktuję je szczególnie jako kolejną prowokację i dezinformację. 🛑 Apeluję o niepowielanie wrogiej narracji i… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) November 11, 2026 Polish fact-checking and investigative journalism service OKO.press also raised doubts about the material shared by Russia. It notes that the alleged Polish-language phone messages released by the FSB have unnatural wording and appear to have been translated from Russian. It also points out that the footage showing the alleged detentions appears to have been recorded much earlier, judging by the green folliage on trees. This assessment was echoed by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the security services from 2016 to 2022. He said that “fabricated propaganda materials” were clearly “prepared in advance” and “fit the Russian security services’ ongoing campaign against Poland”. “It should be assumed that, in its operation against Poland, Moscow will resort to fabricated evidence, and today’s FSB statement will be used to legitimise earlier accusations against Poland of preparing an attack on Kaliningrad,” he added. #InfoAlert. Kolejna rosyjska prowokacja. FSB twierdzi, że rozbiła polską siatkę szpiegowską pracującą w Obwodzie Królewieckim. Analiza komunikacji rosyjskiej wskazuje, że mamy do czynienia z zaplanowaną sekwencją działań informacyjnych. Wpisuje się ona w stałe oddziaływanie… pic.twitter.com/s6bTV9pIK8 — Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) November 11, 2026 The FSB’s announcement came a week after Poland announced that it had detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components, which were smuggled over the border into Kaliningrad. Poland also sent additional security personnel to its regions along the Russian border this month following intelligence reports suggesting a planned act of sabotage or other provocation there. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later claimed that “individuals with flashlights” had been spotted at the border but “we very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and managed to prevent a provocation”. Poland recently launched a special operation along the Russian border after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. For more, see our report from yesterday:https://t.co/RVaXb6SQJI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 Poland has seen a sharp rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Moscow in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates on its territory, prompting Russia to do the same with Polish consulates in a tit-for-tat move. World.title: Poland indicts Ukrainian man for assisting in rail sabotage on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have filed an indictment against a Ukrainian man accused of working on behalf of Russian intelligence and assisting in last year’s sabotage of a rail line in Poland. The accused, who can be named only as Volodymyr B. under Polish privacy law and is pictured above, will stand trial for espionage, sabotage and causing the risk of a major transport accident. He could face up to life in prison if convicted. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego w Warszawie akt oskarżenia przeciwko Volodymyrowi B. w śledztwie dotyczącym aktów dywersji na torach kolejowych, do których doszło jesienią 2025 r. w miejscowości Mika i Gołąb. ⬇️https://t.co/N2vK7thpKe — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In November last year, the Polish authorities discovered acts of sabotage on two sections of a rail line running between Warsaw and the eastern Polish city of Lublin. In one case, a device containing military-grade C4 explosive was detonated in an apparent attempt to derail a freight train near the village of Mika. However, it caused only minor damage to the floor of the train. The following day, in the nearby town of Puławy, a passenger train carrying 475 people had to brake suddenly due to damage to the line. However, no one was injured. Soon after, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that the perpetrators had been identified as two Ukrainian citizens working on behalf of Russia. They had entered Poland from Belarus and then fled back across the border immediately after the incident. In December, Interpol issued red notices for the men, identified as Yevhenii Ivanov and Oleksandr Kononov. However, the pair remain at large. Meanwhile, a third Ukrainian man, Volodymyr B., was detained in Poland a few days after the sabotage and was charged with assisting in carrying out the attack. In their statement regarding the indictment of Volodymyr B., published on Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office says that he assisted Yevhenii Ivanov in conducting reconnaissance of the area, selecting a place to plant the explosives and installing recording devices and metal elements on the rails. “These actions created an imminent threat of a disaster, threatening the lives and health of many people and significant property damage,” wrote prosecutors. “Their goal was to seriously intimidate many people and influence public opinion.” They also say that Volodymyr B. was “participating in the activities of Russian intelligence”. The most serious charge he faces is for acts of sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of ten years, ranging up to life. Interpol has published red notices for two men that Poland says were responsible for carrying out the sabotage of a rail line last month on behalf of Russia The pair immediately fled to Belarus after the incident and their current location is unknown https://t.co/RnahHDQkC8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 18, 2025 Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Such actions have often been carried out by Ukrainians and Belarusians. Last month, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. This week, Poland announced that it had detained and charged two Ukrainians accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. World.title: Polish deputy foreign minister charged over alleged misappropriation of millions of zloty
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish deputy foreign minister has been charged with misappropriating millions of zloty entrusted to him and taking steps to prevent creditors from recovering money owed to them. Prosecutors say that Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski used the money for personal expenses and to buy three apartments in Warsaw. His wife has also been charged in the case. Both of them deny the allegations, and Bartoszewski says he “will defend the truth and my good name”. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela. Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister. From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister. From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki. In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children. “As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said. In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending. Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025 Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife. Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October. At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further. Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026 On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years. A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years. Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt. Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi — Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026 In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP). “I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added. “I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.” Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”. World.title: Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier. Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks. This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”. The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.” On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared. Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji! W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły! 🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx — Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026 The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right. Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march. A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000. That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One. The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government. “It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.” Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”. “Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.” Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu. Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0 — Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026 However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”. While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea. In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident. Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car. Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland. “All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.” Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition. The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister. World.title: Poland and US sign statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries. “Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”. The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared. Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0 — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory. After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December. Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence. “Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending. Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems. “You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war. Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell. American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers. He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers. “We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.” The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries. W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych. Chcemy, by więcej uzbrojenia powstawało i było naprawiane w Polsce. To nowe… pic.twitter.com/j24E2xON66 — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 10, 2026 Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself. In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”. World.title: Bohemian Burlesque Festival Returns to Prague for Its 10th Anniversary
World.content:
The Bohemian Burlesque Festival returns for its 10th anniversary, bringing four nights of international performances and a daytime market to Ostrava (already sold out), Brno, and Prague.

The festival, the largest burlesque event in the Czech Republic, will welcome a record 100 performers from 20 countries for this year’s edition. The programme combines classic burlesque, cabaret, contemporary performances, and vintage glamour.



This year’s theme is French-inspired, with three of the festival’s guest performers and headliners coming from France. Artists from Finland, Lithuania, and Estonia will also join performers from across Europe and beyond, alongside Czech talent.

Two major international names lead the programme. Medianoche, originally from New York and raised in Spain, is one of the industry’s best-known performers and won the prestigious Miss Exotic World title in 2017. Representing France, Chanelle de Mai is an acclaimed performer and costume designer known for her elaborate acts and precise choreography.

They will be joined by French special guests Vicomte Harbourg and drag performer Chantaaaal.

Prague will host three festival events over two days, all taking place at Hotel Belvedere in Prague 7.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bohemian Burlesque Festival (@bohemianburlesquefestival)

The programme opens on Friday, November 20, with Bohemian Cabaret Prague, a gala evening featuring international headliners, professional performers, and local artists. The show starts at 20:00, with doors opening at 19:15.

On Saturday, November 21, the festival continues with the Bohemian Market, running from 12:00 to 18:00. Visitors can browse vintage clothing, accessories, jewellery, lingerie, and burlesque-inspired fashion.

It is also a great opportunity to enjoy plenty of burlesque at an affordable price: tickets cost just CZK 350, making it a good alternative for those who miss out on the evening shows.

The programme also includes fashion shows, retro hair and makeup services, photo sessions, discussions about body image, interviews with festival guests, and performances by 24 emerging burlesque artists. A pin-up competition, live singer, and magician are also planned.

The weekend concludes with Bohemian Queen Night, the festival’s closing gala, starting at 20:30. Twelve performers from around the world will compete for the titles of Bohemian Queen and Bohemian Princess, as well as the Best Costume Award.

A new feature for 2026 will give audience members the opportunity to vote for their favourite performer in an Audience Choice Award. Festival headliners and special guests will serve as judges and perform during the second half of the evening.

Both evening shows will feature a raffle and a Best Dressed Audience competition, with prizes for visitors who arrive in their finest outfits.
