World.title: Prague Adds Special Trams and More Metro Services for Letná Demonstration
World.content:
Prague is preparing for a large demonstration at Letná on Sunday, November 15, with additional public transport services planned to accommodate the expected crowds.

The city will increase the frequency of trains on all three metro lines and introduce two temporary tram routes, numbered 40 and 44, to help transport participants to and from the demonstration.



Organized by the Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek) movement, the event is expected to attract thousands of people from across the Czech Republic. Organizers are anticipating a record turnout.

The additional tram services are intended to ease pressure on regular routes, particularly around Letná and neighbouring districts.

Metro services will run more frequently between 11:30 a.m. and 7 p.m. on Sunday.

Tram 40 will operate from approximately noon until 7 p.m., running every five minutes. It will connect Letná with all three metro lines, travelling from Palmovka through Florenc, Vltavská, Hradčanská and Dejvická before terminating at Červený Vrch.

Tram 44 will also run at five-minute intervals, but only from noon until approximately 3 p.m. Starting at Špejchar, the route will pass through Strossmayerovo náměstí and Výstaviště towards Nádraží Holešovice. It will then continue around Holešovická tržnice, pass Vltavská and return to Letná.

The second route is intended primarily for passengers arriving on Metro Line C.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Milion chvilek pro demokracii (@milionchvilek)

Despite the additional services, transport authorities warn that overcrowding and delays are likely, particularly at Hradčanská, Vltavská and Nádraží Holešovice stations and on connecting tram routes.

According to Prague 7 authorities, the busiest periods are expected shortly before the demonstration starts and immediately after it ends. The greatest pressure on public transport is anticipated before 2 p.m. and at around 4 p.m.

Tram Disruptions Elsewhere in Prague

Passengers should also expect changes to regular tram services in central Prague.

From approximately 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., trams will be temporarily suspended in the area between Palackého náměstí, Národní divadlo, Jiráskovo náměstí and Myslíkova Street.

Tram lines 5 and 17 will be diverted via Karlovo náměstí during this period.

Road Restrictions and Changes to Letná Ice Rink

Drivers heading towards Letná should also expect traffic restrictions and temporary road closures in the surrounding area. The city recommends avoiding car travel to the demonstration and allowing extra time for journeys.

World.title: James Blunt Announces Prague Concert as Part of European Tour
World.content:
British singer-songwriter James Blunt will return to Prague on March 5, 2027, for a concert at O2 universum.

The performance is part of his Airplane Mode Tour, which will see him travel across Europe in support of his upcoming album.

Best known for international hits including “You’re Beautiful,” “Goodbye My Lover” and “Wisemen,” Blunt last performed in Prague three years ago, when he played at Forum Karlín.



His upcoming show will combine songs from his new record with the tracks that established his international career.

Blunt rose to international fame with his debut album, Back to Bedlam, released in 2004 after he left the British Army. Before pursuing music, he had attended the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst and served in Kosovo.

The debut album became a major commercial success, featuring three of his best-known songs: “You’re Beautiful,” “Goodbye My Lover” and “Wisemen.” It went on to rank among the 20 best-selling albums in UK history and earned Blunt several major industry honours, including Brit Awards and MTV Europe Music Awards, as well as five Grammy nominations.

His second album, All the Lost Souls, followed in 2007 and included “1973,” which topped music charts in more than 20 countries.

Titled Airplane Mode, the new album is scheduled for release on November 6, 2026, through Atlantic Records. The 12-track record has been introduced by the single “Tastes Like Summer,” followed by “Weight of It All,” a song addressing the pressures of modern life.

The European tour will run through February, March and April 2027, with Prague among its scheduled stops.

Tickets for the March 5 concert are available through Ticketportal and Ticketmaster.

The concert is organised by Charmenko Czechia.

World.title: What to Know About Czechoslovakia’s Velvet Revolution
World.content:
On Nov. 17, 1989, student protesters filled the streets of Prague. It was eight days after the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the same tide of freedom that had swept Berlin seemed to have come to the Czech capital.

Police tried to beat back the demonstrators, hoping to tamp down the demand for freedom, but the people seemed to have grown immune to the brutality of the regime; the show of force only galvanized the resistance.

The students were joined in the coming days by Czechoslovak citizens of all ages. By Nov. 20, a half-million Czechs and Slovaks filled Prague’s streets and took over Wenceslas Square. The Communists were forced out. By the end of 1989, Czechoslovakia was on its way to having an elected President for the first time since 1948.

The events of those world-changing days would come to be known as the Velvet Revolution. But, while the Velvet Revolution was over relatively quickly, it had been decades in the making.

The Failed “Prague Spring”

In January of 1968, the USSR gave the leadership of Czechoslovakia to someone new: Alexander Dubček. Dubček had fought against German forces during WWII, joining the communist party in his country after the end of the war. He rose through the ranks, serving in the parliament and general assembly as part of a new generation of Slovak communists.

Compared to his successor, the Stalinist Antonin Novotny, Dubček was liberal. Within months, he implemented governmental and economic reforms and allowed citizens increased freedom of speech, including freedom of the press. The people of Czechoslovakia embraced the changes and the period of Dubček’s liberalism became known as Prague Spring.

Like the spring, it was fleeting. By August of 1968 the Soviet Union had enough. A more liberal Czechoslovakia was a threat to its regional power and could signal weakness on the world stage.

Over half a million Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia; Soviet tanks rolled through the narrow streets of Prague, crushing mostly student-led protests. Soviet loyalist Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek and returned the country to an authoritarian communist regime — but something had changed.

Jan Palach

The following January, Jan Palach, a Charles University student in Prague, entered a suicide pact with several fellow students. They were determined to protest the Soviet invasion and combat growing despondency among citizens after the takeover.

On Jan. 16, 1969, Palach climbed the steps of the National Museum near the bustling train station on the edge of Wenceslas Square. There he doused himself with gasoline and lit a match.

In his suicide note, he signed his name as “Torch Number 1” — suggesting more self-immolation and protests to come. (Jan Zajic became “Torch Number 2”; though he couldn’t be directly linked to the original pact, Zajic participated in group hunger-strike after Palach’s death and was part of the resistance.) Palach lived for three days in a hospital after sustaining burns to 85% of his body. Amazingly, he still managed to give interviews. He spoke softly, his voice rough and halting.

When asked why he had done what he did, Palach replied that he wanted to voice opposition to the Soviet invasion and “make people wake up.” He died three days later.

The Velvet Revolution

In the decades that followed, Communist rule in Czechoslovakia continued, and the resistance, although forced underground, continued to grow too. By 1989, intermittent uprisings throughout Warsaw Pact countries, the increasing militarism of Soviet governments across the region and slowing economic growth within the Eastern Bloc set the stage for revolution.

In neighboring Poland, Lech Walesa, Anna Walentynowicz and workers of Lenin Shipyards in the Polish city of Gdańsk founded the Polish trade union Solidarność — Solidarity. Strikes and non-violent civil disobedience tactics employed by Solidarity paralyzed Baltic seaports.

In January 1989, 20 years after Jan Palach’s death, the clandestine resistance movement formed after the Soviets crushed the promise of Prague Spring planned what they dubbed “Palach Week.”

For the first time since Palach’s self-immolation, they would go to the place where he fell in Wenceslas Square for as public memorial and protest against the ongoing Soviet occupation. Nearly 5,000 people came out the first evening of that week — an unthinkable number since the Prague Spring. It set the stage for what became known as the Velvet Revolution.

That autumn, after a simmering year of protests and the fall of the Berlin Wall, students organized another protest. They chose Nov. 17, the 50-year anniversary of the killings of Prague students by invading Nazi troops.

The English phrase “Velvet Revolution,” which the European Parliament Directorate-General for Translation credits to Czech dissident Rita Klímová, signifies the idea that the revolution was brought about without violence — even though the larger process was not always peaceful. Soldiers beat protesters, used water cannons on the crowd and made numerous arrests.

A writer named Vaclav Havel was arrested that night. In 1968, Havel had been in Liberec, a small town outside the capital, when Soviet tanks rolled into his native Prague.

Before the regime was able to shut down Liberec’s radio station, Havel broadcast several speeches advising fellow citizens to engage peacefully but be prepared to defend themselves, encouraging them to remain loyal to the liberal ideals of the Spring and to resist and persist. So by the time the protests began in 1989 he was a well-known dissident turned leader of a coalition of opposition movements, the Civic Forum.

But when the government-controlled newspaper Rudé Právo tried to paint the jailed Havel as a symbol of a supposedly failed freedom movement, it backfired tremendously. By Nov. 28, after constant protests and workers’ strikes, the Communists announced they would cede power, and the parliament then removed the one-party provision from the constitution.

In December, Havel’s name was put forward as the Forum’s candidate for interim president. Two months later, in February 1990, in a speech to a joint session of the U.S. congress, Havel expressed his own disbelief that he was even nominated — yet by that point, he stood before the body as President of Czechoslovakia all the same.

In 1990, the country’s first open and free national elections were held. Havel retained his seat until the Velvet Divorce — the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia into the Czech and Slovak Republics in 1992 — at which point he stepped down. He then served as President of the Czech Republic from 1993-2003.

World.title: Expat Next Door: How One Entrepreneur Is Making Flower Delivery in Prague Easier
World.content:
Originally from Ukraine, Valentyn moved to the Czech Republic in 2015, worked his way into the IT industry and eventually launched Pinflower, a platform connecting customers with the best local florists in Prague.

His journey to becoming a tech entrepreneur didn’t start in an office. After arriving in the Czech Republic in 2015, Valentyn initially settled in Brno, where he worked night shifts in a bakery and washed cars. In 2017, he entered the IT industry through technical support before moving into software engineering.



The idea for Pinflower came from a frustrating experience. While looking for a bouquet for a friend’s birthday, he couldn’t find anything suitable at his usual flower shop. Delivery would take hours, so he ended up driving across Prague himself.

He wondered why there wasn’t a simple way to see which nearby florists had bouquets available, compare prices and arrange pickup or delivery.

Rather than wait for someone else to solve the problem, he built the platform himself, working on it in his spare time. Pinflower launched in July 2026.

Local florists, one platform

Pinflower brings together local flower studios in Prague, allowing customers to compare bouquets, prices and delivery options in one place. The platform makes it easier to find flower delivery in Prague without having to browse individual shop websites.

Unlike anonymous delivery services, every arrangement comes from a named local florist. Customers can choose a specific bouquet or select the Florist’s Style option, allowing the florist to create something inspired by a reference image.

The platform is available in English, Czech, Ukrainian and Russian, making it easier for foreigners to order without having to call a shop or speak Czech. Customers can also arrange deliveries to Prague from abroad and pay by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay.

Another key feature is real-time delivery availability. The system considers each florist’s opening hours, bouquet preparation time and delivery area before showing customers when an order can arrive. One of Pinflower’s partner studios also offers 24/7 flower delivery in Prague, subject to availability.

Ordering flowers through ChatGPT

Since October, Pinflower has also allowed customers to arrange orders through ChatGPT and Claude.

Instead of browsing the website, customers can describe what they need, specify their budget and provide a delivery address. The AI assistant checks available bouquets, prices and delivery times before preparing the order. Customers then receive a secure payment link.

The founder sees this as part of a broader shift in online shopping, where people will increasingly start with a conversation rather than a search engine.

What’s next?

For now, the priority is expanding Pinflower’s network of Prague florists, with other Czech cities potentially coming later.

But the long-term ambition goes beyond flowers. The founder envisions bringing together local bakeries, gift makers and other small businesses, allowing customers to organise celebrations and surprises through a single platform.

The idea is to make it easier to support local businesses while using technology to simplify everyday tasks.

World.title: Prague to Mark 37 Years Since Velvet Revolution With 160 Events
World.content:
Prague will mark the 37th anniversary of the Velvet Revolution on November 17 with more than 160 events taking place along Národní Street as part of this year’s Korzo Národní celebrations.

Organised by the association Díky, že můžem, the annual event will bring together concerts, theatre performances, public discussions, exhibitions and activities exploring democracy and freedom.



This year’s programme carries the motto “Let’s Not Stand on the Sidelines. Democracy Relies on Each of Us.” The organisers say the message reflects growing concerns about declining trust in society and the challenges facing democratic institutions.

One of the central moments of the celebrations will take place at 17:11, when the traditional song Modlitba pro Martu (A Prayer for Marta) will be performed from the balcony of the Metro Palace.

This year, the performance will form the finale of a theatrical production titled DŮM VŠECH (House for All), which begins at 17:00. Visitors unable to gather directly beneath the balcony will be able to watch the performance on large screens along Národní Street or through a live broadcast.

The day’s programme will begin earlier, with the popular Velvet Brunch, a charity event held directly on the street between 10:00 and 13:00. At 13:00, members of the Czech Radio Children’s Choir will perform the national anthem.

Other events include live podcasts, musical performances and discussions on social issues. Among the scheduled speakers and performers are Markéta Foukalová, Martin Brunner, Václav Kopta and Vietnamese community representative Quang Luong.

Havel, the Vietnamese community and Věra Čáslavská

Several parts of this year’s celebrations will focus on important anniversaries.

The programme will commemorate the 90th anniversary of the birth of Václav Havel, the playwright and former Czech president.

His legacy will be explored through the traditional Václav Havel’s Living Room, titled “For Vašek”, at Platýz Palace. Actors including Vojtěch Vondráček and Taťjana Medvecká will read texts dedicated to Havel.

Another anniversary concerns the Vietnamese community, which marks 70 years in the Czech Republic. The programme will include Lost in Translation, a discussion bringing together three generations of Vietnamese residents to examine questions of identity, belonging and life between cultures.

The celebrations will also remember gymnast Věra Čáslavská, ten years after her death. Her life and the relationship between sport and politics will be examined through a special lecture aboard the Educational Tram and a live recording of the Outsider podcast.

World.title: FlixBus Launches Direct Route Between Prague Florenc and Airport
World.content:
FlixBus will introduce a direct bus connection between Prague’s Florenc Central Bus Station and Václav Havel Airport on November 12.

The new service will operate 13 times a day in each direction, with the journey taking approximately 30 minutes.

The first bus will leave Florenc at 3:40 a.m., while the last departure is scheduled for 10:40 p.m. From the airport, services will run between 4:15 a.m. and 11:15 p.m.



Ticket prices will depend on demand and departure times. According to the FlixBus website, the usual fare is around CZK 79, including the booking fee. The cheapest tickets start at CZK 69, while some departures cost up to CZK 89.

The company expects the route to attract business travellers in particular. Passengers will have access to Wi-Fi and power outlets on board.

BusAir joins the competition

FlixBus is not the only company expanding its airport connections. A separate private service, operating under the name BusAir, began running between Prague’s city centre and the airport in late October.

Operated by UBUS, the service offers eight departures a day in each direction, with buses running every two hours. A ticket costs CZK 125 and remains valid for 24 hours.

Due to renovation work on the ceiling at Prague Main Railway Station and traffic restrictions on the city’s main arterial road, BusAir currently departs from Opletalova Street, close to the station. On the way to the airport, it also stops at Hradčanská metro station on Line A.

Both new services are entering a market where the main competitor is the Airport Express, operated by Prague Public Transit Company (DPP).

The Airport Express runs more frequently than the private alternatives, with departures every 20 to 30 minutes during the day and hourly services overnight. It is also currently the only direct bus connection between the city centre and airport operating throughout the night.

Standard Prague public transport tickets are not valid on the service. A single adult ticket costs CZK 200, although passengers can get a lower fare when purchasing it together with a train ticket.

World.title: Říčany Named Czech Republic’s Best Place to Live for Ninth Year
World.content:
Říčany has been named the best municipality in the Czech Republic for quality of life for the ninth consecutive year, retaining its position at the top of a nationwide ranking ahead of Prague.

The Central Bohemian town, located southeast of the capital, again led the Quality of Life Index compiled by the Obce v datech project. The ranking assesses 206 Czech municipalities with extended administrative powers.

At the other end of the table, Orlová in the Karviná District ranked last, while nearby Karviná finished second from bottom.



The geographical divide remains clear: the 14 highest-ranked municipalities are all located within 50 kilometres of Prague or Brno, while many of those at the bottom are found in former industrial and border regions, particularly in the Moravian-Silesian and Ústí nad Labem regions.

There have nevertheless been signs of improvement in parts of the Moravian-Silesian Region. Over the past eight years, Odry, Kopřivnice and Hlučín have each climbed by around 40 places in the ranking.

The picture is less positive in the Ústí nad Labem Region, where only six of the region’s 16 assessed municipalities have improved their position since 2018. Roudnice nad Labem was the only municipality in the region to record a substantial rise.

Pohořelice Makes the Biggest Leap

Pohořelice, in the Brno-Country District, has recorded one of the most striking improvements since the index was introduced in 2018. The town has climbed from 117th place to fifth this year.

Nepomuk, in the Plzeň Region, has made an equally large jump of 112 places and now ranks 24th. Kuřim has moved up 65 positions to 15th, while Mnichovo Hradiště has risen 46 places to 18th.

According to Jan Havránek of AQE Advisors, which developed the project, municipalities do not need to perform at the top in every category to improve their overall ranking.

For around half of the 30 municipalities that have improved the most, the stronger results were linked to a younger population, population growth and, in many cases, longer life expectancy.

The Quality of Life Index evaluates municipalities across several broad areas, including health and the environment, material security and education, and relationships and public services.

World.title: Austrian police shoot 38-year-old Hungarian man after alleged attack on officers
World.content:
A 38-year-old Hungarian man was shot by police in Lower Austria on Thursday morning after allegedly attacking officers and a railway emergency coordinator. He was taken to hospital and is not in a life-threatening condition.

The incident took place near the Westbahn railway line in Michelhausen, in the Tulln district, shortly before 10.30am, according to Austrian broadcaster ORF and Hungarian news outlet Telex.

Police were alerted after the driver of a freight train spotted a man near the tracks who appeared to be confused. He reported the situation to the railway company, whose employee subsequently called the emergency services and requested police assistance.

According to the Lower Austrian police, the 38-year-old Hungarian citizen behaved extremely aggressively towards the officers who arrived at the scene and the railway company’s emergency coordinator. He allegedly attacked them, prompting the officers to use pepper spray.

However, the man reportedly launched another attack, after which one of the police officers fired a shot, injuring him.

If you missed it: Hungarian fugitive on Europol’s most wanted list arrested in Graz after years on the run

Man taken to hospital, investigation launched

The injured man received emergency medical treatment at the scene before being transported to the University Hospital in Tulln. He was not in a life-threatening condition, according to the information available at the time of reporting.

The circumstances of the shooting are now being investigated by Austria’s Investigation and Complaints Office for Allegations of Abuse (EBM), together with staff from the Lower Austrian State Criminal Police Office. The latter’s teams responsible for investigating offences against life and physical integrity, as well as crime scene investigations, have also taken over the case.

No further details about the shooting had been made public at the time of the initial reports.

Westbahn line closed for several hours

The incident also caused significant disruption to rail services. The affected section of the new Westbahn line was closed for several hours to allow investigators to examine the scene and collect evidence.

According to Austrian Federal Railways (ÖBB), services on the line resumed shortly after 3pm.

World.title: Rosatom chief speaks out about Hungary’s Paks II nuclear power plant project
World.content:
The head of Russia’s state-owned nuclear energy company Rosatom has expressed confidence that Hungary’s Paks II nuclear power plant project will be completed, saying the company remains committed to the investment, primarily in Hungary’s interests.

Speaking to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev said the company believed the project would be realised despite the challenges surrounding it.

Rosatom has no plans to drop Paks II

Likhachev made the remarks at the World Atomic Days (WAD) event, held alongside the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

He stressed that Rosatom had never planned to remove the Paks II investment from its list of top-priority projects and had no intention of doing so in the future.

The Russian company’s chief executive said he was confident that the project would be completed in cooperation with the Hungarian government and Hungarian experts. He argued that Hungary needed the new nuclear power plant to secure its energy supply, while the investment would also contribute to the development of the country’s nuclear energy sector.

Likhachev described the cooperation between the two countries as exemplary, noting that it had begun decades ago with the construction of the existing Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

He added that Paks II was progressing according to a timetable agreed with the Hungarian client and approved last year. The project is being overseen by both the Hungarian and Russian governments.

Rosatom ready to provide financial and technical information

Looking ahead, Likhachev said that the financial plan for next year would need to be drawn up first, followed by a schedule for the construction work.

“We are fully prepared to complete the project with our Hungarian partners within the agreed deadline. We are aware that the Hungarian government is conducting an audit of the project, and we respect and understand this,” he told MTI.

He emphasised that Rosatom was ready to provide its Hungarian partners with all the necessary financial and technical information.

The CEO also pointed out that the first concrete had already been poured into the foundation of Unit 5. Construction work on both Units 5 and 6 was continuing without interruption, he said.

“We can implement the project at whatever pace the Hungarian client allows us to,” Likhachev added.

World Atomic Days brings together 700 participants from 50 countries

The international World Atomic Days business event took place in Antalya on 12–13 November, alongside COP31, which is being held in the Turkish city from 9 to 20 November.

World.title: Heavy rainfall brings Hungary November’s average in a single day
World.content:
Large parts of Hungary received exceptionally heavy rainfall on Thursday, with several weather stations recording the equivalent of the country’s entire average November precipitation in just 24 hours. The downpours also brought a new national daily precipitation record.

Record amount of rain reached Hungary

According to Hungary’s national meteorological service, HungaroMet, more than 30 millimetres of downpour fell across extensive areas, while some locations in the north recorded over 50 millimetres. The average monthly precipitation for November is 48.6mm, meaning that several measuring stations reached or exceeded this amount in a single day.

Kékestető recorded 59.9mm in the 24-hour period, while both the Gerecse hills and Balassagyarmat received 55.9mm, according to data shared by HungaroMet.

A month of precipitation in one day

The heaviest recorded downpour was in Tardos, in Komárom-Esztergom County, where 66mm fell on Thursday, 12 November. This set a new national daily precipitation record, surpassing the previous high of 61mm, measured in Letenye in 1997.

HungaroMet said several weather systems arriving from the west brought successive waves of rain to the Carpathian Basin. Rain initially affected mainly southern areas before the extensive precipitation zone associated with Cyclone Charles moved across the country, delivering widespread and substantial rainfall.

World.title: Budapest metro line to undergo maintenance this weekend
World.content:
Budapest’s M2 metro line will operate on a shortened route this weekend due to scheduled track maintenance, with replacement buses running between Deák Ferenc Square and Déli Railway Station.

M2 metro line to undergo maintenance

According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), the changes will begin at 10 PM on Friday, 13 November, and remain in effect throughout Saturday and Sunday, 14–15 November. During this period, metro trains will run only between Örs vezér Square and Deák Ferenc Square.

Passengers travelling between Deák Ferenc Square and Déli Railway Station will be able to use replacement buses marked M2. The buses will cross the Margaret Bridge and also serve Kossuth Lajos Square and Batthyány Square.

Alternative routes for passengers

At Kossuth Lajos Square, passengers heading towards Déli Railway Station should board in Alkotmány Street, while those travelling towards Deák Ferenc Square should use the stop on Bajcsy-Zsilinszky Road. At Batthyány Square, buses towards Déli Railway Station will stop in Csalogány Street, near the junction with Fő Street. Replacement buses heading towards Deák Ferenc Square will stop in front of the church.

To reduce disruption between Buda and Pest, the 4–6 tram service will run more frequently throughout the weekend. The BKK recommends that passengers travelling to Széll Kálmán Square use the 4–6 tram, changing at Blaha Lujza Square. Those coming from Hűvösvölgy or Óbuda and heading towards the city centre are also advised to take the tram.

Plan ahead with BudapestGO

World.title: Police fail to identify women who attacked blind man in Budapest shopping centre
World.content:
Police have suspended an investigation after two women allegedly tried to rob a blind man with a guide dog in a Budapest shopping centre, assaulting him when he resisted. The suspects have not been identified.

Two women attacked a blind man

The incident happened during the summer and was reported by RTL Híradó on Thursday, 12 November. The Baráthegyi Guide Dog School Foundation has now shared video footage of the attack to highlight the vulnerability of people with disabilities.

The victim, Dániel Klabacsek, is a young man with multiple disabilities, including visual impairment, autism and a mobility disability. He was accompanied by his guide dog, Vidra (meaning “otter”), when he encountered the two women at a busy shopping centre in Budapest.

According to his account, the women offered to help him find his way to the metro. He accepted, but instead of taking him there, they led him to the rooftop of the building. He later asked them to help give his dog some water.

One of the women sat him down on a bench and started talking to him before unclipping his waist bag. When he noticed, she reportedly claimed she only wanted to check how much money was inside, then returned it.

Klabacsek subsequently asked the women to escort him back into the building. The situation escalated in the lift, where one of them tried to take his bag again. When he resisted, the women allegedly forced him down and repeatedly banged his head against the lift wall.

According to the victim, one of the women also shouted: “Don’t resist us, you dog!”

Klabacsek said he was deeply affected by the experience and struggling to process what had happened. At one point, he shouted for help inside the shopping centre, but nobody came to his assistance.

Investigation suspended

Klabacsek eventually filed a police report on the advice of his guide dog trainers. The foundation said it released the footage to draw attention to the vulnerability of people with disabilities and the importance of protecting them.

Police told RTL that the investigation into suspected robbery was suspended in mid-October because officers had been unable to establish the identities of the alleged perpetrators. 24.hu also reported that the investigation had been suspended, giving late October as the date.

The two women have therefore not been identified, and no suspects have been brought to justice in connection with the incident.

World.title: Six Southeast Asian countries showcase their cultures at ASEAN Day in Pécs
World.content:
Six Southeast Asian countries presented their traditions, cuisine and cultural heritage at ASEAN Day 2026 in Pécs on 11 November. Organised by the Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest, fellow ASEAN embassies and the University of Pécs, the event aimed to strengthen cultural and diplomatic connections between Southeast Asia and Hungary.

Held at the university’s Faculty of Humanities and Law under the theme “Navigating Our Future Together”, the programme was aligned with the Philippines’ current chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The day-long event brought together six participating embassies: Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. Their representatives introduced visitors to their countries through cultural displays, traditional clothing, tourism information and food.

Southeast Asian cuisine and traditions take centre stage

The country’s exhibition booths opened at midday, offering visitors an opportunity to explore the diversity of Southeast Asia without leaving Pécs.

Food was an important part of the programme, with the participating embassies preparing authentic dishes and snacks for guests. Indonesian specialities included Indomie noodles, klepon (green sticky rice balls) and tahu isi (stuffed tofu). Visitors could also sample Lao stir-fried noodles and traditional Filipino pastries.

Photo: Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest Photo: Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest

The cultural displays and culinary offerings gave students and other attendees an opportunity to discover the participating countries’ traditions and everyday culture.

ASEAN diplomats discuss international relations with students

Beyond the cultural programme, ASEAN Day also included an academic roundtable discussion incorporated into an international relations course at the University of Pécs.

Heads of Mission from the participating ASEAN countries spoke with students about Southeast Asia’s position amid global changes in the 21st century and relations between ASEAN and the European Union.

The diplomats also shared personal experiences from their foreign service careers, offering practical advice to students interested in pursuing a future in diplomacy.

During the discussion, Indonesia’s ambassador emphasised that diplomacy extends far beyond official meetings and formal receptions, highlighting the importance of personal connections between people.

The ambassador also spoke about the adaptability and emotional resilience required in diplomatic careers, explaining that diplomats and their families often have to relocate every few years and adjust to entirely different cultural environments.

Photo: Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest

Traditional performances celebrate ASEAN diversity

The programme concluded with a series of traditional cultural performances featuring students and members of the participating communities.

One of the highlights was Indonesia’s energetic Poco-poco dance, performed by a nine-member troupe. Traditional dances from Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam also featured, showcasing the region’s diverse cultural heritage.

Photo: Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest

Through its combination of cultural exhibitions, culinary experiences, academic discussions and performances, ASEAN Day offered the university community an opportunity to learn more about Southeast Asia while strengthening connections between the region and Hungary.

World.title: Wizz Air to resume domestic flights in Eastern European country after 8-year break
World.content:
Wizz Air is set to resume domestic flights in Romania after an eight-year break, reintroducing a direct connection between Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca from December 2026. The low-cost airline plans to operate up to two flights a day on the route, offering another option for passengers travelling between Romania’s capital and its second-largest city.

According to Romanian news outlet Economedia, flights from Bucharest Otopeni to Cluj-Napoca are scheduled to restart on 18 December, with tickets already available from 199 Romanian lei. The route will operate up to 12 times a week.

From Monday to Friday, passengers will be able to choose between two daily flights, while one service will operate on Saturdays and Sundays. However, during the Christmas and New Year holiday period, between 18 December and 10 January, the twice-daily schedule will only be available on selected days.

Wizz Air becomes the third airline on the route

Wizz Air last operated domestic flights between Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca eight years ago. The route is currently served by Romania’s national carrier TAROM and HiSky, making Wizz Air the third airline to offer direct flights between the two cities.

The connection is one of the busiest domestic routes in Romania. Cluj International Airport recorded more than 366,000 passengers travelling between Cluj-Napoca and Bucharest in 2025. In the first ten months of 2026, the figure exceeded 300,000, accounting for around 10% of the airport’s total passenger traffic.

Wizz Air Group’s network director Samuel Ferrera said the airline had long helped connect Romania with the rest of Europe and that the new service would bring the country’s cities closer together.

Alin Tişe, president of the Cluj County Council, also welcomed the announcement, highlighting the importance of direct air links with the capital for economic development, attracting investment and supporting businesses.

Wizz Air’s growing Romanian network

Wizz Air is the leading airline in Romania, with a market share of more than 50%. It carried 14.5 million passengers on its Romanian routes in 2025, a 13% increase compared with the previous year.

During the 2026–2027 winter season, the airline offers more than 25 destinations from Cluj International Airport. Passengers can choose from around 40 scheduled destinations across approximately 15 countries in Europe and the Middle East.

The airline operates a fleet of 276 Airbus A320 and A321 aircraft.

World.title: EU, UK ‘Concerned’ as Kosovo Moves Against Hague Court’s Powers Again
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Protest in Pristina against the verdict convicting four high-profile Kosovo Liberation Army figures , October 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

The European Union and United Kingdom have warned Kosovo MPs to seek international advice as they review an amended law aimed at curbing the powers of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers on Friday.

The legislation was initiated by the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, after the Hague-based war crimes court convicted PDK ex-leader Hashim Thaci and three other wartime Kosovo Liberation Army officials who fought for liberation from Serbia’s oppression, sparking outrage among Kosovo Albanians.

The EU Office in Kosovo said that “the amendments raise serious concerns regarding Kosovo’s international obligations and compliance with basic rule of law principles, in particular judicial independence, the protection of victims and witnesses, the continuity of procedural rights, and effective accountability”.

In a statement on Facebook, the EU also said that the amendments “also raise concerns regarding their constitutionality”, and stressed “the need for prior consultations before any adoption, in line with Kosovo’s international obligations”.

The British Embassy in Pristina echoed these concerns, saying in a statement on Facebook that “we fear that the proposed amendments will do nothing to serve Kosovo’s essential interests and will undermine its relations with international partners and supporters”.

The British Embassy encouraged MPs to “take the time for further consultations internally and with the EU and other international allies to find a better solution”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court that is located in The Hague and staffed by internationals but is part of Kosovo’s judiciary. It was established in 2015 to try former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters, under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies.

The establishment of the Specialist Chambers was initiated in an exchange of letters between Kosovo’s President and the EU, making it an international agreement, and therefore the EU requires consultations for any changes in its legal framework.

MPs initially voted for the amended law in a rushed procedure on October 6, under pressure from protests that turned violent outside the parliament building and the need to push through the urgent last-minute election of Kosovo’s new president to avoid the continuation of a political crisis that had lasted almost two years.

The vote followed weeks of protests after the four former KLA leaders were convicted of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years respectively. An appeal is expected.

Given the uncertainty over whether the Hague court will indict anyone else, the effect of the proposed legislation is uncertain, however.

Kosovo MPs are also undecided on whether the bill in its current form is adequate.

On Thursday, at the Parliamentary Commission for Legislation, MP Vigan Qorrolli from ruling party Vetevendosje argued that a redraft is needed.

“Our position as the political majority is very clear; we believe that a new legislative initiative – drafted with care and through joint parliamentary participation – would be the most responsible way to address this issue,” Qorrolli said.

However, PDK MP Blerta Deliu-Kodra said that, following discussions with other political parties, “we have agreed to pass the bill, but there is no consensus on amending it. We must proceed with the bill as it stands, and subsequently, we will enter the amendment process.”

World.title: Eight Key Defendants in Istanbul Municipality Mass Trial Freed From Custody
World.content:
Eight defendants in the Istanbul Municipality trial walked free on Friday after a court ordered their release late on Thursday despite prosecutors demanding that all detained defendants remain behind bars.

Those freed included Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu’s lawyer, Mehmet Pehlivan, and Fatos Pinar Turker, manager of Istanbul Municipality’s media company. The decision brought relief in opposition circles, although Imamoglu and other defendants remain in prison.

“I am happy, of course, but also saddened. My brother and my friends are in prison. I want them to regain their freedom soon,” Pehlivan said on Friday after leaving prison.

Turker also focused on those who remained detained: “My only wish is to reunite with my daughters. My thoughts are with the other friends who remain imprisoned,” he said.

Mayor Imamoglu, who is also the main opposition presidential candidate for the next election, is one of the 46 defendants still in custody after the eight were released. A total of 436 people have been indicted in the case, accused of involvement in corruption. They insist that the charges are politically motivated and false.

During the latest hearing, Imamoglu again denied the prosecution’s claims and criticised its reliance on secret witnesses.

“This pile of rubbish built on a secret witness has collapsed. There is not a single tangible witness,” Imamoglu told the court, demanding his release.

Defence lawyers and opposition figures have challenged the use of secret witnesses in the case and demanded the release of those being held, pending trial.

Over the last few years, dozens of opposition mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terror charges.

Imamoglu was arrested on March 19, 2025. The prosecutor’s office is demanding a 2,352-year prison sentence for him. Imamoglu denies all the accusations.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have said the government is using the judiciary to crush its political rivals in what they call an unprecedented crackdown.

World.title: After the Protests: Bulgaria as a Cautionary Tale
World.content:
“The situation is not better, not worse. It’s just the same,” said Vesislava Tancheva, spokesperson for Bulgarians United for One Goal, the civic association behind the protest outside the Russian embassy and which also demonstrated against the previous government. It goes by the acronym BOETS, which in Bulgarian means ‘fighter’.

One thing is different, however – the scale of the protests.

In November and December 2025, tens of thousands of Bulgarians took to the streets across the country. The collapse of the ruling coalition led by the centre-right GERB party, the dominant party in Bulgaria since 2008, was portrayed in media reports as a success story.

Twenty-two-year-old law student Aleksandar Tanev saw firsthand how quickly Gen Z can mobilise. After a few demonstrations, he and some fellow students founded Students Against Mafia. They were soon inundated with requests from young people across the country to join.

A year on, however, Tanev says “it was not enough”.

“This corrupted management that ruled Bulgaria for more than 15 years is responsible for our cities, our roads, our education,” Tanev told BIRN. “They are guilty, but we vote for them. We need to understand our responsibility.”

He was echoed by Asen Lazarov, 27, another of the young people who took to the streets last year and co-founder of the NGO Active Politics, which aims to make politics more accessible to young people.

“Protests are a way to express your democratic participation, but they should not be the final step,” he said. “We should expect more from the politicians that we’ve elected.”

At a time when social movements in France, Albania, Spain or Serbia are challenging the political establishment, Bulgaria offers an instructive case study.

Governments change, system remains

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary Pick Fight with Berlin Over Ukraine Aid
World.content:
Hungarian PM Peter Magyar also criticised the idea of linking Ukraine’s financial support to the ongoing EU budget talks during a visit to Germany this week. “I would like to express, diplomatically and politely but nevertheless firmly, that I do not consider it a good idea to link the European budget, which is ultimately about the EU itself, in any way to another issue,” he said at a press conference with Merz in Berlin, where he otherwise heralded a new beginning in German-Hungarian bilateral relations after years of frosty ties under his predecessor Viktor Orban. Magyar also delivered the renowned State of Europe speech organised by the CDU-affiliated Konrad Adenauer Foundation. Speaking in German, he did not spare Europe’s governing elites, accusing them of having “lost contact with the people”, nor Brussels, which had detected the problems Europe was facing but had been unable to find solutions in recent years. The PM also warned against radical movements offering easy solutions to problems but, in fact, merely end up dividing and polarizing Europe and serving the interests of outside, often hostile forces. His view of the EU sees a gradual shift back towards nation states, which, in his words, know better what their societies need. He also pleaded for cheaper energy sources – though stopped short of saying they should be Russian – and for strengthening the continent’s industrial fabric and competitiveness, and stepping up the fight against illegal migration and climate change.

Fico’s mood this week was not helped by his government losing its parliamentary majority. The prime minister, who spent years demanding early elections whenever his opponents found themselves in the same position, now seems prepared to govern without one. The numbers became clear on Wednesday, when a controversial amendment to the Criminal Procedure Code received just 75 votes in the 150-seat parliament. Two MPs around the recently dismissed environment minister and lawmaker Tomas Taraba voted against it, while former coalition MP Jan Ferencak abstained. The amendment sought to restrict the use of testimony from cooperating defendants. Prosecutors and anti-corruption groups warned that it could undermine ongoing criminal cases, including the “Purgatory” police corruption trial, in which high-profile Smer politician and former police chief Tibor Gaspar is a defendant. Gaspar denies the legislation was intended to help him personally in his legal disputes. Things went wrong again that afternoon. A bill to abolish postal voting from abroad was derailed because none of its sponsors appeared to present it. Under parliamentary rules recently introduced by the coalition itself, the proposal could now be delayed for six months. Gaspar, who was chairing the session and is also among the bill’s sponsors, wants that interpretation reviewed. Fico once had little patience for governments relying on independent MPs. He accused former PM Mikulas Dzurinda of buying support and demanded early elections when Iveta Radicova and Eduard Heger struggled with their majorities. In 2006, he described opaque deals with independent MPs as one of the gravest attacks on parliamentary democracy since 1989. His own coalition now has 75 dependable MPs. Fico says he will negotiate with Taraba’s group and accepts that some bills may fail. Smer still insists this is not a minority government.

World.title: High Bank Fees Hamper Albania’s Crackdown on Cash
World.content:
In Tirana’s 9-Katëshet neighbourhood, people queue for ice cream at 100 lek a scoop.

Previously, the ice cream parlour only accepted cash, but the growing number of tourists among their clientele, many of whom don’t carry cash, has forced the business to start taking bank cards too.

If you pay by card, however, the price is 125 lek.

“We don’t make any extra profit from this,” the woman behind the counter said. “It’s the fee charged by the bank that provides us with the card payment service.”

World.title: On a Bosnian Mountainside, a Quiet Exodus Leaves Only the Elderly Behind
World.content:
As All Saints’ Day approached, Dubravka Jurisic sat down in her home in Straza and counted its residents.

She ran a finger down the handwritten pages where for years she has kept a record of births, deaths and who lives where in this village on the slopes of Mount Majevica, in the far northeast of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Reaching the end, she declared: “Seventy-one people currently live in the village.”

That’s less than half the number counted the last time Bosnia held a census, in 2013. Then, authorities registered 188 residents of Straza, part of Srebrenik municipality, though census totals can include Bosnian citizens who have lived abroad for years. In January 2017, Jurisic made her own count: 138.

Between 1991 and 2013, the population of Srebrenik municipality as a whole shrank from 40,882 to 39,678. The town of Srebrenik itself grew by roughly 1,400 residents. The villages, in other words, are emptying faster than the town.

Those who remain are, by and large, elderly. While Srebrenik municipality is majority Bosniak, Straza is Catholic Croat. Many of its residents hold Croatian passports, easing their departure since Croatia joined the European Union in 2013.

“Before the war, there were about 100 unmarried young men in the village,” said Jurisic, 52, referring to the 1992-95 war in Bosnia during the collapse of federal Yugoslavia. “Today we don’t have a single one.” According to Jurisic, the youngest resident is already a teenager.

World.title: Bulgarian economy grew by 0.6% in Q3 2026 – flash estimate
World.content:
Bulgaria’s economy grew by 0.6 per cent in the third quarter of the year, the National Statistical Institute (NSI) said in a flash estimate on November 13. In real terms, gross domestic product (GDP) in Bulgaria in July-September was 35.51 billion euro.

Year-on-year, the economic growth in the third quarter was 2.5 per cent. NSI is due to announce preliminary growth figures for the quarter on December 4.

The flash estimate’s seasonally-adjusted data showed domestic consumption increase by 1.4 per cent during the third quarter, and it was 6.3 per cent higher on an annual basis. Gross fixed capital formation shrank by 0.8 per cent in July-September, and was 0.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Exports fell by four per cent compared to the second quarter of the year, and were 5.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of last year, while imports shrank by 4.8 per cent on a quarterly basis and were down one per cent year-on-year.

The country recorded a trade surplus of 357.2 million euro in the third quarter, the equivalent of one per cent of GDP, NSI said.
