World.title: Rappler’s Bea Cupin joins FES New York’s 2026 Fall Academy program
World.content:
FALL ACADEMY 2026. Participants of FES NY's flagship programme pose for a photo outside the United Nations headquarters in New York.

The flagship program brings together a diverse group of young professions from all over the world

NEW YORK, USA — Rappler senior reporter Bea Cupin is one of 14 participants in Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (FES) New York’s 2026 Fall Academy.

The Fall Academy is FES New York’s flagship capacity-building program designed for “emerging political changemakers.” The week-long program saw participants in exchanges with United Nations diplomats, officials, advocates, and experts from think tanks and non-governmental organization.

This year’s edition ran from November 9 to 13, 2026.

Bea, who covers foreign affairs and defense, joined a diverse group of young professionals selected from FES’ global network. She is one of three participants from Asia in a cohort of 14.

The 2026 edition of the program is backdropped by challenges to and opportunities for the UN and multilateralism — increased great power competition, and middle powers’ try for a larger role in the international, and the deadline to elect a new Secretary-General. There are shifts, too, in the country that hosts the UN headquarters — just days prior to the start of the program, the United States saw a blue wave in its midterm elections.

It’s a UN that must find its role in a world in turmoil — the most wars and conflicts since World War II, the continuing threat of climate change, and calls for global governance on artificial intelligence, among others.

The Fall Academy is held annually. The last time Filipinos were elected for the program was in the 2022 edition, the first after a two-year hiatus due to COVID-19. – Rappler.com

World.title: 12 Christmas scams to watch out for
World.content:
Here are the commonly launched scams this holiday season

Christmas is right around the corner, and so are scams. The Philippine National Police (PNP) cautioned the public to be wary of their online transactions and the notifications they receive.

The PNP stressed the importance of verifying the legitimacy of sellers and the products and services they are offering. But scams aren’t just in online shopping anymore; they are in text messages, calls, and even in everyday physical stores.

Here are the usual scams and their tactics to look out for this Christmas.

Smishing

Smishing is phishing, but through text messages. Attackers use portable International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers to spoof the sender ID of legitimate banks, digital wallets, and government agencies.

This device acts like a fake cell tower, blasting messages to devices that connect to its signal. Since it can spoof the sender ID, the messages may appear in existing conversations.

These messages often include links that lead users to a spoofed website with a premise that you have a reward, a deadline to meet, or that your account is at risk of hacking. They ask for your information, passwords, and sometimes, one-time PINs (OTPs). Once given, attackers can make unauthorized transactions.

In 2022, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) released BSP Memorandum No. M-2022-015, requiring financial institutions not to include links in their messages and emails. Government agencies and financial institutions also send messages reminding consumers to never interact with links in text messages.

Vishing

Voice phishing, or vishing, uses calls or voice messages to imitate trusted entities and trick victims into revealing sensitive information, according to the BSP. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) says scammers introduce themselves as a bank, digital wallet, or government agency personnel.

They use the same tactics as other forms of phishing. They conduct “verification procedures” by asking for your information and OTP, which banks and government agencies consistently remind customers to never share.

Quishing

The rise of e-wallets and digital banking has allowed users to pay through QR codes. However, the BSP began warning the public about QR code fraud, or quishing.

In this case, fraudsters use QR codes to steal money and sensitive information from unsuspecting users. The code leads to fake login pages for e-wallets or banks, automatically downloads harmful content, or transfers money to unknown recipients.

QR codes usually don’t show website links. This makes it difficult for users to check.

The BSP warned users to be cautious and scan QR codes from verified stores. It added that most smartphones display the link before opening the webpage, which can help in verifying the site.

The institution also warned that attackers may alter or tamper with stores’ QR codes, placing a different code over legitimate ones.

Fake online sellers

This is the most frequent online scam. PNP chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., at a press briefing on November 9, said people should be skeptical of offers that seem too good to be true.

The PNP also reminds people to verify the seller’s credibility, keep communication on the same platform, and never share sensitive information.

Holiday travel, booking

Similar to fake online sellers, fraudsters offer unusually cheap tickets, booking deals, and vacation packages. This also leads users to phishing sites, allowing attackers to steal information and make unauthorized transactions.

Fake cash aid, gifts

Scammers pose as government agencies, such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), and spread links to surveys or registration to receive cash aid or gifts.

Though the department now offers digital payouts, it does not offer an open online application portal or form. Similarly, these fake portals are often phishing sites.

‘High-Yield’ investments

Investment frauds travel faster on social media because of Filipinos’ high usage. It depends on a “trust” mechanism and referrals, allowing users to transact or cooperate with people online with assurance.

Cryptocurrency is also used to lure victims with the promise of high yields.

In the 2026 book The Rogue Compound, these platforms use a “pump-and-dump” scheme where fraudsters artificially inflate the currency’s price and spread false hype to sell their shares. Once people invest, the price crashes, leaving investors with heavy losses.

Fake charity, donation drives

Fraudsters also use charities, donation drives, and generosity to steal money. This does not only happen during disasters. The CICC included this scam in its list last year.

The PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group (ACG) advises users to verify the organization before donating, check official announcements, verified social media pages, and official bank accounts, and be wary of personal accounts soliciting donations and vague or unverifiable details.

Impersonation

Also known as “hijack profile scam.” This happens when scammers gain unauthorized access to social media accounts and message contacts, asking for urgent financial assistance.

Oftentimes, attackers gain access through phishing, hacking, or social engineering techniques. Hackers can also get banking details from those accounts, leading to unauthorized transactions.

Fake raffles, giveaways

Apart from smishing scams telling users that they won in a giveaway, this scam is also prevalent on social media.

The PNP says the usual red flags of these messages is you’re told you won a prize you never registered, asks for sensitive information, pressures you to act immediately, or instructed to make a transaction of investment.

Online gambling

The Rogue Compound book also explained how online gambling lures users through its architecture. According to one source, it operates in a “God-mode panel,” where operators configure the game’s parameters to tailor the user’s experience.

It tricks players into thinking they’re playing fairly by fluctuating between two settings: Newbie Setting and Kill Mode. The Newbie Setting tricks new accounts and first-time depositors by designing early wins to boost their confidence. Kill Mode activates when the victim keeps depositing money despite their losses.

Task/job scams

The book also states that the scam only needs people who look for a quick source of income. “Receptionists” send messages at random on platforms such as Telegram, Viber, or WhatsApp.

It begins by instructing victims to do basic tasks for low-value commissions they can withdraw, which range from P100 to P200. They then instruct victims to deposit a small amount to gain access to an online platform that assigns them tasks. There, the cycle begins, helping establish trust.

Once the user makes bigger investments, the operators will demand more payment for various reasons before disappearing with the invested money. – Rappler.com

World.title: FAST FACTS: What is a Super El Niño, and what should we expect from it?
World.content:
This Super El Niño is expected to bring prolonged dry spells, drought, and water shortages until April 2027

Are you ready for the Super El Niño?

On November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) declared that a very strong El Niño was currently active in the tropical Pacific predicted to peak at the end of 2026 and persist until the first half of 2027.

Because of its intensity, foreign news outlets began referring to it as a “Godzilla El Niño” — referencing the giant mythical creature — or a Super El Niño.

Confused by terms used by government agencies, or curious about the difference between Super El Niño and a regular El Niño? Here are facts you need to know about this complex phenomenon.

First, what is El Niño?

El Niño is a climate event that happens when the Pacific Ocean’s surface temperature is warmer than normal.

This phenomenon occurs as the trade winds across the Pacific weaken or sometimes reverse. These winds typically travel from east to west along the equator, carrying warm surface waters away from South America and toward Southeast Asia.

Because warmer ocean temperatures bring more rainfall, their absence in Southeast Asia during an El Niño brings cooler-than-normal sea surface temperatures and an unusually dry climate.

El Niño is one extreme phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring global climate pattern driven by the Pacific Ocean’s temperature shifts. In contrast, La Niña is its cold phase, marked by colder-than-average sea surface temperatures.

Fishers off the coast of Peru first noticed periods of unusually warm water that come around Christmas time, hence calling them El Niño, meaning “little boy” in Spanish, or “Christ child” when capitalized. Afterwards, they named its contrasting phenomenon La Niña, meaning “little girl.”

El Niño and La Niña events occur every two to seven years and typically last nine to 12 months, but can sometimes last years.

How does it become a Super El Niño?

An El Niño becomes a very strong one when the ocean surface temperature threshold of 28 degrees Celsius (°C) along the monitored region rises by 2.0°C or more for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods. A very strong El Niño is what’s known as the Super El Niño.

PAGASA applies the Relative Oceanic Niño Index or RONI used by the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to determine ENSO conditions. See the classification scale below:

Very Strong El Niño : 2.0°C and above

: 2.0°C and above Strong El Niño : 1.5°C to less than 2.0°C

: 1.5°C to less than 2.0°C Moderate El Niño : 1.0°C to less than 1.5°C

: 1.0°C to less than 1.5°C Weak El Niño : 0.5°C to less than 1.0°C

: 0.5°C to less than 1.0°C Neutral : -0.5°C to less than 0.5°C

: -0.5°C to less than 0.5°C Weak La Niña : -0.5°C to more than -1.0°C

: -0.5°C to more than -1.0°C Moderate La Niña : -1.0°C to more than -1.5°C

: -1.0°C to more than -1.5°C Strong La Niña : -1.5°C to -2.0°C

: -1.5°C to -2.0°C Very Strong La Niña: -2.0°C and below

The last Super El Niño happened about a decade ago, from 2015 to 2016, when the Pacific Ocean’s surface temperature increased, peaking at 2.72°C in November 2015. It lasted for 18 months.

A World Bank assessment report showed that during that particular El Niño, six cities, 16 provinces, and 65 municipalities declared a state of calamity, with over 400,000 farmers and 550,000 hectares affected by drought as of May 2016. Agricultural production losses then reached approximately P20 billion.

Expected weather conditions

This Super El Niño is expected to bring prolonged dry spells, drought, water shortages, food insecurity, and health and energy risks in the Philippines.

A dry spell occurs when rainfall is below normal for three consecutive months, or far below normal for two consecutive months. A drought occurs when rainfall is far below normal for three consecutive months, or below normal for five consecutive months.

Meanwhile, active tropical cyclones that may arrive could bring short-term but heavy rainfall to the western section of the Philippines. In an October announcement, PAGASA said two to six tropical cyclones may still develop within, or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility from November 2026 to April 2027.

PAGASA previously observed that even during El Niño conditions this year, rainfall was also enhanced from August to September due to the southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat.

With the Philippines already in the amihan season (northeast monsoon) — a period typically characterized by cool, dry weather — PAGASA indicated that temperatures could still remain warmer due to the active El Niño.

In its September advisory, the weather bureau emphasized the need for early preparations, including climate information and preparing essential services before the full impact of Super El Niño hits the Philippines.

Affected areas throughout the country

PAGASA’s November forecasts show numerous areas across the country that could be affected by drier climate for the duration of the Super El Niño.

The following areas may experience drought by the end of November:

Luzon – Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes

– Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes Visayas – Capiz, Leyte, Negros Oriental, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte

– Capiz, Leyte, Negros Oriental, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte Mindanao – Isabela City, Misamis Oriental

Meanwhile, these areas could be experiencing dry spells at the same time period:

Luzon – Abra, Apayao, Bataan, Batanes, Batangas, Benguet, Cagayan, Cavite, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Palawan (Kalayaan), Kalinga, La Union, Marinduque, Masbate, Mountain Province, Metro Manila, Nueva Vizcaya, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Pangasinan, Quezon, Quirino, Romblon, Sorsogon, Zambales

– Abra, Apayao, Bataan, Batanes, Batangas, Benguet, Cagayan, Cavite, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Palawan (Kalayaan), Kalinga, La Union, Marinduque, Masbate, Mountain Province, Metro Manila, Nueva Vizcaya, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Pangasinan, Quezon, Quirino, Romblon, Sorsogon, Zambales Visayas – Aklan, Antique, Biliran, Bohol, Cebu, Guimaras, Iloilo, Negros Occidental, Northern Samar

– Aklan, Antique, Biliran, Bohol, Cebu, Guimaras, Iloilo, Negros Occidental, Northern Samar Mindanao – Basilan, Camiguin, Cotabato, Davao del Sur, Davao Occidental, Dinagat Islands, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Misamis Occidental, Sarangani, South Cotabato, Special Geographic Area, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Surigao del Norte, Tawi-Tawi, Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga del Sur, Zamboanga Sibugay

In its November 4 advisory, PAGASA said that five provinces experienced meteorological drought, 11 were under a dry spell, and 10 experienced dry conditions as of October.

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources also reported that one of three barangays nationwide may be extremely vulnerable to water shortages. Based on its geospatial database analysis, the department classified the affected barangays into the following priority levels:

High priority: 14,434 barangays or 34%

Moderate priority: 17,046 barangays or 41%

Low priority: 9,685 barangays or 23%

Not affected: 883 or 2%

By March 2027, the weather bureau forecasted that the whole country may eventually face droughts.

El Niño preparedness

According to the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction’s Climate Impact Outlook for the Philippines, the country has strategies in place to prepare for Super El Niño. See the table below:

It suggested prioritizing food production to lessen disruptions to the food supply, ensure sufficient water resources, and prepare for concurrent hazards that might overlap with Super El Niño, such as volcanic eruptions, typhoons, and earthquakes, which stretch provisions thin.

However, the national government has faced criticism over its preparations for the imminent crisis.

Aksyon Klima Pilipinas’ John Leo Algo pointed out the need for a publicly available El Niño action plan so coordination between the government, civil society groups, and stakeholders will be seamless and effective. Tracking where the budget goes throughout the plan is also easier if it is accessible.

The Federation of Free Farmers also expressed alarm in September over the government’s plans to cut the 2027 budget for agriculture and fisheries by 8%, saying that at this critical time, funding should be increased.

In October, they also demanded swifter distribution of the P45-billion assistance to farmers, saying that it might be too late for some areas if it took too long to arrive. – Rappler.com

World.title: From selling shoes at 8, SM’s Tessie Sy-Coson still sees the perks of being small
World.content:
'My dad always tells his friends that if he can do it, you can do it too,' says Teresita Sy-Coson, recalling her childhood helping out at Henry Sy Sr.'s little shoe shop that would grow into the SM empire

There sat Teresita Sy-Coson, heiress to SM’s multitrillion-peso empire, being asked what hope small businesses had left in the Philippines.

A weak economy, a weak peso, high interest rates, rising living and fuel costs, and now artificial intelligence. Could a small business still thrive?

Tessie, as she’s fondly called, smiled.

“We always have a lot of challenges. But the good thing about a small business is sometimes, those can be just noises,” she said. “You just look into your market, search your market, work hard, and you’ll be able to get over it.”

Play Video

“That’s the good thing about small businesses. You don’t have to worry about government regulator, accounting [principles], compliance, environment,” Tessie added.

Perhaps not the best legal advice, but an amusing observation from the vice chairperson of SM Investments and chairperson of BDO. And there is some truth, especially in red-tape laden Philippines; while small firms have rules to follow too, they don’t face the same compliance demands as a listed mega-company.

Besides, if anyone understood the difference between small and big, literally and figuratively, it was Tessie.

In her shoes

Long before SM became the empire it is today, Tessie was an eight-year-old helping in her father’s shoe store.

At the ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit on Wednesday, November 11, she laughed when veteran broadcaster Rico Hizon brought up this childhood memory.

“I have a small frame. And you can imagine how small I must be when I was small,” she recalled.

A tiny girl fetching shoes for customers to the amusement of adults around her. But it was no matter to her — everyone was expected to help the family business, particularly during the busy Christmas season.

“I have to work to show the family that I can contribute,” she said. By 13, she was spending Saturdays at her father’s store.

She reckoned her father’s business was only micro or small when she was born.

Henry Sy Sr. opened ShoeMart in 1958, and by 22, Tessie was already running the family’s first department store.

SHOEMART. Henry Sy Sr. poses in front of the small shoe store he opened in Manila on October 1958, more than six decades before it transformed into a sprawling mall. Photo from Teresita Sy-Coson’s Facebook page.

Being the eldest of six, however, didn’t automatically make her the heir. Traditional Chinese family customs have often favored sons in leadership positions, though the Sy siblings shared responsibilities.

“I was not meant to lead the group. Even now I am not leading — I maintain the core,” she told Forbes in 2012.

An understated assessment from a woman who helped build SM’s retail operations and BDO’s banking empire, including its 2007 merger with Equitable PCI Bank.

A soft spot for small businesses

Even today, SM hasn’t stopped growing. Its latest flagship mall, SM Nuvali, is opening this November and a new mall on Manila’s former Harrison Plaza site targeted for 2027.

The malls are also evolving to court younger shoppers, with Tessie keeping an eye on Gen Z tastes and trends.

“I have to research, and I look at a lot of social media as well,” she said. Even TikTok, she admitted, is part of her research.

And yet for all its immense size today, SM still has a soft spot for entrepreneurs who started small, just as Henry Sy Sr. did.

Tessie said many mall tenants began at trade fairs, where SM provided customers and foot traffic while entrepreneurs developed their products. Some eventually became permanent tenants. SM also works with the DTI and Go Negosyo on fairs and mentoring events.

“We provide the customers for them,” she explained. “For them, it’s more of selling and the marketing and the traffic is already there.”

“We grow, they grow,” she said.

Tessie hopes more small businesses will emerge and eventually grow into bigger enterprises, even amid difficult economic conditions.

“My dad always tells his friends that if he can do it, you can do it too,” she recalled. – Rappler.com

World.title: US to resume flights after air traffic network failure sparks chaos
World.content:
CANCELED FLIGHTS. A person looks at a departures board showing cancelled flights at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, in Chicago, Illinois, US, November 13, 2026.

(2nd UPDATE) Though the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers is far from over

WASHINGTON, USA – The US Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest nationwide shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened at 8:15 pm Eastern Time (0115 GMT’ 9:15 am Philippine time), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations.

“It’s going to be slow,” Duffy told reporters at the White House.

More than 6,600 flights were canceled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already canceled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country. Duffy said he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office to discuss the outage.

The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m., when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications systems.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” Duffy said, adding that at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and they were able to safely land thousands of planes.

Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the aging air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.

$50-billion aviation overhaul

Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50 billion to modernize it.

Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging airports and air traffic control infrastructure.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said.

“Give us the money to fix it.”

Homeland Security Secretary Mullin said there was “zero evidence” so far that the outage resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, though investigators had not ruled out either possibility.

“It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we’re still looking,” Mullin said.

The National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation, he added.

The outage appeared to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials. The network handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots. L3Harris did not respond to a request for comment.

Pain not over for passengers

Though the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers was far from over. From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted and aircraft remained parked at gates.

Thousands of passengers faced being stranded overnight. Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, had been scheduled to take a 9 pm Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lomé, Togo. Instead, he planned to spend the night at the airport before a rescheduled flight at 6 am on Saturday.

“I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.”

Louise Maher, 47, was also caught up in the disruption at Newark after her British Airways flight to London was caught up in the aviation meltdown.

“I might cry at some point but not yet,” she said.

US airlines will not be required to provide compensation to stranded passengers because the carriers were not responsible for the FAA system failures.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for about 90 minutes.

Investors were already pricing in a financial hit to airlines. Shares of American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines fell between 1% and 2% in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about 3%.

American Airlines said it was prioritizing flights to smaller cities outside its major hubs and international destinations to position aircraft and crews for a faster recovery. – Rappler.com

World.title: Baguio council seeks NBI’s clarification on operation vs lending firm
World.content:
Baguio City Hall in Baguio City (Photo by Maureen Matayew)

BAGUIO CITY—The city council raised questions about the handling of an Aug. 26 operation involving employees of a lending company called 1 Loyalty.

It is particularly inquiring about the decision to transfer to Manila of 24 arrested persons.

The council is also wondering why there was lack of information provided to the local National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) office afterwards.

Article continues after this 

The matter was discussed during the council’s regular session on Nov. 9.

The talks came following concerns about the involvement of the NBI Homicide Division in the operation and the subsequent handling of those who were nabbed.

NBI-Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR) Agent Romano Pangan said his office received a coordination letter from the NBI Homicide Division.

The NBI had informed its CAR unit of a planned surveillance and possible reinforcement operation within its area of responsibility.

However, the letter did not identify the subjects or specify the nature of the case.

Article continues after this 

Pangan said NBI-CAR learned of these details only during the briefing before the operation.

He clarified that his office provided assistance and perimeter security, while the Homicide Division carried out the apprehensions.

Article continues after this 

Pangan confirmed that around 34 to 35 individuals were brought to the NBI-CAR office for processing.

They underwent medical examinations, interviews and booking procedures, while lawyers and relatives were allowed to enter the office and make inquiries, he recalled.

Pangan also said the individual who allegedly received marked money was subjected to a fluorescent powder examination.

However, he said NBI-CAR did not receive a report from the Homicide Division after the individuals were transferred to the NBI headquarters in Manila.

His office was also not informed of the subsequent developments about the case.

Councilor Jose Molintas questioned why the Homicide Division handled an operation involving an alleged estafa or fraud case when no homicide investigation was involved.

He also asked about the transfer of 24 of those arrested to Manila, instead of having the case processed locally, particularly in relation to jurisdiction, preliminary investigation and inquest proceedings.

Molintas spoke about his concerns on the rights of those persons who remained suspects and were still presumed innocent.

He also questioned the circumstances surrounding reports that the case had been dismissed and whether those arrested could seek damages.

Pangan said he had sought an explanation from another agent, who told him that a task force had been created by the Department of Justice (DOJ). However, NBI-CAR was not aware of the task force.

According to Pangan, his office normally files cases arising from its operations within its area of jurisdiction and does not transfer respondents to Manila.

He said he could not explain the decision of the Homicide Division because he was not part of the operating unit.

“If it was me, I would readily file the cases here in Baguio City,” Pangan said.

Molintas requested that the NBI provide the city council with a report on the incident to help determine what policy action may be appropriate.

He also proposed seeking clarification from the NBI national office and the DOJ, and referring the matter to the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) for investigation.

Meanwhile, Councilor Peter Fianza asked whether NBI-CAR had been informed of the purpose of the operation and whether it had records identifying those who were brought to Manila.

Pangan said the coordination letter did not include the names of the subjects or the nature of the case, apparently for confidential reasons.

He added that operational matters are generally kept confidential before an operation to prevent information leaks.

Fianza also asked whether NBI-CAR knew the identities of the Baguio residents brought to Manila, where they were taken and what happened to them.

Pangan said he did not have the names of those transferred.

The city council referred the matter to the Committee on Public Protection and Safety for further review and preparation of a report.

World.title: MILF: No unauthorized recruitments in the name of our military arm
World.content:
Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) logo (Inquirer file)

COTABATO CITY—Officials of Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) clarified that there are no ongoing authorized recruitment activities in the name of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF).

They said that such events are not held without the approval of the MILF’s central committee.

In a statement Friday, Nov. 13, MILF chairman Ahod Balawag Ebrahim made it known that there is only one MILF, with a recognized leadership, organizational structure, and clear chain of command.

Article continues after this 

He is also concurrently the chief of its military arm, the BIAF.

“No individual or group has the authority to claim to represent the MILF or conduct recruitment activities in its name without proper authorization from its legitimate leadership,” Ebrahim said in a statement.

The MILF is urging the public, particularly communities in the Bangsamoro region, to remain vigilant against individuals or groups claiming to be representatives of the MILF or BIAF.

Now a member of the Bangsamoro Parliament, Ebrahim said the issue must be addressed with accountability, honesty and caution, particularly at this critical stage of the Bangsamoro peace process.

He was reacting to reports circulating across the Bangsamoro Region of recruitments reportedly for persons who are interested to join the BIAF in Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur.

He did not say who was behind the recruitments. /apl

World.title: From nursing to courtship: Flying foxes reveal their tender side
World.content:
Photos courtesy of DENR Soccsksargen

MANILA, Philippines — A mother flying fox gently fans her wings to keep her young pup comfortable before wrapping it in a protective embrace as the little bat suckles milk beneath her wing.

This intimate moment of maternal care was among the wildlife behaviors documented by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Soccsksargen during a monitoring activity in Kulaman Valley, Arakan, Cotabato, from Oct. 24 to 26.

The three-day monitoring also revealed a thriving colony of approximately 30,000 endangered large flying foxes (Pteropus vampyrus) roosting across 39 trees, highlighting the valley’s importance as a habitat for the threatened species.

Article continues after this 

Conducted by the DENR’s Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) in Matalam, the monitoring offered a closer look at the daily lives of these mammals, from nurturing their young to courtship, mating and grooming.

Among the observations was a mother flying fox nursing her pup while using her wings to regulate its temperature.

After gently fanning her wings, the mother wrapped them around her young, providing warmth and protection as the pup fed from a specialized teat near her armpit.

The monitoring team also documented courtship and mating behaviors, including prolonged grooming interactions between male and female flying foxes.

Beyond their reproductive activities, the bats were observed meticulously cleaning their fur, bodies and delicate wing membranes with their long, flexible tongues.

Article continues after this 

According to the DENR, grooming helps the animals remove debris, maintain their physical condition and preserve the sensitivity of their wing membranes, which are essential for flight.

A sanctuary for flying foxes

Article continues after this 

The monitoring recorded approximately 30,000 large flying foxes occupying 39 trees belonging to several genera, including Dipterocarpus, Parashorea, Astronia, Ficus and Canarium.

The size of the colony underscores the ecological importance of Kulaman Valley as a roosting habitat for the endangered mammals.

Often described as nature’s “flying farmers,” large flying foxes play an important role in maintaining forest ecosystems through pollination and seed dispersal.

As they move through forest habitats, these fruit bats help spread seeds and support natural forest regeneration, contributing to biodiversity and the continued growth of vegetation.

Their presence in Kulaman Valley highlights the importance of protecting not only the animals themselves but also the trees and forest habitats on which they depend.

Threats to survival

Despite their ecological contributions, large flying foxes continue to face threats from habitat destruction, hunting for bushmeat and persecution fueled by misconceptions about crop damage and disease transmission.

The species is classified as endangered under DENR Administrative Order No. 2019-09 and the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List.

RELATED STORY: In Photos: A glimpse of birdlife in Cabusao wetlands

The DENR stressed the importance of sustained wildlife monitoring, habitat conservation and public awareness to protect the species and its natural roosting sites.

The observations in Kulaman Valley provide a glimpse into the lives of these endangered mammals, showing how nursing, courtship and grooming form part of their natural behavior.

For conservation authorities, protecting the large flying foxes also means safeguarding the forest ecosystems that benefit from their role in pollination and seed dispersal.

World.title: Ilocos Norte centenarian gets P100K cash incentive on 100th birthday
World.content:
Dingras, Ilocos Norte Mayor Joemelle Saguid-Go Sy (third from left) leads the awarding of a P100,000 cash incentive to centenarian Esperanza Longboy Asuncion of Barangay San Francisco, Dingras, Ilocos Norte, under Republic Act No. 10868 or the Centenarians Act of 2016. (Photo from Dingras local government)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — A centenarian from Barangay San Francisco, Dingras, Ilocos Norte received a P100,000 cash incentive from the government for reaching the age of 100.

Esperanza Longboy Asuncion was awarded the incentive under Republic Act No. 10868, or the Centenarians Act of 2016, which grants a cash gift to Filipinos who reach their 100th birthday.

The visit and awarding on Friday (Nov. 13) were led by Dingras Mayor Joemelle Saguid-Go Sy.

Article continues after this 

She was together with Municipal Social Welfare and Development Officer Jessanie Gayya, Office for Senior Citizens Affairs head Madeline Soliman, and Federation of Senior Citizens Associations of the Philippines President Osias Ballesteros.

The local government said the incentive recognizes Asuncion’s milestone and her long life, describing her as an inspiration to the community.

Local officials extended their congratulations and wished her continued good health and happiness. /apl

World.title: Fewer Negros Island Region families are living in poverty in 2025 – PSA
World.content:
Negros Island Region (Inquirer files)

BACOLOD CITY— Poverty incidence among families in the Negros Island Region (NIR) fell to 14.3 percent in 2025 from 22.6 percent in 2023, data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)-NIR showed Friday, Nov. 13.

The PSA estimated that about 178,470 families in the region had incomes below the poverty threshold in 2025.

Among the general population, poverty incidence in the region stood at 20.4 percent, equivalent to approximately 987,200 Filipinos who could not meet their basic food and non-food needs.

Article continues after this 

“Poverty incidence among the population in the Negros Island Region (NIR) was estimated at 20.4 percent in 2025, equivalent to approximately 987.20 thousand Filipinos unable to meet their basic food and non-food needs,” the PSA-NIR said.

Among the region’s provinces and highly urbanized city, Negros Occidental recorded the highest poverty incidence, at 18.7 percent among families and 26.3 percent among the population.

Negros Oriental followed, with poverty incidence at 12 percent among families and 17.6 percent among the population.

Bacolod City posted rates of 2.9 percent among families and 5 percent among its population.

Siquijor recorded the lowest poverty incidence in the region, at 0.4 percent among families and 0.7 percent among the population. /apl

World.title: PCG lifts travel suspension for small vessels in 3 Palawan towns
World.content:
(Inquirer files)

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has lifted the suspension of travel for small vessels in Roxas, Dumaran and Araceli in Palawan following the improved weather.

In Sea Travel Advisory No. 1126-002 issued on Saturday (Nov. 14), the Coast Guard Station North Central Palawan announced that vessels and watercraft with a gross tonnage of 15 and below may resume operations in the three municipalities.

The lifting of the restriction was based on the latest weather forecast issued by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) at 4 a.m. on Saturday.

Article continues after this 

However, the PCG reminded vessel operators and mariners to remain vigilant and take extra precautions against possible adverse weather and sea conditions.

It also advised operators to observe HPCG Memorandum Circular No. 03-01, which provides guidelines on vessel and motorboat movements in the absence of local weather bulletins.

It also cited HPCG Memorandum Circular No. 02-23, which sets revised guidelines for vessel operations during heavy weather conditions. /apl

World.title: UP, NRDC to craft national El Niño response plan
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The University of the Philippines (UP) and the Natural Resources Development Corporation (NRDC) will hold a two-day national consultation on Nov. 20 and 21 in Quezon City to develop a coordinated response to the potential impacts of El Niño

The National Multi-Stakeholder Consultation on El Niño Impact and Response will take place at the GT Toyota Asian Cultural Center in UP Diliman, bringing together government agencies, scientists, community representatives, civil society organizations and businesses.

According to a joint press release dated Nov. 13, the consultation aims to produce a National Multi-Stakeholder El Niño Response Action Matrix, which will form part of a report to be submitted to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Article continues after this 

The proposed matrix will identify priority needs and match them with voluntary interventions, designated lead organizations and partners, implementation timelines, performance measures and reporting arrangements.

The consultation will focus on sectors considered most vulnerable to El Niño, including low-income families, children, students, farmers, fisherfolk, indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities, older persons and workers.

UP will serve as the lead convenor, providing the scientific framework, program design, moderation and synthesis of the discussions.

NRDC, meanwhile, will coordinate with government agencies and other partners, mobilize resources and handle public information.

UP President Angelo Jimenez will deliver the welcome remarks, while NRDC President and CEO Benjamin Turgano will present the consultation’s statement of purpose.

Article continues after this 

Alfredo Mahar Lagmay of the UP Resilience Institute and Project NOAH will discuss the science behind El Niño and its anticipated impacts on the Philippines.

A team from the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), led by Ana Liza Solis, will present the climate outlook and an assessment of geographic risks.

Article continues after this 

Researchers and academics from the UP College of Engineering, UP Los Baños School of Environmental Science and Management, Silliman University and Davao Oriental State University will also share lessons from previous El Niño episodes.

A scientific dialogue will examine which populations face the greatest risks and where they are located.

Community representatives, including students and their families, farmers, fisherfolk, indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities and barangay officials, will discuss their needs and available local resources.

The consultation will also address three priority areas: continuity of basic and higher education, health protection and social services, and food security and agriculture.

Government agencies will be tasked with identifying vulnerable populations and priority geographic areas, assessing existing interventions and determining operational gaps requiring additional support.

Community representatives will also participate in validating the proposed interventions to determine whether they are relevant, accessible and feasible.
