Spoiler alert: This story references major plot-points in You Can See Everything. We all suspected Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, would be a wild ride. The buzz was inescapable since its top-secret premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, where critics described it as “one head-scratching scene after another”. A near perfect Rotten Tomatoes score and talk of a best picture Oscar run further confirmed our suspicions. But nothing could have properly prepared us for what was to come. Nathan Fielder (left) and Elizabeth Holmes (centre) in a scene from You Can See Everything. A24 Shot over 34 days, the documentary captures Holmes’ last moments with her family before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison for an 11-year sentence – while also attempting to get to the bottom of one key question: “Is she telling the truth?” The answer, it turns out, is far from black and white. After watching the documentary, it’s clear the term “head-scratcher” is an understatement. So, here are eight of the film’s most shocking moments, ranked from wild to “what the hell just happened?”.



8. Not one lie While sitting on the deck of Holmes’ rented San Diego home (which she shared with her partner Billy Evans and their two children before going to jail), Fielder asks Holmes if she has ever lied. She insists she hasn’t, not even an innocent white lie. It’s a perplexing moment that forces you to consider whether Holmes, a convicted fraudster, is lying about lying, or if her understanding of truth and deceit differ from others. Despite the absurdity of the claim, she still comes across as somewhat sincere, her wide-eyed look of innocence never breaking from Fielder’s piercing gaze. Even if she has lied before, it appears she genuinely believes she hasn’t. A manipulative liar or an unaware liar – it’s difficult to say which is more terrifying. 7. ‘FYI you can totally see everything’ Soon after claiming she’s never lied, Holmes sends Fielder a text from the beach. She’s only a few paces away, yet she decides to message him, typing “FYI you can totally see everything”. Beyond inspiring the documentary’s title, the message seems random and reeks of a desperation to prove there’s nothing to hide … Or is she genuinely promising total transparency? It’s one of several moments in which Holmes and Fielder share a quasi-intimate moment, further complicating the documentary’s objectivity. Loading



6. Shock revelation dismissed During a brief moment with Holmes’ parents, who are visiting before she begins her prison sentence, Holmes’ father tells Fielder he believes things changed for Holmes when she was raped during her college years. The conversation is brief, frank and entirely unexpected, leaving viewers desperate for elaboration. But it’s never addressed again, and Evans shuts the conversation down entirely shortly after. 5. Full-frontal nudity After a filmed gym session, Evans is captured in the shower – naked and in full view. It’s surprising, confronting and has you second-guessing Evans’ motivations. According to a Vulture interview with Oppenheim, Evans had undressed and stepped into the shower while the cameras were still rolling. However, an anonymous source told People that Evans reportedly felt his trust was violated over that scene, and that he had allegedly only agreed to it if they “kept it PG”. Once again, we’re left wondering if we’ve witnessed a simple misunderstanding or a carefully manipulated conflict.



4. Billy’s egg specificity Evans is an all-round peculiar bloke. Beside the fact that he encouraged total strangers to enter his family’s home during presumably one of the most harrowing periods of their lives, he also admits to being constantly armed (for safety), tells an A-list star that he’s “great at sex”, and cannot for the life of him allow Holmes to beat eggs her way. The latter arose when Holmes is speaking to Fielder while casually whisking eggs in a bowl. Midway through her sentence, Evans abruptly takes the bowl and proceeds to whisk them himself. Fielder addresses the awkward moment, and Holmes explains that Evans simply believes he can do it better. This idea of control returns later when Evans reveals he’s Holmes’ power of attorney and controls her X account while she’s imprisoned. Elizabeth Holmes, with partner Billy Evans, outside the court in 2022. Bloomberg Whether the documentary is intentionally framing him this way or not, Evans comes across as ego-driven and incredibly controlling. His love for Holmes appears genuine (verging into obsessive), but his yearning for exposure seems equally strong. It’s here that sympathy for Holmes begins to grow: Could she once again be caught under a domineering man’s spell (similar to the alleged situation with her ex-partner and Theranos president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani), pressured into saying and doing what ultimately suits him?



3. Who’s on first? Related Article Pop culture How tech geniuses became Hollywood’s favourite monster One of the most bizarre moments comes early in the documentary during a scene in the couple’s living room. Fielder shows Holmes and Evans the 1930s Abbott and Costello’s “who’s on first” comedy skit in an attempt to demonstrate Holmes’ occasionally misleading use of language. Earlier in the documentary, she’d failed to understand the issue around saying her blood-testing device “can” work when it could only theoretically work. Fielder believed the skit, which plays on the word “who” as both a name and pronoun, would clarify his earlier confusion. However, when asked if she understands why the skit is funny, Holmes said she does but then fails to explain why, and can’t point out the connection between the routine and their earlier conversation. She becomes so confused, overwhelmed – whatever her feelings are – that her eyes well with tears. Does she actually not understand the correlation (in which case, we’d pity her) or is it all part of a grand facade of innocence?



2. The Drop-in Given Amanda Seyfried is known for playing Holmes in the 2022 series The Dropout – a role she won an Emmy for – she certainly elicits gasps after suddenly appearing in the documentary’s “second act”. Holmes is in prison, so Fielder and Oppenheim invite Seyfried to watch some of their footage and act as a talking head of sorts. However, Seyfried unexpectedly ends up imitating Holmes, resuming her earlier award-winning role in a bizarre fiction/non-fiction hybrid. The filmmakers decide to go with it, reenacting earlier off-camera moments between Holmes and Fielder. Better yet, Wolf Man star Christopher Abbott plays Evans alongside her. Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. Hulu The reenactments, based entirely on Fielder’s memory of events, capture the fallibility of documentary-making and challenge the notion of truth. Is truth universally understood, and can documentaries ever be entirely objective? Seyfried herself adds an interesting perspective, as someone wrangling with the possibility that the person she embodied for months may (or may not) have been misunderstood.



Related Article Documentaries Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doco could make Oscars history. Here’s what to know before seeing it 1. The matter of payment Usually, documentary subjects do not receive payments as this would impact a production’s credibility. This doesn’t stop Evans from trying though. He asks A24 executives, Fielder and Oppenheim if he and Holmes could be paid for taking part. What makes this scene more intriguing is that it’s recreated using Seyfried as Holmes and Abbott as Evans, throwing into question whether Evans really was that upfront, and what kind of negotiations actually ensued (the documentary claims A24 agreed to pay them, but Evans rescinded his request post-filming). More intriguingly, Seyfried’s Holmes leaves the room to check on her baby before Evans makes the request. Once again, Holmes’ complicity is questioned. On one hand, she could have no idea about Evans’ desire for payment, meaning he’s yet again controlling the situation. Or (and there’s always an “or” in this documentary) Holmes is privy to the plan, and excuses herself intentionally to feign ignorance. She’s either an innocent bystander, frequently pulled into the orbit of domineering men, or she’s a manipulative liar. Come the end of the documentary, it’s still unclear. You Can See Everything is in cinemas now. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Out of the bubble: How a world-first gene therapy gave Matthew a second chance at life
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare Out of the bubble: How a world-first gene therapy gave Matthew a second chance at life Henrietta Cook November 14, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s the tail end of the flu season, and hundreds of shoppers are milling around a food court, searching for a bite to eat. Until recently, sitting among this lunchtime crowd could have killed Matthew Rozek. Matthew Rozek was born with a rare inherited immune disorder sometimes known as “bubble boy disease”. Joe Armao “It’s a big adjustment,” says the 29-year-old, who recently became one of the first people in the world to receive an experimental gene therapy that he hopes will cure him of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) or “bubble boy disease”. Born without a functional immune system, Rozek spent the first few years of his life largely inside a Melbourne hospital.



Everyday germs posed a constant threat. When chickenpox circulated through his primary school, he stayed home for weeks. Parties, shopping malls, flights, public transport and art galleries were off limits, especially during winter, when he retreated to the safety of his home “like a hermit”. The slightest sign of a scratchy throat triggered a wave of anxiety. Would he end up in hospital yet again, requiring intravenous antibiotics for an infection most people shake off within a few days? “Once I was in the teenage years, that’s when you notice that everyone else is normal and I’m not,” he says, sipping a hot chocolate in the food court of the Spencer Outlet Centre in Melbourne’s CBD. “There’s a lot of physical suffering, but mental suffering as well.”



Professor Shalin Naik corrected Rozek’s genetic mutation using a “blood in a dish” system. His life began to change a year ago in a Melbourne laboratory at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, where a research team led by Professor Shalin Naik, with Dr Miles Horton, corrected Rozek’s genetic mutation using a “blood in a dish” system. “We can very quickly take someone like Matthew’s blood, simulate his disease in a dish, and test these brand-new therapies that are coming out to see which one works,” Naik says. “Each person needs their own personalised gene therapy.” Every Australian child is now tested for SCID at birth through the newborn heel prick, and about six new cases are diagnosed a year.



Matthew Rozek is already starting to see the benefits of his gene-editing treatment for SCID. Joe Armao The devastating, life-shortening condition is widely known as “bubble boy disease” because of David Vetter, a Texan boy who was born with SCID in 1971 and spent almost the entirety of his 12 years inside a sterile plastic chamber. Vetter’s confronting situation attracted intense media attention around the world and inspired the movies The Boy in the Plastic Bubble, which starred John Travolta, and Bubble Boy, starring Jake Gyllenhaal. It also spawned comedic references in Seinfeld and The Simpsons. The standard long-term treatment for SCID is a bone marrow transplant from a matched donor, which can carry serious risks including graft failure and death. Rozek had a transplant as a toddler, but it gradually failed over time, leaving him with minimal immunity.



By adulthood, his health had deteriorated to the point where doctors warned he faced up to a 50 per cent chance of dying if he underwent a second bone marrow transplant. Rozek wasn’t prepared to take this risk. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Why doctors are writing medical scripts for fresh air In desperate search of another option, one of Rozek’s team of clinicians at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, Dr Samantha Chan, reached out to Dr Suk See DeRavin, an Australian researcher overseeing gene therapy trials at the US National Institutes of Health in Maryland. For three years, the two doctors corresponded by email, shipping samples of Rozek’s blood to the US on dry ice to test his eligibility for an upcoming trial. Rozek flew to Maryland last August to receive the experimental treatment at the National Institutes of Health.



After three weeks of medical tests and a full genetic panel, he underwent a two-day process called apheresis in which his stem cells were harvested through a line in his neck. Over the next month, scientists genetically edited those cells in a laboratory. He received chemotherapy to make room in his bone marrow for a 30-millilitre infusion of his repaired cells. This allowed his body to build the functioning immune system he was born without. “It’s just crazy that I still am alive,” Rozek says. “I just don’t know how the body can function without the immune system.” Chan says Rozek would have died without access to the trial. “There’s no doubt it’s been a huge success,” she says. “It offers hope at a normal life. Being able to offer them a solution that doesn’t carry the mortality rate of something like a stem cell transplant can be life-changing.”



Rare immune diseases can be devastating for families. Related Article Healthcare One in three babies with suspected peanut allergies cleared of the condition in landmark study “Fear of infection is really debilitating,” says Chan. “They want to be able to go to school, but then they’re afraid of bringing the virus home. It’s a really life-altering disease.” Walter and Eliza Hall Institute researchers are now working to bring similar treatments to Australia. Backed by a $5 million Medical Research Future Fund grant, Naik’s team is developing a way to package gene-editing machinery into microscopic mRNA droplets, similar to those used in COVID-19 vaccines.



This would allow doctors to repair a patient’s stem cells with a simple injection in the arm, avoiding the need for bone marrow transplants. Related Article Science ‘It’s a total game changer’: Australian breakthrough in DNA editing “It will encode the machinery that the patient needs to correct their mutation,” says Naik, who estimates his team is two to three years away from clinical trials. Rozek is already experiencing the benefits of his gene-editing treatment. For the first time in his life, he’s properly absorbing nutrients, which means he has gained a much-needed 10 kilograms.



Chronic gut infections had previously prevented his body from absorbing crucial vitamins and minerals from food. Related Article Good Weekend Matt dug in Patagonia. He made a priceless discovery about Earth’s biggest creatures Blood tests show his immune system is improving, allowing him to come off medications. The full benefits may not be seen for another few years. While the treatment has turned Rozek’s life around, it won’t reverse decades of damage inflicted on his body as a result of not having an immune system. A childhood infection has left him with about 70 per cent lung capacity, and he has ongoing issues with his bones as a result of being malnourished for so long.



“It won’t fully cure everything,” he says of the treatment. “But it was the easiest decision I’ve ever had to make.” It’s also allowed him to step back into normal life, and do many things that other people take for granted. Rozek, who runs agritech start-up Agtuary from his bedroom, recently attended a 300-person conference in Sydney. “I don’t want to jump into the deep end,” he says. “I’m taking it slow.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: In person, in writing and in a weekly newsletter: WorkSafe details CFMEU warnings to minister
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBig Build royal commission In person, in writing and in a weekly newsletter: WorkSafe details CFMEU warnings to minister Mathew Dunckley November 14, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The workplace safety watchdog repeatedly warned the state government about the CFMEU’s escalating use of spurious danger claims to disrupt major projects, particularly the $10 billion West Gate Tunnel. WorkSafe Victoria’s chief health and safety officer Sam Jenkin’s claims in his submission to the royal commission into the construction industry cast fresh doubt on the government’s insistence it was unaware of the CFMEU’s conduct prior to this masthead’s Building Bad investigation in mid-2024. Ingrid Stitt’s department repeatedly warned her about the CFMEU’s conduct. Ruby Alexander Jenkin described regular high-level meetings with then-minister Ingrid Stitt and her staff as one of the ways WorkSafe communicated the CFMEU’s disruption of major projects using unfounded safety claims – particularly on the West Gate Tunnel, which was beset by delays and cost blowouts. “These issues were recorded within WorkSafe in weekly email updates and highlighted in written and oral briefings to the minister’s office, including by the CEO personally,” he said.



Related Article Big Build royal commission Big Build royal commission as it happened: Construction boss says work sites have become ‘more combative’ as unions battle for territory Jenkin’s evidence follows the release of multiple briefing notes from senior bureaucrats seeking to warn then-minister in charge of the major projects, Jacinta Allan, of costly and significant problems caused by the CFMEU. Asked by the commission to reflect on events in 2021 and 2022, Jenkin said WorkSafe had regularly observed CFMEU officials entering projects over matters that “appeared not to relate to genuine safety concerns” as part of the industrial battle it was fighting with the Australian Workers Union. “So far as ‘patterns’ are concerned, although it is highly unlikely that WorkSafe could have proved such matters in a court, CFMEU aligned [officials] may have been raising safety concerns to advance industrial and other interests, including with employers and during a demarcation dispute with a rival union, the Australian Workers’ Union,” he said. “As a general rule … they arose earlier, more consistently and were most pronounced at the West Gate Tunnel Project.”



On several occasions, he said, WorkSafe suggested the officials should be removed by Victoria Police as they were trespassing. Jenkin said another noted pattern was that CFMEU issues “arose with a greater degree of frequency, or intensity, when time-critical works were due to occur” such as road closures or public transport shutdowns. Jenkin said WorkSafe’s chairman and chief executive were among those who briefed Stitt. Loading



“The minister was also briefed on an ongoing basis, including in writing by weekly reports to the minister’s office, on an ad hoc basis when specific incidents occurred, and on a number of occasions, in person by the CEO,” he said. Jenkin said although the Gap Road level crossing removal was of less concern to WorkSafe than the West Gate Tunnel, the agency was asked to brief Stitt on June 6, 2022, at the height of the Gap Road dispute that has occupied the opening week of witness examinations at the royal commission. The West Gate Tunnel was beset by delays and blowouts. He said WorkSafe had not been able to identify Stitt’s response to the briefing, which he said was not unusual. “The 6 June meeting followed earlier meetings in April and May of 2022 at which WorkSafe was requested to advise on similar issues. Notes prepared at the time include a reference to the Gap Road Site, although the majority of communication concerned the West Gate Tunnel Project, where union issues were more pronounced from WorkSafe’s perspective,” he said.



“WorkSafe was regularly requested to advise on issues relating to CFMEU activity on Major [Major Transport Infrastructure Authority] Projects with the Minister for Workplace Safety between June and August 2022, including as part of written weekly reports and at least one meeting on 6 June 2022.” Editor's pick Analysis

Big Build royal commission The company memo that goes to the heart of the Big Build royal commission The WorkSafe chief executive held monthly meetings throughout 2022 with Stitt, which were usually also attended by her chief of staff and a policy adviser. Jenkin said despite WorkSafe inspectors increasingly being called to these projects, they did not have the power to act as an umpire in industrial disputes and had little ability to remove union officials acting improperly. Additionally, there was also “marked hostility” towards WorkSafe from the CFMEU during the period, when the union published highly critical social media posts naming WorkSafe staff, which had resulted in death threats.

World.title: ‘Overloaded’: US flight grounding leaves days of travel chaos in its wake
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAirports ‘Overloaded’: US flight grounding leaves days of travel chaos in its wake Michael Koziol Updated November 14, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published November 14, 2026 — 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: The US is facing days of travel chaos after an extraordinary nationwide order grounded all flight departures for more than four hours, prompting the cancellation of more than 8000 services and delays to thousands more. The Trump administration blamed old and “overloaded” technical infrastructure for the failure, and used it to demand the US Congress appropriate $US50 billion ($74 billion) for new systems, warning that without it, the outage was likely to happen again. Loading The shutdown on a Friday afternoon (Washington time) caused havoc at airports, with airlines cancelling more than 8000 flights, according to flight-tracking service FlightRadar24. Thousands more were delayed, and hold-ups were set to continue throughout the weekend. The ground stop order meant flights in the air could land, but those on the ground could not take off. The disruption quickly spread beyond the US, forcing the cancellation of flights from Canada and Europe. US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day.



Flights departing Australia for the US were temporarily halted before resuming once the order was lifted. Some international flights were able to depart the US despite the shutdown. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”. Planes are parked at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas during the national ground stop. AP Later, at a news conference at the White House, he said the FAA shut the system down after intermittent communications and radar failures in critical air traffic control systems. “It wasn’t a complete blackout ... but when you have issues, and you can’t immediately communicate and immediately see where aircraft are at, that’s a risk that we are unwilling to tolerate,” Duffy said.



He said the failure was caused by an overloaded system, which relies on outdated technology including floppy disks and replacement parts that occasionally have to be purchased on eBay. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy said. “I shouldn’t say ‘went down’ – they started to give us inconsistency in the data. And because of that, we shut the system down. “We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded.” US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy (left) and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin brief media at the White House. AP Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that a cyberattack was to blame for the problem, nor the involvement of a rogue artificial intelligence system. Nothing could be conclusively ruled out at this stage, he said, though he stressed that there was no connection to the outage that hit Microsoft systems the previous day.



Duffy said technicians developed a fix that reduced the overloading on the network switches. “Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem.” Last year, US Congress approved $US12.5 billion to fix the FAA’s ageing communications system, and on Friday – before the communications problem – the FAA and White House asked Congress for another $US30.1 billion to address other issues. Duffy said he now wanted $US50 billion. New switches installed during the Trump administration did not fail, he said – only the old ones. “This is an emergency,” he said. “I want Congress to give us emergency funding.” Passengers wait at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as flights are delayed. AP The lines for rideshares and taxis at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. AP



The FAA has also begun rolling out an AI tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) to help manage air traffic across the country. The rollout, which began in Washington in September, was expanded to other areas only days ago. Asked whether Friday’s issues could be AI-related, Mullin reminded a reporter: “We call it SI around here, remember.” The Trump administration has attempted to rename artificial intelligence to superintelligence. Loading The ground stop was issued at about 4pm Washington time and lifted at 8.15pm (12.15pm Saturday AEDT), lasting a little more than four hours. But the delays are set to continue into the weekend as airlines try to move the backlog of passengers whose travel was disrupted. Duffy said he expected the system to return to normal operations by next Friday. That weekend marks the start of the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel period.



Duffy said he expected the system to return to normal operations by next Friday. That weekend marks the start of the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel period. It was only the third time in US history that a nationwide ground stop has been ordered; the first was during the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and the other was in 2023 when the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system failed. The 2023 problem lasted about 12 hours in total, though departures started to resume after about 90 minutes. Luggage chaos at Los Angeles International Airport. AP Travellers settle in for a long wait at New York’s LaGuardia Airport. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy On Friday afternoon, passengers from New York to Los Angeles, and Chicago to Atlanta waited at crowded gates and terminals while their aircraft remained parked at the gates, and staff had little information about what would happen next.



In some cases, passengers were forced to wait on their planes on the tarmac, with customers sending messages to the airlines on social media begging to be allowed to return to the terminal. Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: Departures to resume as FAA lifts ground directive after citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’; Homeland Security secretary denies cyberattack, Microsoft outage connection Dennis Lennox, a Republican strategist, was on a plane on the tarmac at MBS International Airport in Michigan when the ground stop was ordered. He was due to fly to Detroit and onwards to Los Angeles. “We had backed out of the gate and were starting to go through the taxiing process to take off, and we were ordered to return to the gate,” he said. “The initial report was there were radio issues in this area. Within a minute or two, I was able to find out things quicker. We weren’t even given the chance to stay on the plane. We were kicked off the plane and dumped inside the terminal.”



Related Article Need to know

Airports Here’s what we know about the US flight shutdown – and what it means for travel Other passengers gave up early in the evening and went home or booked hotels. At Washington’s Ronald Reagan National Airport, Madeline DeMaske said the price of hotels increased over the two hours she was waiting, and there was an Uber pricing surge. “This delay is going to cost me several hundred dollars,” she said. Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell told Fox News the ground stop was a sensible measure to “declutter the airspace” and deal with the technical issue. “The ground stop, while a real pain in the neck, is the safest way to go,” he said. World.title: Warner makes bombshell sandpapergate claim involving Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon
World.content:
Updated SportCricketBall tampering Warner makes bombshell sandpapergate claim involving Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon Andrew Wu Updated November 14, 2026 — 3:28pm ,first published 1:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. David Warner has accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal. In another explosive escalation of the saga that has rocked Australian sport, Warner took to Instagram to claim the governing body did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon as part of its investigation in the days after the Cape Town Test of 2018. David Warner appeared on a Kayo Sports panel on Friday. The former opener has thrown his weight behind friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja. AAP Warner made the claim early on Saturday afternoon, a day after he accused Test captain Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja under the bus after the release of his memoir, Sabr. “As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” Warner posted to Instagram.



“If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know? David Warner’s post to Instagram on Saturday. Instagram “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose, and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up.” This masthead has reached out to representatives of Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon for comment. Cricket Australia released a statement in response to Warner’s allegation, saying the organisation respected the differing recollections among the 2018 playing group.



The statement did not say if any of the three players were interviewed by investigator Iain Roy. “As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation [into the ball-tampering saga] and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a CA spokesman said. “Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players’ right to provide their own version of events.” Loading CA chief Todd Greenberg said this week the governing body would not be reopening the investigation, despite Khawaja’s allegations.



Warner hit out at Cummins on Friday, just hours after his former Test captain delivered an extraordinary 69-minute press conference denying any knowledge of the sandpaper plot. “Pat Cummins was very well-prepared this morning and I still stick by what Uzzy [Usman Khawaja] said, what he’s written in that book,” Warner told Fox Cricket. “That is the truth and I really, really support him [Khawaja]. I’m actually feeling for him at the moment. “I actually feel that the captain today actually threw Uzzy under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that. “Each person is going to have their differences, but I’m not going to accept them until the truth is out there.” Earlier on Saturday, former Pakistan captain and legendary swing bowler Wasim Akram – whose family is based in Melbourne – took to X to give his take on Sandpapergate.



“I saw Pat Cummins, who’s a very close friend of mine, [a] great cricketer, one of the top leaders in world cricket, the way he leads his team from the front, and he said he didn’t know [about any plot to tamper with the ball],” Akram said. “It’s my opinion, and it can be right or wrong, but as a bowler, when the cricket ball comes in my hand, either it’s the fifth over, either it’s in the 10th over, either it’s in the 50th over – the old ball – where you look after the ball, you shine the one side if it’s a dry day, a dry square, you one-bounce throw [in from the outfield], you get it scratched a bit, but the sandpaper scratch is totally different than the one-bounce scratch. “As a cricket lover, if you want to check, grab a semi-new cricket ball, grab sandpaper, and rub it in – you know the scratches are totally different. “Again, like I said, I’m not taking anybody’s side … Australians are known and famous for their straightforwardness, hardness on the field, off the field, and, most importantly, honesty.”



Khawaja, who has not spoken publicly since Cummins’ press conference, was due to appear on The Grade Cricketer podcast on Sunday, but that interview has been postponed until Thursday. He was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands in western Sydney on Saturday, but publisher Penguin said it too had been postponed. The former Test opener is scheduled to play in the T20 Gold Clash exhibition game in Cairns on November 22. He’s been named to play alongside the likes of Brian Lara, Adam Gilchrist, Matthew Hayden and Michael Hussey against a team featuring former AFL and NRL stars. South Sydney officials have met with Sam Walker in a bid to lure the premiership-winning halfback from arch rivals the Roosters. Sources not authorised to speak publicly said the Rabbitohs had met with Walker in Brisbane, where he is part of the Kangaroos World Cup squad. Walker remains contracted to the premiers until the end of next year, but they are prepared to get him off the books immediately after contract extension talks spectacularly unravelled two weeks ago after the Queensland half requested additional time to consider the deal. Sam Walker could be on the move. Getty Images The Rabbitohs are open to the prospect of taking Walker straight away, but don’t have the salary cap space to meet his contract figure of about $1 million a year. While several high-profile Rabbitohs are off contract from 2028 – including Latrell Mitchell, Campbell Graham and Jack Wighton – none of them have been asked to make way immediately.



PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters has stated there is interest in Walker after the club missed out on Panthers superstar Nathan Cleary and Titans youngster Zane Harrison. Canterbury has also been touted as a potential contender for Walker, if Matt Burton seeks an immediate release to join Perth. Burton has a three-year deal on the table from the Bears, but will likely make a final decision after speaking with the Bulldogs. Sam Walker scores for the Roosters against South Sydney. Getty The Walker development adds further intrigue to the storied rivalry between the foundation clubs. The Roosters would likely need to chip in part of Walker’s freight to get him to move immediately, given most clubs don’t have the salary cap space to get near his asking price. However, it’s unlikely the Roosters would subsidise a move to their fiercest rivals, as they did to get Brandon Smith off their roster. The Roosters could consider making a play for Graham given they have lost star outside backs Mark Nawaqanitawase (rugby) and Daniel Tupou (retirement).



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL investigates after Eels recruit Leniu allegedly abuses official Cody Walker is close to re-signing with Souths for next year, while other Rabbitohs halves options include Ashton Ward and Jayden Sullivan. Another is utility Jamie Humphreys, who this week signed a two-year contract extension. Prospective clubs are unlikely to be in a rush to take Walker, given the Roosters could continue to pay his salary until just before the 2027 season kicks off. Walker is one of 11 Kangaroos players who officially became free agents on November 1. The World Cup stars are likely to turn their attention to their long-term futures after the final against New Zealand on Sunday.

World.content:

A first home buyer raising her paddle for the first time won the keys to a one-bedroom apartment in Elizabeth Bay on Saturday, paying $760,000 at auction. As a crowd of about 40 people gathered on the footpath outside the art deco building, bidding for 6/39 Roslyn Gardens opened at $620,000. A further bid of $20,000 followed, then it fell into a steady rhythm of $5000 and $10,000 increments. When the price reached $735,000, auctioneer Dave McMahon declared the property was on the market. Five further bids of $5000 followed before the hammer fell. The opening bidder was also the person who eventually won the keys. She had been renting, but had more recently moved in with family in preparation for entering the property market.



Related Article Luxury property Five of the best Sydney homes with facades we love Six parties registered to bid with five active. Most of the underbidders were also first home buyers. The property had a guide of $700,000 and a reserve of $745,000, which was adjusted to $735,000 during the auction. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The apartment has retained many of its original features, including patterned ceilings and timberwork, and has been held as an investment for some time. Sales agent for BresicWhitney East, Melinda Antella said market conditions had created space for new buyers.



“There are some opportunities for first home buyers because they are not competing with investors,” she said. McMahon, the auctioneer, said while he expected little change in the market into 2027, buyer sentiment was linked to stability. “People are looking for more stability [in terms of] interest rate movement, but once we have clarity, it will give them confidence to enter the market,” he said. The apartment’s study enjoys a view of jacarandas. Sitthixay Ditthavong Most bidders took shelter under the trees on a hot and humid morning as auctioneer Dave McMahon competed with passing traffic and the occasional plane during the auction of 6/39 Roslyn Gardens. Sitthixay Ditthavong



The property was one of 646 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. At Mount Kuring-gai, a six-bedroom home passed in on Saturday when the sole bidder failed to attend, citing delays associated with Friday’s Microsoft outage. Two parties were expected to register to bid for 5 High Street, but the strongest bidder was not confident about doing so without seeing the requested changes in the contract documents before the auction. The Microsoft outage hit Australia early Friday morning and affected Copilot, Teams and Microsoft Outlook, resulting in issues accessing and sending emails.



“It all fell apart because the solicitors couldn’t talk to each other,” sales agent for Stone Real Estate, Dean Finch said. “I ended up having to send things through WhatsApp to get the changes requested. Related Article Architecture Renovate or detonate. How two heritage homes had very different fates “But they were still not confident [about bidding].” The auction was held but closed without a bid, although a second party arrived after the auction ended. Both groups were families from the wider local area. The property had a listed guide of $1.95 million and a reserve of $2.3 million.



The six-bedroom home has five bedrooms in the main house – three with ensuite bathrooms – and a self-contained studio above the garage. Finch is hoping to sell the two-storey Hamptons-inspired home in the next fortnight, but if he is unsuccessful, he said the vendors, who want to downsize, will rent it out. In Enmore, a two-bedroom apartment sold under the hammer for $1.34 million, $10,000 below the reserve. Five groups registered to bid for the keys to 7/159 Enmore Road, which is positioned just steps away from the popular Enmore Theatre.



Four parties actively participated with bidding opening at $1.25 million. It went up in increments of $10,000 and $20,000 until it reached $1.32 million. Ray White Erskineville agent Ercan Ersan then negotiated with the bidder to make an additional offer of $1.33 million, and it was called on the market. The opening bidders made a further bid of $10,000 and the property sold. The two-bedroom apartment is at the back of the block of the Encore on Enmore building and has views across to Chatswood Domain It had a guide of $1.3 million and a reserve of $1.35 million. The successful bidders were a brother and sister who plan to use the property as a city bolthole and rent it as short-term accommodation. The underbidder was a first home buyer bidding with the assistance of her mother.



Ersan said he had noticed more interest from investors in recent weeks. “My last three auctions all had some investor activity,” he said. “They tend to come back where they see value and prices have now reached that level. If we’re not [at the bottom of the market], we’re pretty bloody close.” Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: The wildest, most shocking moments from You Can See Everything – ranked
World.content:
CultureMoviesDocumentaries The wildest, most shocking moments from You Can See Everything – ranked Nell Geraets November 14, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Spoiler alert: This story references major plot-points in You Can See Everything. We all suspected Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, would be a wild ride. The buzz was inescapable since its top-secret premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, where critics described it as “one head-scratching scene after another”. A near perfect Rotten Tomatoes score and talk of a best picture Oscar run further confirmed our suspicions. But nothing could have properly prepared us for what was to come. Nathan Fielder (left) and Elizabeth Holmes (centre) in a scene from You Can See Everything. A24 Shot over 34 days, the documentary captures Holmes’ last moments with her family before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison for an 11-year sentence – while also attempting to get to the bottom of one key question: “Is she telling the truth?” The answer, it turns out, is far from black and white. After watching the documentary, it’s clear the term “head-scratcher” is an understatement. So, here are eight of the film’s most shocking moments, ranked from wild to “what the hell just happened?”.



8. Not one lie While sitting on the deck of Holmes’ rented San Diego home (which she shared with her partner Billy Evans and their two children before going to jail), Fielder asks Holmes if she has ever lied. She insists she hasn’t, not even an innocent white lie. It’s a perplexing moment that forces you to consider whether Holmes, a convicted fraudster, is lying about lying, or if her understanding of truth and deceit differ from others. Despite the absurdity of the claim, she still comes across as somewhat sincere, her wide-eyed look of innocence never breaking from Fielder’s piercing gaze. Even if she has lied before, it appears she genuinely believes she hasn’t. A manipulative liar or an unaware liar – it’s difficult to say which is more terrifying. 7. ‘FYI you can totally see everything’ Soon after claiming she’s never lied, Holmes sends Fielder a text from the beach. She’s only a few paces away, yet she decides to message him, typing “FYI you can totally see everything”. Beyond inspiring the documentary’s title, the message seems random and reeks of a desperation to prove there’s nothing to hide … Or is she genuinely promising total transparency? It’s one of several moments in which Holmes and Fielder share a quasi-intimate moment, further complicating the documentary’s objectivity. Loading



6. Shock revelation dismissed During a brief moment with Holmes’ parents, who are visiting before she begins her prison sentence, Holmes’ father tells Fielder he believes things changed for Holmes when she was raped during her college years. The conversation is brief, frank and entirely unexpected, leaving viewers desperate for elaboration. But it’s never addressed again, and Evans shuts the conversation down entirely shortly after. 5. Full-frontal nudity After a filmed gym session, Evans is captured in the shower – naked and in full view. It’s surprising, confronting and has you second-guessing Evans’ motivations. According to a Vulture interview with Oppenheim, Evans had undressed and stepped into the shower while the cameras were still rolling. However, an anonymous source told People that Evans reportedly felt his trust was violated over that scene, and that he had allegedly only agreed to it if they “kept it PG”. Once again, we’re left wondering if we’ve witnessed a simple misunderstanding or a carefully manipulated conflict.



4. Billy’s egg specificity Evans is an all-round peculiar bloke. Beside the fact that he encouraged total strangers to enter his family’s home during presumably one of the most harrowing periods of their lives, he also admits to being constantly armed (for safety), tells an A-list star that he’s “great at sex”, and cannot for the life of him allow Holmes to beat eggs her way. The latter arose when Holmes is speaking to Fielder while casually whisking eggs in a bowl. Midway through her sentence, Evans abruptly takes the bowl and proceeds to whisk them himself. Fielder addresses the awkward moment, and Holmes explains that Evans simply believes he can do it better. This idea of control returns later when Evans reveals he’s Holmes’ power of attorney and controls her X account while she’s imprisoned. Elizabeth Holmes, with partner Billy Evans, outside the court in 2022. Bloomberg Whether the documentary is intentionally framing him this way or not, Evans comes across as ego-driven and incredibly controlling. His love for Holmes appears genuine (verging into obsessive), but his yearning for exposure seems equally strong. It’s here that sympathy for Holmes begins to grow: Could she once again be caught under a domineering man’s spell (similar to the alleged situation with her ex-partner and Theranos president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani), pressured into saying and doing what ultimately suits him?



3. Who’s on first? Related Article Pop culture How tech geniuses became Hollywood’s favourite monster One of the most bizarre moments comes early in the documentary during a scene in the couple’s living room. Fielder shows Holmes and Evans the 1930s Abbott and Costello’s “who’s on first” comedy skit in an attempt to demonstrate Holmes’ occasionally misleading use of language. Earlier in the documentary, she’d failed to understand the issue around saying her blood-testing device “can” work when it could only theoretically work. Fielder believed the skit, which plays on the word “who” as both a name and pronoun, would clarify his earlier confusion. However, when asked if she understands why the skit is funny, Holmes said she does but then fails to explain why, and can’t point out the connection between the routine and their earlier conversation. She becomes so confused, overwhelmed – whatever her feelings are – that her eyes well with tears. Does she actually not understand the correlation (in which case, we’d pity her) or is it all part of a grand facade of innocence?



2. The Drop-in Given Amanda Seyfried is known for playing Holmes in the 2022 series The Dropout – a role she won an Emmy for – she certainly elicits gasps after suddenly appearing in the documentary’s “second act”. Holmes is in prison, so Fielder and Oppenheim invite Seyfried to watch some of their footage and act as a talking head of sorts. However, Seyfried unexpectedly ends up imitating Holmes, resuming her earlier award-winning role in a bizarre fiction/non-fiction hybrid. The filmmakers decide to go with it, reenacting earlier off-camera moments between Holmes and Fielder. Better yet, Wolf Man star Christopher Abbott plays Evans alongside her. Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. Hulu The reenactments, based entirely on Fielder’s memory of events, capture the fallibility of documentary-making and challenge the notion of truth. Is truth universally understood, and can documentaries ever be entirely objective? Seyfried herself adds an interesting perspective, as someone wrangling with the possibility that the person she embodied for months may (or may not) have been misunderstood.



Related Article Documentaries Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doco could make Oscars history. Here’s what to know before seeing it 1. The matter of payment Usually, documentary subjects do not receive payments as this would impact a production’s credibility. This doesn’t stop Evans from trying though. He asks A24 executives, Fielder and Oppenheim if he and Holmes could be paid for taking part. What makes this scene more intriguing is that it’s recreated using Seyfried as Holmes and Abbott as Evans, throwing into question whether Evans really was that upfront, and what kind of negotiations actually ensued (the documentary claims A24 agreed to pay them, but Evans rescinded his request post-filming). More intriguingly, Seyfried’s Holmes leaves the room to check on her baby before Evans makes the request. Once again, Holmes’ complicity is questioned. On one hand, she could have no idea about Evans’ desire for payment, meaning he’s yet again controlling the situation. Or (and there’s always an “or” in this documentary) Holmes is privy to the plan, and excuses herself intentionally to feign ignorance. She’s either an innocent bystander, frequently pulled into the orbit of domineering men, or she’s a manipulative liar. Come the end of the documentary, it’s still unclear. You Can See Everything is in cinemas now. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Out of the bubble: How a world-first gene therapy gave Matthew a second chance at life
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare Out of the bubble: How a world-first gene therapy gave Matthew a second chance at life Henrietta Cook November 14, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s the tail end of the flu season, and hundreds of shoppers are milling around a food court, searching for a bite to eat. Until recently, sitting among this lunchtime crowd could have killed Matthew Rozek. Matthew Rozek was born with a rare inherited immune disorder sometimes known as “bubble boy disease”. Joe Armao “It’s a big adjustment,” says the 29-year-old, who recently became one of the first people in the world to receive an experimental gene therapy that he hopes will cure him of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) or “bubble boy disease”. Born without a functional immune system, Rozek spent the first few years of his life largely inside a Melbourne hospital.



Everyday germs posed a constant threat. When chickenpox circulated through his primary school, he stayed home for weeks. Parties, shopping malls, flights, public transport and art galleries were off limits, especially during winter, when he retreated to the safety of his home “like a hermit”. The slightest sign of a scratchy throat triggered a wave of anxiety. Would he end up in hospital yet again, requiring intravenous antibiotics for an infection most people shake off within a few days? “Once I was in the teenage years, that’s when you notice that everyone else is normal and I’m not,” he says, sipping a hot chocolate in the food court of the Spencer Outlet Centre in Melbourne’s CBD. “There’s a lot of physical suffering, but mental suffering as well.”



Professor Shalin Naik corrected Rozek’s genetic mutation using a “blood in a dish” system. His life began to change a year ago in a Melbourne laboratory at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, where a research team led by Professor Shalin Naik, with Dr Miles Horton, corrected Rozek’s genetic mutation using a “blood in a dish” system. “We can very quickly take someone like Matthew’s blood, simulate his disease in a dish, and test these brand-new therapies that are coming out to see which one works,” Naik says. “Each person needs their own personalised gene therapy.” Every Australian child is now tested for SCID at birth through the newborn heel prick, and about six new cases are diagnosed a year.



Matthew Rozek is already starting to see the benefits of his gene-editing treatment for SCID. Joe Armao The devastating, life-shortening condition is widely known as “bubble boy disease” because of David Vetter, a Texan boy who was born with SCID in 1971 and spent almost the entirety of his 12 years inside a sterile plastic chamber. Vetter’s confronting situation attracted intense media attention around the world and inspired the movies The Boy in the Plastic Bubble, which starred John Travolta, and Bubble Boy, starring Jake Gyllenhaal. It also spawned comedic references in Seinfeld and The Simpsons. The standard long-term treatment for SCID is a bone marrow transplant from a matched donor, which can carry serious risks including graft failure and death. Rozek had a transplant as a toddler, but it gradually failed over time, leaving him with minimal immunity.



By adulthood, his health had deteriorated to the point where doctors warned he faced up to a 50 per cent chance of dying if he underwent a second bone marrow transplant. Rozek wasn’t prepared to take this risk. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Why doctors are writing medical scripts for fresh air In desperate search of another option, one of Rozek’s team of clinicians at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, Dr Samantha Chan, reached out to Dr Suk See DeRavin, an Australian researcher overseeing gene therapy trials at the US National Institutes of Health in Maryland. For three years, the two doctors corresponded by email, shipping samples of Rozek’s blood to the US on dry ice to test his eligibility for an upcoming trial. Rozek flew to Maryland last August to receive the experimental treatment at the National Institutes of Health.



After three weeks of medical tests and a full genetic panel, he underwent a two-day process called apheresis in which his stem cells were harvested through a line in his neck. Over the next month, scientists genetically edited those cells in a laboratory. He received chemotherapy to make room in his bone marrow for a 30-millilitre infusion of his repaired cells. This allowed his body to build the functioning immune system he was born without. “It’s just crazy that I still am alive,” Rozek says. “I just don’t know how the body can function without the immune system.” Chan says Rozek would have died without access to the trial. “There’s no doubt it’s been a huge success,” she says. “It offers hope at a normal life. Being able to offer them a solution that doesn’t carry the mortality rate of something like a stem cell transplant can be life-changing.”



Rare immune diseases can be devastating for families. Related Article Healthcare One in three babies with suspected peanut allergies cleared of the condition in landmark study “Fear of infection is really debilitating,” says Chan. “They want to be able to go to school, but then they’re afraid of bringing the virus home. It’s a really life-altering disease.” Walter and Eliza Hall Institute researchers are now working to bring similar treatments to Australia. Backed by a $5 million Medical Research Future Fund grant, Naik’s team is developing a way to package gene-editing machinery into microscopic mRNA droplets, similar to those used in COVID-19 vaccines.



This would allow doctors to repair a patient’s stem cells with a simple injection in the arm, avoiding the need for bone marrow transplants. Related Article Science ‘It’s a total game changer’: Australian breakthrough in DNA editing “It will encode the machinery that the patient needs to correct their mutation,” says Naik, who estimates his team is two to three years away from clinical trials. Rozek is already experiencing the benefits of his gene-editing treatment. For the first time in his life, he’s properly absorbing nutrients, which means he has gained a much-needed 10 kilograms.



Chronic gut infections had previously prevented his body from absorbing crucial vitamins and minerals from food. Related Article Good Weekend Matt dug in Patagonia. He made a priceless discovery about Earth’s biggest creatures Blood tests show his immune system is improving, allowing him to come off medications. The full benefits may not be seen for another few years. While the treatment has turned Rozek’s life around, it won’t reverse decades of damage inflicted on his body as a result of not having an immune system. A childhood infection has left him with about 70 per cent lung capacity, and he has ongoing issues with his bones as a result of being malnourished for so long.



“It won’t fully cure everything,” he says of the treatment. “But it was the easiest decision I’ve ever had to make.” It’s also allowed him to step back into normal life, and do many things that other people take for granted. Rozek, who runs agritech start-up Agtuary from his bedroom, recently attended a 300-person conference in Sydney. “I don’t want to jump into the deep end,” he says. “I’m taking it slow.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The workplace safety watchdog repeatedly warned the state government about the CFMEU’s escalating use of spurious danger claims to disrupt major projects, particularly the $10 billion West Gate Tunnel. WorkSafe Victoria’s chief health and safety officer Sam Jenkin’s claims in his submission to the royal commission into the construction industry cast fresh doubt on the government’s insistence it was unaware of the CFMEU’s conduct prior to this masthead’s Building Bad investigation in mid-2024. Ingrid Stitt’s department repeatedly warned her about the CFMEU’s conduct. Ruby Alexander Jenkin described regular high-level meetings with then-minister Ingrid Stitt and her staff as one of the ways WorkSafe communicated the CFMEU’s disruption of major projects using unfounded safety claims – particularly on the West Gate Tunnel, which was beset by delays and cost blowouts. “These issues were recorded within WorkSafe in weekly email updates and highlighted in written and oral briefings to the minister’s office, including by the CEO personally,” he said.



Related Article Big Build royal commission Big Build royal commission as it happened: Construction boss says work sites have become ‘more combative’ as unions battle for territory Jenkin’s evidence follows the release of multiple briefing notes from senior bureaucrats seeking to warn then-minister in charge of the major projects, Jacinta Allan, of costly and significant problems caused by the CFMEU. Asked by the commission to reflect on events in 2021 and 2022, Jenkin said WorkSafe had regularly observed CFMEU officials entering projects over matters that “appeared not to relate to genuine safety concerns” as part of the industrial battle it was fighting with the Australian Workers Union. “So far as ‘patterns’ are concerned, although it is highly unlikely that WorkSafe could have proved such matters in a court, CFMEU aligned [officials] may have been raising safety concerns to advance industrial and other interests, including with employers and during a demarcation dispute with a rival union, the Australian Workers’ Union,” he said. “As a general rule … they arose earlier, more consistently and were most pronounced at the West Gate Tunnel Project.”



On several occasions, he said, WorkSafe suggested the officials should be removed by Victoria Police as they were trespassing. Jenkin said another noted pattern was that CFMEU issues “arose with a greater degree of frequency, or intensity, when time-critical works were due to occur” such as road closures or public transport shutdowns. Jenkin said WorkSafe’s chairman and chief executive were among those who briefed Stitt. Loading



“The minister was also briefed on an ongoing basis, including in writing by weekly reports to the minister’s office, on an ad hoc basis when specific incidents occurred, and on a number of occasions, in person by the CEO,” he said. Jenkin said although the Gap Road level crossing removal was of less concern to WorkSafe than the West Gate Tunnel, the agency was asked to brief Stitt on June 6, 2022, at the height of the Gap Road dispute that has occupied the opening week of witness examinations at the royal commission. The West Gate Tunnel was beset by delays and blowouts. He said WorkSafe had not been able to identify Stitt’s response to the briefing, which he said was not unusual. “The 6 June meeting followed earlier meetings in April and May of 2022 at which WorkSafe was requested to advise on similar issues. Notes prepared at the time include a reference to the Gap Road Site, although the majority of communication concerned the West Gate Tunnel Project, where union issues were more pronounced from WorkSafe’s perspective,” he said.



“WorkSafe was regularly requested to advise on issues relating to CFMEU activity on Major [Major Transport Infrastructure Authority] Projects with the Minister for Workplace Safety between June and August 2022, including as part of written weekly reports and at least one meeting on 6 June 2022.” Editor's pick Analysis

Big Build royal commission The company memo that goes to the heart of the Big Build royal commission The WorkSafe chief executive held monthly meetings throughout 2022 with Stitt, which were usually also attended by her chief of staff and a policy adviser. Jenkin said despite WorkSafe inspectors increasingly being called to these projects, they did not have the power to act as an umpire in industrial disputes and had little ability to remove union officials acting improperly. Additionally, there was also “marked hostility” towards WorkSafe from the CFMEU during the period, when the union published highly critical social media posts naming WorkSafe staff, which had resulted in death threats.

World.title: ‘Overloaded’: US flight grounding leaves days of travel chaos in its wake
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAirports ‘Overloaded’: US flight grounding leaves days of travel chaos in its wake Michael Koziol Updated November 14, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published November 14, 2026 — 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: The US is facing days of travel chaos after an extraordinary nationwide order grounded all flight departures for more than four hours, prompting the cancellation of more than 8000 services and delays to thousands more. The Trump administration blamed old and “overloaded” technical infrastructure for the failure, and used it to demand the US Congress appropriate $US50 billion ($74 billion) for new systems, warning that without it, the outage was likely to happen again. Loading The shutdown on a Friday afternoon (Washington time) caused havoc at airports, with airlines cancelling more than 8000 flights, according to flight-tracking service FlightRadar24. Thousands more were delayed, and hold-ups were set to continue throughout the weekend. The ground stop order meant flights in the air could land, but those on the ground could not take off. The disruption quickly spread beyond the US, forcing the cancellation of flights from Canada and Europe. US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day.



Flights departing Australia for the US were temporarily halted before resuming once the order was lifted. Some international flights were able to depart the US despite the shutdown. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”. Planes are parked at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas during the national ground stop. AP Later, at a news conference at the White House, he said the FAA shut the system down after intermittent communications and radar failures in critical air traffic control systems. “It wasn’t a complete blackout ... but when you have issues, and you can’t immediately communicate and immediately see where aircraft are at, that’s a risk that we are unwilling to tolerate,” Duffy said.



He said the failure was caused by an overloaded system, which relies on outdated technology including floppy disks and replacement parts that occasionally have to be purchased on eBay. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy said. “I shouldn’t say ‘went down’ – they started to give us inconsistency in the data. And because of that, we shut the system down. “We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded.” US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy (left) and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin brief media at the White House. AP Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that a cyberattack was to blame for the problem, nor the involvement of a rogue artificial intelligence system. Nothing could be conclusively ruled out at this stage, he said, though he stressed that there was no connection to the outage that hit Microsoft systems the previous day.



Duffy said technicians developed a fix that reduced the overloading on the network switches. “Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem.” Last year, US Congress approved $US12.5 billion to fix the FAA’s ageing communications system, and on Friday – before the communications problem – the FAA and White House asked Congress for another $US30.1 billion to address other issues. Duffy said he now wanted $US50 billion. New switches installed during the Trump administration did not fail, he said – only the old ones. “This is an emergency,” he said. “I want Congress to give us emergency funding.” Passengers wait at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as flights are delayed. AP The lines for rideshares and taxis at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. AP



The FAA has also begun rolling out an AI tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) to help manage air traffic across the country. The rollout, which began in Washington in September, was expanded to other areas only days ago. Asked whether Friday’s issues could be AI-related, Mullin reminded a reporter: “We call it SI around here, remember.” The Trump administration has attempted to rename artificial intelligence to superintelligence. Loading The ground stop was issued at about 4pm Washington time and lifted at 8.15pm (12.15pm Saturday AEDT), lasting a little more than four hours. But the delays are set to continue into the weekend as airlines try to move the backlog of passengers whose travel was disrupted. Duffy said he expected the system to return to normal operations by next Friday. That weekend marks the start of the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel period.



Duffy said he expected the system to return to normal operations by next Friday. That weekend marks the start of the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel period. It was only the third time in US history that a nationwide ground stop has been ordered; the first was during the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and the other was in 2023 when the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system failed. The 2023 problem lasted about 12 hours in total, though departures started to resume after about 90 minutes. Luggage chaos at Los Angeles International Airport. AP Travellers settle in for a long wait at New York’s LaGuardia Airport. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy On Friday afternoon, passengers from New York to Los Angeles, and Chicago to Atlanta waited at crowded gates and terminals while their aircraft remained parked at the gates, and staff had little information about what would happen next.



In some cases, passengers were forced to wait on their planes on the tarmac, with customers sending messages to the airlines on social media begging to be allowed to return to the terminal. Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: Departures to resume as FAA lifts ground directive after citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’; Homeland Security secretary denies cyberattack, Microsoft outage connection Dennis Lennox, a Republican strategist, was on a plane on the tarmac at MBS International Airport in Michigan when the ground stop was ordered. He was due to fly to Detroit and onwards to Los Angeles. “We had backed out of the gate and were starting to go through the taxiing process to take off, and we were ordered to return to the gate,” he said. “The initial report was there were radio issues in this area. Within a minute or two, I was able to find out things quicker. We weren’t even given the chance to stay on the plane. We were kicked off the plane and dumped inside the terminal.”



Related Article Need to know

Airports Here’s what we know about the US flight shutdown – and what it means for travel Other passengers gave up early in the evening and went home or booked hotels. At Washington’s Ronald Reagan National Airport, Madeline DeMaske said the price of hotels increased over the two hours she was waiting, and there was an Uber pricing surge. “This delay is going to cost me several hundred dollars,” she said. Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell told Fox News the ground stop was a sensible measure to “declutter the airspace” and deal with the technical issue. “The ground stop, while a real pain in the neck, is the safest way to go,” he said. World.title: Warner makes bombshell sandpapergate claim involving Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon
World.content:
Updated SportCricketBall tampering Warner makes bombshell sandpapergate claim involving Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon Andrew Wu Updated November 14, 2026 — 3:28pm ,first published 1:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

David Warner has accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal. In another explosive escalation of the saga that has rocked Australian sport, Warner took to Instagram to claim the governing body did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon as part of its investigation in the days after the Cape Town Test of 2018. David Warner appeared on a Kayo Sports panel on Friday. The former opener has thrown his weight behind friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja. AAP Warner made the claim early on Saturday afternoon, a day after he accused Test captain Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja under the bus after the release of his memoir, Sabr. “As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” Warner posted to Instagram.



“If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know? David Warner’s post to Instagram on Saturday. Instagram “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose, and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up.” This masthead has reached out to representatives of Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon for comment. Cricket Australia released a statement in response to Warner’s allegation, saying the organisation respected the differing recollections among the 2018 playing group.



The statement did not say if any of the three players were interviewed by investigator Iain Roy. “As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation [into the ball-tampering saga] and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a CA spokesman said. “Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players’ right to provide their own version of events.” Loading CA chief Todd Greenberg said this week the governing body would not be reopening the investigation, despite Khawaja’s allegations.



Warner hit out at Cummins on Friday, just hours after his former Test captain delivered an extraordinary 69-minute press conference denying any knowledge of the sandpaper plot. “Pat Cummins was very well-prepared this morning and I still stick by what Uzzy [Usman Khawaja] said, what he’s written in that book,” Warner told Fox Cricket. “That is the truth and I really, really support him [Khawaja]. I’m actually feeling for him at the moment. “I actually feel that the captain today actually threw Uzzy under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that. “Each person is going to have their differences, but I’m not going to accept them until the truth is out there.” Earlier on Saturday, former Pakistan captain and legendary swing bowler Wasim Akram – whose family is based in Melbourne – took to X to give his take on Sandpapergate.



“I saw Pat Cummins, who’s a very close friend of mine, [a] great cricketer, one of the top leaders in world cricket, the way he leads his team from the front, and he said he didn’t know [about any plot to tamper with the ball],” Akram said. “It’s my opinion, and it can be right or wrong, but as a bowler, when the cricket ball comes in my hand, either it’s the fifth over, either it’s in the 10th over, either it’s in the 50th over – the old ball – where you look after the ball, you shine the one side if it’s a dry day, a dry square, you one-bounce throw [in from the outfield], you get it scratched a bit, but the sandpaper scratch is totally different than the one-bounce scratch. “As a cricket lover, if you want to check, grab a semi-new cricket ball, grab sandpaper, and rub it in – you know the scratches are totally different. “Again, like I said, I’m not taking anybody’s side … Australians are known and famous for their straightforwardness, hardness on the field, off the field, and, most importantly, honesty.”



Khawaja, who has not spoken publicly since Cummins’ press conference, was due to appear on The Grade Cricketer podcast on Sunday, but that interview has been postponed until Thursday. He was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands in western Sydney on Saturday, but publisher Penguin said it too had been postponed. The former Test opener is scheduled to play in the T20 Gold Clash exhibition game in Cairns on November 22. He’s been named to play alongside the likes of Brian Lara, Adam Gilchrist, Matthew Hayden and Michael Hussey against a team featuring former AFL and NRL stars. World.title: Rabbitohs meet with Roosters halfback Sam Walker
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Rabbitohs meet with Roosters halfback Sam Walker Adrian Proszenko November 14, 2026 — 3:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
