South Sydney officials have met with Sam Walker in a bid to lure the premiership-winning halfback from arch rivals the Roosters. Sources not authorised to speak publicly said the Rabbitohs had met with Walker in Brisbane, where he is part of the Kangaroos World Cup squad. Walker remains contracted to the premiers until the end of next year, but they are prepared to get him off the books immediately after contract extension talks spectacularly unravelled two weeks ago after the Queensland half requested additional time to consider the deal. Sam Walker could be on the move. Getty Images The Rabbitohs are open to the prospect of taking Walker straight away, but don’t have the salary cap space to meet his contract figure of about $1 million a year. While several high-profile Rabbitohs are off contract from 2028 – including Latrell Mitchell, Campbell Graham and Jack Wighton – none of them have been asked to make way immediately.



PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters has stated there is interest in Walker after the club missed out on Panthers superstar Nathan Cleary and Titans youngster Zane Harrison. Canterbury has also been touted as a potential contender for Walker, if Matt Burton seeks an immediate release to join Perth. Burton has a three-year deal on the table from the Bears, but will likely make a final decision after speaking with the Bulldogs. Sam Walker scores for the Roosters against South Sydney. Getty The Walker development adds further intrigue to the storied rivalry between the foundation clubs. The Roosters would likely need to chip in part of Walker’s freight to get him to move immediately, given most clubs don’t have the salary cap space to get near his asking price. However, it’s unlikely the Roosters would subsidise a move to their fiercest rivals, as they did to get Brandon Smith off their roster. The Roosters could consider making a play for Graham given they have lost star outside backs Mark Nawaqanitawase (rugby) and Daniel Tupou (retirement).



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL investigates after Eels recruit Leniu allegedly abuses official Cody Walker is close to re-signing with Souths for next year, while other Rabbitohs halves options include Ashton Ward and Jayden Sullivan. Another is utility Jamie Humphreys, who this week signed a two-year contract extension. Prospective clubs are unlikely to be in a rush to take Walker, given the Roosters could continue to pay his salary until just before the 2027 season kicks off. Walker is one of 11 Kangaroos players who officially became free agents on November 1. The World Cup stars are likely to turn their attention to their long-term futures after the final against New Zealand on Sunday.

World.title: Sculpture on 10-year loan to Kaikōura to combat 'negative attitude' towards fur seals
World.content:
Seals are often misunderstood in Kaikōura's marine environment, local artist Ben Foster says.

Foster is loaning his sculpture 'Kekeno' (New Zealand fur seal) to the Kaikōura District Council for 10 years, in a bid to raise awareness about respecting Kaikōura's marine environment.

''There's often a negative attitude towards seals and I want to change that.''

Kekeno was first designed in 2009 for an exhibition hosted by an art gallery in Auckland, with the theme to create a work which ''represented your environment'', Foster said.

He hopes the sculpture, installed in Kaikōura's West End on Thursday, November 5, becomes a focal point and reminds people to give wildlife some space.

Made out of marine-grade stainless steel, the sculpture ''literally reflects its environment''.

''I'm hoping it will help people to see themselves as part of the environment and not separate from it.''

Kaikōura District Council chief executive Will Doughty said Foster's generosity in making the sculpture available to the community on a 10-year loan was ''absolutely incredible''.

Ben Foster’s ‘Kekeno’ sculpture now features in Kaikōura’s West End. Supplied by Ben Foster

''It touches on an area of environment close to his heart and hopefully it will raise some awareness.

''It will be a fantastic addition for people to enjoy, both visitors and locals alike.''

As a contemporary sculptor, Foster draws upon the physical landscape of his home, with his abstract figurative works mirroring the dramatic surroundings of the Kaikōura mountains and sea.

As a surfer, diver and climber, he enjoys interacting with the local environment and has a particular affinity for the seal.

''I hold the seals in high regard, so this was a beautiful representation of this environment for me personally.''

As a trustee of the Kaikōura Wildlife Centre Trust, Foster hopes to create awareness and inspire a sense of community guardianship in the region.

In a growing community focused on tourism, advocacy and sustainability are critical, Foster said.

Once hunted to near extinction, New Zealand fur seals have recovered from 10,000 individuals to 200,000 since legislation was passed to protect them in 1978.

But numbers are still only five to 10 percent of the historic population numbering two to three million nationwide.

The seals remain threatened by fisheries depletion, bycatch, boat strike, climate change, disease, marine debris and human disturbance.

Their scarcity means seals are misunderstood, Foster said.

"For decades post-fur sealing, seals no longer remained in the region.

''Pre the 1960s, local generations lived in an environment completely devoid of seals.

''So to some their gradual return may seem like a new species has turned up, or they're taking too many fish, when they have always belonged here and used to persist in far greater numbers."

At sites such as Point Kean on the Kaikōura Peninsula, seals are a visitor attraction, with encroachment being a daily occurrence.

While Department of Conservation guidelines require a viewing distance from seals of 20 metres, people are often observed approaching or disturbing seals to take photos.

World.title: Health expert accuses NZ Food Safety of 'very poor' performance over campylobacter rates
World.content:
A leading public health expert is accusing the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) of not protecting consumers from contaminated fresh chicken meat.

Professor of Public Health at the University of Otago Michael Baker said the performance of MPI's food safety unit, New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS), had been "very poor".

He said the country not being close to eliminating campylobacter infection from raw chicken was a "regulatory failure".

In a press release this week, NZFS warned against washing uncooked chicken, while announcing a new goal to lower the campylobacter infection rate by 15 percent (from 76 to 65 cases per 100,000 people) by 2030.

NZFS deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said many people incorrectly thought washing raw chicken made it safer to eat.

"In fact, washing chicken increases the risk of getting sick. That's because, when you rinse raw chicken under the tap, bacteria such as Campylobacter can be spread in water droplets onto sinks, benches, utensils and other foods around the kitchen."

But Baker said the onus should not be on the public.

"Putting out a media release telling consumers, 'Don't wash your chicken'. Is that it? They have to do better than that."

"There's a whole list of behaviours we'd have to change to make [raw chicken] even remotely safe in the kitchens of New Zealand. Even if you're very careful, you can still make mistakes.

"I think it's more responsible for our food safety regulator to put more effort into possibly not entirely eliminating but significantly reducing contamination of fresh chicken. We've got an industry that has huge sales of fresh chilled chicken, which is often contaminated, and that's what has caused this preventable foodborne epidemic."

Professor of Public Health at the University of Otago Michael Baker. Supplied

Baker wanted MPI to require poultry producers to label how heavily contaminated their product was.

"Consumers can then say, I'm not so keen on buying that heavily contaminated fresh chicken. I'd rather buy the one that has got very low or no contamination. That would be one way of giving the market and good producers an incentive to get this right."

Baker said a 2018 study he co-authored found consumers had "huge gaps in their knowledge" about preparing chicken meat safely, including that a majority did not know it should not be washed.

His study recommended safety labels indicating that a product was contaminated with campylobacter.

"I think it's very reasonable to have a labelling requirement as we have on other hazardous goods and services."

He said contaminated fresh chicken meat caused an estimated 77 percent of human campylobacter infections, and resulted in upwards of 500 hospitalisations and tens of thousands of community illnesses each year.

Symptoms included stomach cramps, diarrhoea, and vomiting, which could last for a week or longer.

Baker said a Public Health Communication Centre (PHCC) analysis from 2025, which he was the lead author of, showed hospitalisation rates for campylobacter infection increased by almost 70 percent in 17 years.

"If you look at the numbers since when we had an independent regulator, I think that's a very robust indicator that we're not succeeding here."

He said the former New Zealand Food Safety Authority, which was amalgamated in 2010, was very successful.

"They introduced a big programme of work to try and cut down the contamination levels of fresh chicken leaving the processor, and it was one of the most successful programmes in the world. It halved the rate of human disease in just three months.

"But that's almost 20 years ago now, and since then, rates [of campylobacter infection from fresh chicken] have stayed very high by world standards. They may even be increasing at the moment based on the rise of hospitalisations."

Food Safety deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle. Supplied / MPI

But Arbuckle said between 2006 and 2020 reported rates of foodborne campylobacter infections had halved and that they had decreased by a further 20 percent since then.

He said its figures were based on public notifications of infections provided by the health system.

He said it was working with the Ministry of Health to "better understand the drivers behind changes in hospitalisation rates over time".

"It's notable that campylobacteriosis case rates are dropping, which suggests that there are other reasons behind some hospitalisations, such as people deciding to delay looking for medical care, changes in the way that people access primary health care, and changes in definitions of hospital care over time."

But Baker believed MPI was missing the mark as a food safety regulator.

"MPI has two very different briefs. One is to support the agriculture sector, which is great, and we all applaud that. But whether they can also at the same time be the regulator of food safety, I think their performance at the moment suggests that they shouldn't be.

"There are very few other infectious disease problems that are coming from just one source, one contaminated food. This problem can be ended very rapidly in New Zealand, and it is a choice."

Arbuckle said that while Food Safety welcomed changes that would contribute to reducing campylobacter infection rates, it was not convinced labels were necessary.

Campylobacter jejuni bacteria 123rf

He said its 2023 Consumer Insights Survey indicated most consumers had a high level of awareness of the risks associated with raw chicken.

"We're not alone in our approach to labelling. Most other countries also do not require raw chicken to be labelled.

"Before making any changes to rules, we need to be sure that the benefits outweigh the costs. There's no evidence that labelling would have a significant benefit, and the costs, including to consumers, are not known."

He said the press release about its 'Skip the Wash' campaign Baker was referring to was just one way it was responding to the problem and educating consumers.

"NZFS has worked with supermarkets to ensure that this message also reaches consumers where they are buying raw chicken over the summer period, which is when we typically see a spike in case numbers.

"We know the increase in cases is partly due to more people gathering to eat and cook outdoors in warmer weather."

He said Food Safety had led changes to the way the industry processed poultry, including making changes to the equipment used and applying an antimicrobial wash.

World.title: Have I made an investing mistake? Ask Susan
World.content:
I am a single, mid-30s female. About a month-and-a-half ago, I started a new permanent job with a significant pay cut.

I also invested a significant amount (about 30 percent) of my life savings ($200,000-plus) in managed funds, with about 50 percent in balanced, 25 percent in growth and 25 percent in global share funds (high risk). I felt like I had done my research when taking out these investments and that I wouldn't need access to the funds within the next three years.

I had been planning to transfer more money into these investments each payday, but since opening these investments, the value has now dropped. This is causing me a lot of anxiety and fear that I might lose a lot of money that I worked hard for, and can't afford to lose.

Added to this is the large component tech stocks have in the US share markets, and political and global economic uncertainty.

I have stopped contributing to my investment funds and am too scared to look at the balances. I know that you cannot time the market - it's about time in the market.

I feel like I overestimated my risk appetite, but I also know that it's too late to change my funds to lower risk funds, as I would be realising a loss. Plus, if you are going to change the fund type, you should only do it once.

I also have KiwiSaver, which is high growth. I have seen the balance of this fluctuate over time (eg during Covid and with the recent oil crisis), but this hasn't caused me the anxiety and fear like my new investment funds have.

Are you able to please provide any advice or reassurance (or otherwise!) for my situation? I thought I might restart my contributions or take out some short term PIEs, after the OCR announcement, and elections here and the US, but I am feeling anxious that I will make another poor decision.

I don't think you've made as poor a decision as you think you have. Everything you've done actually looks fine to me and it sounds like you just need to keep going.

Koura founder Rupert Carlyon agrees with me and says you seem quite switched on, although you are suffering normal anxieties.

"She has done her risk assessment properly and has made it clear that she will not be taking any money out for at least three years, which is good.

"One thing worth thinking about is whether she will be withdrawing everything in three years or only a part of it. If it is all in three years, then she might want to think about whether the global share allocation is appropriate.

"Over the next few years, she can expect some material ups and downs. She has already been through this with her KiwiSaver and her managed funds will not be different at all.

"If she is truly invested for the long term - longer than the three years, in my view - she might want to take advantage of the falling prices and invest in the markets while they are down."

Carlyon is correct that, if you are investing when prices are down, you have an opportunity to benefit from the recovery, when it comes. Provided your strategy is still appropriate for your goals and risk profile, I would stick with your plans, if I were you.

I am in my 80s. I have no living relatives, so I sold my house and have been spending most of the money I received from the sale on things I couldn't afford before.

I am now living comfortably in a flat. I have a reasonable amount left, after ticking off all the things on my 'bucket list'. What I'd like to know is whether or not I should donate to my favourite charities now, so I can see the good results, or leave the bequests until I die.

Should I require rest home care in the future, can any monies I've donated be clawed back?

I asked the Ministry of Social Development about this. General group manager of service delivery Shannon Soughtton said, when someone applied for the rest home subsidy, a range of factors were assessed, including income and assets.

"This assessment is complex and is done on a case-by-case basis, looking at the individual person or couple's circumstances. However, all donations, including to charities, are assessed under the gifting rules for residential care subsidy asset testing.

"We won't count up to $8500 of assets gifted each year in the last five years, from when the subsidy application is made. This is a total of $42,500 gifted in the last five years.

"In terms of gifted assets from longer than five years ago, we won't count up to $27,000 a year of assets that are gifted or donated.

"Everyone's situation is different and we strongly encourage people to get in touch with us, if they want to understand how donations may affect their eligibility for the residential care subsidy."

Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

World.title: Moa Point treatment plant restarts after months of repairs
World.content:
The Moa Point wastewater treatment plant has restarted, following months of recovery work after catastrophic flooding in February.

Wellington's water agency Tiaki Wai says the restart of the plant is part of a gradual recommissioning process, with wastewater from central and southern Wellington progressively returning to treatment at the plant.

Tiaki Wai chief executive Mike Brewster says getting the plant operating at full capacity will take time as it re-establishes biological treatment processes.

The agency says that process may result in residents occasionally noticing odours coming from the plant.

It will monitor the water quality daily throughout the recommissioning period.

Wellington surfer Jamie McCaskill said he "looked forward to getting some barrels when there's no poos in the way".

"It's kept a lot of people out of the water, but a lot of us still just went in there, which is not ideal," the Wellington Boardriders committee member said. "I've swallowed the water a few times, I'll tell you that.

"Sometimes, there was a yellow, foamy substance sitting on the water, which kind of stuck to your wetsuit, so you knew you were swimming in... waste. We always made sure we had our hoods on or earplugs in."

Asked why he kept getting in the water: "Well, surfing's an addiction," he laughed.

McCaskill hoped the kaimoana would become edible again, as the bay's health improved.

World.title: Businesses suffering a loss from Microsoft outage could have grounds for insurance claim, lawyer says
World.content:
While the economic impact of the global Microsoft outage could be in the billions, a lawyer says businesses may have a chance to get their money back through insurance.

The outage affected Microsoft 365, a cloud-based subscription service popular for applications like Outlook, Copilot, and Teams. On Saturday morning, the company confirmed the technical problems were finally easing.

Barrister John Gibbered, who specialises in insurance law, said businesses whose insurance policies include "business interruption" could well have a claim with their insurer.

"Business interruption is when an unexpected or unforeseen occurs which prevents a business from carrying out its normal activities.

"As a result of the interruption, the business suffers a loss."

Making a claim to Microsoft would be more difficult, he said.

"Those claims are rarer and harder to establish, but in theory, such a claim would be possible."

Gobbard said moving forward, businesses should be reading terms and conditions thoroughly, and weighing up the damage an outage could cause.

"This is the lesson from today, that businesses need to check they have good system and processes in place to ensure that their businesses can continue even when events like this occur."

AUT associate professor of computer and information sciences, Kenneth Johnson, said as businesses become more reliant on Microsoft platforms, they have to accept some risk for outages.

Johnson said the outage could lead to a loss in productivity.

He said businesses could set up alternative contact pathways - like using personal email addresses.

World.title: Russia sets cull limits to help control bear population after attacks kill 36 people
World.content:
The Russian government has established a cull of up to 30 percent of brown bear populations to keep numbers in check after bear attacks killed 36 people this year, the Ministry of Natural Resources was quoted as saying on Friday.

A ministry statement, quoted by the state RIA news agency, said the limit sought to better control bear populations and reduce the number of attacks, and was already registered with Russia's Justice Ministry.

"Since the beginning of the year, more than 12,000 reports have been received in Russia about brown bears approaching people. There have been 87 attacks, with 36 people killed," RIA quoted the ministry as saying.

"In view of the situation, a decision was taken to remove limits and set a maximum quota for culling at 30 percent of the brown bear population in each region."

The RIA report gave no indication when the cull was to begin or how long it was to remain in effect.

The figure for deaths was one more than reported earlier this week by RIA following the killing of a security guard at a holiday camp in the far eastern Kamchatka peninsula.

The ministry put Russia's bear population at 308,000 and said culling quotas varied from region to region, including 14 percent on Kamchatka and 19 percent in western Siberia's Krasnoyarsk region.

The ministry allocated funds totalling more than the equivalent of NZ$1.75 million to finance the cull of bears known to approach people and feed at landfills.

According to government data, the brown bear population has more than doubled in the last three decades, in part due to shorter and milder winters.

World.title: RNZ chief executive Paul Thompson announces early departure from organisation
World.content:
RNZ CEO Paul Thompson is to leave the organisation on Monday, six weeks early, after controversy over a financial blowout at the public broadcaster.

Thompson, RNZ's CEO for 13 years and a former president of the global Public Media Alliance, was due to leave on December 31.

In a statement this morning, Thompson said he felt it was best for himself, his family and RNZ to leave.

Thompson made a bombshell announcement on Monday that RNZ was facing a shock $12 million loss and will axe 58 jobs - around one in six staff.

It has seen questions raised about whether his position was tenable and protests planned by staff unions.

The broadcaster's chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigned unexpectedly in October.

The $11.8m loss is more than 25 times the $470,000 RNZ had expected to lose over the year to June.

RNZ has commissioned an independent review of how it got its finances wrong.

RNZ chairman Brent Impey - who was appointed to the Board of Directors in 2024 and became chair in July - said Thompson had responded to a difficult situation "with courage and integrity".

"As I said on Tuesday, I have considerable empathy for him as a chief executive who was provided with inaccurate financial information. He has responded to a difficult situation with courage and integrity.

"We wish him all the best."

Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Media and Communications Minister Paul Goldsmith said it "was the right thing to do".

His office said there was no indication of him stepping in over RNZ's governance decisions at this stage.

Associate Finance Minister David Seymour, a shareholding minister in RNZ, also welcomed the decision.

"I hope the board will reflect carefully on this recent period and make their next appointments very carefully.

"The chief executive is responsible for the performance of the company, and RNZ has fallen well short of what taxpayers have a right to expect.

"The people who suffer most from that underperformance are the hard-working staff and the public who fund it."

Earlier this week Thompson was questioned by Checkpoint's Lisa Owen if he should quit early but pushed back saying, the government had reduced RNZ's funding.

"We thought we were addressing that. We weren't."

In a statement to staff today, Thompson said it had been a privilege to lead RNZ.

"The last few weeks have, of course, been difficult. As Chief Executive and Editor-in-Chief I take responsibility for the financial issues we are dealing with. It is a sad note to end on. I will contribute to the independent review to help ensure RNZ robustly examines what went wrong and identifies improvements."

He said he was proud of work to modernize the organisation, "including leading on trust, diversifying and growing audiences and content, improving journalism and connecting with more New Zealanders than ever before".

He said public media played a vital role and urged staff to keep up "the great and important work".

World.title: A friendship forged on the rugby league fields of New Zealand a century ago
World.content:
Awhina Hetet and Rita McRae Kingi share a drink on a blistering November day, on the balcony of Awhina's Logan business.

The women and their families met and became close mates in Brisbane, after moving to the city from Rotorua and Marton and in New Zealand.

But the families' close bond was first forged more than a century ago, on the rugby league fields of New Zealand.

Awhina's great-great-great grandfather Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Māori All Stars in 1909.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Rita's great-great grandfather Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae was a coach, captain, and player.

The players had all anglicised their names before making the trip across the ditch for the campaign 117 years ago.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet (far left) was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909 and Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae (far right) was a coach, captain, and player. (Supplied)

"New Zealand was a nation of union players," Awhina says. "When they came over in 1909 to Australia … we brought with us our haka, our culture. They had two guides with them … they came with a campaign to show, 'this is who we are, we're Māori. We love this game.'"

"You see how proud they are and I think our people absolutely displayed that proudness when they put on the shirt."

Rob Hetet, Awhina Hetet, Rita McRae King, Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi and Harley Kingi. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

One of the guides was Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator who was posthumously awarded a Master of Philosophy in Anthropology from the University of Oxford.

Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator, was a guide. (Supplied)

At the time, rugby league was struggling financially in Australia. But the Aussie-Kiwi clashes attracted more than 30,000 to their games.

The Maori side left victorious, taking the cup back to New Zealand. It is now in the care of Awhina's family "in an undisclosed location," she laughs, in New Zealand.

Rob Hetet with the 1909 cup. (Supplied)

"That cup's still standing, it's one of the oldest rugby league cups in existence," she says.

"Beautiful history," adds her father, Rob Hetet. "That's probably why I am really passionate."

The Hetet family also has distant links to star Kiwi player Kalyn Ponga, who is part of the starting side for the World Cup Final in Brisbane this Sunday.

Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi, Harley Kingi and Rob Hetet. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The Hetet and McRae families will be in the stands at Lang Park, with a closer link to the game than most other revellers.

"It's been 13 years since we were in the finals," says Awhina.

"Our boys have been amazing throughout this whole campaign … may the best team win!"

World.title: Australia wins six Youth Olympics medals as African Games hailed
World.content:
Australia has come away from the 2026 Youth Olympic Games with six medals as Senegal held up its hands for the Olympic movement in Africa.

The Dakar Games were the first Olympic event to be hosted in Africa, with organisers hailing the success as further proof of the continent's ability to host major international competitions.

South Africa, which staged the men's FIFA World Cup in 2010, is among countries in talks with the IOC about hosting the 2036 Olympic Games.

Nearly 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 competed across 25 sports and 153 medal events over two weeks in Senegal.

"I think that everyone came here with certain expectations and I think those expectations have been far exceeded," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said on Thursday.

"It has been an magnificent journey. It has been extremely magical.

"I think we've shown the world the capability that we have and now we need to choose to take that forward," the Zimbabwean two-time Olympic champion added.

Australia's six medals included four silvers and two bronzes.

Boxer Marley Dodd claimed silver in the men's 55kg event, while Mackenzie Macdonald claimed Australia's first ever taekwondo Youth Olympic Games medal in the 49kg category.

Marley Dodd won silver on the penulimate day of the competition. (Supplied: AOC)

Australia's cyclists excelled, with Elsie Apps winning silver and Caleb McKenzie bronze on the same day in the women's and men's road races.

Tasmania's McKenzie, who was diagnosed with the autoimmune illness Hashimoto’s disease earlier this year, led the race via a brave breakaway right up until the final lap before sprinting for bronze.

"I wasn't on the bike for a long time," McKenzie told Olympics.com.

"I couldn't ride my bike, I couldn't train and nothing really went well for me.

Caleb McKenzie rode in the breakaway for the majority of the men's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

"I finally pulled it together at the end of this year and had a really good ride. I had the confidence. We talked about it before we raced about having confidence in yourself, and we said, 'If you believe, you achieve'."

Apps, meanwhile, sprinted to silver.

"I'm so grateful for the opportunity that I was given to be able to go out there and get a medal," Apps said.

"It's been really inspiring. To have a little taste of what it would be like, it really makes you want more and hopefully I can make it there [to Brisbane 2032]."

Elsie Apps came second in the women's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

Queensland's beach volleyball pairing Thomas Turner and Ryan Edgar won bronze, while the women's rugby sevens teams were only denied gold in an extra-time thriller against Kenya, which claimed a first ever Olympic rugby sevens title for the nation.

Apps and Dodd were named as closing ceremony flag bearers, with Chef de Mission Kenny Wallace said the success gave him a lot of positivity heading to Brisbane 2032.

"To summarise the last two weeks … it would come down to being proud," he said.

"I'm inspired by what our Australian sporting ecosystem has in store leading into LA28 and into Brisbane 2032.

"When we came into this campaign, we hoped Dakar would become that important milestone for our emerging athletes with Brisbane 2032 on the horizon.

"It's been incredibly inspiring to see the athletes developing even further here in Dakar and understanding what it means to be part of an Australian team.

"That is what a Youth Olympic Games can do. I really look forward to seeing some of the faces that we've had in the team here in Brisbane."

First African Games hailed but future questioned

Elisabeth Diatta was one of Senegal's gold medal winners at her country's first home Olympic event. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Beach wrestling's Olympic debut brought particular pride to Senegal, where wrestling is a national sport, with 16-year-old Elisabeth Diatta's win the first for the host nation.

Other Youth Olympic debuts included baseball5, a simplified version of baseball, skateboarding, and the Chinese martial art wushu.

China finished with the most gold medals, 18, followed by Japan with 11 and Russia with eight.

Three African countries came next: Egypt with six, and Ethiopia and Senegal with five each.

The IOC staged the first summer Youth Olympic Games in 2010 in Singapore, however it has delayed naming the host for the next event, set to take place in 2030.

Kirsty Coventry hailed Africa's first Olympic event. (Supplied: AOC)

"We took a pause … and we are analysing and that's where we are. We are still analysing. The data we will collect from Dakar will be added," Coventry said.

"As we move forward, the way we want to engage with young people is extremely important. We have to analyse what will be the best way for the movement to continue in the future."

Coventry noted that just 15 per cent of athletes who have competed at the Youth Olympic Games have gone on to compete at the full Olympics.

Jess Fox and Emma McKeown are notable Australians who made the leap, winning gold at the Youth Olympic Games before going on to claim 20 Summer Olympic Games medals between them.

"We have to be very realistic about what we want the Youth Olympics to be," Coventry said.

ABC/wires

World.title: Australian cricket urged to stop 'eating itself' as Sandpapergate rolls on
World.content:
Greg Chappell has urged Australia's past and present cricket stars to end their civil war as the ghosts of Sandpapergate continue to haunt the game.

Usman Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin last week when he claimed the ball tampering scandal in Cape Town in 2018 was everyone in the team's responsibility.

Cameron Bancroft, who was in charge of using sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball, copped a nine-month ban in the wake of the cheating scandal, while Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for a year and stripped of their leadership roles.

The fallout continues to this very day.

Test skipper Pat Cummins delivered an extraordinary 70-minute press conference in Sydney on Friday where he provided an open floor for journalists to ask whatever they wanted in regards to Sandpapergate 2018 and ball tampering in general, among other hot topics.

The 33-year-old steadfastly rejected claims he had any prior knowledge of the 2018 plot to use sandpaper on the ball in order to gain reverse swing.

He also hit out at Khawaja, saying the accusations were "complete nonsense" and suggested they were "probably defamatory".

Warner returned serve just hours after the press conference, saying he stood by all of Khawaja's claims and wouldn't rest until the full truth came out.

The former Test opener also accused Cummins of throwing Khawaja under the bus with his sandpaper denials.

Usman Khawaja has stood by his comments. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Chappell knows a thing or two about controversy.

In 1981, and with NZ requiring six runs off the final ball to force a draw in a one-day match at the MCG, then-Australia captain Chappell ordered his younger brother Trevor Chappell to bowl the last delivery underarm.

While technically legal at the time, the move caused a massive backlash and forced a rule change, with the incident still brought up to this very day.

"Good luck with that. I think 45 years tells me it will probably be a while before it gets trumped," Chappell replied when asked if 'Sandpapergate' had finally trumped the underarm controversy.

"Mistakes have been made, I think you have to own them.

Cummins faces the music In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

"It would've been a tough time back in 2018 with all of that going on. I don't think you're always ready for these disasters when they happen, but we all make mistakes and they're all human beings.

"They're going to make mistakes, and I think we have to accept that and own those decisions, as I had to do 45 years ago."

Chappell doesn't want the in-fighting in Australian cricket to continue.

"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," Chappell said.

"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket.

"It'll be a distraction, but I think they've all had enough experience that when they walk out on the cricket field there's only one thing they're thinking about."

As for Cummins' claims of having no knowledge of the plan to tamper with the ball?

"We have to believe it," Chappell said.

"Pat's a very honourable man and very talented on the field, but I think he's very talented off the field as well.

"I think from a cricket point of view they just need to move on and focus on what's in front of them."

Khawaja was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands on Saturday, but publishers Pelican said it unfortunately had to be postponed.

AAP

World.title: Flag football takes flight as young Aussie athletes compete in China
World.content:
A team of high school athletes has travelled from the Gold Coast to China to compete against some of the world's best NFL flag football players.

The fast-emerging sport is a non-contact take on the United States's most beloved game and looks a bit like OzTag.

Teams of five run plays to pass a football down the field in the hope of scoring touchdowns, pulling flags from the belt of their opponents to stop play.

Khodi Fabian, 15, had spent most of her life excelling at Australian sports, including touch football, before putting on the flag belt.

Khodi plays the role of wide receiver, catching long balls down the field thrown by the quarterback.

"I never thought I'd get into NFL. My life has been all touch," she said.

Despite that, the teen didn't shy away from the new sport, and represented Queensland in a competition earlier this year.

Coco Gillett (left) and Khodi Fabian say playing touch football has opened the door to competing in a future Olympic Games. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Kodhi is among 10 Palm Beach-Currumbin State High School students competing in this weekend's NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championship in Shanghai.

The team is the only Australian side invited to play in the competition.

"It's really fun to do something different, especially since it's a new sport. It's exciting to play," Khodi said.

Rapid growth on way to Olympics

In flag football, teammates work together to pull flags from the belt of their opposition to stop play. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

Flag football will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles in 2028, generating rapid growth in participation since the move was announced in 2023.

The fast-approaching showcase has prompted major investment by the NFL in Australia, headquartered on the Gold Coast.

A 2022 pilot of 10 local schools helped the sport gather steam, before it was expanded to 750 schools across Australia with free flag kits announced by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell in April.

"There's over 20 million people playing in a very short period of time. By the time we get to [Brisbane] 2032 that number will be exponentially higher," Mr Goodell said.

Bindy McCormack says flag football presents huge career opportunities and professional pathways for her students. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Teacher Bindy McCormack agreed the growth had been rapid.

After first seeing the game three years ago during state championships on the Gold Coast, Ms McCormack said she was hooked.

"We took a team to compete and we'd never played before, we just learnt on the run," the coach said.

"We ended up winning and there were lots of selectors, lots of talk about the opportunities moving forward, so I think that locked me in to embed it within the school."

Fun keeps girls playing sport

A team of 10 Gold Coast students are the only Australians competing at the NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championships in Shanghai. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

NFL Australia and New Zealand general manager Charlotte Offord said the league was footing the bill for the team of 10 plus two coaches to travel and compete in the one-day international event.

She said the investment aimed to break down barriers for women in sport and create more pathways for young people, regardless of the outcome of the China championship.

"There's US colleges for young athletes to go and play flag now," Ms Offord said.

"We've recently announced we'll launch a professional flag league in the next five years … where people will be paid to play in the US."

Charlotte Offord says footing the bill for the trip is an investment by NFL Flag in the future of the game domestically. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Coco Gillett, 13, plays centre for the team heading abroad and said she had been "gobsmacked" to get a call-up to compete internationally.

Despite the difference to her usual sports, Coco said the culture of the game had helped her enjoy playing flag.

"All coming together and scoring and having fun with your friends … there's lots of celebrating," she said.

Unlike some of her teammates, Coco will be too young to qualify for the LA Games in 2028, something she said would drive her to keep her sights set on the big leagues.

"The Olympics would be great … I just want to try and get better each year and progress," Coco said.

World.title: Tears for Pochettino as Man Utd turn to former Spurs boss
World.content:
Tears filled Mauricio Pochettino's eyes as he discussed quitting the US national team for his dream job with Manchester United.

"A decision that in some parts, it's a very sad decision, in other parts, we are professional and we need also to try to find the next step, to try and make your dreams come true," he said.

Just three months after the US Soccer Federation announced his contract to lead the Americans through to the 2030 World Cup, Pochettino said he will depart next week for Old Trafford.

The Argentine will try to revive the 20-time English champions, who sit in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.

"They know that there's not too many opportunities [that] can happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives, it's difficult to turn down," Pochettino said during an emotional news conference at the US team training camp.

He signed a two-and-a-half-year contract and will take over on November 18 ahead of a crucial Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield four days later, becoming United's eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino choked up at a news conference, speaking while seated between USSF president Cindy Parlow Cone and chief executive JT Batson.

"One of the most difficult decision in our career," he said, crying and rubbing his hands as Cone put a supportive hand on his back.

He did not want to speak about the state of United.

Mauricio Pochettino has coached from the visitors dug out at Old Trafford in the Premier League. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

The English club said the 54-year-old was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".

It said he had "consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues".

Pochettino's appointment came one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United's worst league start in 40 years.

Manchester United sits in 18th place in the Premier League.

Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the US for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.

The former Spurs coach took over the US team in 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year's World Cup.

The USSF is likely to inquire about Pep Guardiola's interest and also could consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender.

The Americans' next game with the full player pool after Tuesday is likely to be in late March, so the US could take its time with its search.

Going into his final two games, Pochettino led the US to 21 wins, 12 losses and two draws — counting a penalty shootout win over Costa Rica as a draw. He was the first long-term US coach not to win any titles since Steve Sampson from 1995-98.

Pochettino said he told his US players and staff of his decision in a meeting on Thursday.

"I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation," Pochettino said.

"And they know us, how committed we are for the next two games."

Mauricio Pochettino will lead the USA in two more matches against Haiti this international window. (Getty Images: Press Association/PA Images)

After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a near 27-year tenure.

United has not won the league since Ferguson's last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.

Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United's expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.

Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino's greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.

He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.

It is not known how much Pochettino will earn at United, as typically European soccer teams do not disclose the salaries of coaches and players.

United has spent huge sums on coaches and executives over the past 13 years and paid well in excess of $100 million in severance payments alone.

AP

World.title: McKeown returns, Pallister stars at Swim GP
World.content:
Lani Pallister produced the race of the evening and Kaylee McKeown made a successful return in the opening session of the inaugural Swim GP.

This is McKeown's return to competition after the backstroke star pulled out of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games because of glandular fever.

She won the 50m backstroke skins event, beating Iona Anderson in the last round on Friday night at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre.

Asked if she was having fun immediately after the backstroke skins, a breathless McKeown groaned "no".

Pallister won the 400m freestyle in 3 minutes 53.73 seconds, just two seconds off her personal best.

At the start of next month, the Australian distance freestyle ace will compete at the world short-course championships in Beijing.

Lani Pallister of team KingTide was superb, as ever. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Wahoo team leads on 105 points, 11 ahead of Kraken, with McKeown's Tsunami team next on 77 and Pallister's King Tide scoring 63 and with work to do in Saturday's final session.

Swim GP format Traditional swimming competitions are no longer enough, as Swimming Australia continues to explore alternative formats with the Swim GP in Melbourne, and the return of the International Swimming League in London this December.

Kyle Chalmers is captaining the Kraken team, but he is not competing in the made-for-TV novelty event.

On doctor's orders the 28-year-old is in the midst of a six-week break from swimming after the latest MRI scan on his troublesome back.

Six weeks is manageable, especially with three Olympics under his belt and all the faith that experience brings.

But an injury tweak at the Swim GP could turn that into 10 weeks, with next year's national trials looming large, and the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away.

"Earlier, when I was going through surgeries, I'd always try to force myself back in the pool and set myself back further — taking more anti-inflammatory tablets or getting a cortisone injection as a quick fix," he told AAP.

"But my doctor has advised me to have six weeks of no swimming and it's very important to take that seriously, so I don't push that six weeks out to 10 weeks.

"Then I'm really behind the eight ball of where I need to be."

Kyle Chalmers is resting his back for this event. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

After qualifying for the Paris Olympics two years ago, Chalmers revealed he had needed four epidural injections into his spine. That is as brutal as it sounds and he'd prefer not to go through it again.

"It would have been up there as one of the worst experiences for an athlete," he said.

"At some point you have to step back and say 'I am a human being first, I'm not just a racehorse that needs to be jabbed'.

"I don't want the quick fix, I need the long-term solution so I can run around in the backyard with my daughter — hopefully also future children."

Chalmers also noted that he usually takes time out of the water around this time of year.

He calls this enforced lay-off a small road bump.

But Chalmers was keen to be in Melbourne and lead the Kraken team, calling the Swim GP a great opportunity for the sport.

"I know I could race here and it could be fine, but does it put me back a little bit further in my rehab, and trying to get my body right for what matters most?" he said.

"That's why it's still cool to be able to be here and be part of the team."

Fellow Olympic gold medallist Mollie O'Callaghan also pulled out of the event as she manages a skin infection.

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Wallabies ring changes ahead of Scotland Test
World.content:
Carter Gordon is back at five-eighth to steer the creaking ship as the Wallabies seek to urgently get back on course against Scotland at Murrayfield in the Nations Championship.

After the calamitous 45-22 thrashing by England at Twickenham, the Wallabies have made three changes, with Declan Meredith paying the price for a woeful outing against England.

Gordon is recalled just two months after breaking his leg against Argentina, with Ben Donaldson remaining as cover on the bench.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted from the left wing to inside centre alongside Len Ikitau as coach Les Kiss changes the midfield partnership for the sixth successive Test.

Star flanker Rob Valetini returns as the starting number 6 after the two-time John Eales Medal winner started from the bench last time out, in a familiar back-row partnership with skipper Harry Wilson and current player-of-the-year Fraser McReight.

With Tom Hooper and Brandan Paenga-Amosa making welcome comebacks on the bench after injury, Kiss wants to see a big response from his team who've suffered three heavy defeats on the bounce.

"We've had a good week of training but after falling short of our own expectations last week it's vital we transfer our hard work onto the field for the 80 minutes on Sunday," Kiss said.

"Playing Scotland on their home turf is a massive Test and we're all determined to make our supporters proud by elevating our game to the level it needs to be."

The Wallabies were well beaten by England at Twickenham. (Getty Images: RFU/Dan Mullan )

Winger Harry Potter is also back at the venue of his Test debut, with Suaalii back in midfield to replace the injured Isaac Henry. He'll be partnering with Ikitau for the 18th time at Test level.

Western Force skipper Jeremy Williams shifts back to lock alongside Josh Canham after the experiment of playing him in the back row against England didn't pay dividends.

Lachlan Shaw will play his first Test in Europe as the lock cover, while Hooper should be a valuable addition in the back row after his recent shoulder injury.

Scotland, meanwhile, have made two changes from their team that faded so badly against New Zealand last weekend, with Blair Kinghorn and record try-scorer Darcy Graham taking up positions in the back three.

Australia-born players Sione Tuipulotu, captaining the side at centre, and number 8 Jack Dempsey, will both start for the Scots, who were well beaten by the All Blacks 21-43 last time out.

Former Australian under 20s star Tuipulotu played a big part in Scotland's win over the Wallabies at Murrayfield two years ago.

Former Waratah's player Dempsey played 14 times for the Wallabies, most recently in 2019.

World.title: Socceroos crush Qatar in Doha demolition
World.content:
The Socceroos have enjoyed one of their most emphatic outings under Tony Popovic, outclassing woeful Asian Cup holders Qatar 3-0 with a statement win in front of the champions' home fans in Doha.

Goals from Riley McGree, Tete Yengi and Nestory Irankunda in a dominant first-half display put the one-sided friendly to bed by the break on Friday (Saturday AEDT) with the help of dreadful defending from the back-to-back continental champions.

The fare did get totally disjointed after the break amid a bewildering raft of personnel changes, as subs Eli Adams, Sam Klein, Kasey Bos and Diesel Herrington all earned their Socceroos debuts, but Australia remained in complete control with the hosts only firing their first tame shot after 72 minutes.

"The win was what we wanted and we set the game up with a very good first-half," Popovic told Paramount+.

"We won some balls high up the pitch, which is always encouraging, in difficult conditions. A lot of the boys have come from Europe where it's a lot cooler, so we were tested physically to be that aggressive."

Relieved that they won't have to travel to Amman for their second match next Tuesday (Wednesday AEDT) and that Asian Cup finalists Jordan will come to Doha to face them, Popovic's men seemed relaxed and confident from the start.

It certainly helped when in the fifth minute, new Qatar goalkeeper Mahmoud Abunada had a complete brain fade, attempting a short pass to his central defenders only to deliver it straight to a grateful Riley McGree, who slotted home left-footed into an unguarded net.

It was the Middlesbrough creator's second international goal, a gift four years after his first.

McGree, who missed the World Cup through injury, showed what the Socceroos had missed as he ran the midfield show early on, also firing over narrowly with a 17th minute volley.

Nestory Irankunda scored the Socceroos' third. (Getty Images: Mohamed Farag)

With Julen Lopetegui's hosts looking strangely lethargic and toothless, it was no surprise when another aimless clearance from Abunada resulted in Connor Metcalfe pouncing to put Yengi in the clear to finish neatly just after the half-hour.

Irankunda had a ball on the left flank tormenting the Qatari defence and another neat bit of midfield thieving and distribution from Metcalfe enabled him to free the Sporting Lisbon star to smash home his eighth international goal five minutes before the break.

It was the first time in five years the Socceroos had scored three in an overseas international, and it could have been six at the break, such was their dominance.

Popovic rang the changes in abundance after half time, conceding: "We lost a bit of cohesion and fluency, but we got a lot of debuts as well, so special moment for them."

Brotherly love was the order of the day. Kusini Yengi replaced Tete at the break, while on 65 minutes, Bos joined his absent older sibling Jordy as a full-fledged Socceroo before Diesel replaced Lucas Herrington, who'd had an armchair ride all match, in the final 10 minutes.

Popovic, while looking frustrated on the bench that his side hadn't kicked on with more goals, couldn't complain at a fine night's work after 14 Australian shots on goal were answered by just three from Qatar, and not one on target except for an offside goal in the 88th minute.

The Socceroos can now face Jordan with confidence, perhaps just a little miffed they won't be back in the Middle East in January for the Asian Cup now that it's been rescheduled to December 2027 in Saudi Arabia because of the regional conflict.

Tech.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled.

In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency. An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. L3Harris has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET.

According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday afternoon, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recent Microsoft Outlook outage, but that so far no cause has been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”

When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system that was activated nationwide on November 10th, he said they were looking into that. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems. He said the problems disrupted both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

Updated, Friday, November 13th: Added that the stop has been lifted.

Tech.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
Tech.content:
Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters. The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages.

Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters, an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models.

Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date.

Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”

Tech.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.”

After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

Users have to approve every purchase from ChatGPT Wallet. Image: OpenAI

After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.”

ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

Tech.title: CMF’s milk carton-shaped Bluetooth speaker is down to a new low price
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bluetooth speakers are often boring boxes in plain colors, but not this one! As part of Nothing’s ongoing early Black Friday promo, you can grab its unique, milk carton-shaped CMF Speaker S from Amazon and Nothing for just $39. That’s a solid $20 discount and the lowest price we’ve seen on Nothing’s newfangled wireless speaker, which hit the market about a month ago.

The CMF Speaker S is the smaller of the two recently-released models — the larger Series M is also on sale at Amazon for $79 ($30 off) — and sports a 45mm driver with two passive radiators to help with low-end frequencies. It can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge and carries an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance. Despite its carefree aesthetic, it also supports stereo pairing with a second Seris S speaker, Bluetooth 6, fast pairing via multiple methods (including NFC and Google Fast Pair), and audio over USB-C.

In addition to their great sound and compact footprint, both the Speaker S and Speaker M feature removable faceplates and multifunction front knobs. Not only can you swap them out to customize the colors, but CMF plans to share STL files so anyone with a 3D printer can create their own attachments and looks.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
